padaccheda.m: தம்புதல்வரைத் தம்பொருளென்று சொல்லுவர் (அறிந்தோர்)(
அப்புதல்வர் செய்தபொருள் தம்மை நோக்கி (அவர்) செய்யும் நல்வினையானே (தம்பால்) வரும் (ஆதலான்)

en.1: People say their children are their wealth. That wealth comes by each one’s own deeds.
en.2: The wise call a man’s sons his wealth, because what those sons earn comes to him through the good deeds they do for his sake. Sons who earn are called wealth as a manner of speaking. These two couplets tell the reward of good sons in the next life.
en.4: Children are the veritable riches of a man: for they pass to him by their own acts all the merits that they acquire.
en.5:
‘Man’s children are his fortune,’ say the wise;
From each one’s deeds his varied fortunes rise.
en.6: Men will call their sons their wealth, because it flows to them through the deeds which they (sons) perform on their behalf.

padaccheda.m: (சுவையான்) அமிழ்தத்தினும் மிக வினிமை யுடைத்து
தம் மக்களது சிறுகையான் அளாவப்பட்ட சோறு

en.1: Sweeter by far than ambrosia is the porridge your own children have stirred with their small hands.
en.2: Rice mixed by the small hands of your own children tastes far sweeter than ambrosia. To mix it is to drop it, touch it, bite it, stir it and scatter the ghee-soaked food over themselves.
en.4: Sweeter verily than ambrosia is the plain soup bespattered by the tender hands of one’s own children.
en.5:
Than gods’ ambrosia sweeter far the food before men laid,
In which the little hands of children of their own have play’d.
en.6: The rice in which the little hand of their children has dabbled will be far sweeter (to the parent) than ambrosia.

padaccheda.m: (ஒருவன்) மெய்க்கு இன்பமாவது மக்களது மெய்யைத் தீண்டுதல்
செவிக்கின்பமாவது அவரது சொல்லைக் கேட்டல்

en.1: Touching your children’s bodies is joy to the body, and hearing their words is joy to the ear.
en.2: The body’s joy is touching your children’s bodies, and the ear’s joy is hearing their words. “Words” is left general because what they say once they are learned is a joy too, not only their baby talk.
en.4: The touch of children is the delight of the body: the delight of the ear is the hearing of their speech.
en.5:
To parent sweet the touch of children dear;
Their voice is sweetest music to his ear.
en.6: The touch of children give pleasure to the body and the hearing of their words, pleasure to the ear.

padaccheda.m: குழலிசை யினிது யாழிசை யினிது என்று சொல்லுவர்
தம் புதல்வருடைய குதலைச் சொற்களைக் கேளாதவர்

en.1: “The flute is sweet, the harp is sweet,” say those who have not heard the babble of their own children.
en.2: Those who haven’t heard the lisping words of their own sons say the music of the flute and the harp is sweet. Those who have heard them would call those words sweeter. These three couplets tell the reward of children in this life.
en.4: The flute is sweet and the guitar dulcet: so say they who have not heard the babbling speech of their little ones.
en.5:
‘The pipe is sweet,’’ the lute is sweet, ‘by them ’twill be averred,
Who music of their infants’ lisping lips have never heard.
en.6: “The pipe is sweet, the lute is sweet, ’’ say those who have not heard the prattle of their own children.

padaccheda.m: தந்தை புதல்வனுக்குச் செய்யும் நன்மையாவது
(கற்றார்) அவையத்தின்கண் (அவரினும்) மிக்கிருக்குமாறு கல்வியுடையனாக்குதல். பொருளுடையனாக்குதல் முதலாயின, துன்பம் பயத்தலின் நன்மையாகாவென்பது கருத்து. இதனால் தந்தை கடன் & கூறப்பட்டது. (&. கடன்= கடமை)

en.1: The good a father does his son is to put him in the front rank of the assembly.
en.2: The good a father does his son is to make him so learned that he stands above others in the assembly of the learned. Making him rich and the like isn’t good, because that brings suffering. This tells the father’s duty.
en.4: What is the duty of the father to his son? It is to make him worthy to sit in the front rank in the assembly.
en.5:
Sire greatest boon on son confers, who makes him meet
In councils of the wise to fill the highest seat.
en.6: The benefit which a father should confer on his son is to give him precedence in the assembly of the learned.

padaccheda.m: தம் மக்களதறிவுடைமை

padaccheda.w: மா நிலத்து மன் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் தம்மின் இனிது
padaccheda.m: பெரிய நிலத்து மன்னாநின்ற உயிர்கட்கெல்லாம் தம்மினுமினிதாம்

en.1: That your children know more than you is sweet to every living being on this great earth.
en.2: Your children’s understanding is sweeter to all those on this great earth than it is to you. Understanding here means learning joined to natural intelligence. “Living beings” means the wise, since only they can delight in seeing it. So the assembly rejoices even more than the father.
en.4: To find oneself eclipsed in intelligence by one’s children is a delight to all the world.
en.5:
Their children’s wisdom greater than their own confessed,
Through the wide world is sweet to every human breast.
en.6: That their children should possess knowledge is more pleasing to all men of this great earth than to themselves.

reading.note: தம்மின், “than oneself”, can go with the children’s understanding, as here. He joins it to “sweet”: their understanding is sweeter to the world than to the parent.

padaccheda.m: (தான்) பெற்ற பொழுதை மகிழ்ச்சியினும் மிக மகிழும்
தன்மகனைக் (கல்வி கேள்விகளான்) நிறைந்தானென்று (அறிவுடையார்) சொல்லக் கேட்ட தாய்

en.1: A mother who hears her son called a man of worth feels more joy than when she bore him.
en.2: A mother who hears the wise call her son complete in learning rejoices more than at the time she bore him. A mother’s joy in her child has no measure, so it is told on its own here.
en.4: Great is the joy of the mother when a male child is born unto her: but greater far is her delight when she heareth him called worthy.
en.5:
When mother hears him named ‘f ulfill’d of wisdom’s lore,’
Far greater joy she feels, than when her son she bore.
en.6: The mother who hears her son called “a wise man” will rejoice more than she did at his birth.

padaccheda.m: (கல்வியுடையனாக்கிய) தந்தைக்கு மகன் செய்யும் கைம்மாறாவது
(தன் அறிவும் ஒழுக்கமுங் கண்டார்), இவன் தந்தை (இவனைப்) பெறுதற்கு என்ன தவஞ் செய்தான்கொல்லோவென்று சொல்லுஞ் சொல்லை நிகழ்த்துதல்

en.1: What a son does in return for his father is to make people say, “What penance did his father do to have him?”
en.2: The return a son makes to the father who had him taught is to live so that people who see his understanding and conduct say, “What penance did his father do to get him?” This tells the son’s duty.
en.4: What is the duty of the son to his father? It is to make the world ask, For what austerities of his hath he been blessed with such a son?
en.5:
To sire, what best requital can by grateful child be done?
To make men say, ‘What merit gained the father such a son?’
en.6: (So to act) that it may be said “by what great penance did his father beget him,” is the benefit which a son should render to his father.

padaccheda.m: அன்பிற்கும் (பிறரறியாமல்) அடைத்து வைக்குந் தாழுளதோ? ஆர்வலர் புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும் = (தம்மாலன்பு செய்யப்பட்டாரது துன்பங்கண்டுழி) அன்புடையார்கண் பொழிகின்ற புல்லிய கண்ணீரே (உள் நின்ற அன்பினை எல்லாரும்) அறியத் தூற்றும் (ஆதலான்)

en.1: Can any lock keep loving-kindness hidden? The tears of those who have it will give it away.
en.2: Can loving-kindness be locked away so that no one knows? When people who have it see those dear to them suffer, their tears tell everyone. It can’t be seen, but it can be inferred.
en.4: Where is the bar that can close in the gates of love? The gentle teardrops of lovers’ eyes are sure to proclaim its presence.
en.5:
And is there bar that can even love restrain?
The tiny tear shall make the lover’s secret plain.
en.6: Is there any fastening that can shut in love? ‘Tears of the affectionate will publish the love that is within.

padaccheda.m: அன்பிலாதார் (பிறர்க்குப் பயன்படாமையின்) எல்லாப் பொருளானுந் தமக்கே யுரியர்
அன்பு உடையார், (அவற்றானேயன்றித் தம்) உடம்பானும் பிறர்க்குரியர்

en.1: People without loving-kindness keep everything for themselves. People with it would give even their bones for others.
en.2: Those without it are of no use to others, so all they own stays theirs alone. Those who have it belong to others with their bodies too, not only with what they own. “Bones” stands for the body.
en.4: Those that love not live only for themselves: as to those that love, their very bones are for others’ occasions.
en.5:
The loveless to themselves belong alone;
The loving men are others’ to the very bone.
en.6: Those who are destitute of love appropriate all they have to themselves; but those who possess love consider even their bones to belong to others.

padaccheda.m: (பெறுதற்கு) அரிய மக்களுயிர்க்கு உடம்போடுண்டாகிய தொடர்ச்சியினை
அன்போடு பொருந்துதற்கு வந்த நெறியின் பயனென்று சொல்லுவர் அறிந்தோர்

en.1: They say the precious soul is joined to a body of bone so that it can practise loving-kindness.
en.2: Human life is hard to obtain. Its bond with the body exists for loving-kindness, because it can’t be practised without a body. So the purpose of being embodied is loving-kindness.
en.4: They say it is to taste again of love that the soul hath consented once more to be encased in bone.
en.5:
Of precious soul with body’s flesh and bone,
The union yields one fruit, the life of love alone.
en.6: They say that the union of soul and body in man is the fruit of the union of love and virtue (in a former birth).

padaccheda.m: (ஒருவனுக்குத் தொடர்புடையார்மாட்டுச் செய்த) அன்பு, (அத்தன்மையாற் பிறர்மாட்டும்) விருப்பமுடைமையைத் தரும்

padaccheda.w: அது நண்பு என்னும் நாடாச் சிறப்பு ஈனும்
padaccheda.m: அவ்விருப்பமுடைமைதான் (இவற்குப் பகையும் நொதுமலுமில்லையாய்) யாவரும் நண்பு என்று சொல்லப்படும் அளவிறந்த சிறப்பினைத் தரும்

en.1: Loving-kindness makes you warm towards people, and that warmth brings friendship, a gift beyond measure.
en.2: Loving-kindness shown to your own people grows into goodwill towards others. That goodwill leaves you with no enemies and no strangers, so that everyone is your friend, and this is a distinction beyond measure.
en.4: Love maketh the heart tender towards all: and tenderness yieldeth that priceless treasure called friendship.
en.5:
From love fond yearning springs for union sweet of minds;
And that the bond of rare excelling friendship binds.
en.6: Love begets desire: and that (desire) begets the immeasurable excellence of friendship.

padaccheda.m: அன்புடையராய் (இல்லறத்தோடு) பொருந்திய நெறியின் பயன் என்று சொல்லுவர் (அறிந்தோர்)
இவ்வுலகத்து (இல்வாழ்க்கைக்கணின்று) இன்பநுகர்ந்து (அதன்மேல் துறக்கத்துச் சென்று) எய்தும் பேரின்பத்தினை

en.1: They say the happiness of those who are happy in this world comes from a life settled in loving-kindness.
en.2: The reward is heaven. People who are happy in household life with wife, children and kin become gods through the sacrifices they performed, and are happy there too. Ascetics suffer to reach that heaven. Only loving-kindness lets you reach it through happiness.
en.4: The blessing of the blessed, they say, is only the reward of a constant love.
en.5:
Sweetness on earth and rarest bliss above,
’These are the fruits of tranquil life of love.
en.6: They say that the felicity which those who, after enjoying the pleasure (of the conjugal state) in this world, obtain in heaven is the result of their domestic state imbued with love.

reading.note: parimēlaḻagar moves the reward from this world to the next.

padaccheda.m: அன்பு துணையாவது அறத்திற்கே என்று சொல்லுவர் (சிலர்), அறியார்
(ஏனை) மறத்திற்கும் அவ்வன்பே துணையாவது

en.1: Only the ignorant say loving-kindness helps righteousness alone. It helps against hostility too.
en.2: Some say loving-kindness supports righteousness only, and they are ignorant. When someone wrongs you and hostility rises in your heart, treat that person as a friend and show them loving-kindness, and the hostility goes.
en.4: They are fools who say that love is for the righteous alone: for even against the evil-minded love is the only ally for a man.
en.5:
The unwise deem love virtue only can sustain,
It also helps the man who evil would restrain.
en.6: The ignorant say that love is an ally to virtue only, but it is also a help to get out of vice.

reading.note: He reads the hostility as your own, not someone else’s.

padaccheda.m: என்பில்லாத வுடம்பை, வெயில் காய்ந்தாற்போலக் காயும்

அன்பில்லாதவுயிரை அறக்கடவுள். 'என்பிலது' என்றதனான் உடம்பென்பதூஉம், 'அன்பிலது' என்றதனான் உயிரென்பதூஉம் பெற்றாம். வெறுப்பின்றி எங்குமொருதன்மைத்தாகிய வெயிலின்முன், என்பில்லது தன்னியல்பாற் சென்று கெடுமாறு போல, அத்தன்மைத்தாகிய அறத்தின்முன் அன்பில்லது தன்னியல்பாற் கெடுமென்பதாம். அதனைக் 'காயு'மென வெயிலறங்களின் மேலேற்றினார், அவவற்றிற்கும் அவ்வியல்பு உண்மையின். இவ்வாறு "அல்லவை செய்தார்க் கறங்கூற்றம்" (நான்மணிக்கடிகை, 84) எனப் பிறருங் கூறினார். இக்குறள் உவமையணி

en.1: As the sun scorches a creature with no bones, righteousness scorches a person with no loving-kindness.
en.2: The god of righteousness burns the soul without loving-kindness, as the sun burns a body without bones. The sun has no malice: the boneless thing perishes before it by its own nature, and so does such a soul before righteousness.
en.4: Behold how the sun burneth the boneless worm: even so doth Righteousness burn the man that doth not love.
en.5:
As sun’s fierce ray dries up the boneless things,
So loveless beings virtue’s power to nothing brings.
en.6: Virtue will burn up the soul which is without love, even as the sun burns up the creature which is without bone, i. e. worms.

padaccheda.m: மனத்தின்கண் அன்பி்ல்லாத உயிர் (இல்லறத்தோடு கூடி) வாழ்தல்
வன்பாலின்கண் வற்றலாகிய மரந் தளிர்த்தாற்போலும்

en.1: A life with no loving-kindness inside is like a dead tree trying to sprout on barren ground.
en.2: For someone with no loving-kindness in the heart, living a household life is like a dried tree sprouting on hard ground. It can’t happen.
en.4: Behold the man that loveth not: he will know prosperity only when the sapless tree of the desert putteth forth leaves.
en.5:
The loveless soul, the very joys of life may know,
When flowers, in barren soil, on sapless trees, shall blow.
en.6: The domestic state of that man whose mind is without love, is like the flourishing of a withered tree upon the parched desert.

padaccheda.m: யாக்கை யகத்தின்கண் (நின்று) (இல்லறத்திற்கு) உறுப்பாகிய அன்பு உடையரல்லாதார்க்கு
ஏனைப் புறத்தின்கணின்று உறுப்பாவனவெல்லாம் (அவ்வறஞ் செய்தற்கண்) என்ன உதவியைச் செய்யும்?

en.1: What use is everything on the outside to someone who lacks loving-kindness, the part within?
en.2: The outer parts of a household are place, wealth and servants. What use are they without loving-kindness, the inner part? He rejects the reading that this means eyes and other parts of the body, because that has nothing to do with household life.
en.4: Of what avail is a lovely outside, if love, the soul’s ornament, hath no place in the heart?
en.5:
Though every outward part complete, the body’s fitly framed;
What good, when soul within, of love devoid, lies halt and maimed?
en.6: Of what avail are all the external members (of the body) to those who are destitute of love, the internal member.

padaccheda.m: அன்பு முதலாக அதன்வழி நின்ற உடம்பே, உயிர்நின்ற உடம்பாவது

padaccheda.w: அஃது இலார்க்கு உடம்பு என்பு தோல் போர்த்த
padaccheda.m: அவ்வன்பில்லாதார்க்கு (உளவான) உடம்புகள் என்பினைத் தோலாற் போர்த்தனவாம்

en.1: A living body is one that loving-kindness moves. Without it, a body is just bones wrapped in skin.
en.2: Only a body led by loving-kindness is one with life in it. The bodies of those without it are bones covered in skin, because they yield none of the righteousness of household life.
en.4: The seat of life is in Love: who hath it not is only a mass of skin-encased bone.
en.5:
Bodies of loveless men are bony framework clad with skin;
Then is the body seat of life, when love resides within.
en.6: That body alone which is inspired with love, contains a living soul: if void of it, (the body) is bone overlaid with skin.

padaccheda.m: மனைவியோடும் வனத்திற் செல்லாது இல்லின்கணிருந்து பொருள்களைப் போற்றிவாழுஞ் செய்கையெல்லாம்
விருந்தினரைப்பேணி அவர்க்குபகாரஞ் செய்தற்பொருட்டு

en.1: The whole point of staying at home and keeping things up is to care for guests and do them good.
en.2: All the work of staying at home with your wife, not going to the forest, and looking after your wealth, is so that you can care for guests and help them. Without that help, staying at home and the toil of earning wealth have no use.
en.4: What for do the wise toil and set up homes? It is to feed the guest and help the pilgrim.
en.5:
All household cares and course of daily life have this in view,
Guests to receive with courtesy, and kindly acts to do.
en.6: The whole design of living in the domestic state and laying up (property) is (to be able) to exercise the benevolence of hospitality.

padaccheda.m: உண்ணப்படும் பொருள் அமிர்தமேயெனினும்
தன்னை நோக்கிவந்த விருந்து தன்னில்லின் புறத்ததாகத் தானே உண்டல்
விரும்புதன் முறைமை யுடைத்ன்று

en.1: To eat while your guest stays outside is not to be wished for, even if it is the medicine against death.
en.2: Even if what you eat is ambrosia, you shouldn’t want to eat it alone while a guest who came to you stays outside your home. It can also be read: even if some call eating once without a guest a medicine against death, leave it. These two couplets tell the excellence of caring for guests.
en.4: Were it even the draught of immortality, it shall not be tasted alone when the guest is in the hall.
en.5:
Though food of immortality should crown the board,
Feasting alone, the guests without unfed, is thing abhorred.
en.6: It is not fit that one should wish his guests to be outside (his house) even though he were eating the food of immortality.

padaccheda.m: தன்னை நோக்கி வந்தவிருந்தை நாடோறும் புறந்தருவான தில்வாழ்க்கை
நல்குரவான் வருந்திக் கெடுதலில்லை

en.1: The life of one who cares for the guests who come each day will not suffer and fall to ruin.
en.2: The home life of one who cares every day for the guests who come to him isn’t ruined by the misery of poverty. His wealth doesn’t shrink by this but grows more and more.
en.4: No evil befalleth the man who never faileth to honour the incoming guest.
en.5:
Each day he tends the coming guest with kindly care;
Painless, unfailing plenty shall his household share.
en.6: The domestic life of the man that daily entertains the guests who come to him, shall not be laid waste by poverty.

padaccheda.m: திருமகள் மனமகிழ்ந்து வாழாநிற்கும்
முகமினியனாய்த் தக்கவிருந்தினரைப் பேணுவானதில்லின்கண்

en.1: With a glad heart the goddess of fortune lives in the home of one who cares for good guests with a glad face.
en.2: The goddess of fortune lives gladly in the home of one who cares for worthy guests with a pleasant face. She is glad because her wealth is going the right way. Worthy means high in knowledge and conduct. This gives the reason why his wealth grows.
en.4: Behold the man who receiveth the worthy guest with his best smile: Lakshmi delighteth to abide in his home.
en.5:
With smiling face he entertains each virtuous guest;
‘Fortune’ with gladsome mind shall in his dwelling rest.
en.6: Lakshmi with joyous mind shall dwell in the house of that man who with cheerful countenance entertains the good as guests.

padaccheda.m: முன்னே விருந்தினரை மிசைவித்துப் பின் மிக்கதனைத் தான் மிசைவானது விளைபுலத்திற்கு
வித்திடுதலும் வேண்டுமோ? வேண்டா

en.1: Need you even sow seed in the field of one who feeds guests and eats what is left?
en.2: Does the field of one who first feeds his guests and then eats what is left even need seed sown? No. It yields by itself. These three couplets tell what those who care for guests gain in this life.
en.4: Behold the man who feedeth his guest first and then only eateth what is left: standeth his land in need even of sowing?
en.5:
Who first regales his guest, and then himself supplies,
O’er all his fields, unsown, shall plenteous harvests rise.
en.6: Is it necessary to sow the field of the man who having feasted his guests eats what may remain?

padaccheda.m: தன்கட் சென்ற விருந்தைப் பேணிப் பின் செல்லக்கடவ விருந்தைப் பார்த்துத் தான் அதனோடு உண்ணவிருப்பான்
மறுபிறப்பிற் றேவனாய் வானினுள்ளார்க்கு நல்விருந்தாம்

en.1: One who looks after the guest who is leaving and watches for the guest still to come is a good guest to those in the sky.
en.2: One who has tended the guests who came, and then watches for those still to come so as to eat with them, becomes a god in his next birth and a good guest to those in the sky. A good guest means one they seldom get. This tells the reward in the next world.
en.4: Behold the man who hath tended the outgoing guest and waiteth for the incoming one: he is a welcome guest unto the Gods.
en.5:
The guest arrived he tends, the coming guest expects to see;
To those in heavenly homes that dwell a welcome guest is he.
en.6: He who, having entertained the guests that have come, looks out for others who may yet come, will be a welcome guest to the inhabitants of heaven.

padaccheda.m: விருந்தோம்பலாகிய வேள்வியின் பயன் இன்ன அளவிற்று என்பதோர் அளவுடைத்தன்று
அதற்கு அவ்விருந்தின் தகுதியளவே அளவு

en.1: There is no saying how great the fruit of the sacrifice is. It is measured by the worth of the guest.
en.2: The reward of the sacrifice of caring for guests has no fixed measure. Its only measure is the worth of the guest. It is called a sacrifice because it is one of the five great sacrifices. The amount given doesn’t decide it, since a small gift in worthy hands grows huge. This is why it brings reward in both worlds.
en.4: We cannot say of any hospitable act by itself, So much is the merit of this act: it is the worth of the guest that is the measure of the sacrifice.
en.5:
To reckon up the fruit of kindly deeds were all in vain;
Their worth is as the worth of guests you entertain.
en.6: The advantages of benevolence cannot be measured: the measure (of the virtue) of the guests (entertained) is the only measure.

padaccheda.m: நிலையாப் பொருளை வருந்திக் காத்துப் பின் அதனை இழந்து இதுபொழுது யாம் பற்றுக்கோடு இலமாயினேம் என்று இரங்குவர்
அப்பொருளான் விருந்தினரையோம்பி வேள்விப் பயனையெய்தும் பொறியிலாதார்

en.1: After anxious guarding they will say “We have nothing to hold on to”: those who never took up the sacrifice of caring for guests.
en.2: Those without the good fortune to care for guests with their wealth and gain the reward of sacrifice guard that passing wealth with pain, then lose it and lament, “Now we have no support.” Even guarding wealth is hard pain, so he says they guarded it anxiously.
en.4: Behold the man who performeth not the sacrifice of hospitality: he will say one day, I have toiled hard and laid me up a great treasure: but it is all in vain, for there is none to comfort me.
en.5:
With pain they guard their stores, yet ‘All forlorn are we,’ they’ll cry
Who cherish not their guests, nor kindly help supply.
en.6: Those who have taken no part in the benevolence of hospitality shall (at length lament) saying, “we have laboured and laid up wealth and are now without support.”

padaccheda.m: உடைமைக்காலத்து இன்மையாவது விருந்தோம்பலை இகழும் பேதைமை
அஃது அறிந்தார்மாட்டு உளதாகாது, பேதையர்மாட்டே உளதாம்

en.1: Poverty amid plenty is the folly of neglecting guests. It is found among fools.
en.2: Poverty in a time of plenty is the stupidity that scorns caring for guests. It isn’t found in those who know, only in fools. It loses what wealth is for and so turns having into not having. Even if the wealth stays, it is useless. These two couplets tell the fault of not caring for guests.
en.4: Not to honour the pilgrim is veritable indigence in the midst of wealth: such a thing is found only with fools.
en.5:
To turn from guests is penury, though worldly goods abound;
’Tis senseless folly, only with the senseless found.
en.6: That stupidity which exercises no hospitality is poverty in the midst of wealth. It is the property of the stupid.

padaccheda.m: அனிச்சப்பூ மோந்துழியன்றிக் குழையாது
விருந்தினர் முகம் வேறுபட்டு நோக்கக் குழைவர்

en.1: The aṉiccam flower wilts when you smell it. A guest wilts when you look at them with a changed face.
en.2: The aṉiccam flower wilts only when smelled. Guests wilt when looked at with a changed face. A host needs a pleasant face from afar, sweet words as they come near and good deeds once they accept. Without the first, they wilt and leave while still far off, so guests are more delicate than the flower. A pleasant face comes first.
en.4: The anitcha flower fadeth by smelling: but a look is enough to break the heart of the guest.
en.5:
The flower of the ‘Anicha’ withers away,
If you do but its fragrance inhale;
If the face of the host cold welcome convey,
The guest’s heart within him will fail.
en.6: As the Anicham flower fades in smelling, so fades the guest when the face is turned away.

padaccheda.m: இன்சொலாவன

padaccheda.w: ஈரம் அளைஇப் படிறு இலவாம் செம்பொருள் கண்டார் வாய்ச்சொல்
padaccheda.m: அன்போடு கலந்து வஞ்சனையிலவாய் இருக்கின்ற அறத்தினை உணர்ந்தார் வாயிற்சொற்கள். 'ஆல்' அசைநிலை. அன்போடு கலத்தல்= அன்புடைமையை வெளிப்படுத்தல். படிறின்மை= வாய்மை. மெய்யுணர்ந்தார் நெஞ்சிற்கெல்லாம் செம்மையுடைத்தாய்த் தோன்றலின், 'செம்பொரு'ளெனப் பட்டது. இலவாஞ் சொ்ல்லென இயையும். 'வாய்' என வேண்டாது கூறினார், தீய சொற் பயிலாவென்பது அறிவித்தற்கு. இதனான் இன்சொற்கு இலக்கணங் கூறப்பட்டது

en.1: Sweet words are what come from the mouths of those who have seen the truth: steeped in tenderness and free of deceit.
en.2: Sweet words are the words from the mouths of those who know righteousness, mixed with loving-kindness and free of deceit. To mix them is to show loving-kindness, and to be free of deceit is to be true. Righteousness is called the straight thing because it seems straight to all who know the truth. “Mouths” shows they never practise evil words.
en.4: The speech that is truly kind is the speech of the righteous men which is full of tenderness and free from dissimulation.
en.5:
Pleasant words are words with all pervading love that burn;
Words from his guileless mouth who can the very truth discern.
en.6: Sweet words are those which, imbued with love and free from deceit, flow from the mouth of the virtuous.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சுவந்து ஒருவற்கு வேண்டிய பொருளைக் கொடுத்தலினும் நன்று
கண்டபொழுதே முகம் இனியனாய் அதனோடு இனிய சொல்லையும் உடையனாகப் பெறின்

en.1: Better than giving with a glad heart is to have a glad face and sweet words.
en.2: Better than gladly giving someone what they need is to have a pleasant face the moment you see them, and sweet words with it. Unlike giving, this depends on you and not on wealth, yet it doesn’t come naturally except to those with righteous hearts, so it is rarer.
en.4: Better even than a generous gift is sweet speech and a kind and gracious look.
en.5:
A pleasant word with beaming smile’s preferred,
Even to gifts with liberal heart conferred.
en.6: Sweet speech with a cheerful countenance is better than a gift made with a joyous mind.

padaccheda.m: கண்டபொழுதே முகத்தான் விரும்பி இனிதாக நோக்கி
பின் நண்ணியவழி மனத்துடனாகிய இனிய சொற்களைச் சொல்லுதலின் கண்ணே அறம்

en.1: Righteousness lies in a glad face, a kind look and sweet words that come from the heart.
en.2: On seeing someone, welcome them with your face and look on them kindly. Then, when they come near, say sweet words from the heart. Righteousness lies in that, not in giving. These two couplets say a pleasant face with sweet words wins people over at once, and so comes first in caring for guests.
en.4: Behold the sweet and gracious look and the kind speech that cometh from the heart: Righteousness hath its dwelling place there.
en.5:
With brightly beaming smile, and kindly light of loving eye,
And heart sincere, to utter pleasant words is charity.
en.6: Sweet speech, flowing from the heart, (uttered) with a cheerful countenance and a sweet look, is true virtue.

padaccheda.m: எல்லார் மாட்டும் இன்பத்தை மிகுவிக்கும் இன்சொல்லை உடையார்க்கு
துன்பத்தை மிகுவிக்கும் நல்குரவு இல்லையாம்

en.1: The poverty that brings sorrow will not come to those whose sweet words bring joy to everyone.
en.2: Poverty, which increases sorrow, won’t come to those whose sweet words increase everyone’s joy. Poverty is the senses lacking what they would enjoy. Such people have no enemies and no strangers, only friends, and so gain all wealth.
en.4: Behold the man who always speaketh words which gladden all hearts: Poverty, the increaser of sorrow, will never come to him.
en.5:
The men of pleasant speech that gladness breathe around,
Through indigence shall never sorrow’s prey be found.
en.6: Sorrow-increasing poverty shall not come upon those who use towards all, pleasure-increasing sweetness of speech.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு அணியாவது தன்னால் தாழப்படுவார்கண் தாழ்ச்சி உடையனாய் எல்லார்கண்ணும் இனிய சொல்லையும் உடையனாதல்
இவை யிரண்டுமன்றி மெய்க்கணியும் பிற அணிகள் அணியாகா

en.1: Humility and sweet words are a person’s ornaments. Nothing else is.
en.2: A person’s ornament is to bow to those one should bow to and to have sweet words for all. The other ornaments worn on the body aren’t ornaments, because they don’t give such beauty. Humility is named because it goes with sweet words. These two couplets tell the reward of sweet words in this life.
en.4: Modesty and a loving speech, these alone are the ornaments of man and none other.
en.5:
Humility with pleasant speech to man on earth,
Is choice adornment; all besides is nothing worth.
en.6: Humility and sweetness of speech are the ornaments of a man; all others are not (ornaments).

padaccheda.m: பொருளாற் பிறர்க்கு நன்மை பயக்குஞ் சொற்களை மனத்தான் ஆராய்ந்து இனியவாக ஒருவன் சொல்லுமாயின்
அவனுக்குப் பாவங்கள் தேய அறம் வளரும்

en.1: If you seek out what is good and say it sweetly, wrongs will wear away and righteousness will grow.
en.2: If you weigh in your mind words whose meaning does others good, and say them sweetly, your sins wear away and righteousness grows. Sin wastes away because its enemy, righteousness, is growing and it has no footing. Even what is good isn’t righteousness if it is said harshly. This tells the reward in the next life.
en.4: Sinfulness will wane away and righteousness will increase if thy thoughts are good and thy speech is kind.
en.5:
Who seeks out good, words from his lips of sweetness flow;
In him the power of vice declines, and virtues grow.
en.6: If a man, while seeking to speak usefully, speaks also sweetly, his sins will diminish and his virtue increase.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு இம்மைக்கு நீதியையும் உண்டாக்கி மறுமைக்கு அறத்தையும் பயக்கும்
பொருளாற் பிறர்க்கு நன்மையைக் கொடுத்து இனிமைப் பண்பின் நீங்காத சொல்

en.1: Words that are useful and never part from courtesy give rise to fairness and bring good.
en.2: Words whose meaning does others good, and which never lose their sweetness, bring the speaker justice in this life and righteousness in the next. Justice means being in accord with the world. Courtesy here means sweetness.
en.4: The word that is serviceable and kind createth friends and bringeth forth benefits.
en.5:
The words of sterling sense, to rule of right that strict adhere,
To virtuous action prompting, blessings yield in every sphere.
en.6: That speech which, while imparting benefits ceases not to please, will yield righteousness (for this world) and merit (for the next world).

padaccheda.m: பொருளாற் பிறர்க்கு நோய் செய்யாத இனிய சொல்
ஒருவனுக்கு இருமையினும் இன்பத்தைப் பயக்கும்

en.1: Sweet words free of all meanness bring joy in the next life and in this one.
en.2: Sweet words that cause others no pain by their meaning give you joy in both worlds. The next life is named first because its joy is greater. Joy in this life is gaining good things, because the world is on your side. These two couplets stress that both rewards come together.
en.4: Words that are kind and are removed from all littleness yield good in this life and in the next also.
en.5:
Sweet kindly words, from meanness free, delight of heart
In world to come and in this world impart.
en.6: Sweet speech, free from harm to others, will give pleasure both in this world and in the next.

padaccheda.m: பிறர்கூறும் இன்சொல் தனக்கின்பம் பயத்தலை அனுபவித்து அறிகின்றவன்
அது நிற்கப் பிறர்மாட்டு வன்சொல்லைச் சொல்லுவது என்ன பயன் கருதி?

en.1: If you have seen what joy sweet words bring, why use hard words?
en.2: Someone who has felt the joy that others’ sweet words give him: what does he hope to gain by speaking hard words to others? Hard words are unpleasant to others too, so they shouldn’t be said.
en.4: Why doth not a man cease from violent words, even after he hath felt the sweetness that kind words give?
en.5:
Who sees the pleasure kindly speech affords,
Why makes he use of harsh, repellant words?
en.6: Why does he use harsh words, who sees the pleasure which sweet speech yields?

padaccheda.m: அறம் பயக்கும் இனிய சொற்களும் தனக்கு உளவாயிருக்க அவற்றைக் கூறாது பாவம் பயக்கும் இன்னாத சொற்களை ஒருவன் கூறல்
இனிய கனிகளும் தன் கைக்கண் உளவாயிருக்க அவற்றை நுகராது இன்னாத காய்களை நுகர்ந்ததனோடு ஒக்கும்

en.1: To speak harsh words when sweet ones are there is like picking unripe fruit when ripe fruit is there.
en.2: To say harsh words that bring sin, when you have sweet words that bring righteousness, is like eating bitter unripe fruit when sweet ripe fruit is in your hand. The ripe fruit is like ambrosia and the unripe like poison. Harsh words end by hurting the one who says them. These two couplets tell the fault of harsh words.
en.4: Behold the man who useth hard words when sweet ones serve: he preferreth the unripe fruit to the ripe.
en.5:
When pleasant words are easy, bitter words to use,
Is, leaving sweet ripe fruit, the sour unripe to choose.
en.6: To say disagreeable things when agreeable are at hand, is like eating unripe fruit when there is ripe.

padaccheda.m: தனக்கு முன்னோர் உதவி செய்யாதிருக்க ஒருவன் பிறனுக்குச் செய்த உதவிக்கு
மண்ணுலகும் விண்ணுலகுங் கைமாறாகக் கொடுத்தாலும் ஒத்தல்அரிது

en.1: For help you did nothing to earn, even earth and sky are hardly a fair return.
en.2: For help a person gives when you had done them no good first, even earth and heaven given in return can hardly match it. Every return has a cause, so none can match help with no cause. Some read a variant that makes this help given where it can’t be repaid.
en.4: Behold the kindness done without any obligation: even the heavens and the earth are too poor to repay it.
en.5:
Assistance given by those who ne’er received our aid,
Is debt by gift of heaven and earth but poorly paid.
en.6: (The gift of) heaven and earth is not an equivalent for a benefit which is conferred where none had been received.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு இறுதிவந்த எல்லைக்கண் ஒருவன் செய்த உபகாரம்
தன்னை நோக்கச் சிறிதாயிருந்ததாயினும் அக்காலத்தை நோக்க நிலவுலகத்தினும் மிகப் பெரிது

en.1: A good deed done at the right time, though small, is far greater than the world.
en.2: Help given when someone’s end has come may be small in itself, but judged by that moment it is far greater than the earth. You should look at the moment, not at the thing given.
en.4: A kindness done in the hour of need may look small: but it outweigheth the whole world.
en.5:
A timely benefit,—though thing of little worth
The gift itself,—in excellence transcends the earth.
en.6: A favour conferred in the time of need, though it be small (in itself,) is (in value) much larger than the world.

padaccheda.w: பயன் தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி நயன் தூக்கின்
padaccheda.m: இவர்க்கு இதுசெய்தால் இன்னது பயக்கும் என்று ஆராய்தல் இலராய்ச் செய்த உதவியாகிய ஈரமுடைமையை ஆராயின்
அதன் நன்மை கடலினும் பெரிதாம்

en.1: Weigh the goodness of help given with no thought of return, and it is greater than the sea.
en.2: If you weigh the kindness in help given by those who never ask what it will bring, its goodness is greater than the sea. These three couplets say that help given without cause, at the right time, or without thought of return is boundless.
en.4: Behold the kindness done without thought of recompense: it is mightier than the ocean.
en.5:
Kindness shown by those who weigh not
What the return may be;
When you ponder right its merit,
’Tis vaster than the sea.
en.6: If we weigh the excellence of a benefit which is conferred without weighing the return, it is larger than the sea.

padaccheda.m: தமக்குத்தினை அளவிற்றாய உபகாரத்தை ஒருவன் செய்தானாயினும்
அதனை அவ்வளவிற்றாகக் கருதாது பனையளவிற்றாகக் கருதுவர் அக்கருத்தின் பயன் தெரிவார்

en.1: Though the good done them is the size of a millet seed, those who know its worth take it as the size of a palmyra.
en.2: Though someone does them a good the size of a millet seed, those who know what comes of thinking so take it as the size of a palmyra. Millet and palmyra are the usual measures of small and large.
en.4: The benefit received may be small even like a millet seed: but in the eyes of the just its measure is that of a palmyra tree.
en.5:
Each benefit to those of actions’ fruit who rightly deem,
Though small as millet-seed, as palm-tree vast will seem.
en.6: Though the benefit conferred be as small as a millet seed, those who know its advantage will consider it as large as a palmyra fruit.

padaccheda.m: கைம்மாறான உதவி காரணத்தானும் பொருளானும் காலத்தானுமாகிய் மூவகையானும் முன்செய்த உதவியளவிற்றன்று
அதனைச் செய்வித்துக் கொண்டவர்தம் அமைதி யளவிற்று

en.1: The measure of help is not the help itself. It is the worth of those who received it.
en.2: The help given back isn’t measured by the earlier help, in its cause, substance or timing. It is measured by the character of those who received that help. As great as their character is, so great is the help. These two couplets say that even ordinary help is great when done to those who know its worth.
en.4: Gratitude is not limited by the assistance given: it is bounded only by the nobility of him that receiveth it.
en.5:
The kindly aid’s extent is of its worth no measure true;
Its worth is as the worth of him to whom the act you do.
en.6: The benefit itself is not the measure of the benefit; the worth of those who have received it is its measure.

padaccheda.m: துன்பக்காலத்துத் தனக்குப் பற்றுக்கோடாயினாரது நட்பை விடாதொழிக
அறிவு ஒழுக்கங்களிற் குற்றம் அற்றாரது கேண்மையை மறவாது ஒழிக

en.1: Don’t forget the bond of the stainless. Don’t give up the friendship of those who stood by you in trouble.
en.2: Don’t give up the friendship of those who were your support in trouble. Don’t forget the bond of those without fault in knowledge and conduct. Along with what serves you in this life, he names what serves you in the next.
en.4: Disregard not the friendship of the holy ones: forsake not those that succoured thee in difficulty.
en.5:
Kindness of men of stainless soul remember evermore!
Forsake thou never friends who were thy stay in sorrow sore!
en.6: Forsake not the friendship of those who have been your staff in adversity. Forget not the benevolence of the blameless.

padaccheda.m: தங்கண் எய்திய துன்பத்தை நீக்கினவருடைய நட்பினை
எழுமையினையுடைய தம் எழுவகைப் பிறப்பினும் நினைப்பர் நல்லோர்

en.1: Through seven lives and seven births, people remember the friendship of those who wiped away their sorrow.
en.2: The good remember the friendship of those who removed their sorrow, through all seven kinds of birth, in the seven births that the fruit of deeds follows. “Wiped” shows how quickly it was done. To remember is for the loving-kindness felt for them to go on birth after birth.
en.4: He that hath relieved from affliction shall be remembered with gratitude in every birth.
en.5:
Through all seven worlds, in seven-fold birth,
Remains in mem’ry of the wise,
Friendship of those who wiped on earth,
The tears of sorrow from their eyes.
en.6: (The wise) will remember throughout their seven-fold births the love of those who have wiped away their affliction.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் முன் செய்த நன்மையை மறப்பது ஒருவற்கு அறனன்று
அவன் செய்த தீமையைச் செய்தபொழுதே மறப்பது அறன்

en.1: It is not good to forget a good deed. It is good to forget what is not good, that very day.
en.2: Forgetting the good someone did you before isn’t righteous. Forgetting the harm that same person did you, at the moment it is done, is righteous. This sorts what to forget and what to keep, when one person has done both.
en.4: It is ignoble to forget a kindness: but an ill turn received it is the part of nobility to forget at once.
en.5:
’Tis never good to let the thought of good things done thee pass away;
Of things not good, ’tis good to rid thy memory that very day.
en.6: It is not good to forget a benefit: it is good to forget an injury even in the very moment (in which it is inflicted.)

padaccheda.m: தமக்கு முன்னொரு நன்மை செய்தவரு பின் கொன்றால் ஒத்த இன்னாதவற்றைச் செய்தாராயினும்
அவையெல்லாம் அவர்செய்த நன்மை ஒன்றினையும் நினைக்க இல்லையாம்

en.1: Though someone hurts you as if they were killing you, it all dies when you recall one good thing they did.
en.2: If someone who once did you good later does you harm equal to killing you, all of it vanishes when you think of that one good. A millet seed of good is taken as a palmyra, so that one good destroys it all. This tells how to forget harm that very day.
en.4: The mortallest injury is forgiven the moment the mind recalleth a single kindness received from the injurer.
en.5:
Effaced straightway is deadliest injury,
By thought of one kind act in days gone by.
en.6: Though one inflict an injury great as murder, it will perish before the thought of one benefit (formerly) conferred.

padaccheda.m: பெரிய அறங்களைச் சிதைத்தார்க்கும் பாவத்தின் நீங்கும் வாயில் உண்டாம்
ஒருவன் செய்த நன்றியைச் சிதைத்த மகனுக்கு அஃதில்லை

en.1: Those who have killed any good may still escape. There is no escape for the man who killed the good done to him.
en.2: Those who wreck great righteous acts still have a way out of their sin. The man who wrecks a good done to him has none. Wrecking great righteousness means crimes such as cutting a cow’s udder, destroying a woman’s unborn child and killing Brahmins. This tells how terrible it is to kill a kindness.
en.4: There is redemption for men who are guilty of every other crime: but the ingrate wretch shall know of none.
en.5:
Who every good have killed, may yet destruction flee;
Who ‘benefit’ has killed, that man shall ne’er ’scape free!
en.6: He who has killed every virtue may yet escape: there is no escape for him who has killed a benefit.

en.1: What is called fairness is good, if you can give each side its due.
en.2: The one righteousness called impartiality is good, if you can keep to your rule with each of the three groups, enemies, strangers and friends. “If you can” shows how hard it is to live this way. This tells the excellence of impartiality.
en.4: The just and the fair that giveth each man his due whether he is friend or foe, that is the good: nought else.
en.5:
If justice, failing not, its quality maintain,
Giving to each his due,—’tis man’s one highest gain.
en.6: That equity which consists in acting with equal regard to each of (the three) divisions of men [enemies, strangers and friends] is a pre-eminent virtue.

padaccheda.m: நடுவுநிலைமையை உடையவனது செல்வம்
பிறர் செல்வம்போல் அழிவின்றி அவன் வழியின் உள்ளார்க்கும் வலியாதலை உடைத்து

en.1: The gains of one who is upright don’t fall apart, and are a strength to those who come after.
en.2: The wealth of an impartial man doesn’t perish as others’ wealth does, and it is a strength even to those of his line. It serves him too as long as he lives. It lasts because it comes with righteousness. Descendants are called what remains after you die.
en.4: The prosperity of the just groweth not less: it endureth even unto their remotest posterity.
en.5:
The just man’s wealth unwasting shall endure,
And to his race a lasting joy ensure.
en.6: The wealth of the man of rectitude will not perish, but will bring happiness also to his posterity.

padaccheda.m: தீங்கன்றி நன்மையே பயந்ததாயினும்

padaccheda.w: நடுவு இகந்து ஆம் ஆக்கத்தை அன்றே ஒழிய விடல்
padaccheda.m: நடுவுநிற்றலை ஒழிதலான் உண்டாகின்ற ஆக்கத்தை அப்பொழுதே யொழிய விடுக

en.1: Even if it brings only good, let go at once of gain that comes from leaving the middle.
en.2: Even if it brings nothing but good, give up at once any gain that comes from abandoning impartiality. He says “even if” because such gain brings no good. These two couplets say that wealth from impartiality does good and other wealth does harm.
en.4: Though nought but profit come of it, touch not the wealth that cometh by deviating from the right.
en.5:
Though only good it seem to give, yet gain
By wrong acquired, not e’en one day retain!
en.6: Forsake in the very moment (of acquisition) that gain which though it should bring advantage is without equity.

padaccheda.m: இவர் நடுவுநிலைமை யுடையர், இவர் நடுவு நிலைமையிலர் என்னும் விசேடம்
அவரவருடைய நன்மக்களது உண்மையானும், இன்மையானும் அறியப்படும்

en.1: Whether people are worthy or unworthy is seen by what each leaves behind.
en.2: Whether someone is impartial or not can be known from whether they have good sons. It is certain that the worthy have descendants and the unworthy don’t, so this is the sign for telling the two apart.
en.4: The righteous and the unrighteous are known by their offspring.
en.5:
Who just or unjust lived shall soon appear:
By each one’s offspring shall the truth be clear.
en.6: The worthy and unworthy may be known by the existence or otherwise of good offsprings.

reading.note: எச்சம், what is left after you, could be a name or deeds as well as children. He takes it as good sons.

padaccheda.m: தீவினையாற் கேடும் நல்வினையாற் பெருக்கமும் யாவர்க்கு முன்னே அமைந்து கிடந்தன
அவ்வாற்றை அறிந்து அவை காரணமாக மனததின்கட் கோடாமையே அறிவான் அமைந்தார்க்கு அழகாவது

en.1: Loss and gain will always come. A heart that doesn’t lean is the ornament of the worthy.
en.2: Ruin from bad deeds and increase from good deeds are laid down beforehand for everyone. Knowing this, not to lean in your heart because of them is the beauty of the wise. To lean is to take one side, thinking these come now, to avoid ruin or win increase. Their cause is past deeds, not leaning.
en.4: Evil and good come unto all: but an upright heart is the glory of the wise.
en.5:
The gain and loss in life are not mere accident;
Just mind inflexible is sages’ ornament.
en.6: Loss and gain come not without cause: it is the ornament of the wise to preserve evenness of mind (under both).

padaccheda.w: தன் நெஞ்சம் நடுவு ஒரீஇ அல்ல செயின்
padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் தன்னெஞ்சம் நடுவுநிற்றலை யொழிந்து நடுவல்லவற்றைச் செய்ய நினைக்குமாயின்
அந்நினைவை யான் கெடக்கடவேன் என்று உணரும் உற்பாதமாக அறிக. விளககம்: நினைத்தலும் செய்தலோடு ஒக்கும் ஆகலின், செயின் என்றார்

en.1: If your heart leaves the middle and does wrong, know this: “I will be ruined.”
en.2: If your heart leaves impartiality and thinks of doing otherwise, take that thought as the omen that says “I am bound for ruin.” Thinking is the same as doing, so he says “does”.
en.4: When thy heart swerveth from the right and turneth unto evil, know that thy destruction is near at hand.
en.5:
If, right deserting, heart to evil turn,
Let man impending ruin’s sign discern!
en.6: Let him whose mind departing from equity commits sin well consider thus within himself, “I shall perish.”

padaccheda.m: நடுவாக நின்று அறததின்கண்ணே தங்கினவனது வறுமையை
வறுமையென்று கருதார் உயர்ந்தோர்

en.1: The world does not count it ruin when someone who stays in the middle and in the good falls low.
en.2: The high-minded don’t count as poverty the poverty of one who stood impartial and stayed in righteousness. They take it as wealth. These three couplets say that loss and gain don’t come from leaning, that leaning brings ruin, and that the lowness of one who doesn’t lean isn’t ruin.
en.4: The world looketh not down on the poverty of the upright and virtuous man.
en.5:
The man who justly lives, tenacious of the right,
In low estate is never low to wise man’s sight.
en.6: The great will not regard as poverty the low estate of that man who dwells in the virtue of equity.

padaccheda.m: முன்னே தான்சமனாகநின்று பின் தன்கண் வைத்த பாரத்தை வரையறுக்குந் துலாம்போல அமைந்து ஒருபால் கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி= இலக்கணங்களான் அமைந்து ஒருபக்கத்துக் கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அழகாம்

en.1: To be like the balance that rests level and then weighs true, leaning to neither side, is the ornament of the worthy.
en.2: Like a balance that first stands level and then fixes the weight placed on it, to be sound and lean to no side is the beauty of the wise. Their weighing is grasping, in due order, what is heard through question and answer. Not leaning is stating it as it is, hiding nothing, to enemies, strangers and friends alike.
en.4: Behold the weighing beam, for it is straight in itself and weigheth justly: the glory of the wise is to be like unto it and to incline neither to this side nor to that.
en.5:
To stand, like balance rod that level hangs and rightly weighs,
With calm unbiassed equity of soul, is sages’ praise.
en.6: To incline to neither side, but to rest impartial as the even fixed scale is the ornament of the wise.

padaccheda.m: நடுவுநிலைமையாவது, சொல்லின்கட் கோடுதல் இல்லாததாம்
அஃது அன்னதாவது, மனத்தின்கட் கோட்டம் இன்மையைத் திண்ணிதாகப் பெறின்

en.1: Uprightness is speech that does not bend, if you have made sure there is no bend within.
en.2: Impartiality is having no bend in your speech, provided you firmly have no bend in your mind. The speech is the verdict given in due order. Joined to a mind that leans for no reason, saying what righteousness requires is impartial. Without that mind, the same words are not.
en.4: Behold the man who swerveth not at all from the right in his own mind: the upright speech of his lips is a judgment.
en.5:
Inflexibility in word is righteousness,
If men inflexibility of soul possess.
en.6: Freedom from obliquity of speech is rectitude, if there be (corresponding) freedom from bias of mind.

padaccheda.m: பிறர் பொருளையுந் தம் பொருள்போலப் பேணிச் செய்யின்
வாணிகஞ் செய்வார்க்கு நன்றாய வாணிகமாம்

en.1: For traders, good trade is to care for others’ goods as their own.
en.2: If traders tend others’ goods as their own, that is good trade for them. That means taking no more and giving no less, weighing evenly. Of these last three couplets, the first two look to those in the assembly and this one to traders, because for both this righteousness matters most.
en.4: Behold the businessman that looketh after the interests of others as his own: his business will expand.
en.5:
As thriving trader is the trader known,
Who guards another’s interests as his own.
en.6: The true merchandize of merchants is to guard and do by the things of others as they do by their own.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனை அடக்கமாகிய அறம் பின் தேவருலகத்து உய்க்கும்
அடங்காமையாகிய பாவம் தங்குதற்கரிய இருளின்கட் செலுத்தும்

en.1: Restraint will carry you among the immortals. Lack of restraint will drive you into deep darkness.
en.2: The righteousness of restraint later carries you to the world of the gods. The sin of lacking it drives you into a darkness hard to endure. That darkness is one particular hell.
en.4: Self-control leadeth unto heaven, but uncontrolled passion is the royal road to endless darkness.
en.5:
Controul of self does man conduct to bliss th’ immortals share;
Indulgence leads to deepest night, and leaves him there.
en.6: Self-control will place (a man) among the Gods; the want of it will drive (him) into the thickest darkness (of hell).

padaccheda.m: உயிர்கட்கு அடக்கத்தின் மிக்க செல்வமில்லை
ஆகலான் அவ் வடக்கத்தை உறுதிப்பொருளாகக் கொண்டு அழியாமற் காக்க

en.1: Guard restraint as wealth. There is no greater gain for a life.
en.2: No wealth for living beings is greater than restraint, so take it as your true treasure and guard it from loss. “Living beings” here means human life, since only humans know restraint and benefit from it.
en.4: Guard thy self-control as a very treasure: life hath no richer wealth here below.
en.5:
Guard thou as wealth the power of self-controul;
Than this no greater gain to living soul!
en.6: Let self-control be guarded as a treasure; there is no greater source of good for man than that.

padaccheda.m: அடங்குதலே நமக்கு அறிவாவது என்று அறிந்து நெறியானே ஒருவன் அடங்கப்பெறின்
அவ்வடக்கம் நல்லோரான் அறியப்பட்டு அவனுக்கு விழுப்பத்தைக் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: If you know what is worth knowing and hold yourself in by the right way, your restraint will be noticed and bring you honour.
en.2: If you understand that restraint is your true knowledge and hold yourself in by the right path, the good will recognise that restraint and it will bring you distinction. For a householder the path of restraint is to keep body, speech and mind under his own control.
en.4: Behold the man who controlleth his passions consciously and by the right way: wisdom and every other blessing will come unto him.
en.5:
If versed in wisdom’s lore by virtue’s law you self restrain,
Your self-repression known will yield you glory’s gain.
en.6: Knowing that self-control is knowledge, if a man should control himself, in the prescribed course, such self-control will bring him distinction among the wise.

padaccheda.m: இல்வாழ்க்கையாகிய தன் நெறியின் வேறுபடாது நின்று அடங்கியவனது உயர்ச்சி
மலையின் உயர்ச்சியினும் மிகப் பெரிது

en.1: One who holds steady in their place and keeps restraint stands taller than a mountain.
en.2: The stature of one who stays on his path of home life and keeps restraint is far greater than the height of a mountain. This is restraint kept while still enjoying the objects of the senses.
en.4: Behold the man who hath triumphed over his passions and who swerveth not from duty: his form is more imposing than a mountain.
en.5:
In his station, all unswerving, if man self subdue,
Greater he than mountain proudly rising to the view.
en.6: More lofty than a mountain will be the greatness of that man who without swerving from his domestic state controls himself.

padaccheda.m: பெருமிதம் இன்றி அடங்குதல் எல்லார்க்கும் ஒப்ப நன்றே யெனினும்
அவ்வெல்லாருள்ளுஞ் செல்வம் உடையார்க்கே வேறொரு செல்வமாஞ்சிறப்பினையுடைத்து

en.1: Humility is good in everyone, but in the rich it is a further wealth.
en.2: Restraint without pride is good in everyone alike, but among them only the rich gain from it a distinction that is another wealth. Those with learning and good birth are held in by these very things, so their restraint doesn’t stand out. These five couplets tell the excellence of restraint in general.
en.4: Humility is beautiful in all man: but alone on the rich doth it shine in all its splendour.
en.5:
To all humility is goodly grace; but chief to them
With fortune blessed,—’tis fortune’s diadem.
en.6: Humility is good in all; but especially in the rich it is (the excellence of) a higher riches.

padaccheda.m: ஆமைபோல ஒருவன் ஒருபிறப்பின்கண் ஐம்பொறிகளையும் அடக்கவல்லனாயின்
அவ்வன்மை அவனுக்கு எழுபிற்ப்பின்கண்ணும் அரணாதலை உடைத்து

en.1: If in one life you can draw in the five senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs, it will shelter you through seven lives.
en.2: If in one birth you can hold in the five senses as a tortoise holds in its five limbs against danger, that power shields you in all seven births. As it keeps out danger, you must keep out sin. The fruit of deeds done in one birth follows you for seven. This tells restraint of the body.
en.4: Behold the man who can draw in into himself his five senses even as the tortoise doth its limbs: he hath laid up for himself a treasure for all his future births.
en.5:
Like tortoise, who the five restrains
In one, through seven worlds bliss obtains.
en.6: Should one throughout a single birth, like a tortoise keep in his five senses, the fruit of it will prove a safe-guard to him throughout the seven fold births.

padaccheda.m: தம்மாற் காக்கப்படுவன எல்லாவற்றையும் காக்கமாட்டாராயினும் நாவொன்றனையும் காக்க
அதனைக் காவாராயின் சொற்குற்றத்தின்கட் பட்டுத் தாமே துன்புறுவர்

en.1: Whatever else you fail to guard, guard your tongue. If you don’t, you will suffer from the slips of your speech.
en.2: Even if you can’t guard all you should guard, guard the tongue alone. Those who don’t guard it fall into the faults of speech and suffer for it themselves.
en.4: Whatever else thou rein not in, rein in thy tongue: for an unbridled tongue leadeth unto grief.
en.5:
Whate’er they fail to guard, o’er lips men guard should keep;
If not, through fault of tongue, they bitter tears shall weep.
en.6: Whatever besides you leave unguarded, guard your tongue; otherwise errors of speech and the consequent misery will ensue.

padaccheda.m: தீயவாகிய சொற்களின் பொருள்களாற் பிறர்க்குவருந் துன்பம் ஒன்றாயினும் ஒருவன்பக்கல் உண்டாவதாயின்
அவனுக்குப் பிற அறங்களால் உண்டான நன்மை தீதாய் விடும்

en.1: If a single evil word does its harm, the good you have done turns bad.
en.2: If even one hurt comes to others through the meaning of your evil words, the good that your other righteous acts brought you turns bad. Evil words are harmful lies, slander and harsh speech. Some read it as one evil word among many good ones.
en.4: If even one word of thine causeth pain to another, all thy virtue is lost.
en.5:
Though some small gain of good it seem to bring,
The evil word is parent still of evil thing.
en.6: If a man’s speech be productive of a single evil, all the good, by him will be turned into evil.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனை யொருவன் தீயினால் சுட்ட புண் மெய்க்கண் கிடப்பினும் மனத்தின்கண் அப்பொழுதே ஆறும்
அவவாறு அன்றி வெவ்வுரையை உடைய நாவினால் சுட்டவடு அதன்கண்ணும் எஞ்ஞான்றும் ஆறாது

en.1: A wound burned by fire heals within. A scar burned by the tongue never heals.
en.2: A wound someone burns on you with fire stays on the body but heals at once in the mind. The scar burned by a tongue of hot words never heals, even there. So one is called a wound and the other a scar. Both burn, but hot words are crueller than fire. These three couplets tell restraint of speech.
en.4: The burn caused by fire healeth in its time: but the wound burned in by the tongue remaineth green forever.
en.5:
In flesh by fire inflamed, nature may throughly heal the sore;
In soul by tongue inflamed, the ulcer healeth nevermore.
en.6: The wound which has been burnt in by fire may heal, but a wound burnt in by the tongue will never heal.

padaccheda.w: கதம் காத்துக் கற்று அடங்கல் ஆற்றுவான் செவ்வி
padaccheda.m: மனத்தின்கண் வெகுளி தோன்றாமல் காத்துக் கலவியுடையனாய் அடங்குதலை வல்லவனது செவ்வியை
அறக்கடவுள் பாராநிற்கும் அவனை அடையும்நெறியின்கண் சென்று

en.1: Righteousness finds the path to someone who holds back anger, learns and keeps restraint, and waits for the moment to see them.
en.2: The god of righteousness goes down the path to one who keeps anger from rising, is learned and can hold back, and watches for the right moment. Holding back is the mind staying in righteousness and not spreading outward. The right moment is when he is pleasant in mind, speech and face. Righteousness itself comes to such a person. This tells restraint of the mind.
en.4: Behold the man who hath learned wisdom and whose mind is tranquil and under perfect control: Righteousness pilgrimageth to his home in order to have a look at him.
en.5:
Who learns restraint, and guards his soul from wrath,
Virtue, a timely aid, attends his path.
en.6: Virtue, seeking for an opportunity, will come into the path of that man who, possessed of learning and self control, guards, himself against anger.

padaccheda.m: ஒழுக்கம் எல்லார்க்கும் சிறப்பினைத் தருதலான்
அவ்வொழுக்கம் உயிரினும் பாதுகாக்கப்படும்

en.1: Conduct brings excellence, so guard your conduct more closely than your life.
en.2: Conduct gives distinction to everyone, high and low alike, so it is to be guarded more than life. Life is the best of all things, but it doesn’t give distinction as conduct does.
en.4: The man whose conduct is pure is honoured by all: purity of conduct is therefore to be prized even above life.
en.5:
‘Decorum’ gives especial excellence; with greater care
‘Decorum’ should men guard than life, which all men share.
en.6: Propriety of conduct leads to eminence, it should therefore be preserved more carefully than life.

padaccheda.m: ஒழுக்கத்தினை ஒன்றானும் அழிவுபடாமற் பேணி வருந்தியும் காக்க
அறங்கள் பலவற்றையு்ம் ஆராய்ந்து இவற்றுள் இருமைக்கும் துணையாவது யாதென்று மனத்தை யொருக்கித் தேர்ந்தாலும் துணையாய் முடிவது அவ்வொழுக்கமே யாகலான்

en.1: Guard your conduct with anxious care. Search and test as you will, it alone is your companion.
en.2: Protect conduct, even with pain, letting none of it perish. Examine all kinds of righteousness, ask with a settled mind which helps in both worlds, and conduct is the one that proves your help. These two couplets tell the excellence of conduct.
en.4: Watch anxiously over thy conduct: for wheresoever thou mayest search thou canst not find a firmer ally than right conduct.
en.5:
Searching, duly watching, learning,—‘decorum’ still we find
Man’s only aid: toiling, guard thou this with watchful mind.
en.6: Let propriety of conduct be laboriously preserved and guarded; though one know and practise and excel in many virtues, that will be an eminent aid.

padaccheda.m: எல்லார்க்கும் தத்தம் வருணத்திற்கு ஏற்ற ஒழுக்கமுடைமை குலனுடைமையாம்
அவ்வொழுக்கத்தில் தவறுதல் அவ்வருணத்தில் தாழ்ந்த வருணமாய்விடும்

en.1: Good conduct is noble family. A lapse in it becomes low birth.
en.2: For everyone, the conduct right for their varna is high family. Lapsing from it becomes a lower varna. Those of a low family within their varna become high by conduct. Those born in a high varna become low by lapsing. The result follows at once, so the deeds themselves are named as the results.
en.4: Good conduct bespeaketh an honourable family: but low conduct placeth a man amongst the ignoble.
en.5:
‘Decorum’ ’s true nobility on earth;
‘Indecorum’s’ issue is ignoble birth.
en.6: Propriety of conduct is true greatness of birth, and impropriety will sink into a mean birth.

padaccheda.m: கற்ற வேதத்தினை மறந்தான் ஆயினும் அவ்வருணம் கெடாமையிற் பின்னும் அஃது ஓதிக் கொளலாம்
அந்தணனது உயர்ந்த வருணம் தன்னொழுக்கம் குன்றக் கெடும்

en.1: A Brahmin who forgets his scripture can learn it again. If his conduct falls, his birth is ruined.
en.2: A Brahmin who forgets the Veda he learned can study it again, because his varna isn’t lost. But his high varna is lost when his conduct falls. “Forgets” is no licence, since forgetting too would lower him. This is said of the highest varna, and it holds for the others as well.
en.4: Even the Vedas if forgotten can be learned again: but once fallen from virtuous conduct the Brahman is fallen from his place forever.
en.5:
Though he forget, the Brahman may regain his Vedic lore;
Failing in ‘decorum due,’ birthright’s gone for evermore.
en.6: A Brahman though he should forget the Vedas may recover it by reading; but if he fail in propriety of conduct even his high birth will be destroyed.

padaccheda.m: அழுக்காறு உடையான்மாட்டு ஆக்கம் இல்லாதாற்போல
ஒழுக்கம் இல்லாதவன் மாட்டும் உயர்ச்சியில்லை

en.1: Just as the envious have no gain, those without good conduct have no standing.
en.2: As the envious have no gain, those without conduct have no height. From the comparison it follows that their kin have none either, because the kin of the envious go poor too. Height here means belonging to a high family.
en.4: Prosperity is not for the envious: even so dignity is not for men of ill conduct.
en.5:
The envious soul in life no rich increase of blessing gains,
So man of ‘due decorum’ void no dignity obtains.
en.6: Just as the envious man will be without wealth, so will the man destitute of propriety of conduct be without greatness.

padaccheda.m: செய்தற்கு அருமை நோக்கி ஒழுக்கத்திற் சுருங்கார் மனவலியுடையார்
அவ்விழுக்கத்தால் தமக்கு இழிகுலமாகிய குற்றம் உண்டாமாற்றை அறிந்து

en.1: The strong-minded don’t slacken in their conduct, for they know the harm that comes of a lapse.
en.2: Those strong of mind don’t cut back on conduct because it is hard, for they know that a lapse brings them the fault of low family. They are called strong because they don’t give up the vow they have taken.
en.4: The firm-minded swerve not from virtuous conduct: for they know the evils brought on by such swerving.
en.5:
The strong of soul no jot abate of ‘strict decorum’s’ laws,
Knowing that ‘due decorum’s’ breach foulest disgrace will cause.
en.6: Those firm in mind will not slacken in their observance of the proprieties of life, knowing, as they do, the misery that flows from the transgression from them.

padaccheda.m: எல்லாரும் ஒழுக்கத்தானே மேம்பாட்டை எய்துவர்
அதனினின்று இழுக்குதலானே தாம் எய்துதற்கு உரித்தல்லாத பழியை எய்துவர்

en.1: By good conduct people reach greatness. By a lapse they reach blame they didn’t deserve.
en.2: Everyone reaches eminence by conduct. By falling from it they get blame they don’t deserve. When enemies bring a false charge, the world believes it because of the lapse. These five couplets tell the good of having conduct and the fault of lacking it.
en.4: The man of right conduct is honoured among men: but ignominy alone is the portion of those who fall therefrom.
en.5:
’Tis source of dignity when ‘true decorum’ is preserved;
Who break ‘decorum’s’ rules endure e’en censures undeserved.
en.6: From propriety of conduct men obtain greatness; from impropriety comes insufferable disgrace.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு நல்லொழுக்கம் அறத்திற்குக் காரணமாய் இருமையினும் இன்பம் பயக்கும்
தீய ஒழுக்கம் பாவத்திற்குக் காரணமாய் இருமையினும் துன்பம் பயக்கும்

en.1: Good conduct is the seed of good. Bad conduct brings suffering always.
en.2: Good conduct is the cause of righteousness and gives joy in both worlds. Bad conduct is the cause of sin and gives suffering in both. Naming one half of each implies the other. This tells what follows from conduct later.
en.4: Good conduct soweth the seed of prosperity: but an evil course is the mother of endless ills.
en.5:
‘Decorum true’ observed a seed of good will be;
‘Decorum’s breach’ will sorrow yield eternally.
en.6: Propriety of conduct is the seed of virtue; and impropriety will ever cause sorrow.

padaccheda.m: மறந்துந் தீயசொற்களைத் தம் வாயாற் சொல்லும் தொழில்கள்
ஒழுக்கம் உடையவர்க்கு முடியா

en.1: Those with good conduct can’t say evil things with their mouths, even by a slip.
en.2: Those with conduct can’t utter evil words with their mouths, even by forgetting. Evil words are lies and the like that harm others, and words not fit for their varna. “Mouths” is added to say their mouths are practised in good words.
en.4: Foul words can never fall from the lips of the well-bred even when off their guard.
en.5:
It cannot be that they who ‘strict decorum’s’ law fulfil,
E’en in forgetful mood, should utter words of ill.
en.6: Those who study propriety of conduct will not speak evil even forgetfully.

padaccheda.m: உலகத்தோடு பொருந்த ஒழுகுதலைக் கல்லாதார்
பல நூல்களையுங் கற்றாராயினும் அறிவிலாதார்

en.1: Those who don’t learn to move in step with the world may learn much, but they are still without understanding.
en.2: Those who haven’t learned to live in accord with the world have no understanding, though they have read many books. To accord with the world is to live as the high-minded have lived. That drops what the law books say that no longer suits the time, and takes up what suits it though unsaid. The use of learning is knowledge, and the use of knowledge is conduct.
en.4: Fools may be as instructed as thou pleasest: but they never learn to conform to the ways of the Righteous.
en.5:
Who know not with the world in harmony to dwell,
May many things have learned, but nothing well.
en.6: Those who know not how to act agreeably to the world, though they have learnt many things, are still ignorant.

padaccheda.m: பிறனுக்குப் பொருளாந் தன்மையை உடையாளைக் காதலித்து ஒழுகுகின்ற அறியாமை
ஞாலத்தின்கண் அறநூலையும் பொருள்நூலையும் ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்தார்மாட்டு இல்லை

en.1: The folly of chasing a woman who is another man’s property is not found in those who know righteousness and wealth.
en.2: The ignorance of loving and pursuing a woman who is another man’s property isn’t found in those on earth who have studied the books of righteousness and of wealth. Those who study the books of pleasure, and look to pleasure alone, even give this wicked conduct a name, so he names only the two. Those with this folly have neither righteousness nor wealth.
en.4: Behold the men whose eyes are turned towards righteousness and towards wealth: they commit not the folly of desiring another man’s wife.
en.5:
Who laws of virtue and possession’s rights have known,
Indulge no foolish love of her by right another’s own.
en.6: The folly of desiring her who is the property of another will not be found in those who know (the attributes of) virtue and (the rights of) property.

padaccheda.m: காமம் காரணமாகப் பாவத்தின்கண் நின்றார் எல்லாருள்ளும்
பிறன் இல்லாளைக் காதலித்து அவன் வாயிற்கண் சென்றுநின்றார் போலப் பேதையார் இல்லை

en.1: Of all who stand outside righteousness, none is a greater fool than those who stand at another man’s door.
en.2: Of all who stand in sin because of desire, none are as foolish as those who love another man’s wife and stand at his door. Sinners who follow women, or go with prostitutes or women of low family, lose righteousness and wealth. Those at another’s door lose even the pleasure they sought, through fear. So they have no pleasure either.
en.4: Among those that have fallen from virtue there is no greater fool than he that standeth at his neighbour’s threshold.
en.5:
No fools, of all that stand from virtue’s pale shut out,
Like those who longing lurk their neighbour’s gate without.
en.6: Among all those who stand on the outside of virtue, there are no greater fools than those who stand outside their neighbour’s door.

padaccheda.m: தம்மை ஐயுறாதார் இல்லாள் கண்ணே பாவம் செய்தலை விரும்பி ஒழுகுவார்
உயிருடையவரேனும் இறந்தாரே யாவர்

en.1: Those who do evil in the home of someone who trusts them are surely no different from the dead.
en.2: Those who like to sin with the wife of a man who doesn’t suspect them are dead, though they have life. They are no different from the dead because their souls gain none of righteousness, wealth and pleasure. “One who trusts” is said because they can do this only through the husband’s trust.
en.4: Verily they are in the jaws of death who invade the home of an unsuspecting friend.
en.5:
They’re numbered with the dead, e’en while they live,—how otherwise?
With wife of sure confiding friend who evil things devise.
en.6: Certainly they are no better than dead men who desire evil towards the wife of those who undoubtingly confide in them.

padaccheda.m: எத்துணைப் பெருமைஉடையர் ஆயினும் ஒருவர்க்கு யாதாய் முடியும்

padaccheda.w: தினைத் துணையும் தேரான் பிறன் இல் புகல்
padaccheda.m: காம மயக்கத்தால் தினையளவமு தம் பிழையை ஓராது பிறனுடைய இல்லின்கண் புகுதல்

en.1: However great you may be, what good is it, if you enter another man’s home without a millet seed’s worth of thought?
en.2: However great someone is, what does it come to if, in the delusion of desire, they enter another man’s home without weighing their fault even by a millet seed? Like Indra, they lose all greatness and fall low. Some take “not weighing” with the other man, as the husband who suspects nothing.
en.4: Let a man be ever so great: what availeth it all if he committeth adultery without thinking ever so little of the shame that floweth therefrom?
en.5:
How great soe’er they be, what gain have they of life,
Who, not a whit reflecting, seek a neighbour’s wife?
en.6: However great one may be what does it avail if without at all considering his guilt he goes unto the wife of another.

padaccheda.m: எய்துதல் எளிது என்று கருதிப் பின்விளைவு கருதாது பிறன் இல்லின்கண் இறப்பான்
மாய்தலின்றி எஞ்ஞான்றும் நிலைநிற்கும் குடிப்பழியினை எய்தும்

en.1: Whoever trespasses on a home, thinking it easy, earns blame that will never die.
en.2: One who thinks “It is easy” and, with no thought of what follows, trespasses on another’s home earns a blame on his family that stands for all time and never dies. To trespass on a home is to cross the line with the wife of the house.
en.4: Behold the man who hangeth on to his neighbour’s wife because she is accessible: his name is sullied forever.
en.5:
‘Mere trifle!’ saying thus, invades the home; so he ensures
A gain of guilt that deathless aye endures.
en.6: He who thinks lightly of going unto the wife of another acquires guilt that will abide with him imperishably and for ever.

padaccheda.m: பிறன் இல்லாள்கண் நெறிகடந்து செல்வானிடத்து

padaccheda.w: பகை பாவம் அச்சம் பழி என நான்கும் இகவாவாம்
padaccheda.m: பகையும் பாவமும் அச்சமும் குடிப்பழியும் என்னும் இந்நான்கு குற்றமும் ஒருகாலும் நீங்காவாம்

en.1: Enmity, sin, fear and blame: these four never leave the one who trespasses on a home.
en.2: Enmity, sin, fear and blame on his family: these four faults never leave the man who crosses the line with another’s wife. So he loses both worlds. These six couplets tell the fault in one who wants another’s wife.
en.4: The adulterer knoweth no respite from four things, hatred, sin, fear, and shame.
en.5:
Who home invades, from him pass nevermore,
Hatred and sin, fear, foul disgrace: these four.
en.6: Hatred, sin, fear, disgrace; these four will never leave him who goes in to his neighbour’s wife.

padaccheda.m: அறனாகிய இயல்போடு கூடி இல்வாழ்வான் என்று சொல்லப்படுவான்
பிறனுக்குரிமை பூண்டு அவனுடைய இயல்பின்கண்ணே நிற்பாளது பெண்தன்மையை விரும்பாதவன்

en.1: The one who doesn’t crave the womanhood of a woman who is another’s is the one called a householder who lives by righteousness.
en.2: The one called a householder, living with righteousness as his nature, is the man who doesn’t want the womanhood of one who belongs to another and stays in his ways. Only he is said to practise household righteousness.
en.4: He is the righteous householder who careth not for the charms of his neighbour’s wife.
en.5:
Who sees the wife, another’s own, with no desiring eye,
In sure domestic bliss he dwelleth ever virtuously.
en.6: He who desires not the womanhood ‘of her who should walk according to the will of another will be praised as a virtuous house-holder.

padaccheda.m: பிறன் மனையாளை உட்கொள்ளாத பெரிய ஆண்டகைமை
சால்புடையார்க்கு அறனுமாம், நிரம்பிய ஒழுக்கமுமாம்

en.1: The great manhood that won’t look at another’s wife is, for the worthy, not only righteousness but full conduct.
en.2: The great manhood that doesn’t hold another’s wife in mind is, for the worthy, both righteousness and complete conduct. Even men who can defeat outer enemies find it hard to subdue desire, the enemy within, so this is called great manhood. Merely not doing this wrong brings both, which are otherwise hard to do.
en.4: Behold the high-souled man that looketh not on another’s wife: he is more than righteous: he is saintly.
en.5:
Manly excellence, that looks not on another’s wife,
Is not virtue merely, ’tis full ‘propriety’ of life.
en.6: That noble manliness which looks not at the wife of another is the virtue and dignity of the great.

padaccheda.m: அச்சந் தரும் கடலாற் சூழப்பட்ட உலகத்து
எல்லா நன்மைகளும் எய்துதுற்கு உரியார் யாவரெனின்
பிறன் ஒருவனுக்கு உரிமையாகியாள் உடைய தோளைச் சேராதார்

en.1: Who in this world ringed by the fearsome sea deserves every good? Those who don’t embrace the shoulders of a woman who is another’s.
en.2: Who in the world ringed by the fearsome sea is fit to gain every good? Those who don’t join the shoulders of a woman who belongs to another. The sea is fearsome because its width, depth and contents can’t be measured. They gain good in both worlds.
en.4: Who on earth deserve all the good things of the world? It is they who clasp not the arms of her who belongeth to another.
en.5:
Who’re good indeed, on earth begirt by ocean’s gruesome tide?
The men who touch not her that is another’s bride.
en.6: Is it asked, “who are those who shall obtain good in this world surrounded by the terror-producing sea?” Those who touch not the shoulder of her who belongs to another.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் அறத்தைத் தனக்கு உரித்தாகச் செய்யாது பாவங்களைச் செய்யுமாயினும்
அவனுக்குப் பிறன் எல்லைக்கண் நிற்பாளது பெண்மையை விரும்பாமை உண்டாயின் அது நன்று

en.1: Even if you keep no bounds of righteousness and do wrong, it is good not to crave the womanhood of one within another’s bounds.
en.2: Even if a man doesn’t make righteousness his own and does sinful things, if he doesn’t want the womanhood of one within another’s bounds, that is good. This quality alone will stand out. These four couplets tell the quality of one who doesn’t want another’s wife.
en.4: Though thou shouldst transgress and yield to every other sin, it were well for thee if thou desire not thy neighbour’s wife.
en.5:
Though virtue’s bounds he pass, and evil deeds hath wrought;
At least, ’tis good if neighbour’s wife he covet not.
en.6: Though a man perform no virtuous deeds and commit (every) vice, it will be well if he desire not the womanhood of her who is within the limit (of the house) of another.

padaccheda.m: தன்னை அகழ்வாரை வீழாமல் தாங்கும் நிலம்போல
தம்மை அவமதிப்பாரைப் பொறுத்தல் தலையாய அறம்

en.1: As the earth holds up those who dig into it, the highest thing is to bear with those who scorn you.
en.2: As the earth holds up those who dig it and doesn’t let them fall, bearing with those who scorn you is the foremost righteousness. Scorn covers both what is done and what is said beyond measure.
en.4: The earth supporteth even those that dig into her: even so bear thou with those that traduce thee; for that is greatness.
en.5:
As earth bears up the men who delve into her breast,
To bear with scornful men of virtues is the best.
en.6: To bear with those who revile us just as the earth bears up those who dig it, is the first of virtues.

en.1: Always bear a wrong done to you. Forgetting it is better still.
en.2: Since patience is good, bear what others do beyond measure even when you have the power to punish. Better than that is to forget it at once and not take it in. While you bear a wrong you still hold it in mind, which is why forgetting is better.
en.4: Forgive thou always the injuries that others may do thee: but if thou forget them, it were even better.
en.5:
Forgiving trespasses is good always;
Forgetting them hath even higher praise.
en.6: Bear with reproach even when you can retaliate; but to forget it will be still better than that.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு வறுமையுள் வைத்து வறுமையாவது, விருந்தினரை யேற்றுக்கொள்ளாது நீக்குதல்
அதுபோல வன்மையுள் வைத்து வன்மையாவது, அறிவின்மையான் மிகைசெய்தாரைப் பொறுத்தல்

en.1: The deepest poverty is to turn a guest away. The greatest strength is to bear with fools.
en.2: The poverty of all poverty is refusing to receive guests. In the same way, the strength of all strength is bearing with those who wrong you out of ignorance. Turning guests away is unrighteous and never counts as wealth, and bearing with fools is never weakness but strength.
en.4: The most shameful poverty is the refusal of hospitality: and the greatest strength is to bear with the dullness of fools.
en.5:
The sorest poverty is bidding guest unfed depart;
The mightiest might to bear with men of foolish heart.
en.6: To neglect hospitality is poverty of poverty. To bear with the ignorant is might of might.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் நிறையுடைமையை தன்கண் நின்று நீங்காமை வேண்டுவனாயின்
அவனாற் பொறையுடைமை தன்கண் அழியாமல் காத்து ஒழுகப்படும்

en.1: If you want your integrity never to leave you, guard your patience and live by it.
en.2: Someone who wants their integrity never to leave them must guard their patience so that it doesn’t perish. There is no nobility except through patience.
en.4: If thou want to be grand always, be forgiving unto all.
en.5:
Seek’st thou honour never tarnished to retain;
So must thou patience, guarding evermore, maintain.
en.6: If you desire that greatness should never leave you preserve in your conduct the exercise of patience.

padaccheda.m: பிறன் தமக்குத் தீங்கு செய்தவழிப் பொறாது அவனை ஒறுத்தாரை அறிவுடையார் ஒருபொருளாக மனத்துக் கொள்ளார்
அதனைப் பொறுத்தாரைப் பொன்போற் பொதிந்து கொள்வர்

en.1: Those who punish a wrong are counted as nothing. Those who bear it are wrapped up and kept like gold.
en.2: The wise give no place in their minds to those who can’t bear an injury and punish the one who did it, since they have become no better than that person. Those who bear it they keep like wrapped gold, thinking of them without pause for their nobility.
