en.4: The fledgeling abandoneth the broken shell of the egg and flieth away: that is the symbol of the love between the soul and the body.
en.5:
Birds fly away, and leave the nest deserted bare;
Such is the short-lived friendship soul and body share.
en.6: The love of the soul to the body is like (the love of) a bird to its egg which it flies away from and leaves empty.

reading.note: குடம்பை can mean egg or nest. The plain reading follows him.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்குச் சாக்காடு வருதல் உறக்கம் வருதலோடு ஒக்கும்
அதன்பின் பிறப்பு வருதல் உறங்கி விழித்தல் வருதலோடு ஒக்கும்

en.1: Death is like falling asleep. Birth is like waking after sleep.
en.2: Death comes as sleep comes, and birth follows as waking follows sleep. As sleeping and waking alternate quickly and naturally, so do death and birth. Birth is named too, to show that impermanence is the one thing that lasts.
en.4: Death is like unto a sleep: and life is like the waking after that sleep.
en.5:
Death is sinking into slumbers deep;
Birth again is waking out of sleep.
en.6: Death is like sleep; birth is like awaking from it.

padaccheda.m: வாதமுதலியவற்றின் இல்லாய உடம்புகளுள் ஒதுக்கிருந்தே போந்த உயிர்க்கு
எஞ்ஞான்றும் இருப்பதோர் இல் இதுகாறும் அமைந்தில்லைபோலும்!

en.1: The soul has been lodging in the body. Has it still found no home of its own?
en.2: The soul has only ever taken shelter in bodies, which are the houses of wind and the other humours. It seems that until now no lasting house has been found for it. It stays while those ailments allow and leaves when they rage, settling in no body. If it had a home it never had to leave, it wouldn’t lodge in others’ houses.
en.4: Hath the soul no home of its own, that it taketh shelter in this worthless body?
en.5:
The soul in fragile shed as lodger courts repose:—
Is it because no home’s conclusive rest it knows?
en.6: It seems as if the soul, which takes a temporary shelter in a body, had not attained a home.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் யாதொருபொருளின் யாதொருபொருளின் நீங்கினான்

அவன் அப்பொருளால் அப்பொருளால் துன்பம் எய்துதல் இலன். அடுக்குக்கள் பன்மை குறித்து நின்றன. நீங்குதல்= துறத்தல். ஈண்டுத் 'துன்பம்' என்றது இம்மைக்கண் அவற்றைத் தேடுதலானும், காத்தலானும், இழத்தலானும் வருவனவும், மறுமைக்கட் பாவத்தான் வருவனவுமாகிய இருவகைத் துன்பங்களையுமாம். எல்லாப் பொருளையும் ஒருங்கே விடுதல் தலை. அஃதன்றி ஒரோவொன்றாக விடினும் அவற்றான் வரும் துன்பம் இலனாம் என்பது கருத்து

en.1: From each thing you have let go of, you suffer no more pain.
en.2: From each thing you have renounced, you suffer no pain. The pain is of two kinds: in this life, from seeking, guarding and losing it, and in the next, from sin. Giving up everything at once is best, but even giving things up one by one frees you from the pain they bring.
en.4: Whatsoever thing a man hath renounced, from the grief arising from that thing hath he liberated himself.
en.5:
From whatever, aye, whatever, man gets free,
From that, aye, from that, no more of pain hath he!
en.6: Whatever thing a man has renounced, by that thing, he cannot suffer pain.

padaccheda.m: எல்லாப் பொருள்களையும் துறந்தால் ஒருவர்க்கு இம்மைக்கண்ணே உளவாம் முறைமையையுடைய இன்பங்கள் பல
அவ்வின்பங்களைவேண்டின் அவற்றைக் காலம் பெறத் துறக்க

en.1: If you want them, renounce while you can. Once you have renounced, many things are yours here.
en.2: If you renounce everything, many joys are yours in this very life. If you want them, renounce in good time. They come from mind, speech and body no longer being driven about by things, and from moving on the good path. Whoever renounces in youth has them longest. So renouncing brings joys, not only freedom from pain.
en.4: If thou want joy, renounce early: for many are the delights that thou shalt enjoy after renouncing.
en.5:
‘Renunciation’ made—ev’n here true pleasures men acquire;
‘Renounce’ while time is yet, if to those pleasures you aspire.
en.6: After a man has renounced (all things), there will still be many things in this world (which he may enjoy); if he should desire them, let him, while it is time, abandon (the world).

reading.note: He supplies “joys” and “time”. The Tamil names neither.

padaccheda.m: வீடு எய்துவார்க்குச் செவி முதலிய ஐம்பொறிகட்கு உரியவாய ஓசை முதலிய ஐம்புலன்களையும் கெடுத்தல் வேண்டும்
கெடுக்குங்கால் அவற்றை நுகர்தற் பொருட்டுத் தாம் படைத்த பொருள் முழுதையும் ஒருங்கே விடுதல் வேண்டும்

en.1: You must crush the hold of the five senses and give up, all together, everything you wanted.
en.2: Those seeking release must crush the enjoyment of the five senses, and in doing so give up, all at once, everything they gathered to enjoy. That enjoyment drives the mind towards things won only by pain and sin, away from yoga and wisdom. Fed with such things it flares up like fire given firewood, and can’t be crushed.
en.4: Crush thou the five senses: and everything in which thou takest delight, give up utterly.
en.5:
‘Perceptions of the five’ must all expire;—
Relinquished in its order each desire.
en.6: Let the five senses be destroyed; and at the same time, let every thing be abandoned that (the ascetic) has (formerly) desired.

padaccheda.m: பற்றப் படுவது ஒருபொருளும் இல்லாமை தவம் செய்வார்க்கு இயல்பாம்
அஃதன்றி, ஒன்றாயினும் உடைமை அத்தவத்தைப் போக்குதலான், மீண்டும் மயங்குதற்கு ஏதுவாம்

en.1: Having nothing at all is the way of penance. Owning even one thing brings back delusion.
en.2: Having nothing to cling to is natural to those who do penance. Owning even one thing drives the penance away and becomes a cause of delusion again. If you give up all but one thing, everything you gave up comes back through it, breaks your penance and troubles your mind.
en.4: To possess nothing, that is the law of the man of vows: the possession of even one thing is a coming back to the snares that he hath left.
en.5:
‘Privation absolute’ is penance true;
‘Possession’ brings bewilderment anew.
en.6: To be altogether destitute is the proper condition of those who perform austerities; if they possess anything, it will change (their resolution) and bring them back to their confused state.

padaccheda.m: பிறப்பு அறுத்தலை மேற்கொண்டார்க்கு அதற்குக் கருவியாகிய உடம்பும் மிகையாம்
ஆனபின் அதற்கு மேலே இயைபு இல்லனவும் சில தொடர்ப்பாடு உளவாதல் என்னாம்!

en.1: For those out to cut off birth, even the body is too much. Why then any other ties?
en.2: For those set on cutting off birth, even the body, their tool for it, is surplus. Then why have any further ties? “Body” means both the visible one and the subtle one, the mind joined with the senses, the vital airs and the results of desire and deeds. Seeing the constant suffering of these, they can’t bear the bond a moment and hurry to release.
en.4: To those that desire to put an end to their reincarnations, even the body is a superfluity: how much more then are other bonds?
en.5:
To those who sev’rance seek from being’s varied strife,
Flesh is burthen sore; what then other bonds of life?
en.6: What means the addition of other things to those who are attempting to cut off (future) births, when even their body is too much (for them).

padaccheda.m: தான் அல்லாத உடம்பை யான் என்றும், தன்னோடு இயைபில்லாத பொருளை எனது என்றும் கருதி அவற்றின்கண் பற்றுச் செய்தற்கு ஏதுவாகிய மயக்கத்தைக் கெடுப்பான்
வானோர்க்கும் எய்தற்கு அரிய வீட்டுலகத்தை எய்தும்

en.1: Whoever cuts away the pride that says “I” and “mine” will enter a world higher than the gods’.
en.2: Whoever destroys the delusion that calls the body “I” and unrelated things “mine” reaches the world of release, hard even for the gods to reach. Destroying it means seeing, through a teacher’s words and the practice of yoga, that these are neither I nor mine, and letting go. Release is only for those who give up both kinds of attachment.
en.4: The feelings of I and Mine are nought but vanity and pride: he who crusheth them entereth a higher world than the world of the Gods.
en.5:
Who kills conceit that utters ‘I’ and ‘mine,’
Shall enter realms above the powers divine.
en.6: He who destroys the pride which says “I,” “mine,” will enter a world which is difficult even to the Gods to attain.

padaccheda.m: இருவகைப் பற்றினையும் இறுகப்பற்றி விடாதாரை
பிறவித்துன்பங்கள் இறுகப்பற்றி விடா. இறுகப்பற்றுதல்= காதல்கூர்தல். விடாதவர்க்கு என்பது வேற்றுமைமயக்கம். இதனால் இவை விடாதவர்க்கு வீடில்லை என்பது கூறப்பட்டது

en.1: Suffering holds on and won’t let go of those who hold on to attachment and won’t let go.
en.2: Those who grip both kinds of attachment and won’t let go are gripped by the sufferings of birth, which won’t let them go. Gripping means loving fiercely. So those who don’t let go have no release.
en.4: Behold the man who holdeth on to attachments and giveth not them up: Grief shall take hold of him and shall not give him up.
en.5:
Who cling to things that cling and eager clasp,
Griefs cling to them with unrelaxing grasp.
en.6: Sorrows will never let go their hold of those who give not up their hold of desire.

padaccheda.m: முற்றத்துறந்தார் வீட்டினைத் தலைப்பட்டார்
அங்ஙனம் துறவாதார் மயங்கிப் பிறப்பாகிய வலையுட்பட்டார்

en.1: Those who renounce completely have arrived. All others are deluded, and caught in a net.
en.2: Those who renounce completely have reached release. To renounce completely is to sicken of all things and of both bodies, and to let them go with no attachment. Those who don’t, who keep even a little attachment to any of these, have been deluded by false paths and caught in the net of birth.
en.4: They that have renounced utterly are on the path to salvation: but the others are caught in a snare.
en.5:
Who thoroughly ‘renounce’ on highest height are set:
The rest, bewildered, lie entangled in the net.
en.6: Those who have entirely renounced (all things and all desire) have obtained (absorption into God); all others wander in confusion, entangled in the net of (many) births.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் இருவகைப்பற்றும் அற்றபொழுதே, அப்பற்றுஅறுதி அவன் பிறப்பை அறுக்கும்
அவை அறாதபொழுது அவற்றால் பிறந்து இறந்து வருகின்ற நிலையாமை காணப்படும்

en.1: The moment attachment ends, birth is cut off. Otherwise you will see impermanence.
en.2: The moment both kinds of attachment are gone, their ending cuts off birth. While they remain, you see the impermanence of being born and dying through them. When a cause goes, its effect goes at once.
en.4: The moment that attachments are broken, that very moment reincarnations cease: the man who breaketh them not continueth in vanity.
en.5:
When that which clings falls off, severed is being’s tie;
All else will then be seen as instability.
en.6: At the moment in which desire has been abandoned, (other) births will be cut off; when that has not been done, instability will be seen.

padaccheda.m: எல்லாப் பொருளையும் பற்றிநின்றே பற்றற்ற இறைவன் ஓதிய வீட்டு நெறியை இதுவே நன்னெறியென்று மனத்துட் கொள்க
கொண்டு, அதன்கண் உபாயத்தை அம்மனத்தாற் செய்க, விடாது வந்த பற்று விடுதற்கு

en.1: Hold to the attachment of the one who has no attachment. Hold to that attachment, so that you can let go of attachment.
en.2: God holds all things yet is free of attachment. Take the path to release that god taught as the good path, and hold it in your mind. Then with that mind practise its means, meditation and absorption, to let go of the attachment to the body that has come with you from no beginning.
en.4: Take thou refuge in Him who hath conquered all attachments: and hold fast to that ark in order that all thy bonds may be broken.
en.5:
Cling thou to that which He, to Whom nought clings, hath bid thee cling,
Cling to that bond, to get thee free from every clinging thing.
en.6: Desire the desire of him who is without desire; in order to renounce desire, desire that desire.

padaccheda.w: பொருள் அல்லவற்றைப் பொருள் என்று உணரும் மருளான் ஆம்
padaccheda.m: மெய்ப்பொருள் அல்லவற்றை மெய்ப்பொருள் என்று உணரும் விபரீத உணர்வானே உளதாம்
இன்பம் இல்லாத பிறப்பு

en.1: A wretched birth comes from the delusion that takes what isn’t real for what is.
en.2: A birth without joy comes from false understanding: trusting books that deny rebirth, the fruit of deeds and god as true books, or taking a post for a man or a shell for silver. All four kinds of birth, in hell, as beasts, as humans and as gods, are only suffering. Delusion is the first cause of birth.
en.4: From the delusion of taking vanities for the Reality a man cometh by a life of sorrow.
en.5:
Of things devoid of truth as real things men deem;—
Cause of degraded birth the fond delusive dream!
en.6: Inglorious births are produced by the confusion (of mind) which considers those things to be real which are not real.

padaccheda.m: அவிச்சையின் நீங்கி மெய்யுணர்வு உடையராயினார்க்கு
அம்மெய்யுணர்வு பிறப்பினை நீக்கி வீட்டினைக் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: For those who have left delusion behind and see without stain, darkness goes and joy comes.
en.2: For those free of delusion who have true knowledge, that knowledge removes birth and gives release. The darkness is hell, which stands for birth, its cause. Release is joy beyond compare, and seeing without stain means knowing the one absolute reality.
en.4: Behold the man who is freed from delusion and who hath an unclouded vision: darkness ceaseth for him and joy cometh unto him.
en.5:
Darkness departs, and rapture springs to men who see
The mystic vision pure, from all delusion free.
en.6: A clear, undimmed vision of things will deliver its possessors from the darkness of future births, and confer the felicity (of heaven).

padaccheda.m: ஐயத்தினின்று நீங்கி மெய்யுணர்ந்தார்க்கு
எய்திநின்ற நிலவுலகத்தினும் எய்தக்கடவதாகிய வீட்டுலகம் நணித்தாதல் உடைத்து

en.1: For those who have left doubt behind and see clearly, heaven is nearer than the earth.
en.2: For those free of doubt who know the truth, the world of release they are to reach is nearer than the earth they stand on. Doubt is wavering over whether rebirth, the fruit of deeds and god exist, like “mirage or water, rope or snake”. Those ripe in yoga clear it by experience, and their old worldly sense fades.
en.4: Behold the man who hath freed himself from uncertainties and who hath realised the Truth: heaven is nearer to him than the earth.
en.5:
When doubts disperse, and mists of error roll
Away, nearer is heav’n than earth to sage’s soul.
en.6: Heaven is nearer than earth to those men of purified minds who are freed from doubt.

padaccheda.m: செல்லப்படுகின்ற புலன்கள் வேறுபாட்டான் ஐந்தாகிய உணர்வு அவற்றை விட்டுத் தம் வயத்தாய வழியும், அதனாற் பயன் இல்லையேயாம்
மெய்யினையுணர்தல் இல்லாதார்க்கு

en.1: Even if you have mastered the awareness of the five senses, there is no gain in it without knowledge of the truth.
en.2: The fivefold awareness is the mind, five because of the senses it runs to. Even when it leaves them, comes under control and stays fixed in concentration, there is no gain for those who don’t know the truth, because it can’t give release. That fixed state is hard to reach, and still it isn’t enough.
en.4: Though risen to human birth, nought is gained if the soul realiseth not the Truth.
en.5:
Five-fold perception gained, what benefits accrue
To them whose spirits lack perception of the true?
en.6: Even those who have all the knowledge which can be attained-by the five senses, will derive no benefit from it, if they are without a knowledge of the true nature of things.

reading.note: ஐயுணர்வு can mean simply the five senses. He reads it as the mind held still in concentration.

padaccheda.m: யாதொரு பொருள் யாதோர் இயல்பிற்றாய்த் தோன்றினும்
அத்தோன்றியவாற்றைக் கண்டொழியாது, அப்பொருளின்கண்நின்று மெய்யாகிய பொருளைக் காண்பதே மெய்யுணர்வாவது

en.1: Whatever a thing may be, and however it may seem, understanding is seeing the reality in it.
en.2: Whatever a thing appears to be, true knowledge doesn’t stop there. It removes what the world imagines and sees the truth within. A ruler’s caste, family, looks and titles are all imagined. See him as a gathering of elements, from earth up to the soul, resolve each into its cause, and you reach what is left at the end. All things are known this way.
en.4: To separate the true from the false in everything, whatever its nature may be, that is the part of a wise understanding.
en.5:
Whatever thing, of whatsoever kind it be,
’Tis wisdom’s part in each the very thing to see.
en.6: (True) knowledge is the perception concerning every thing of whatever kind, that that thing is the true thing.

padaccheda.m: இம் மக்கட் பிறப்பின்கண்ணே உபதேசமொழிகளை அனுபவமுடைய தேசிகர்பாற் கேட்டு அதனான் மெய்ப்பொருளை உணர்ந்தவர்
மீண்டு இப்பிறப்பின்கண் வாராத நெறியை எய்துவர்

en.1: Those who learn here and see the truth will reach the path that doesn’t come back here.
en.2: Those who in this human birth hear the teaching from an experienced teacher and so know the truth reach the path of no return to this birth, the path to release. “Learn” means hearing many teachers many times, and “here” shows how hard a human birth is to get. There are three means of knowing the truth: hearing, reflection and meditation. This is the first.
en.4: Behold the man who hath studied deeply and hath realised the Truth: he shall enter the path that leadeth not again into this world.
en.5:
Who learn, and here the knowledge of the true obtain,
Shall find the path that hither cometh not again.
en.6: They, who in this birth have learned to know the true being, enter the road which returns not into this world.

padaccheda.m: அங்ஙனங் கேட்ட உபதேசமொழிப்பொருளை ஒருவன் உள்ளம் அளவைகளானும் பொருந்துமாற்றானும் தெளிய ஆராய்ந்து, அதனான் முதற்பொருளை உணருமாயின்
அவனுக்கு மாறிப் பிறப்புள்ளதாக நினைக்கவேண்டா

en.1: If your mind examines and surely knows what truly is, you need not think of being born again.
en.2: If your mind tests the teaching it has heard by the means of knowledge and by reason, examines it clearly and so knows the first reality, you need not think there is any birth for you again. This is the second means, reflection.
en.4: Verily those that have meditated upon and attained to the Truth need not think at all of future incarnations.
en.5:
The mind that knows with certitude what is, and ponders well,
Its thoughts on birth again to other life need not to dwell.
en.6: Let it not be thought that there is another birth for him whose mind having thoroughly considered (all it has been taught), has known the true being.

padaccheda.m: பிறப்பிற்கு முதற்காரணமாய அவிச்சைகெட
வீட்டிற்கு நிமித்தகாரணமாய செவ்விய பொருளைக் காண்பதே ஒருவர்க்கு மெய்யுணர்வாவது

en.1: To end the folly called birth and see the pure reality called excellence: that is understanding.
en.2: True knowledge is seeing the pure reality that leads to release, so that delusion, first cause of birth, is destroyed. Release is called excellence as the best of all things. This reality is eternal, pure and changeless. To see it is to meditate without a break until the soul is one with it, since at death the soul becomes what it dwells on. This is the third means.
en.4: It is the part of Wisdom to desire to escape the folly called birth, and to aim at realising the Supreme and the Good.
en.5:
When folly, cause of births, departs; and soul can view
The truth of things, man’s dignity—’tis wisdom true.
en.6: True knowledge consists in the removal of ignorance, which is (the cause of) births, and the perception of the true being who is (the bestower of) heaven.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் எல்லாப்பொருட்கும் சார்பாய அச்செம்பொருளை உணர்ந்து இருவகைப் பற்றும் அற ஒழுகவல்லனாயின்
அவனை முன் சாரக்கடவனவாய் நின்ற துன்பங்கள் அவ்வுணர்வொழுக்கங்களை அழித்துப் பின்சாரமாட்டா

en.1: If you know what to rest on and live so that attachment dies, the ills that would come to you are destroyed and won’t come.
en.2: If you know the pure reality that all things rest on and live so that both attachments end, the sufferings due to reach you can’t reach you. Living here means the eight limbs of yoga. Those sufferings are the stored fruit of deeds from endless births, and they vanish before wisdom and yoga like darkness before a lamp. Even the fruit of good deeds counts as ills.
en.4: Behold the man who understandeth the means of his salvation and laboureth to conquer all attachments: the ills that he is yet to suffer depart from him.
en.5:
The true ‘support’ who knows—rejects ‘supports’ he sought before—
Sorrow that clings and all destroys, shall cling to him no more.
en.6: He, who so lives as to know him who is the support of all things and abandon all desire, will be freed from the evils which would otherwise cleave to him and destroy (his efforts after absorption).

padaccheda.w: காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் இவை மூன்றன் நாமம் கெட
padaccheda.m: ஞானயோகங்களின் முதிர்ச்சியுடையார்க்கு விழைவு, வெறுப்பு, அவிச்சை என்னும் இக்குற்றங்கள் மூன்றனுடைய பெயருங்கூடக் கெடுதலான்
அவற்றின் காரியமாய வினைபபயன்கள் உளவாகா

en.1: When even the names of these three, desire, anger and delusion, are gone, pain is gone.
en.2: For those ripe in wisdom and yoga, even the names of these three faults, desire, hatred and delusion, perish, so the fruits of deeds no longer arise. Before unbroken wisdom and yoga they are like cotton before a forest fire. With the cause gone, no new deeds are done and no new suffering comes. Only this body and the deeds that brought it remain.
en.4: As desire and anger and delusion leave a man, his ills also follow their pace and slowly melt away.
en.5:
When lust and wrath and error’s triple tyranny is o’er,
Their very names for aye extinct, then pain shall be no more.
en.6: If the very names of these three things, desire, anger, and confusion of mind, be destroyed, then will also perish the evils (which flow from them).

padaccheda.w: எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் எஞ்ஞான்றும் தவாஅப் பிறப்பு ஈனும் வித்து
padaccheda.m: எல்லா உயிர்கட்கும் எக்காலத்தும் கெடாது வருகின்ற பிறப்பினை விளைவிக்கும் வித்து
அவா என்று சொல்லுவர் நூலோர்

en.1: They say craving is the seed that yields, for all living things at all times, birth that never ends.
en.2: The books call craving the seed that yields unending birth for all living things at all times. As the body is left, the next deed, the signs of the next state and craving for that state arise in turn. Delusion hides knowledge, and the craving carries the soul there. All religions agree on this.
en.4: Desire is the seed that yieldeth unto every soul, and always, a never-failing crop of births.
en.5:
The wise declare, through all the days, to every living thing
That ceaseless round of birth from seed of strong desire doth spring.
en.6: (The wise) say that the seed, which produces unceasing births, at all times, to all creatures, is desire.

padaccheda.m: பிறப்புத்துன்பமாதல் அறிந்தவன் ஒன்றை வேண்டிற் பிறவாமையை வேண்டும்
அப்பிறவாமைதான் ஒரு பொருளையும் அவாவாமையை வேண்ட அவனுக்குத் தானேயுண்டாம்

en.1: If you must want something, want not to be born. That comes from wanting to want nothing.
en.2: Knowing that birth is suffering, if you are to want anything, want not to be born. That comes of itself when you want to want nothing. Someone who has seen the endless pain of birth, illness, age and death wants only joy, and craving any small pleasure here is the seed of more birth and more pain.
en.4: If thou must needs long for anything, long for freedom from reincarnation: and that freedom shall come to thee if thou long to conquer longing.
en.5:
If desire you feel, freedom from changing birth require!
’Twill come, if you desire to ’scape, set free from all desire.
en.6: If any thing be desired, freedom from births should be desired; that (freedom from births) will be attained by desiring to be without desire.

padaccheda.w: வேண்டாமை அன்ன விழுச் செல்வம் ஈண்டு இல்லை
padaccheda.m: ஒரு பொருளையும் அவாவாமையை ஒக்கும் விழுமிய செல்வம் காணப்படுகின்ற இவ்வுலகின்கண் இல்லை
இனி அவ்வளவேயன்று, கேட்கப்படுகின்ற துறக்கத்தின்கண்ணும் அதனை ஒப்பதில்லை

en.1: There is no great wealth here to match wanting nothing. Even there, nothing equals it.
en.2: In this world that we see, no excellent wealth equals wanting nothing. And not only here: in heaven, which we only hear of, nothing equals it either. The wealth of humans and of gods each looks low beside something higher, but wanting nothing has nothing above it.
en.4: There is no greater wealth here below than desirelessness: and wherever thou goest thou canst find no treasure that equalleth it.
en.5:
No glorious wealth is here like freedom from desire;
To bliss like this not even there can soul aspire.
en.6: There is in this world no excellence equal to freedom from desire; and even in that world, there is nothing like it.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவர்க்கு வீடு என்று சொல்லப்படுவது அவாஇல்லாமை
அவ்வவாஇல்லாமைதான் மெய்ம்மையை வேண்டத் தானே உண்டாம்

en.1: Purity is having no craving. That comes from wanting truthfulness.
en.2: What is called release is having no craving, and that comes of itself when you seek the truth. Release is the soul’s freedom from delusion and other stains, so it is called purity. The truth here is the supreme reality, and seeking it means dwelling on it without a break. Cutting off craving is the direct cause of release.
en.4: Purity is nought but freedom from desire: and this freedom is achieved by yearning for perfect truthfulness.
en.5:
Desire’s decease as purity men know;
That, too, from yearning search for truth will grow.
en.6: Purity (of mind) consists in freedom from desire; and that (freedom from desire) is the fruit of the love of truth.

reading.note: The Tamil says purity and truthfulness. He takes purity to mean release, and truthfulness to mean the supreme reality.

padaccheda.m: பிறவி அற்றவர் என்று சொல்லப்படுவார் அதற்கு நேரே ஏதுவாகிய அவா அற்றவர்கள்
பிற ஏதுக்கள் அற்று அஃது ஒன்றும் அறாதவர்கள், அவற்றால் சில துன்பங்கள் அற்றதல்லது அவர்போல் பிறவியற்றிலர்

en.1: Those who are called free are the ones free of craving. The others are not free in the same way.
en.2: Those called free of birth are the ones free of craving, its direct cause. Others who have cut away other causes but not this one lose some sufferings by doing so, but they aren’t free of birth as these are.
en.4: It is those that have conquered their desire that are called the liberated ones: the others appear to be free but they are verily in bondage.
en.5:
Men freed from bonds of strong desire are free;
None other share such perfect liberty.
en.6: They are said to be free (from future birth) who are freed from desire; all others (who, whatever else they may be free from, are not freed from desire) are not thus free.

padaccheda.m: மெய்யுணர்தல் ஈறாகிய காரணங்கள் எல்லாம் எய்தி அவற்றான் வீடு எய்தற்பாலனாய ஒருவனை மறவிவழியாற் புகுந்து பின்னும் பிறப்பின்கண்ணே வீழ்த்துக் கெடுக்கவல்லது அவா
ஆகலான், அவ்வவாவை அஞ்சி்க் காப்பதே துறவறமாவது

en.1: Craving is what deceives you. To fear it is righteousness.
en.2: Someone may have gained every cause of release up to true knowledge, yet craving can slip in through a lapse, throw him back into birth and ruin him. So fearing craving and guarding against it is the righteousness of renunciation. Guarding means never stopping the practice of seeking the truth.
en.4: If thou love righteousness, flee from desire: for desire is a snare and a disappointment.
en.5:
Desire each soul beguiles;
True virtue dreads its wiles.
en.6: It is the chief duty of (an ascetic) to watch against desire with (jealous) fear; for it has power to deceive (and destroy) him.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் அவாவினை அஞ்சித் துவரக்கெடுக்க வல்லனாயின்

padaccheda.w: தவா வினை தான் வேண்டும் ஆற்றான் வரும்
padaccheda.m: அவனுக்குக் கெடாமைக்கு ஏதுவாகிய வினை தான் விரும்புநெறியானே உண்டாம்

en.1: If you cut off craving completely, deeds that never fail you will come the way you want them.
en.2: If you fear craving and can destroy it wholly, the deeds that keep you from ruin come in the way you wish, the way with no strain on the body. Those deeds are the righteous acts of renunciation. Someone who has fully cut off craving needs no other righteousness: all they do is righteousness.
en.4: If a man cutteth off utterly all his desires, salvation shall come to him by any path that he commandeth to it.
en.5:
Who throughly rids his life of passion-prompted deed,
Deeds of unfailing worth shall do, which, as he plans, succeed.
en.6: If a man thoroughly cut off all desire, the deeds, which confer immortality, will come to him, in the path in which he seeks them.

padaccheda.m: அவா இல்லாதார்க்கு வரக்கடவதொரு துன்பமுமில்லை
ஒருவற்குப் பிற காரணங்கள் எல்லாம் இன்றி அஃதுஒன்றும் உண்டாயின், அதனானே எல்லாத் துன்பங்களும் முடிவின்றி இடைவிடாமல் வரும்

en.1: Those without craving have no suffering. Where it exists, suffering comes on and on, without end.
en.2: Those without craving have no suffering to come. Someone with this one cause, even with no other, has all sufferings come endlessly, without a break. The suffering the body already carries was earned earlier, so “suffering” here means what craving earns now. Craving alone is the cause of suffering.
en.4: He that hath no desires hath no grief: but ills on ills descend on the man that hankereth after things.
en.5:
Affliction is not known where no desires abide;
Where these are, endless rises sorrow’s tide.
en.6: There is no sorrow to those who are without desire; but where that is, (sorrow) will incessantly come, more and more.

padaccheda.m: அவாவென்று சொல்லப்படுகின்ற மிக்க துன்பம் ஒருவற்குக் கெடுமாயின்
அவன் வீடுபெற்ற வழியேயன்றி உடம்போடு நின்றவழியும் இன்பம் இடையறாது

en.1: Destroy craving, the worst suffering of all, and joy goes on unbroken, even here.
en.2: If craving, the great suffering, is destroyed, joy doesn’t break off, not only after release but even in the body. It is the suffering that makes all others seem joys, painful even as it arises. With it gone, the mind stops wavering and stays full. Some read ஈண்டும் as “grows”, and he doesn’t follow them.
en.4: Even here a man shall have everlasting joy if he killeth that greatest misery of all, desire.
en.5:
When dies away desire, that woe of woes,
Ev’n here the soul unceasing rapture knows.
en.6: Even while in this body, joy will never depart (from the mind, in which) desire, that sorrow of sorrows, has been destroyed.

reading.note: ஈண்டும் can mean “even here” or “grows”. The plain reading follows him.

padaccheda.m: ஒருகாலும் நிரம்பாத இயல்பினை உடைய அவாவினை ஒருவன் நீக்குமாயின்
அந்நீப்பு அவனுக்கு அப்பொழுதே எஞ்ஞான்றும் ஒரு நிலையனாம் இயல்பைக் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: If you give up craving, whose nature is never to be filled, that very moment gives you a nature that never changes.
en.2: Craving is never filled: it grows on and on after useless things whose fruit doesn’t last. If you give it up, that act at once gives you a state that stays the same for ever. That state is release, free of elation and worry, of birth, illness, age and death, in joy beyond compare. Sanskrit writers call such a person liberated while living.
en.4: Desire is never filled: but if a man giveth it up he attaineth perfection even at that very moment.
en.5:
Drive from thy soul desire insatiate;
Straightway is gained the moveless blissful state.
en.6: The removal of desire, whose nature it is never to be satisfied, will immediately confer a nature that can never be changed.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவற்குக் கைப்பொருள் ஆதற்குக் காரணமாகிய ஊழான் முயற்சி உண்டாம்
அஃது அழிதற்குக் காரணம் ஆகிய ஊழான் மடி உண்டாம்

en.1: The fate that brings you wealth also brings the drive to work. The fate that takes it away brings laziness.
en.2: The fate that causes wealth to come produces effort, and the fate that causes it to go produces laziness. So fate creates even the effort and laziness that seem to win or lose wealth.
en.4: Resolution cometh to a man when Fortune is about to smile on him; but Indolence appeareth when Fortune is about to leave.
en.5:
Wealth-giving fate power of unflinching effort brings;
From fate that takes away idle remissness springs.
en.6: Perseverance comes from a prosperous fate, and idleness from an adverse fate.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு எல்லா அறிவும் உளவாயினும் கைப்பொருள் இழத்தற்கு ஏதுவாகிய ஊழ் வந்துற்றவிடத்து அஃது அதனைப் பேதையாக்கும்
இனி அவன் அறிவு சுருங்கியிருப்பினும் கைப்பொருளாதற்கு ஏதுவாகிய ஊழ் வந்துற்றவிடத்து அஃது அதனை விரிக்கும்

en.1: Fate that is taking things from you makes you foolish. Fate that is bringing you gain widens your mind.
en.2: However much you know, the fate of loss makes you a fool when it arrives. However little you know, the fate of gain widens your mind. Fate changes even natural intelligence.
en.4: Evil fate dulleth the faculties: but when Fortune is about to smile she first expandeth the intelligence.
en.5:
The fate that loss ordains makes wise men’s wisdom foolishness;
The fate that gain bestows with ampler powers will wisdom bless.
en.6: An adverse fate produces folly, and a prosperous fate produces enlarged knowledge.

padaccheda.m: பேதைப்படுக்கும் ஊழ்உடையான் ஒருவன் நுண்ணிய பொருள்களை உணர்த்தும் நூல் பலவற்றையும் கற்றானாயினும்
அவனுக்குப் பின்னும் தன் ஊழான் ஆகிய பேதைமை உணர்வே மேற்படும்

en.1: You may study many subtle books, yet the understanding you were born with still wins out.
en.2: Take someone fated to be foolish. Though they study many books on subtle matters, the foolish understanding their fate gave them still comes out on top. Fate overrides even learned intelligence.
en.4: What doth learning avail and all subtleties? It is the Spirit that is inside that prevaileth over all.
en.5:
In subtle learning manifold though versed man be,
The wisdom, truly his, will gain supremacy.
en.6: Although (a man) may study the most polished treatises, the knowledge which fate has decreed to him will still prevail.

reading.note: The words say only “your own true understanding”. He reads உண்மை as fate, one of the words he lists for it in his chapter introduction, and so finds fated foolishness here.

padaccheda.m: உலகத்து ஊழினாய இயற்கை இரண்டு கூறு
ஆதலாற் செல்வமுடையர் ஆதலும் வேறு, அறிவுடையர் ஆதலும் வேறு

en.1: The world runs two separate ways: being rich is one thing, being wise is another.
en.2: By fate the world is of two kinds, so being wealthy and being wise are separate. We see the wise stay poor and others grow rich, so the fate that makes you wise doesn’t make you rich.
en.4: There are two things in the world which have nothing in common: Riches is one thing and Saintliness is quite another.
en.5:
Two-fold the fashion of the world: some live in fortune’s light;
While other some have souls in wisdom’s radiance bright.
en.6: There are (through fate) two different natures in the world, hence the difference (observable in men) in (their acquisition of) wealth, and in their attainment of knowledge.

padaccheda.m: செல்வத்தை ஆக்குதற்கு
நல்லவை எல்லாம் தீயவாய் அழிக்கும்
அதுவே அன்றித் தீயவை தாமும் நல்லவாய் ஆக்கும், ஊழ்வயத்தான்

en.1: When making money, everything that should help can go wrong, and everything that should hurt can turn out well.
en.2: In making wealth, the good and bad things are time, place, means and action. By fate the favourable ones ruin you and the unfavourable ones build you up.
en.4: When the tide is against thee even good things turn to evil: and even evil things turn to good when the tide is on.
en.5:
All things that good appear will oft have ill success;
All evil things prove good for gain of happiness.
en.6: In the acquisition of property, every thing favourable becomes unfavourable, and (on the other hand) every thing unfavourable becomes favourable, (through the power of fate.)

padaccheda.m: தமக்கு ஊழ் அல்லாத பொருள்கள் வருந்திக் காப்பினும் தம்மிடத்து நில்லாவாம்
ஊழால் தமவாய பொருள்கள் புறத்தே கொண்டுபோய்ச் சொரிந்தாலும், தம்மை விட்டுப் போகா

en.1: What isn’t yours by fate won’t stay, however hard you guard it. What is yours won’t leave, even if you throw it out.
en.2: What fate hasn’t made yours won’t stay though you guard it painfully. What fate has made yours won’t leave though you carry it out and scatter it. Keeping and losing are fate’s work, not care’s or neglect’s.
en.4: What Destiny denieth thou canst not keep even with the utmost care: and even if thou scatter abroad, the things that are thine will not go away from thee.
en.5:
Things not your own will yield no good, howe’er you guard with pain;
Your own, howe’er you scatter them abroad, will yours remain.
en.6: Whatever is not conferred by fate cannot be preserved although it be guarded with most painful care; and that, which fate has made his, cannot be lost, although one should even take it and throw it away.

padaccheda.m: ஐம்பொறிகளான் நுகரப்படும் பொருள்கள் கோடியை முயன்று தொகுத்தார்க்கும்
தெய்வம் வகுத்த வகையான் அல்லது நுகர்தல் உண்டாகாது

en.1: Even someone who has piled up millions can enjoy only what fate has allotted.
en.2: Though you gather ten million things to enjoy, you can enjoy them only as the deity allotted. He is called the Allotter because the fruit of one being’s deeds goes to that being and no other. Effort can create wealth, but enjoying it takes fate.
en.4: Even the man who hath amassed ten million cannot enjoy his riches except as the Ordainer hath ordained.
en.5:
Save as the ‘sharer’ shares to each in due degree,
To those who millions store enjoyment scarce can be.
en.6: Even those who gather together millions will only enjoy them, as it has been determined by the disposer (of all things).

padaccheda.m: வறுமையான் நுகர்ச்சி இல்லாதார் துறக்கும் கருத்துடையர் ஆவர்
ஊழ்கள் உறுதற்பாலவாய துன்பங்களை உறுவியாது ஒழியுமாயின்

en.1: The poor would renounce the world, if only fate didn’t make them live out the suffering still due to them.
en.2: Those too poor to enjoy anything would think of renouncing, if fate let them skip the pain that is due. Poverty has already taken what renunciation would give up, yet they still suffer. That is the strength of fate.
en.4: Verily the destitute poor would turn their hearts towards renunciation but that Destiny reserveth them for the miseries that are their portion.
en.5:
The destitute might with ascetics merit share,
If fate to visit with predestined ills would spare.
en.6: The destitute will renounce desire (and become ascetics), if (fate) do not make them suffer the hindrances, to which they are liable, and they pass away.

padaccheda.m: நல்வினை விளையுங்கால் அதன் விளைவாய இன்பங்களைத் துடைக்கும் திறன் நாடாது இவை நல்லவென்று இயைந்து அனுபவிப்பார்
ஏனைத் தீவினை விளையுங்கால் அதன் விளைவாய துன்பங்களையும் அவ்வாறு அனுபவியாது துடைக்குந் திறன் நாடி அல்லல் உழப்பது என் கருதி?

en.1: If you welcome good times as good, why be distressed when the bad ones come?
en.2: When good deeds ripen, people enjoy the pleasures without trying to end them. When bad deeds ripen, why struggle to end the pains? You made both yourself and neither passes unlived, so accept both alike.
en.4: He that rejoiceth when good cometh, why should he fret when he receiveth evil?
en.5:
When good things come, men view them all as gain;
When evils come, why then should they complain?
en.6: How is it that those, who are pleased with good fortune, trouble themselves when evil comes, (since both are equally the decree of fate)?

padaccheda.m: தன்னை விலக்குதற் பொருட்டுத் தனக்கு மறுதலை ஆவதோர் உபாயத்தைச் சூழினும், தான் அவ்வுபாயமேயானும் பிறிதொன்றானும் வழியாக வந்து அச்சூழ்ச்சியின் முற்பட்டு நிற்கும்
அதனால் ஊழ்போல மிக்க வலியுடையன யாவை யுள?

en.1: What is stronger than fate? Even as you plan a way around it, it gets there first.
en.2: Think up a way to stop it, and fate arrives by that very way or by another, ahead of your plan. Nothing is as strong. It leaves no time even for planning, let alone acting.
en.4: What is there that is mightier than Destiny? For even as its victim is meditating a plan to overcome it, it forestalleth him and bringeth him down.
en.5:
What powers so great as those of Destiny? Man’s skill
Some other thing contrives; but fate’s beforehand still.
en.6: What is stronger than fate? If we think of an expedient (to avert it), it will itself be with us before (the thought).

padaccheda.w: படைகுடிகூழ் அமைச்சு நட்பு அரண் ஆறும் உடையான்
padaccheda.m: படையும், குடியும் கூழும் அமைச்சும் நட்பும் அரணும் என்று சொல்லப்பட்ட ஆறு அங்கங்களையும் உடையவன்
அரசருள் ஏறு போல்வான் என்றவாறு

en.1: An army, people, food, ministers, friends and forts: whoever has all six is a bull among rulers.
en.2: A ruler with all six limbs, the army, the land and its people, wealth, ministers, allies and forts, is like a bull among rulers. Without even one of them, rule doesn’t work, which is why Sanskrit writers call them limbs. Having them all is the cause of his victory.
en.4: He is a lion among princes who is well endowed in respect of the six things: troops, population, substance, council, alliances, and fortifications.
en.5:
An army, people, wealth, a minister, friends, fort: six things—
Who owns them all, a lion lives amid the kings.
en.6: He who possesses these six things, an army, a people, wealth, ministers, friends, and a fortress, is a lion among kings.

en.1: Fearlessness, giving, understanding and drive: a ruler’s nature is never to lack these four.
en.2: It is a ruler’s nature to have these four without a break: firmness, giving, understanding and drive. Drive is the mind rising to action. Understanding serves all six limbs, giving serves the army and the others serve action. Qualities recede as others show, but if these recede a ruler loses much, so they must always show.
en.4: Four qualities should never be wanting in the prince, namely, courage, liberality, wisdom, and energy.
en.5:
Courage, a liberal hand, wisdom, and energy: these four
Are qualities a king adorn for evermore.
en.6: Never to fail in these four things, fearlessness, liberality, wisdom, and energy, is the kingly character.

en.1: Wakefulness, learning and resolve: these three never leave those who rule the land.
en.2: For one with the fortune to rule the land, these three never leave: speed in the matters at hand, the learning to understand them, and manliness. Manliness means doing a thing quickly, looking at nothing else, so it is called resolve here. Learning serves all six limbs, and the others serve action.
en.4: Behold the men that are destined to rule the earth: the three virtues, alertness, learning, and decision, leave them not.
en.5:
A sleepless promptitude, knowledge, decision strong:
These three for aye to rulers of the land belong.
en.6: These three things, viz vigilance, learning, and bravery, should never be wanting in the ruler of a country.

reading.note: தூங்காமை is literally not sleeping. He reads it as not delaying.

padaccheda.m: தனக்கு ஓதிய அறத்தின் வழுவாது ஒழுகி
அறன் அல்லவை தன் நாட்டின் கண்ணும் நிகழாமல் கடிந்து
வீரத்தின் வழுவாத தாழ்வின்மையினை உடையான் அரசன் என்றவாறு

en.1: A ruler keeps to righteousness, removes what is wrong, and has an honour that never slips from valour.
en.2: A ruler keeps without fail to the righteousness laid down for him: studying, sacrificing and giving, and also bearing arms, protecting life and crushing enemies. He stops unrighteousness such as killing and theft in his land. His honour never falls short of valour: he won’t strike the young, the old or those who flee.
en.4: The prince shall not fail in virtue and shall abolish unrighteousness: he shall guard his honour jealously but shall not sin against the laws of valour.
en.5:
Kingship, in virtue failing not, all vice restrains,
In courage failing not, it honour’s grace maintains.
en.6: He is a king who, with manly modesty, swerves not from virtue, and refrains from vice.

padaccheda.m: தனக்குப் பொருள்கள் வரும் வழிகளை மேன்மேல் உளவாக்கலும்: ஈட்டலும் = அங்ஙனம் வந்தவற்றை ஒருவழித் தொகுத்தலும்
தொகுத்தவற்றைப் பிறர் கொள்ளாமல் காத்தலும்
காத்தவற்றை அறம் பொருள் இன்பங்களின் பொருட்டு விடுத்தலும்
வல்லவனே அரசன் என்றவாறு

en.1: A ruler is one who can create, gather and guard, and share out what is guarded.
en.2: He alone is a ruler who can open new ways for wealth to come, gather what comes, guard it from enemies, thieves, kin and officials, and spend it on righteousness, wealth and pleasure. Giving to gods, sages, the poor and renown serves righteousness. Elephants, army and forts serve wealth. Halls, pools and groves serve pleasure.
en.4: The prince shall know how to develop the resources of his kingdom and how to enrich his treasury: how to preserve his wealth and how to spend it worthily.
en.5:
A king is he who treasure gains, stores up, defends,
And duly for his kingdom’s weal expends.
en.6: He is a king who is able to acquire (wealth), to lay it up, to guard, and to distribute it.

reading.note: The Tamil doesn’t say what is created and gathered. He supplies wealth.

padaccheda.m: முறைவேண்டினார்க்கும் குறைவேண்டினார்க்கும் காண்டற்கு எளியனாய்
யாவர்மாட்டும் கடுஞ்சொல்லன் அல்லனுமாயின்
அம்மன்னனது நிலத்தை எல்லா நிலங்களினும் உயர்த்துக்கூறும் 'உலகம்' என்றவாறு

en.1: If a ruler is easy to see and not harsh in speech, his land will be praised above all others.
en.2: If a ruler is easy to see for those who seek justice and those who beg for help, and speaks harshly to no one, the world will rank his land above all lands, and so him too. Being easy to see means sitting in the great hall with sages and the worthy, in a good mood. They will call his land better than heaven, free of hunger, disease and enemies.
en.4: If the prince is accessible to all his subjects and is never harsh of word, his kingdom will be esteemed above every other.
en.5:
Where king is easy of access, where no harsh word repels,
That land’s high praises every subject swells.
en.6: The whole world will exalt the country of the king who is easy of access, and who is free from harsh language.

reading.note: He supplies “the world” as the one who praises. The Tamil can also mean that the land praises its ruler.

padaccheda.m: இனிய சொல்லுடனே ஈதலைச் செய்து அளிக்கவல்ல அரசனுக்கு
இவ்வுலகம் தன் புகழோடு மேவித் தான் கருதிய அளவிற்றாம் என்றவாறு

en.1: Whoever can give and protect with sweet words will find the world is just as their own word would have it.
en.2: For a ruler who can give with sweet words and protect, this world joins with his renown and is all he intends: it yields everything he wishes. Giving means giving people what they need, and protecting means keeping them from harm by his retinue and his enemies. These are hard, so it says “can”. He will rule the whole earth.
en.4: Behold the prince who can give with grace and rule with love: his name will fill the world.
en.5:
With pleasant speech, who gives and guards with powerful liberal hand,
He sees the world obedient all to his command.
en.6: The world will praise and submit itself to the mind of the king who is able to give with affability, and to protect all who come to him.

reading.note: சொல் can mean his word or, as he takes it, his renown.

padaccheda.m: தான் முறைசெய்து, பிறர் நலியாமல் காத்தலையும் செய்யும் அரசன்
பிறப்பான் மகனேயாயினும் செயலான் மக்கட்குக் கடவுள் என்று வேறு வைக்கப்படும் என்றவாறு

en.1: A ruler who does justice and protects will be held the lord of his people.
en.2: A ruler who does justice himself and protects the people from others is a man by birth, yet by his deeds he is set apart from men and raised up as their god. Justice is the way the books on righteousness and statecraft lay down.
en.4: Behold the prince who administereth impartial justice and protecteth his subjects: he shall be called a God among men.
en.5:
Who guards the realm and justice strict maintains,
That king as god o’er subject peoples reigns.
en.6: That king, will be esteemed a God among men, who performs his own duties, and protects (his subjects).

reading.note: இறை can mean lord or god. The plain reading says lord. He says god, set apart from men by his deeds.

padaccheda.w: சொல் செவி கைப்பப் பொறுக்கும் பண்பு உடை வேந்தன்
padaccheda.m: இடிக்கும் துணையாயினார் சொற்களைத் தன் செவி பொறாதாகவும், விளைவு நோக்கிப் பொறுக்கும் பண்புடைய அரசனது
குடை நிழற்கண்ணே தங்கும் உலகம் என்றவாறு

en.1: The world rests under the umbrella of a ruler with the character to bear words bitter to his ears.
en.2: The world rests in the shade of the umbrella of a ruler who can bear the words of those who rebuke him, though his ears can’t stand them, looking to what comes of them. Good character here means fine discernment. Since he doesn’t fail in righteousness and statecraft, he will rule the whole earth himself.
en.4: Behold the prince who hath the virtue to bear with words that are bitter to the ear: the world will rest permanently under his umbrella.
en.5:
The king of worth, who can words bitter to his ear endure,
Beneath the shadow of his power the world abides secure.
en.6: The whole world will dwell under the umbrella of the king, who can bear words that embitter the ear.

padaccheda.m: வேண்டுவார்க்கு வேண்டுவன கொடுத்தலும்
யாவர்க்கும் தலையளி செய்தலும்
முறை செய்தலும்
தளர்ந்த குடிகளைப் பேணலும் ஆகிய
இந்நான்கு செயலையும் உடையவன்
வேந்தர்க்கு எல்லாம் விளக்காம் என்றவாறு

en.1: Giving, kindness, a straight sceptre and care for the people: a ruler with these four is a light among rulers.
en.2: A ruler with these four is a lamp to all rulers: giving people what they need, showing everyone warmth with a bright face and sweet words, doing justice, and caring for people who have fallen on hard times. From such people he takes his sixth share only once their poverty has ended, and gives it up if he must.
en.4: Behold the prince who is liberal and gracious and just, and who tendeth his people with care: he is a light among kings.
en.5:
Gifts, grace, right sceptre, care of people’s weal:
These four a light of dreaded kings reveal.
en.6: He is the light of kings who has these four things, beneficence, benevolence, rectitude, and care for his people.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் கற்கப்படு நூல்களைப் பழுதறக் கற்க
அங்ஙனங் கற்றால்அக்கல்விக்குத்தக அவை சொல்லுகின்ற நெறிக்கண்ணே நிற்க

en.1: Learn what should be learned, and learn it without flaw. Once you have learned it, live up to it.
en.2: Learn what is worth learning without flaw, then stand on the path it teaches. Worth learning means what teaches righteousness, wealth, pleasure and release, since other subjects are no use to people of short lives, many ills and small minds. Flawless learning clears error and doubt through long study with good people.
en.4: Acquire thoroughly the knowledge that is worth acquiring and after acquiring it walk thou in accordance therewith.
en.5:
So learn that you may full and faultless learning gain,
Then in obedience meet to lessons learnt remain.
en.6: Let a man learn thoroughly whatever he may learn; and let his conduct be worthy of his learning.

padaccheda.w: எண் என்ப ஏனை எழுத்து என்ப இவ்விரண்டும்
padaccheda.m: அறியாதார் எண்ணென்று சொல்லுவனவும் மற்றை எழுத்து என்று சொல்லுவனுமாகிய கலைகள் இரண்டினையும்
அறிந்தார் சிறப்புடை உயிர்கட்குக் கண் என்று சொல்லுவர்

en.1: What they call numbers and what they call letters: these two, they say, are the eyes of those who live.
en.2: The ignorant speak of numbers and of letters. Those who know call these two arts the eyes of those lives distinguished by greater understanding. Letters take in words too. They are eyes because they are the tools for seeing righteousness and the other aims of life.
en.4: Two are the eyes of living kind: the one is called Numbers, and the other, Letters.
en.5:
The twain that lore of numbers and of letters give
Are eyes, the wise declare, to all on earth that live.
en.6: Letters and numbers are the two eyes of man.

padaccheda.m: கண்ணுடையர் என்று உயர்த்துச் சொல்லப்படுவார் கற்றவரே
மற்றைக் கல்லாதவர் முகத்தின்கண் இரண்டு புண்ணுடையர், கண்ணிலர்

en.1: Those said to have eyes are the learned. The unlearned have two sores on their faces.
en.2: Only the learned are praised as having eyes, because theirs is the eye of wisdom, which sees what is distant in place and time. The unlearned have two sores on their faces, for they have only eyes of flesh, which bring pain through disease and the like.
en.4: The learned alone can be said to possess eyes: the unlettered have but two sores in their head.
en.5:
Men who learning gain have eyes, men say;
Blockheads’ faces pairs of sores display.
en.6: The learned are said to have eyes, but the unlearned have (merely) two sores in their face.

padaccheda.m: யாவரையும் அவர் உவக்குமாறு தலைப்பெய்து, இனி அவரை யாம் எங்ஙனங் கூடுதும் என நினையுமாறு நீங்குதலாகிய அத்தன்மைத்து
கற்றறிந்தாரது தொழில்

en.1: To meet so that people are glad, and to part so that they long to meet again: that is the way of the learned.
en.2: The way of the learned is to meet everyone so that they rejoice, and to leave so that they wonder how they can meet again. Seeing their good conduct and hearing their sweet, helpful words, everyone comes to feel loving-kindness for them.
en.4: The scholar bringeth joy with him wherever he cometh: but when he departeth he leaveth regrets behind.
en.5:
You meet with joy, with pleasant thought you part;
Such is the learned scholar’s wondrous art!
en.6: It is the part of the learned to give joy to those whom they meet, and on leaving, to make them think (Oh! when shall we meet them again).

padaccheda.m: "பிற்றைநிலைமுனியாது கற்றல் நன்று" 2 ஆதலான், செல்வர்முன் நல்கூர்ந்தார் நிற்குமாறு போலத் தாமும் ஆசிரியர்முன் ஏக்கற்று நின்றும் கற்றார் தலையாயினார்
அந்நிலைக்கு நாணிக் கல்லாதவர் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இழிந்தாரேயாவர்

en.1: Some learn, though it means yearning like the poor before the rich. Those who don’t learn are the lowest.
en.2: Learning is good even at the cost of a humble stance. So those who learn, standing before their teachers as the poor stand before the rich, are the highest. Those too ashamed to do it are always the lowest. They lost true learning for a false sense of honour, and they never gain understanding.
en.4: Though thou hast to humble thyself before the teacher even as a beggar before a man of wealth thou yet acquirest learning: it is those that refuse to learn that are the lowest among men.
en.5:
With soul submiss they stand, as paupers front a rich man’s face;
Yet learned men are first; th’ unlearned stand in lowest place.
en.6: The unlearned are inferior to the learned, before whom they stand begging, as the destitute before the wealthy.

padaccheda.m: தோண்டிய அவ்வளவிற்கு சுரக்கும் (நீர்), மணற்கேணி மாந்தர்க்கு = மணல் கிணறு மக்களுக்கு, கற்ற அனைத்து ஊறும் அறிவு = (அதுபோன்றே) கல்வி கற்ற அவ்வளவிற்கு சுரக்கும் அறிவு அதாவது, "மணற்கேணி எவ்வளவுக்கெவ்வளவு தோண்டுகிறோமோ அவ்வளவிற்கு நீர் சுரப்பதுபோல, மக்கள் எவ்வளவுக்கெவ்வளவு கல்வி கற்க முயற்சி எடுக்கின்றனறோ அம்முயற்சிக்கேற்ப கல்வி அறிவும் சுரக்கும்" என்பதாக பெறப்படும்

en.1: A well in the sand gives water as far as you dig. People’s understanding flows as far as they learn.
en.2: A well in sand yields water in measure with the digging, and people’s understanding flows in measure with their learning. So don’t stop at a little: go on learning more. This holds where fate doesn’t oppose it, so it doesn’t clash with the earlier saying that inborn understanding wins out.
en.4: Knowledge is like unto a sand-spring: the more thou diggest and drawest thereat, the more excellent is the flow thereof.
en.5:
In sandy soil, when deep you delve, you reach the springs below;
The more you learn, the freer streams of wisdom flow.
en.6: Water will flow from a well in the sand in proportion to the depth to which it is dug, and knowledge will flow from a man in proportion to his learning.

padaccheda.m: கற்றவனுக்குத் தன்நாடும் தன் ஊருமேஅன்றி, யாதானும் ஒருநாடும் நாடாம், யாதானும் ஓர் ஊரும் ஊராம்
இங்ஙனமாயின் ஒருவன் தான் இறக்கும் அளவும், கல்லாது கழிகின்றது என்கருதி?

en.1: To the learned, every country is their country and every town their town. Why then does anyone go without learning until they die?
en.2: For a learned person, any land and any town is as good as their own. So why do people pass their days unlearned until they die? Other lands and towns take such a person in as their own, with gifts and honour, so nothing is better than learning. Do it always. It says “until death” because learning goes on with the soul.
en.4: Everywhere is his home to the learned man, and everywhere his native land: why then doth a man neglect instruction up to his dying day?
en.5:
The learned make each land their own, in every city find a home;
Who, till they die, learn nought, along what weary ways they roam!
en.6: How is it that any one can remain without learning, even to his death, when (to the learned man) every country is his own (country) and every town his own (town)?

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு
தான் ஒருபிறப்பின்கண் கற்ற கல்வி
எழுபிறப்பினும் சென்று உதவுதலை உடைத்து

en.1: What you learn in one birth shelters you for seven.
en.2: The learning gained in one birth goes on to help you through seven. Like deeds, it stays in the soul and enters wherever the soul enters. Helping means guiding you onto the good path.
en.4: The learning that a man hath acquired in one birth will exalt him; even in all his succeeding incarnations.
en.5:
The man who store of learning gains,
In one, through seven worlds, bliss attains.
en.6: The learning, which a man has acquired in one birth, will yield him pleasure during seven births.

padaccheda.m: தாம் இன்புறுவதற்கு ஏதுவாகிய கல்விக்கு உலகம் இன்புறுதலால் அச்சிறப்பு நோக்கி
கற்றறிந்தார் பின்னும் அதனையே விரும்புவர்

en.1: Seeing that the world delights in what delights them, the learned desire it all the more.
en.2: The learned delight in learning, and seeing that the world delights in it too, they desire it all the more. They delight in tasting words and meanings, in renown, wealth and honour, and in the righteousness and release to come. The world delights in learning from them. Wealth brings trouble and enemies, so they want this instead.
en.4: The learned man seeth that the learning that delighteth him delighteth also all that listen to him: and he loveth instruction all the more on that account.
en.5:
Their joy is joy of all the world, they see; thus more
The learners learn to love their cherished lore.
en.6: The learned will long (for more learning), when they see that while it gives pleasure to themselves, the world also derives pleasure from it.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு அழிவில்லாத சீரிய செல்வமாவது கல்வி
அஃது ஒழிந்த மணியும் பொன்னும் முதலாயின செல்வம் அல்ல

en.1: Learning is the great wealth that can’t be destroyed. All else is not wealth.
en.2: The excellent wealth that can’t perish is learning. All the rest, such as gems and gold, is not wealth. It can’t perish because heirs, thieves, the strong and rulers can’t take it, and giving it to those who serve you doesn’t lessen it. It is excellent because it stays with the worthy.
en.4: An imperishable and flawless treasure is learning to a man: other wealth is as nothing before it.
en.5:
Learning is excellence of wealth that none destroy;
To man nought else affords reality of joy.
en.6: Learning is the true imperishable riches; all other things are not riches.

en.1: Speaking in an assembly without having studied fully is like playing at counters with no board.
en.2: To speak in an assembly without having learned the books that would make you complete is like rolling counters without first marking out the board. Being complete means knowing all that needs knowing. Neither your words nor your meaning will follow any order.
en.4: Ascending the rostrum without abundant knowledge is like the playing of dice without the chequered board.
en.5:
Like those at draughts would play without the checquered square,
Men void of ample lore would counsels of the learned share.
en.6: To speak in an assembly (of the learned) without fullness of knowledge, is like playing at chess (on a board) without squares.

padaccheda.m: கல்வி இல்லாதான் ஒருவன் அவையின்கண் ஒன்று சொல்லுதலை அவாவுதல்
இயல்பாகவே முலையிரண்டும் இல்லாதாள் ஒருத்தி பெண்மையை அவாவினாற் போலும்

en.1: An unlearned man’s desire to speak is like a woman with no breasts at all desiring womanhood.
en.2: An unlearned man wanting to speak in an assembly is like a woman born with no breasts at all wanting womanhood. The want won’t reach its end, and if it does it will only bring laughter.
en.4: Behold the man without learning who desireth to be called eloquent: he is like unto a woman without busts who yearneth to be admired of men.
en.5:
Like those who doat on hoyden’s undeveloped charms are they,
Of learning void, who eagerly their power of words display.
en.6: The desire of the unlearned to speak (in an assembly), is like a woman without breasts desiring (the enjoyment of) woman-hood.

padaccheda.m: கல்லாதாரும் மிக நல்லர் ஆவர்
தாமே தம்மை அறிந்து, கற்றார் அவையின்கண் ஒன்றனையும் சொல்லாது இருத்தல் கூடுமாயின்

en.1: Even the unlearned are very good, if they can keep from speaking in front of the learned.
en.2: Even the unlearned are very good if they know themselves and can stay silent in an assembly of the learned. They don’t know themselves, so this is unlikely, which is why it says “if”. If they manage it they won’t expose themselves, and they may come to want learning.
en.4: Even a fool shall be counted wise if he can hold his peace before the learned.
en.5:
The blockheads, too, may men of worth appear,
If they can keep from speaking where the learned hear!
en.6: The unlearned also are very excellent men, if they know how to keep silence before the learned.

padaccheda.m: கல்லாதவனது ஒண்மை ஒரோவழி மிக நன்றாய் இருப்பினும்
அறிவுடையார் அதனை ஒண்மையாகக் கொள்ளார். ஒண்மை= அறிவுடைமை. அது நன்றாகாது, ஆயிற்றாயினும் ஏரல் எழுத்துப் 4 போல்வதோர் விழுக்காடாகலின், நிலைபெற்ற நூலறிவுடையார் அதனை மதியார் என்பதாம்

en.1: Even when an unlearned man’s cleverness is very good, the wise don’t accept it.
en.2: Even if an unlearned man’s intelligence happens at times to be very good, the wise don’t count it as intelligence. It can’t be good, and if it is, that is mere chance, like letters traced in sand by a snail. So those with settled knowledge of the books pay it no regard.
en.4: The opinion of an ignorant man will be rejected by the wise even though it may be perfectly sensible.
en.5:
From blockheads’ lips, when words of wisdom glibly flow,
The wise receive them not, though good they seem to show.
en.6: Although the natural knowledge of an unlearned man may be very good, the wise will not accept for true knowledge.

padaccheda.m: நூல்களைக் கல்லாத ஒருவன் யான் அறிவுடையேன் எனத் தன்னை மதிக்கும் மதி்ப்பு
அவற்றைக் கற்றவன் கண்டு உரையாடக் கெடும்

en.1: An unlearned man’s standing falls away when he comes face to face with others and speaks.
en.2: The self-regard of a man who hasn’t learned, who thinks himself wise, collapses when he meets a learned man and talks with him. It lasts only until he says something. Once he speaks he blunders, and it is gone.
en.4: Behold the ignorant man who is wise in his own eyes: he will be put to shame directly he openeth his lips in an assembly.
en.5:
As worthless shows the worth of man unlearned,
When council meets, by words he speaks discerned.
en.6: The self-conceit of an unlearned man will fade away, as soon as he speaks in an assembly (of the learned).

padaccheda.m: கல்லாதவர்
காணப்படுதலான் இலரல்லர் உளர் என்று சிலர் சொல்லும் அளவினர் ஆதலன்றி
தமக்கும் பிறர்க்கும் பயன்படாமையால் விளையாத களர்நிலத்தோடு ஒப்பர்

en.1: All you can say of the unlearned is that they exist. They are like salt land that yields nothing.
en.2: The unlearned can be seen, so some will say they exist, and no more. They are like salt land that grows nothing, of no use to themselves or to others. Such land is neglected and gives no creature food, and they are given no regard and give no one knowledge.
en.4: Like unto a wasteland that yieldeth no harvests is the man that hath neglected instruction: all that men can say about him is that he liveth, and nothing more.
en.5:
‘They are’: so much is true of men untaught;
But, like a barren field, they yield us nought!
en.6: The unlearned are like worthless barren land: all that can be said of them is, that they exist.

padaccheda.w: நுண் மாண் நுழை புலம் இல்லான் எழில் நலம்
padaccheda.m: நுண்ணிதாய் மாட்சிமைப்பட்டுப் பல நூல்களினும் சென்ற அறிவு இல்லாதவனுடைய எழுச்சியும் அழகும்
சுதையான் மாட்சிமைப்படப் புனைந்த பாவையுடைய எழுச்சியும் அழகும் போலும்

en.1: The fine looks of a man with no subtle, searching mind are like those of a well-made clay doll.
en.2: The bearing and beauty of a man without a fine, excellent mind that has entered many books are like those of a doll skilfully made of plaster. An excellent mind grasps things quickly and doesn’t forget. A handsome body is rare and is some benefit, but without learning it counts for nothing.
en.4: Behold the man whose understanding hath not been penetrated by the Grand and the Subtle: the comeliness of his person is no better than the beauty of an image of clay.
en.5:
Who lack the power of subtle, large, and penetrating sense,
Like puppet, decked with ornaments of clay, their beauty’s vain pretence.
en.6: The beauty and goodness of one who is destitute of knowledge gained by the study of great and exquisite works, is like (the beauty and goodness) of a painted earthen doll.

padaccheda.m: கற்றார்மாட்டு நின்ற வறுமையினும் இன்னாது
கல்லாதார்மாட்டு நின்ற செல்வம்

en.1: Wealth in the hands of the unlearned is worse than poverty falling on the good.
en.2: Wealth with the unlearned is worse even than poverty with the learned. Each is out of its proper place, and both bring trouble to those who have them and suffering to the world. But wealth ruins the unlearned, while poverty doesn’t ruin the good, so wealth is the worse.
en.4: Bitter verily is the poverty of the man of learning: but far worse is riches in the hands of the fool.
en.5:
To men unlearned, from fortune’s favour greater evil springs
Than poverty to men of goodly wisdom brings.
en.6: Wealth, gained by the unlearned, will give more sorrow than the poverty which may come upon the learned.

padaccheda.m: கல்லாதார் உயர்ந்த சாதிக்கண் பிறந்தாராயினும்
தாழ்ந்த சாதிக்கண் பிறந்துவைத்தும் கற்றாரது பெருமை அளவிற்றாய பெருமை இலர்

en.1: The unlearned, though born high, don’t have the standing of the learned, though born low.
en.2: The unlearned, though born into a high caste, lack the greatness of the learned, though those are born into a low one. The height of caste ends with the body, while the height of learning goes on with the soul, so it is greater. Caste pride is of no use to the unlearned.
en.4: The fool though born of a higher family is esteemed much less than a learned man who is of inferior descent.
en.5:
Lower are men unlearned, though noble be their race,
Than low-born men adorned with learning’s grace.
en.6: The unlearned, though born in a high caste, are not equal in dignity to the learned, though they may have been born in a low caste.

padaccheda.m: விலங்கோடு நோக்க மக்களை எத்துணை நன்மையுடையார் அத்துணைத் தீமையுடையர்

விளங்கிய நூலைக் கற்றாரோடு நோக்கக் கல்லாதவர். 'விலங்கு', 'நூல்' சாதிப்பெயர். விளங்குதல்=மேம்படுதல். விலங்கின் மக்கட்கு ஏற்றமாய உணர்வுமிகுதி காணப்படுவது கற்றார் கண்ணே யாகலின், கல்லாதாரும் அவரும் ஒத்த பிறப்பினர் அல்லர் என்பதாம். மயக்க நிரனிறை. இதனால் அவர் மக்கட்பிறப்பாற் பயன் எய்தாமை கூறப்பட்டது

en.1: As beasts are to humans, so others are to those who have learned bright books.
en.2: However much better humans are than beasts, that much worse are the unlearned than those who have learned shining books. The understanding that raises humans above beasts is seen only in the learned, so the two aren’t of the same birth. The unlearned gain nothing from being born human.
en.4: How much better are men than beasts? Even so much are the learned better than those that have not cared for instruction.
en.5:
Learning’s irradiating grace who gain,
Others excel, as men the bestial train.
en.6: As beasts by the side of men, so are other men by the side of those who are learned in celebrated works.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவற்குச் சிறப்புடைய செல்வமாவது செவியான் வருஞ் செல்வம்
அச்செல்வம் பிற செல்வங்கள் எல்லாவற்றினுந் தலையாகலான்

en.1: The wealth of wealth is the wealth of the ear. That wealth is first among all wealth.
en.2: The wealth that stands out is the wealth that comes through the ear, knowing all things by listening. It is first of all wealth because other wealth comes from possessions, doesn’t last and ends in suffering. The hint is to leave those and pursue this alone.
en.4: The most precious of treasures is the treasure of the ear: verily it is the crown of all kinds of wealth.
en.5:
Wealth of wealth is wealth acquired by ear attent;
Wealth mid all wealth supremely excellent.
en.6: Wealth (gained) by the ear is wealth of wealth; that wealth is the chief of all wealth.

padaccheda.m: செவிக்கு உணவாகிய கேள்வி இல்லாத பொழுது
வயிற்றுக்குஞ் சிறிது உணவு இடப்படும்

en.1: When there is no food for the ear, give the stomach a little too.
en.2: When there is no listening, the ear’s food, a little is given to the stomach as well. While there is listening, with its great taste and later benefit, food is scorned. A little, because much food means the labour of seeking it, and more illness and desire. Even that is only to stay alive and listen. “Give” shows how low the stomach is.
en.4: Even unto the stomach some food will be offered when there is no more food to be offered to the ear.
en.5:
When ’tis no longer time the listening ear to feed,
With trifling dole of food supply the body’s need.
en.6: When there is no food for the ear, give a little also to the stomach.

padaccheda.m: செவி உணவாகிய கேள்வியனை உடையார்
நிலத்தின்கண்ணராயினும் அவி உணவினை யுடைய தேவரோடு ஒப்பர்

en.1: Those who have listening, the food of the ear, are on this earth the equals of the gods who feed on offerings.
en.2: Those who have listening, the food taken in by the ear, are equal to the gods whose food is offerings, though they live on earth. The gods’ food is given through the sacrificial fire. They are full of understanding and know no suffering, so they are like gods.
en.4: Behold the men who have listened to much instruction: they are very Gods on earth.
en.5:
Who feed their ear with learned teachings rare,
Are like the happy gods oblations rich who share.
en.6: Those who in this world enjoy instruction which is the food of the ear, are equal to the Gods, who enjoy the food of the sacrifices.

padaccheda.m: உறுதி நூல்களைத் தான் கற்றிலன் ஆயினும், அவற்றின் பொருள்களைக் கற்றறிந்தார் சொல்லக் கேட்க
அக்கேள்வி ஒருவனுக்குத் தளர்ச்சி வந்துழிப் பற்றுக்கோடாந் துணையாகலான்

en.1: Even if you have no learning, listen. It will be a prop to lean on when you falter.
en.2: Even if you haven’t learned the books that do you good, listen as the learned explain them, because that becomes your support when you falter. Faltering is the mind giving way in trouble, from poverty or lack of understanding, and the knowledge gained by listening removes it. “Even if” means that you should learn as well.
en.4: Let a man hear instruction even though he hath no learning: for it will be a stay unto him when he is encompassed by difficulty.
en.5:
Though learning none hath he, yet let him hear alway;
In weakness this shall prove a staff and stay.
en.6: Although a man be without learning, let him listen (to the teaching of the learned); that will be to him a staff in adversity.

padaccheda.m: வழுக்குதலையுடைய சேற்றுநிலத்து இயங்குவார்க்கு ஊன்றுகோல் போல் உதவும்
காவற் சாகாடு உகைப்பார்க்கு ஒழுக்கமுடையார் வாயிற்சொற்கள்

en.1: The words of people of good conduct are like a staff on slippery ground.
en.2: To those who drive the cart of rule, words from the mouths of people of good conduct help as a staff helps those walking on slippery mud. A staff saves you when you slip. The learned without good conduct are ignorant, so they are not to be listened to. “Mouths” shows that these people know no evil words.
en.4: The counsel of the righteous is like unto a strong staff: for it keepeth those that listen to it from slipping.
en.5:
Like staff in hand of him in slippery ground who strays,
Are words from mouth of those who walk in righteous ways.
en.6: The words of the good are like a staff in a slippery place.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் சிறிதாயினும் உறுதிப்பொருள்களைக் கேட்க
அக்கேள்வி அத்துணையாயினும் நிறைந்த பெருமையை தரும் ஆகலான்

en.1: Listen to good things, however little. Even that little will bring you full greatness.
en.2: Listen to things that do you good, however little, because even that much brings full greatness. “However little” covers both how much you hear and for how long. Listening gathers like raindrops and gives rise to all knowledge, so don’t scorn it as small.
en.4: Listen to good words though they be but few: even those few will add to thee a proportionate dignity.
en.5:
Let each man good things learn, for e’en as he;
Shall learn, he gains increase of perfect dignity.
en.6: Let a man listen, never so little, to good (instruction), even that will bring him great dignity.

padaccheda.m: பிறழ உணர்ந்தவழியும் தமக்குப் பேதைமை பயக்கும் சொற்களைச் சொல்லார்
பொருள்களைத் தாமும் நுண்ணிதாக ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்து அதன்மேலும் ஈண்டிய கேள்வியினை யுடையார்

en.1: Even when they have misunderstood, those who have studied closely and gathered much listening don’t speak folly.
en.2: Even when they grasp something wrongly, they don’t say words that would show folly. These are people who examine things finely themselves and have also gathered listening from many sources. Having tested the truth against those who know, they won’t speak otherwise, even if dullness clouds them.
en.4: Behold the man that hath meditated much in himself and hath laid by a store of instruction by listening to the wise: he talketh not nonsense even when in error.
en.5:
Not e’en through inadvertence speak they foolish word,
With clear discerning mind who’ve learning’s ample lessons heard.
en.6: Not even when they have imperfectly understood (a matter), will those men speak foolishly, who have profoundly studied, and diligently listened (to instruction).

padaccheda.m: தம் புலமாய ஓசை மாத்திரத்தைக் கேட்குமாயினும் செவிடாம் தன்மையவேயாம்
கேள்வியால் துளைக்கப்படாத செவிகள்

en.1: Ears not pierced by listening are deaf, even though they hear.
en.2: Ears not bored through by listening may hear sound, which is their field, yet they are deaf. Mere sound brings no benefit. Listening opens the way for the meaning of the books to enter the mind. The old hole isn’t a hole at all.
en.4: Deaf indeed though it heareth is the ear that hath not been drilled by words of instruction.
en.5:
Where teaching hath not oped the learner’s ear,
The man may listen, but he scarce can hear.
en.6: The ear which has not been bored by instruction, although it hears, is deaf.

padaccheda.m: நுண்ணிதாகிய கேள்வியுடையர் அல்லாதார்
பணிந்த மொழியினை உடையராதல் கூடாது

en.1: Those without subtle listening can hardly have humble mouths.
en.2: Those without fine listening can’t have speech that bows, that is, speech that shows humility. Those who don’t listen lack understanding, so they praise themselves.
en.4: Humility of speech is hard to be attained by those who have not listened to the subtle words of the wise.
en.5:
’Tis hard for mouth to utter gentle, modest word,
When ears discourse of lore refined have never heard.
en.6: It is a rare thing to find modesty,—a reverend mouth—with those who have not received choice instruction.

padaccheda.w: செவியிற் சுவை உணரா வாய் உணர்வின் மாக்கள்
padaccheda.m: செவியான் நுகரப்படும் சுவைகளை உணராத வாயுணர்வினையுடைய மாந்தர்
சாவினும் வாழினும் உலகிற்கு வருவுது என்னை?

en.1: People who know the tastes of the mouth but not the tastes of the ear: what does it matter if they die or live?
en.2: People who know only the tastes of the mouth, and not those enjoyed by the ear: what does the world gain or lose if they die or live? The ear’s tastes are the savours of words and of meaning. The mouth’s are the six, such as bitter and sweet. Nothing is lost by their death or gained by their life, so the two are the same.
en.4: Behold the men that taste with the tongue but know not the taste of the ear: what doth it matter to the world whether they live or die?
en.5:
His mouth can taste, but ear no taste of joy can give!
What matter if he die, or prosperous live?
en.6: What does it matter whether those men live or die, who can judge of tastes by the mouth, and not by the ear?

padaccheda.m: அரசர்க்கு அறிவென்பது இறுதிவாராமற் காக்கும் கருவியாம்
அதுவேயுமன்றிப் பகைவர்க்கு அழிக்காலாகாத உள்அரணுமாம்

en.1: Understanding is a tool that guards against ruin, and a fort inside that even enemies can’t destroy.
en.2: For rulers, understanding is the tool that keeps ruin from coming: to guard is to see ahead and prevent it. More than that, it is an inner fort that enemies can’t destroy. It can also mean a fort they can’t enter and destroy.
en.4: The understanding is an armour against all surprise: it is a fortress which even enemies cannot storm.
en.5:
True wisdom wards off woes,
A circling fortress high;
Its inner strength man’s eager foes
Unshaken will defy.
en.6: Wisdom is a weapon to ward off destruction; it is an inner fortress which enemies cannot destroy.

padaccheda.m: மனத்தை அது சென்ற புலத்தின்கட் செல்லவிடாது

padaccheda.w: தீது ஒரீஇ நன்றின் பால் உய்ப்பது அறிவு
padaccheda.m: அப்புலத்தின் நன்மைதீமைகளை ஆராய்ந்து தீயதனின் நீக்கி நல்லதன்கட் செலுத்துவது அறிவு

en.1: Understanding doesn’t let the mind go wherever it goes. It turns it from evil and guides it to good.
en.2: Understanding doesn’t let the mind go to whichever sense it has gone to. It weighs the good and bad there, draws the mind off the bad and drives it to the good. There are five senses, but the mind goes to one at a time. As a groom knows the ground and steers a horse, understanding knows the sense and steers the mind.
en.4: It is the understanding that curbeth the senses from roving about, keepeth them from evil, and directeth them towards the Good.
en.5:
Wisdom restrains, nor suffers mind to wander where it would;
From every evil calls it back, and guides in way of good.
en.6: Not to permit the mind to go where it lists, to keep it from evil, and to employ it in good, this is wisdom.

reading.note: The Tamil doesn’t name what is steered. He supplies the mind, and the plain reading follows him.

padaccheda.m: யாதொரு பொருளை யாவர் யாவர் சொல்லக் கேட்பினும்
அப்பொருளின் மெய்யாய பயனைக் காணவல்லது அறிவு

en.1: Whatever you hear, from whoever’s mouth, understanding is seeing the reality in it.
en.2: Whatever is said, by whoever says it, understanding can see its true worth. All people shift between the three qualities, so high things may come from low mouths, low things from the high, good counsel from enemies and ruin from friends. So take or leave a thing by its worth, not by the nature of the speaker.
en.4: To separate the true from the false in every utterance, whoever it be that speaketh, that is the part of a wise understanding.
en.5:
Though things diverse from divers sages’ lips we learn,
’Tis wisdom’s part in each the true thing to discern.
en.6: To discern the truth in every thing, by whomsoever spoken, is wisdom.

padaccheda.m: தான் சொல்லும் சொற்களை அரிய பொருளவாயினும் கேட்பார்க்கு எளிய பொருளவாமாறு சொல்லி
பிறர் வாய்க் கேட்கும் சொற்களின் நுண்ணிய பொருள் காண அரிதாயினும், அதனைக் காண வல்லது அறிவு

en.1: Understanding is saying things so that they go home and are easy to grasp, and seeing the subtle meaning in what others say.
en.2: Understanding can say hard things so that they come easily to the listener, and can see the fine meaning in the words of others, however hard that is. Say what you say clearly and without fault. What you hear may be faulty and unclear, but take what is useful in it.
en.4: What he speaketh, the wise man speaketh so as to be understood by all: and from the lips of others he gathereth their subtle meanings.
en.5:
Wisdom hath use of lucid speech, words that acceptance win,
And subtle sense of other men’s discourse takes in.
en.6: To speak so as that the meaning may easily enter the mind of the hearer, and to discern the subtlest thought which may lie hidden in the words of others, this is wisdom.

padaccheda.m: உலகத்தை நட்பாக்குவது ஒருவனுக்கு ஒட்பமாம்
அந்நட்பின்கண் முன் மலர்தலும், பின் கூம்புதலும் இன்றி ஒருநிலையனாவது அறிவாம்

en.1: To embrace the world is cleverness. Not to bloom and then close is understanding.
en.2: Making the world your friend is brightness, and staying constant in that friendship, not blooming at first and closing later, is understanding. The world here means the great. Be their friend unchanging, like a flower on a tree and not one on a pond, and you gain every joy. Some read it as not blooming in wealth and not closing in poverty.
