en.4: The wise man is sociable with all the world: and his temper is ever even, expanding not nor contracting to excess.
en.5:
Wisdom embraces frank the world, to no caprice exposed;
Unlike the lotus flower, now opened wide, now petals strictly closed.
en.6: To secure the friendship of the great is true wisdom; it is (also) wisdom to keep (that friendship unchanged, and) not opening and closing (like the lotus-flower).

padaccheda.m: உலகம் யாதொருவாற்றான் ஒழுகுவதாயிற்று
அவ்வுலகத்தோடு மேவித் தானும் அவ்வாற்றான் ஒழுகுவது அரசனுக்கு அறிவு

en.1: However the world lives, understanding is living that way with the world.
en.2: Whichever way the world goes, it is a ruler’s understanding to go that way with it. A ruler who thinks “I rule the world and no one rules me” and acts as he pleases earns sin and blame, and that isn’t understanding.
en.4: It is a part of wisdom to conform to the ways of the world.
en.5:
As dwells the world, so with the world to dwell
In harmony—this is to wisely live and well.
en.6: ‘To live as the world lives, is wisdom.

padaccheda.m: அறிவுடையராவார் வரக்கடவதனை முன் அறியவல்லார்
அறிவிலராவார் அதனை முன்னறிய மாட்டாதார்

en.1: Those with understanding know what will be. Those without it can’t know that.
en.2: Those with understanding can know in advance what is to come, by thinking ahead. Those without it can’t know until it has arrived. Some read “what will be” as what is good for them.
en.4: The man of understanding knoweth what is coming: but the fool foreseeth not what is before.
en.5:
The wise discern, the foolish fail to see,
And minds prepare for things about to be.
en.6: The wise are these who know beforehand what will happen; those who do not know this are the unwise.

en.1: Not to fear what should be feared is folly. To fear what should be feared is the way of those who understand.
en.2: Not fearing what should be feared, such as sin, blame and ruin, is folly: acting without thought. Fearing it, thinking and holding back, is the work of those with understanding. Don’t scorn it as weakness. Fearlessness was praised in a ruler, and this shows where fear is needed.
en.4: It is folly to rush headlong into danger: it is the part of the wise to fear what ought to be feared.
en.5:
Folly meets fearful ills with fearless heart;
To fear where cause of fear exists is wisdom’s part.
en.6: Not to fear what ought to be feared, is folly; it is the work of the wise to fear what should be feared.

en.1: Those with the understanding to guard against what is to come have no suffering that comes and shakes them.
en.2: Those with the understanding to foresee what is coming and guard against it have no suffering that comes to make them tremble. Guarding means removing its cause.
en.4: Behold the man of foresight who is armed for every contingency: he will never know the blow that causeth trembling.
en.5:
The wise with watchful soul who coming ills foresee;
From coming evil’s dreaded shock are free.
en.6: No terrifying calamity will happen to the wise, who (foresee) and guard against coming evils.

en.1: Those with understanding have everything. Those without it, whatever they have, have nothing.
en.2: Those with understanding have everything, even if they have nothing else. Those without it have nothing, even if they have everything. All things are made and guarded by understanding. Without it you have no means to keep what you have, or to make it again when god brings ruin.
en.4: He that hath understanding hath everything: but the fool though he possess everything hath nothing.
en.5:
The wise is rich, with ev’ry blessing blest;
The fool is poor, of everything possessed.
en.6: Those who possess wisdom, possess every thing; those who have not wisdom, whatever they may possess, have nothing.

padaccheda.m: மதமும் வெகுளியும் காமமுமாகிய குற்றங்களில்லாத அரசரது செல்வம்
மேம்பாட்டு நீர்மையினை உடைத்து

en.1: Those without pride, anger or pettiness have a prosperity with greatness in it.
en.2: The wealth of rulers free of these three faults, drunkenness with wealth, anger and desire, has the nature of eminence. Desire beyond measure is called pettiness because it is the way of petty people. These faults lead to unjust acts, so the wealth of those who remove them goes the good way, lasts and is respected.
en.4: Behold the man who is free from haughtiness and anger and the vulgar passion: there is a dignity about him that adorneth his prosperity.
en.5:
Who arrogance, and wrath, and littleness of low desire restrain,
To sure increase of lofty dignity attain.
en.6: Truly great is the excellence of those (kings) who are free from pride, anger, and lust.

reading.note: சிறுமை is literally smallness. He reads it as desire beyond measure.

padaccheda.m: வேண்டும்வழிப் பொருள் கொடாமையும்
நன்மையின் நீங்கிய மானமும்
அளவிறந்த உவகையும்
அரசனுக்குக் குற்றம்

en.1: Miserliness, honour that has lost its nobility, and joy with no measure are faults in a ruler.
en.2: Not giving where you should, honour that has parted from what is good, and joy beyond measure are faults in a ruler. Such honour means not bowing to sages, the worthy, great ascetics, elders, father and mother, and forcing through what you set out to do even when it can’t be done. Joy beyond measure means excessive favour to others.
en.4: Parsimony, overconfidence, and excessive amour propre are faults in the prince.
en.5:
A niggard hand, o’erweening self-regard, and mirth
Unseemly, bring disgrace to men of kingly birth.
en.6: Avarice, undignified pride, and low pleasures, are faults in a king.

padaccheda.m: பழியை அஞ்சுவார்

padaccheda.w: தினைத்துணையாம் குற்றம் வரினும் பனைத் துணையாக் கொள்வர்
padaccheda.m: தங்கண் திணையளவாம் குற்றம் வந்ததாயினும் அதனை அவ்வளவாகவன்றிப் பனையின் அளவாகக் கொள்வர்

en.1: Those who fear blame treat even a fault the size of a millet seed as if it were as big as a palmyra tree.
en.2: If a fault the size of a millet seed arises in those who fear blame, they take it to be the size of a palmyra. It doesn’t suit them, so they won’t excuse it as small. They take it as great, grieve over it and guard against its coming again.
en.4: Behold the men who are jealous of their reputation: though their fault be small even like a millet seed, they look upon it as of the measure of a palmyra tree.
en.5:
Though small as millet-seed the fault men deem;
As palm-tree vast to those who fear disgrace ’twill seem.
en.6: Those who fear guilt, if they commit a fault small as a millet seed, will consider it to be as large as a palmyra tree.

padaccheda.m: தனக்கு இறுதி பயக்கும் பகை குற்றமே
ஆகலான், அக்குற்றம் தன்கண் வராமையே பயனாகக் கொண்டு காக்க வேண்டும்

en.1: Guard against fault as your one aim. Fault is the enemy that brings your end.
en.2: The enemy that brings your end is fault, so guard against it, making its absence your aim. As Sanskrit writers hold, enemies can bring no ruin except through these faults, so these are the real enemies. Having none of them is the same as having every good quality.
en.4: Guard thyself jealously against weaknesses: for they are the foes that will lead thee to ruin.
en.5:
Freedom from faults is wealth; watch heedfully
’Gainst these, for fault is fatal enmity.
en.6: Guard against faults as a matter (of great consequence; for) faults are a deadly enemy.

padaccheda.m: குற்றம் வரக் கடவதாகின்ற முற்காலத்திலே அதனைக் காவாத அரசன் வாழ்க்கை
அது வந்தால் எரி முகத்து நின்ற வைக்குவை போல அழிந்துவிடும்

en.1: Someone who doesn’t guard in advance will see their life perish, like a stack of straw before a fire.
en.2: A ruler who doesn’t guard against a fault in the time before it comes will see his life destroyed when it comes, like a stack of straw facing a fire. However small the fault, great wealth is wholly ruined by it, as the simile shows.
en.4: Behold the man who provideth not beforehand against surprise: he will be destroyed even like a stack of straw before a spark of fire.
en.5:
His joy who guards not ’gainst the coming evil day,
Like straw before the fire shall swift consume away.
en.6: The prosperity of him who does not timely guard against faults, will perish like, straw before fire.

padaccheda.w: தன் குற்றம் நீங்கிப் பிறர் குற்றம் காண்கிற் பின்
padaccheda.m: முன்னர்த் தன் குற்றத்தைக் கண்டு கடிந்து பின்னர்ப் பிறர் குற்றம் காணவல்லனாயின்
அரசனுக்கு ஆகக்கடவ குற்றம் யாது?

en.1: If a ruler removes his own faults first, and then looks at those of others, what fault can he have?
en.2: If a ruler first sees and removes his own faults and can then see the faults of others, what fault is left to him? Punishing others’ faults with his own uncorrected is itself a fault. With his own removed, it is justice. So only a ruler who has removed his own faults is fit to give justice.
en.4: If the prince correcteth his own faults and then looketh into those of others, where is the ill that can approach him?
en.5:
Faultless the king who first his own faults cures, and then
Permits himself to scan the faults of other men.
en.6: What fault will remain in the king who has put away his own evils, and looks after the evils of others.

padaccheda.m: பொருளால் தனக்குச் செய்துகொள்ளப்படுமவற்றைச் செய்துகொள்ளாது அதன்கட் பற்றுள்ளஞ் செய்தானது செல்வம்
பின் உளதாம் பான்மைத்தன்றி வறிதே கெடும்

en.1: The wealth of a miser who leaves undone what should be done won’t stay. It will perish.
en.2: The wealth of someone who clings to it and doesn’t do what should be done with it perishes for nothing, with no chance of staying. What should be done is righteousness, more wealth and pleasure. Without righteousness and growth it can’t stay, and without pleasure from it, it simply perishes.
en.4: Behold the miser that spendeth not where he ought to spend: his wealth will come to an inglorious wreck.
en.5:
Who leaves undone what should be done, with niggard mind,
His wealth shall perish, leaving not a wrack behind.
en.6: The wealth of the avaricious man, who does not expend it for the purposes for which he ought to expend it, will waste away and not continue.

padaccheda.m: பொருளைவிடத் தகுமிடத்து விடாது பற்றுதலைச் செய்யும் உள்ளமாகிய உலோபத்தினது தன்மை
குற்றத்தன்மைகள் எல்லாவற்றுள்ளும் வைத்து எண்ணப்படுவது ஒன்றன்று, மிக்கது

en.1: The miserliness called a clinging heart is not to be counted with anything else.
en.2: The clinging heart that won’t let wealth go where it should is not to be counted among other faults. It is worse than them all. Its nature is that, even where every good quality is present, it can push them down and rise above them. Other faults can’t do that.
en.4: Closefisted parsimony is not a vice to be classed with other vices: it formeth a class apart.
en.5:
The greed of soul that avarice men call,
When faults are summed, is worst of all.
en.6: Griping avarice is not to be reckoned as one among other faults; (it stands alone—greater than all.)

padaccheda.m: தான் இறப்ப உயர்ந்த ஞான்றும் மதத்தால் தன்னை நன்கு மதியாது ஒழிக
தனக்கு நன்மை பயவா வினைகளை மானத்தால் விரும்பாது ஒழிக

en.1: Never admire yourself. Don’t set your heart on deeds that bring no good.
en.2: Even when you rise very high, don’t in your arrogance think highly of yourself, and don’t out of pride want deeds that bring you no good. Self-admiration keeps you from seeing place, time and strength, and makes you scorn righteousness and wealth. Deeds pursued only to finish what you set out to do bring sin, blame and ruin.
en.4: Exult not at anything at any time: embark not on enterprises that would bring thee no good.
en.5:
Never indulge in self-complaisant mood,
Nor deed desire that yields no gain of good.
en.6: Let no (one) praise himself, at any time; and let him not desire to do useless things.

padaccheda.m: தான காதலித்த பொருள்களை அவர் அக்காதலறியாமல் அனுபவிக்கவல்லனாயின்
பகைவர் தன்னை வஞ்சித்தற்கு எண்ணும் எண்ணம் பழுதாம்

en.1: If you can enjoy what you love without letting your love be known, the schemes of your enemies are useless.
en.2: If you can enjoy the things you love without enemies knowing of your love, their plans to deceive you come to nothing. If they know, they enter by that door and deceive you. Desire, anger and joy aren’t to be wiped out entirely, so this shows how to enjoy desire, the chief of them. The others fall under the general ban.
en.4: If thou canst keep from the knowledge of others the things in which thy heart taketh delight, the machinations of thy foes will be in vain.
en.5:
If, to your foes unknown, you cherish what you love,
Counsels of men who wish you harm will harmless prove.
en.6: If (a king) enjoys privately the things which he desires, the designs of his enemies will be useless.

padaccheda.m: அறத்தினது நுண்மையை அறிந்து தன்னின் மூத்த அறிவுடையாரது கேண்மையை
அரசன் அதனது அருமையை ஓர்ந்து, கொள்ளும் திறமறிந்து கொள்க

en.1: Learn how it is done, then choose with care the friendship of the wise, who know righteousness and have grown old in it.
en.2: A ruler should weigh how rare it is, then find the right way to win the friendship of wise men older than himself, who know the fine points of righteousness. Older means mature in knowledge, conduct and years. The wise know sound policy and the ways of the world. The way to win them is to esteem them, raise them up and defer to them.
en.4: Esteem thou the men that have grown old in righteousness, and acquire their friendship.
en.5:
As friends the men who virtue know, and riper wisdom share,
Their worth weighed well, the king should choose with care.
en.6: Let (a king) ponder well its value, and secure the friendship of men of virtue and of mature knowledge.

padaccheda.m: தெய்வத்தானாக, மக்களானாகத் தனக்கு வந்த துன்பங்களை நீக்குமாறு அறிந்து நீக்கி
பின் அப்பெற்றியன வாராவண்ணம் முன்னறிந்து காக்கவல்ல தன்மையினை உடையாரை
அரசன் அவர் உவப்பன செய்து துணையாகக் கொள்க

en.1: Cherish and keep close those who can end the suffering that has come and guard against it before it comes.
en.2: A ruler should please those who can remove his troubles and foresee new ones, and take them as helpers. Troubles from the gods, such as drought, flood, wind, fire and disease, are met with rites and foreseen through omens. Troubles from people, such as enemies, thieves, kin and officers, are met with the four means of statecraft. So he means priests and ministers.
en.4: Behold the men who can cure the evils that have already befallen thee and who can guard thee from future ones: cultivate thou their friendship with ardour.
en.5:
Cherish the all-accomplished men as friends,
Whose skill the present ill removes, from coming ill defends.
en.6: Let (a king) procure and kindly care for men who can overcome difficulties when they occur, and guard against them before they happen.

padaccheda.m: அப்பெரியவர்களை அவர் உவப்பன அறிந்து செய்து தமக்குச் சிறந்தாராகக் கொள்ளுதல்
அரசர்க்கு அரிய பேறுகள் எல்லாவற்றுள்ளும் அரிது

en.1: Of all rare things the rarest is to cherish the great and make them your own.
en.2: To learn what pleases the great, do it, and so make them dear to you is, for rulers, the rarest of all rare gains. Rulers can obtain everything rare in the world, and this one stands highest because through it all the others come.
en.4: It is the rarest of rare good fortunes if a man can secure to himself the devotion of men of worth.
en.5:
To cherish men of mighty soul, and make them all their own,
Of kingly treasures rare, as rarest gift is known.
en.6: To cherish great men and make them his own, is the most difficult of all difficult things.

padaccheda.m: அறிவு முதலியவற்றால் தம்மின் மிக்கார் தமக்குச் சிறந்தாராகத் தாம் அவர்வழி நின்று ஒழுகுதல்
அரசர்க்கு எல்லா வலியுடைமையினும் தலை

en.1: Conducting yourself so that those greater than you become your own people is the highest of all strengths.
en.2: For rulers, the highest of all strengths is to follow the lead of those who surpass them in wisdom and other things, so that these become dear to them. This strength of helpers is better than wealth, armies and forts, because such men can also remove troubles sent by the gods, which those can’t.
en.4: If those that are worthier than thyself have become thy intimates, thou hast acquired a strength before which all other strength paleth.
en.5:
To live with men of greatness that their own excels,
As cherished friends, is greatest power that with a monarch dwells.
en.6: So to act as to make those men, his own, who are greater than himself, is of all powers the highest.

padaccheda.m: தன்பாரம் அமைச்சரைக் கண்ணாகக் கொண்டு நடத்தலான்
அரசன் அத்தன்மையராய அமைச்சரை ஆராய்ந்து தனக்குத் துணையாகக் கொள்க

en.1: A ruler goes forward with his advisers as his eyes, so he should choose them with care.
en.2: A ruler carries his burden with his ministers as his eyes, so he should examine such ministers and take them as helpers. Even one who can plan alone is overwhelmed by countless tasks, and his burden goes well only through ministers whose whole work it is. Examining means testing them against the marks of a minister set out later.
en.4: As the eyes of the prince are his own ministers, let him use his discretion and choose them wisely.
en.5:
The king, since counsellors are monarch’s eyes,
Should counsellors select with counsel wise.
en.6: As a king must use his ministers as eyes (in managing his kingdom), let him well examine their character and qualifications before he engages them.

padaccheda.m: தக்காராகிய இனத்தை உடையனாய்த் தானும் அறிந்தொழுக வல்ல அரசனை
பகைவர் செய்யக்கிடந்ததொரு துன்பமும் இல்லை

en.1: If you keep worthy company and can conduct yourself well, there is nothing your enemies can do to you.
en.2: Enemies can do no harm to a ruler who has worthy people around him and knows how to conduct himself. The worthy are those fit in wisdom and conduct. Conducting himself means not straying from righteousness and sound policy. Enemies work by deceit, by splitting allies, by stirring up new foes and by force, but none of this reaches one who knows and heeds those who know.
en.4: Behold the man who can move with the worthy as their intimate: his foes will be powerless against him.
en.5:
The king, who knows to live with worthy men allied,
Has nought to fear from any foeman’s pride.
en.6: There will be nothing left for enemies to do, against him who has the power of acting (so as to secure) the fellowship of worthy men.

padaccheda.m: தீயன கண்டால் நெருங்கிச் சொல்லும் துணையாம் தன்மையை உடையாரை இவர் நமக்குச் சிறந்தார் என்று ஆளும் அரசரை
கெடுக்கும் பெருமையுடைய பகைவர் உலகத்து யாவர்?

en.1: If you keep companions who will rebuke you, who has the power to ruin you?
en.2: What enemy in the world has the greatness to ruin rulers who value and keep helpers who come close and speak up when they see wrong? Wrong means sin and what goes against sound policy. Such helpers are free of these faults and have loving-kindness towards the ruler. They never let him stray, so no one can ruin him.
en.4: Who can ruin the man that commandeth the friendship of those that can reprove him?
en.5:
What power can work his fall, who faithful ministers
Employs, that thunder out reproaches when he errs.
en.6: Who are great enough to destroy him who has servants that have power to rebuke him?

padaccheda.m: கழறுதற்கு உரியாரைத் தனக்குத் துணையாகக் கொள்ளாமையின் காவலற்ற அரசன்
பகையாய்க் கெடுப்பார் இல்லையாயினும் தானே கெடும்

en.1: A ruler with no one to rebuke him has no protection, and will fall even with no one to bring him down.
en.2: A ruler who doesn’t take as helpers those fit to reprove him has no protection. Even if no enemy works to ruin him, he ruins himself, like an elephant without a driver that leaves the path. “Even with no one” hints that such people will appear.
en.4: Behold the prince who reposeth not on the support of men who can rebuke him: he will perish even when he hath no foes.
en.5:
The king with none to censure him, bereft of safeguards all,
Though none his ruin work, shall surely ruined fall.
en.6: The king, who is without the guard of men who can rebuke him, will perish, even though there be no one to destroy him.

padaccheda.m: முதற்பொருள் இல்லாத வணிகர்க்கு அதனால் வரும் ஊதியம் இல்லையாம்
அதுபோலத் தம்மைத் தாங்குவதாந் துணை இல்லாத அரசர்க்கு அதனான் வரும் நிலையில்லை

en.1: Without capital there is no profit. Without a prop to lean on there is no standing firm.
en.2: Merchants without capital have no profit from it. In the same way, rulers without helpers to bear them up have no stability. As you must have capital before you can profit, you must have people to hold you up before you can stand. Standing means bearing a ruler’s burden without faltering.
en.4: Profit is not for those that have no capital: even so stability is not for them that repose not on the firm support of the wise.
en.5:
Who owns no principal, can have no gain of usury;
Who lacks support of friends, knows no stability.
en.6: There can be no gain to those who have no capital; and in like manner there can be no permanence to those who are without the support of adherents.

padaccheda.w: பல்லார் பகை கொளலின் பத்து அடுத்த தீமைத்தே
padaccheda.m: தான் தனியனாய்வைத்துப் பலரோடும் பகை கொள்ளுதலிற் பதிற்றுமடங்கு தீமை உடைத்து
அரசன் பெரியாரோடு நட்பினைக் கொள்ளாது ஒழிதல்

en.1: Letting go of your bond with good people is ten times worse than making enemies of many.
en.2: For a ruler to fail to keep friendship with the great is ten times worse than standing alone and making enemies of many. Even with many enemies, he can get away by one means or another, setting them against each other or splitting them. Once he has let go of the good, there is no way out, so this is worse.
en.4: It is foolish to make a multitude of foes: but it is ten times worse to give up the intimacy of the good.
en.5:
Than hate of many foes incurred, works greater woe
Ten-fold, of worthy men the friendship to forego.
en.6: It is tenfold more injurious to abandon the friendship of the good, than to incur the hatred of the many.

padaccheda.m: பெரியோர் இயல்பு சிறிய இனத்தை அஞ்சாநிற்கும்
ஏனைச் சிறியோர் இயல்பு அது சேர்ந்தபொழுது அதனைத் தனக்குச் சுற்றமாக எண்ணித் துணியும்

en.1: Greatness fears petty company. Pettiness treats it as kin.
en.2: The nature of the great is to fear petty company. The nature of the petty is to settle on it as their kin the moment they join it. The wise fear it because they see how it would twist their understanding and the suffering that would follow. The unwise, being of one mind with it, look no further.
en.4: Men of worth fear vulgar company: but little-minded men mix with it as if they made one family with it.
en.5:
The great of soul will mean association fear;
The mean of soul regard mean men as kinsmen dear.
en.6: (True) greatness fears the society of the base; it is only the low-minded who will regard them as friends.

padaccheda.m: தான் சேர்ந்த நிலத்தினது இயல்பானே நீர் தன் தன்மை திரிந்து அந்நிலத்தின் தன்மைத்தாம்
அதுபோல மாந்தர்க்குத் தாம் சேர்ந்த இனத்தினது இயல்பானே அறிவும் தன் தன்மைதிரிந்து அவ்வினத்தின் தன்மைத்தாம்

en.1: Water changes and takes on the nature of the ground it meets. People’s understanding takes on the nature of their company.
en.2: Water loses its own nature and takes on that of the ground it joins. In the same way, people’s understanding changes and takes on the nature of the group they join. In the sky water is itself, and on earth its colour and taste change. Alone, understanding is itself, and in a group its way of seeing changes.
en.4: Water altereth and taketh the character of the soil through which it floweth: even so the mind taketh the colour of the company with which it consorteth.
en.5:
The waters’ virtues change with soil through which they flow;
As man’s companionship so will his wisdom show.
en.6: As water changes (its nature) from the nature of the soil (in which it flows), so will the character of men resemble that of their associates.

padaccheda.m: மாந்தர்க்குப் பொதுஉணர்வு தம் மனம் காரணமாக உண்டாம்
இவன் இத்தன்மையன் என்று உலகத்தாரால் சொல்லப்படும் சொல், இனம் காரணமாக உண்டாம்

en.1: What a person perceives comes from their mind. What people call them comes from their company.
en.2: Ordinary awareness comes from the mind. The word by which the world says “he is this sort of man” comes from his company. Bare sense perception is natural and needs no group. Being called good or bad rests on a finer, acquired understanding, and that needs one. This answers those who won’t accept the water comparison and say that change also comes from the mind.
en.4: The understanding of a man belongeth unto his mind: but his reputation dependeth on the company he keepeth.
en.5:
Perceptions manifold in men are of the mind alone;
The value of the man by his companionship is known.
en.6: The power of knowing is from the mind; (but) his character is from that of his associates.

padaccheda.m: அவ்விசேட உணர்வு
ஒருவற்கு மனத்தி்ன்கண்ணே உளதாவது போலத் தன்னைப் புலப்படுத்தி
அவன் சேர்ந்த இனத்தின்கண்ணே உளதாம்

en.1: A person’s understanding seems to be in their mind, but it lies in their company.
en.2: This finer understanding shows itself as if it were in a person’s mind, but it lies in the group they have joined. Before you look closely it seems to be in the mind. When you look, it is in the company they have kept. It only appears in the mind, and its root is the group.
en.4: The disposition of a man seemeth to reside in his mind: but its veritable abode is the company in which he moveth.
en.5:
Man’s wisdom seems the offspring of his mind;
’Tis outcome of companionship we find.
en.6: Wisdom appears to rest in the mind, but it really exists to a man in his companions.

padaccheda.m: அவ்விசேட உணர்வு புலப்படுதற்கு இடனாய மனம் தூயனாதல்தன்மையும் செய்யும் வினை தூயனாதல் தன்மையுமாகிய இரண்டும்
ஒருவற்கு இனம் தூயனாதல்தன்மை பற்றுக்கோடாக உளவாம்

en.1: A pure mind and pure deeds both depend on pure company.
en.2: Purity of mind, where finer understanding shows itself, and purity of deeds both come with pure company as their support. A pure mind is one freed from its natural ignorance. Pure deeds are good acts of speech and body. When your group is pure, long contact with it purifies your mind, understanding appears there, and your words and acts become pure.
en.4: Purity of heart and purity of action depend upon the purity of a man’s company.
en.5:
Both purity of mind, and purity of action clear,
Leaning on staff of pure companionship, to man draw near.
en.6: Chaste company is the staff on which come, these two things, viz. purity of mind and purity of conduct.

padaccheda.m: மனம் தூயராயினார்க்கு மக்கட்பேறு நன்றாகும்

padaccheda.w: இனம் தூயார்க்கு நன்று ஆகா வினை இல்லை
padaccheda.m: இனம் தூயர் ஆயினார்க்கு நன்றாகாத வினை யாதொன்றும் இல்லை

en.1: What the pure of mind leave behind is good. For those in pure company, no deed fails to turn out well.
en.2: Those pure of mind are blessed with good children, because an effect doesn’t differ from its cause. For those whose company is pure, no undertaking fails to turn out well, because they think it through with good people before they act.
en.4: The pure of heart shall have a righteous progeny: and everything prospereth unto those that consort with good company.
en.5:
From true pure-minded men a virtuous race proceeds;
To men of pure companionship belong no evil deeds.
en.6: To the pure-minded there will be a good posterity. By those whose associates are pure, no deeds will be done that are not good.

reading.note: எச்சம் is what remains after you. He takes it as children.

padaccheda.m: நிலைபெற்ற உயிர்கட்கு மனத்தது நன்மை செல்வத்தைக் கொடுக்கும்
இனத்தது நன்மை அதனோடு எல்லாப் புகழையும் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: A good mind brings living beings prosperity. Good company brings every kind of glory.
en.2: Goodness of mind gives people wealth, and goodness of company gives all renown along with it. Living beings here means humans. A good mind is itself righteousness, so it brings wealth, and only good people can bestow renown. This answers those who say people born with a good mind don’t need good company: it gives much besides, so they need it too.
en.4: Purity of heart is a treasure unto a man: and virtuous company bringeth him every glory.
en.5:
Goodness of mind to lives of men increaseth gain;
And good companionship doth all of praise obtain.
en.6: Goodness of mind will give wealth, and good society will bring with it all praise, to men.

padaccheda.m: மனநன்மையை முன்னை நல்வினையால் தாமே உடையராயினும்
அமைந்தார்க்கு இனநன்மை அதற்கு வலிமையாதலை உடைத்து

en.1: Even the noble, though their minds are thoroughly good, find protection in good company.
en.2: Even when the noble have goodness of mind of their own through good deeds done before, good company gives it strength. Those past deeds may be there, yet good company goes on making the mind’s goodness grow.
en.4: Though themselves are endowed with every virtue, the wise looks upon the company of the pure as a tower of strength.
en.5:
To perfect men, though minds right good belong,
Yet good companionship is confirmation strong.
en.6: Although they may have great (natural) goodness of mind, yet good society will tend to strengthen it.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவற்கு மனநன்மையானே மறுமை இன்பம் உண்டாம்

padaccheda.w: மற்று அஃதும் இன நலத்தின் ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து
padaccheda.m: அதற்கு அச் சிறப்புத்தானும் இனநன்மையான் வலி பெறுதலை உடைத்து

en.1: The next world comes from a good mind, and even that finds its protection in good company.
en.2: Joy in the next world comes from goodness of mind. He grants the view that nothing else yields it. Even so, it draws strength from good company. If the mind slips now and then through the quality of dullness, good company steadies it and still brings the next world’s joy. So keeping away from petty company is praised here through seeking good company.
en.4: Virtue leadeth unto heaven: and the company of the good steadieth a man in the practice thereof.
en.5:
Although to mental goodness joys of other life belong,
Yet good companionship is confirmation strong.
en.6: Future bliss is (the result) of goodness of mind; and even this acquires strength from the society of the good.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவற்கு நல்லினத்தின் மிக்க துணையும் இல்லை
தீய இனத்தின் மிக்க பகையும் இல்லை

en.1: There is no help greater than good company, and nothing causes more grief than bad company.
en.2: No helper is greater than good company, and no enemy is greater than bad company. Good company draws you out of ignorance and keeps you from suffering, so it is a helper. Bad company draws you away from understanding and brings you suffering, so it is an enemy.
en.4: There is no greater ally to a man than good company: and nothing injureth so much as evil company.
en.5:
Than good companionship no surer help we know;
Than bad companionship nought causes direr woe.
en.6: There is no greater help than the company of the good; there is no greater source of sorrow than the company of the wicked.

padaccheda.m: வினைசெய்யுங்கால் அப்பொழுது அதனால் அழிவதனையும்
அழிந்தால் பின்ஆவதனையும்
ஆய்நின்று பிற்பொழுது தரும் ஊதியத்தையும்
சீர்தூக்கி உறுவதாயிற் செய்க

en.1: Weigh what will be lost, what will be gained, and the profit it will bring later, then act.
en.2: Weigh what the work will cost now, what will come back after that loss, and the profit it will bring later, and act if it is worthwhile. Worthwhile means that the return now exceeds the loss and keeps growing later. If that later profit is there, the work shouldn’t be dropped even when loss and return are equal now. See gain at both times, then act.
en.4: Take into thy consideration the output and the wastage and the profit that the undertaking will yield: and then put thy hand to it.
en.5:
Expenditure, return, and profit of the deed
In time to come: weigh these—then to the act proceed.
en.6: Let a man reflect on what will be lost, what will be acquired and (from these) what will be his ultimate gain, and (then, let him) act.

padaccheda.m: தாம் தெரிந்துகொண்ட இனத்துடனே செய்யத்தகும் வினையை ஆராய்ந்து பின் தாமேயும் எண்ணி்ச்செய்து முடிக்கவல்ல அரசர்க்கு
எய்துதற்கரிய பொருள் யாது ஒன்றும் இல்லை

en.1: For those who examine a task with people they have chosen, think it over and then act, nothing is out of reach.
en.2: For rulers who examine a fit task with the group they have chosen, then think it over themselves and can carry it through, nothing is hard to obtain. The task means everything from marching out to victory. Since they don’t fail in what is the source of wealth, all rare things come to them easily.
en.4: Behold the prince who decideth upon action only after consulting with men chosen for their worth: there is nothing that is impossible for him.
en.5:
With chosen friends deliberate; next use thy private thought;
Then act. By those who thus proceed all works with ease are wrought.
en.6: There is nothing too difficult to (be attained by) those who, before they act, reflect well themselves, and thoroughly consider (the matter) with chosen friends.

padaccheda.m: மேல்எய்தக்கடவ ஊதியத்தினை நோக்கி முன் எய்திநின்ற முதல்தன்னையும் இழத்தற்கு ஏதுவாய செய்வினையை
அறிவுடையார் மேற்கொள்ளார்

en.1: The wise won’t start a venture that looks for profit and loses the capital.
en.2: The wise won’t take up work that, for the sake of future profit, may lose even the capital they already hold. Such work is like setting out to seize another’s land, without knowing your strength, the time or the place, and losing your own. This holds even for work already begun.
en.4: There are enterprises that tempt with a great profit but which perish even the capital itself: the wise undertake them not.
en.5:
To risk one’s all and lose, aiming at added gain,
Is rash affair, from which the wise abstain.
en.6: Wise men will not, in hopes of profit, undertake works that will consume their principal.

padaccheda.m: இனத்தொடும் தனித்தும் ஆராய்ந்து துணிதலில்லாத வினையைத் தொடங்கார்
தமக்கு இளிவரவு என்னும் குற்றம் உண்டாதலை அஞ்சுவார்

en.1: Those who fear the stain of disgrace won’t begin what they are not sure of.
en.2: Those who fear the fault of disgrace won’t start work they haven’t examined and settled, with their group and alone. Once begun, it can’t be dropped halfway. Disgrace is the scorn the world adds when the work fails, saying they have neither sense nor honour. That scorn is certain, so begin only where you are clear.
en.4: Behold the men who fear to be ridiculed by others: they start not on any enterprise without previous deliberation.
en.5:
A work of which the issue is not clear,
Begin not they reproachful scorn who fear.
en.6: Those who fear reproach will not commence any thing which has not been (thoroughly considered) and made clear to them.

padaccheda.m: சென்றால் நிகழும் திறங்களையெல்லாம் முற்ற எண்ணாது சில எண்ணிய துணையானே அரசன் பகைவர் மேற் செல்லுதல்
அவரை வளரும் நிலத்திலே நிலைபெறச் செய்வதொரு நெறியாம்

en.1: To march out without thinking through every side of it is a way of planting your enemies in a prepared bed.
en.2: For a ruler to march on his enemies having weighed only some of what may happen is a way of settling them in ground where they will grow. All of it means the position of both sides in strength, time and place, how to begin, the obstacles and how to clear them, how to win, and what is gained. Leave any of it out and the enemy has an opening.
en.4: To make war without planning every detail of it beforehand is only to transplant thy enemy on carefully prepared soil.
en.5:
With plans not well matured to rise against your foe,
Is way to plant him out where he is sure to grow!
en.6: One way to promote the prosperity of an enemy, is (for a king) to set out (to war) without having thoroughly weighed his ability (to cope with its chances).

padaccheda.m: அரசன் தன் வினைகளுட் செய்யத்தக்கன அல்லவற்றைச் செய்தலாற் கெடும்
இனி, அதனானே யன்றிச் செய்யத்தக்கனவற்றைச் செய்யாமைதன்னானுங் கெடும்

en.1: You are ruined by doing what should not be done. You are ruined too by not doing what should.
en.2: A ruler is ruined by doing what he should not, and ruined as well by not doing what he should. What he should not do is work that takes great effort, that gives little or no result, that is uncertain, or that brings sorrow later. What he should do is the reverse. Either error shrinks his wealth and army, so his enemies find him easy.
en.4: There are things that ought not to be done and if thou do them thou wilt be ruined: and there are things that ought to be done and if thou do them not thou will be ruined also.
en.5:
’Tis ruin if man do an unbefitting thing;
Fit things to leave undone will equal ruin bring.
en.6: He will perish who does what it is not fit to do; and he also will perish who does not do what it is fit to do.

padaccheda.m: செய்யத்தக்க கருமமும் முடிக்கும் உபாயத்தை எண்ணித் தொடங்குக
தொடங்கி வைத்துப் பின் எண்ணக் கடவேம் என்றொழிதல் குற்றம்ஆதலான்

en.1: Think, then commit to the task. To say you will think after you have committed is a mistake.
en.2: Even when a task is fit to do, think out the means of finishing it before you start, because saying you will start now and think later is a fault. The means are four: gifts, sweet words, division and punishment. Start without thinking these through and the enemy blocks the work, it can’t be dropped halfway, and the ruler suffers.
en.4: Decide not upon any action except after careful deliberation: it is a fool who undertaketh first and sayeth in his heart, I shall think afterwards.
en.5:
Think, and then dare the deed! Who cry,
‘Deed dared, we’ll think,’ disgraced shall be.
en.6: Consider, and then undertake a matter; after having undertaken it, to say “We will consider,” is folly.

padaccheda.m: முடியும் உபாயத்தால் கருமத்தை முயலாத முயற்சி
துணைவர் பலர்நின்று புரைபடாமல் காப்பினும் புரைபடும்

en.1: Effort not made the right way will crack, though many stand by to guard it.
en.2: Effort without the means that work will go wrong, though many helpers stand guard. It brings harm you didn’t intend instead of the good you did. The right means are gifts for the greedy, sweet words for the upright, the lazy and the battle-worn, division for those with allies or at odds with their own side, and force where these fail and on base men who can’t be trusted.
en.4: Behold the man that goeth not to his work the right way about: all his labour will be a waste even if numbers come to his aid.
en.5:
On no right system if man toil and strive,
Though many men assist, no work can thrive.
en.6: The work, which is not done by suitable methods, will fail though many stand to uphold it.

padaccheda.m: வேற்று வேந்தர்மாட்டு நன்றான உபாயஞ் செய்தற்கண்ணுங் குற்றமுண்டாம்
அவரவர் குணங்களை ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்து அவற்றிற்கு இயையச் செய்யாவிடின்

en.1: Even doing good can go wrong, if you don’t do it knowing each person’s nature.
en.2: Even using the good means on other rulers can fail, unless you study each one’s character and act to suit it. The good means are gifts and sweet words, which are pleasant to everyone. Not suiting them means using them on those they aren’t fit for. Going wrong means the task isn’t finished.
en.4: Even in doing good thou mayest err, it thou suit not the benefit to the character of him that receiveth.
en.5:
Though well the work be done, yet one mistake is made,
To habitudes of various men when no regard is paid.
en.6: There are failures even in acting well, when it is done without knowing the various dispositions of men.

reading.note: He takes நன்று as gifts and sweet words used on other rulers, not as kindness in general.

padaccheda.m: அரசர் வினைமுடித்தற்பொருட்டுத் தந்நிலைமையோடு பொருந்தாத உபாயங்களைச் செய்வாராயின் உலகந் தம்மை இகழாநிற்கும்
ஆகலான் அஃது இகழா உபாயங்களை நாடிச்செய்க

en.1: Think first, and do what no one will scorn. The world won’t accept what doesn’t suit you.
en.2: If rulers, to finish a task, use means that don’t suit their position, the world scorns them, so they should seek means it won’t scorn. Not suiting means a strong ruler using gifts and the two other means fit for the weak, or a weak ruler using force, which is fit for the strong. Only fools do these. Match the means to your own strength or weakness.
en.4: Let the thing that thou decidest on be above reproach: for the world despiseth the man who stoopeth to a thing that is beneath himself.
en.5:
Plan and perform no work that others may despise;
What misbeseems a king the world will not approve as wise.
en.6: Let a man reflect, and do things which bring no reproach; the world will not approve, with him, of things, which do not become of his position to adopt.

padaccheda.m: தான் செய்யக் கருதிய வினைவலியையும்
அதனைச்செய்து முடிக்கும் தன் வலியையும்
அதனை விலக்கலுறும் மாற்றான் வலியையும்
இருவர்க்கும் தூணையாவார் வலியையும்
சீர்தூக்கித் தன் வலி மிகுமாயின் அவ்வினையைச் செய்க

en.1: Weigh the strength of the task, your own strength, your enemy’s strength and the strength of allies, then act.
en.2: Weigh the strength of the work you plan, your own strength to finish it, the strength of the enemy who will try to stop it, and the strength of allies on both sides, and act if yours is greater. The work’s strength is judged by what it involves, such as besieging a fort. If you are weaker, defeat is certain. If you are equal, victory is in doubt. Drop it in both cases.
en.4: Weigh justly the difficulty of the enterprise, thy own strength and the strength of thy enemy, and the strength also of your allies; and then enter thou upon it.
en.5:
The force the strife demands, the force he owns, the force of foes,
The force of friends: these should he weigh ere to the war he goes.
en.6: Let (one) weigh well the strength of the deed (he purposes to do), his own strength, the strength of his enemy, and the strength of the allies (of both), and then let him act.

padaccheda.m: தமக்கியலும் வினையையும் அதற்கறிய வேண்டுவதாய வலியையும் அறிந்து
எப்பொழுதும் மன மொழி மெய்களை அதன்கண் வைத்துப் பகைமேற் செல்லும் அரசர்க்கு
முடியாத பொருள் இல்லை

en.1: For those who know what they can do, know what must be known, and stay fixed on it as they go, nothing is out of reach.
en.2: Rulers who know what task they can manage and what strength it calls for, and who march on the enemy with mind, word and body fixed on it, find nothing impossible. They obtain everything. What they can do covers the task, themselves and the enemy, so what must be known is the strength of allies.
en.4: Behold the prince who knoweth his own force and hath learned what he ought to learn, and who oversteppeth not the limits his force and information: his invasions will never fail.
en.5:
Who know what can be wrought, with knowledge of the means, on this
Their mind firm set, go forth, nought goes with them amiss.
en.6: There is nothing which may not be accomplished by those who, before they attack (an enemy), make themselves acquainted with their own ability, and with whatever else is (needful) to be known, and apply themselves wholly to their object.

padaccheda.m: கருத்தாவாதலை உடைய தம் வலியின் அளவு அறியாதே
மன எழுச்சியால் தம்மின் வலியாரோடு வினை செய்தலைத் தொடங்கி
அவர் அடர்த்தலான் அது செய்து முடிக்கப்பெறாது இடையே கெட்ட அரசர் உலகத்துப் பலர்

en.1: Many, not knowing the strength they have, set out on a surge of zeal and broke halfway.
en.2: Many rulers in the world, not knowing the measure of their own strength, began in a rush of spirit to act against those stronger than them, were pressed hard and fell halfway with the work undone. Those with wisdom, the best of the three powers, are few, which is why he says many. So begin only when you know your strength.
en.4: Many there have been who in the sanguineness of their hearts overestimated their strength and adventured, but were cut off in the middle.
en.5:
Ill-deeming of their proper powers, have many monarchs striven,
And midmost of unequal conflict fallen asunder riven.
en.6: There are many who, ignorant of their (want of) power (to meet it), have haughtily set out to war, and broken down in the midst of it.

padaccheda.m: அயல் வேந்தரோடு பொருந்தி ஒழுகுவதுஞ் செய்யாது
தன் வலியளவு அறிவதுஞ்செய்யாது
தன்னை வியந்து அவரோடு பகைத்த அரசன்
விரையக் கெடும்

en.1: Those who won’t live at peace, don’t know their measure and admire themselves are quickly ruined.
en.2: A ruler who neither lives in accord with neighbouring rulers nor knows the measure of his strength, but admires himself and makes enemies of them, is quickly ruined. There are only two courses with neighbours: be friends, or make an enemy knowing your strength. One who does neither and takes them on while weak never has a firm place.
en.4: Behold the men who know not to live in peace, who know not their own measure and who are full of self-conceit: they will have a swift end.
en.5:
Who not agrees with those around, no moderation knows;
In self-applause indulging, swift to ruin goes.
en.6: He will quickly perish who, ignorant of his own resources flatters himself of his greatness, and does not live in peace with his neighbours.

padaccheda.m: பீலி ஏற்றிய சகடமும் அச்சு முரியும்
அப் பீலியை அது பொறுக்கும் அளவின்றி மிகுத்து ஏற்றின்

en.1: Even a cart loaded with peacock feathers will break its axle, if you pile them too high.
en.2: Even a cart carrying peacock feathers will break its axle if they are loaded beyond what it can bear. “Even” marks both the cart’s strength and the feathers’ lightness. It says something else by this: a ruler who makes enemies of many because each is weak loses his strength, strong as he is, when they unite. So don’t make enemies of many who may join together.
en.4: Put too many of them and even peacock’s feathers would break the wagon’s axle.
en.5:
With peacock feathers light you load the wain;
Yet, heaped too high, the axle snaps in twain.
en.6: The axle tree of a bandy, loaded only with peacocks’ feathers will break, if it be greatly overloaded.

padaccheda.w: கொம்பர் நுனி ஏறினார் அஃது இறந்து ஊக்கின்
padaccheda.m: ஒரு மரக்கோட்டினது நுனிக்கண்ணே ஏறிநின்றார் தம் ஊக்கத்தால் அவ்வளவினைக் கடந்து மேலும் ஏற ஊக்குவராயின்
அவ்வூக்கம் அவர் உயிர்க்கு இறுதியாய் முடியும்

en.1: Those who have climbed to the tip of a branch and try to go further will lose their life.
en.2: People who have climbed to the end of a branch and, in their zeal, strive to climb beyond it will find that zeal the end of their life. It says something else by this: a ruler who has marched on his enemy as far as he can, and then pushes on in a surge of spirit, will end not the work but his own life. Know the limit and stop there.
en.4: Those that have climbed to the top of the tree will lose their lives if they attempt to climb still higher.
en.5:
Who daring climbs, and would himself upraise
Beyond the branch’s tip, with life the forfeit pays.
en.6: There will be an end to the life of him who, having climbed out to the end of a branch, ventures to go further.

padaccheda.m: ஈயும் நெறியானே தமக்குள்ள பொருளின் எல்லையை அறிந்து அதற்கு ஏற்ப ஈக
அங்ஙனம் ஈதல் பொருளைப் பேணிக்கொண்டு ஒழுகும் நெறியாம்

en.1: Give in the right way, knowing your limit. That is how to look after your wealth as you spend it.
en.2: Give in the proper way, knowing the limit of your wealth, because that is how to live while taking care of it. Split what you have into four: spend two parts on yourself, keep one against trouble, and give one. Taking care means making wealth, which is no one’s friend, a friend to you. If spending stays below income, wealth never leaves.
en.4: Keep thou in mind the extent of thy wealth and let thy gifts be commensurate therewith: that is the way to conserve and divide thy substance.
en.5:
With knowledge of the measure due, as virtue bids you, give!
That is the way to guard your wealth, and seemly live.
en.6: Let a man know the measure of his ability (to give,) and let him give accordingly; such giving is the way to preserve his property.

padaccheda.w: ஆகு ஆறு அளவு இட்டிதாயினும் கேடு இல்லை
padaccheda.m: அரசர்க்குப் பொருள் வருகின்ற நெறியளவு சிறிதாயிற்றானும் அதனாற் கேடில்லையாம்
போகின்ற நெறியளவு அதனிற் பெருகாதாயின்

en.1: The way in may be narrow, but there is no harm, as long as the way out is no wider.
en.2: Even if the path by which wealth comes to rulers is small, no harm comes of it, as long as the path by which it goes is no larger. Income and spending may even be equal, and there is still no harm.
en.4: It mattereth not if the feeder channel is strait, provided that the draining channel is not wider.
en.5:
Incomings may be scant; but yet, no failure there,
If in expenditure you rightly learn to spare.
en.6: Even though the income (of a king) be small, it will not cause his (ruin), if his outgoings be not larger than his income.

padaccheda.m: தனக்கு உள்ள பொருளின் எல்லையை அறிந்து அதற்கு ஏற்ப வாழமாட்டாதான் வாழ்க்கைகள்
உள்ளனபோலத் தோன்றி, மெய்ம்மையான் இல்லையாய்ப் பின்பு அத்தோற்றமும் இன்றிக் கெட்டுவிடும்

en.1: A life not lived within its limit seems to be there, then is not, then vanishes without a trace.
en.2: The life of someone who can’t live within the limit of their wealth seems to exist but in truth does not, and later even the appearance goes. Living within the limit means giving and enjoying no more than you have. At first the ruin doesn’t show, which is why it seems to be there. This is the harm of spending more than your income.
en.4: Behold the man that taketh not account of his measure nor liveth within the bounds thereof: he may look like prospering, but he will perish leaving no trace behind.
en.5:
Who prosperous lives and of enjoyment knows no bound,
His seeming wealth, departing, nowhere shall be found.
en.6: The prosperity, of him who lives without knowing the measure (of his property), will perish, even while it seems to continue.

padaccheda.m: தனக்குள்ள அளவு தூக்காமைக்கு ஏதுவாய ஒப்புரவாண்மையால்
ஒருவன் செல்வத்தின் எல்லை விரையக் கெடும்

en.1: Helping others without weighing what you have will quickly destroy your wealth.
en.2: Helping others in a way that doesn’t weigh how much you have quickly destroys the extent of your wealth. Even helping others must not go too far. These last four couplets single out the strength of wealth, a part of greatness among the three powers, because it matters so much.
en.4: Behold the man that measureth not his wealth and lavisheth it with an unsparing hand: his substance will quickly come to nought.
en.5:
Beneficence that measures not its bound of means,
Will swiftly bring to nought the wealth on which it leans.
en.6: The measure of his wealth will quickly perish, whose liberality weighs not the measure of his property.

padaccheda.m: தன்னின் வலிதாய கூகையைக் காக்கை பகற்பொழுதின்கண் வெல்லாநிற்கும்
அதுபோலப் பகைவரது இகலை வெல்லக் கருதும் அரசர்க்கு அதற்கேற்ற காலம் இன்றியமையாதது

en.1: By day the crow beats the owl. Rulers who would beat their enemies need the right time.
en.2: By day the crow beats the owl, which is stronger than it. In the same way, rulers who mean to overcome their enemies must have a fitting time, because without it strength is useless. The fitting time is when heat and cold are even and bring no sickness, when water and food are at hand, and when the army can march without hardship.
en.4: The crow triumpheth over the owl when it is day: so opportunity is a great thing to the prince who would vanquish his enemy.
en.5:
A crow will conquer owl in broad daylight;
The king that foes would crush, needs fitting time to fight.
en.6: A crow will overcome an owl in the day time; so the king who would conquer his enemy must have (a suitable) time.

padaccheda.m: அரசன் காலத்தோடு பொருந்த வினைசெய்து ஒழுகுதல்
ஒருவர்கண்ணும் நில்லாது நீங்கும் செல்வத்தைத் தன்கண் நீங்காமற் பிணிக்கும் கயிறாம்

en.1: Acting in step with the season is a rope that ties good fortune down so that it can’t leave.
en.2: For a ruler to act in keeping with the time is a rope that binds to him the wealth that stays with no one and always moves on. It means doing things without missing the moment. Since the work then succeeds, the wealth it brings never leaves.
en.4: To follow closely on the pace of Time: that is the cord that will bind Fortune to thee firmly.
en.5:
The bond binds fortune fast is ordered effort made,
Strictly observant still of favouring season’s aid.
en.6: Acting at the right season, is a cord that will immoveably bind success (to a king.)

en.1: Is any task hard, if you have the means and know the time?
en.2: Are there any tasks that can be called too hard for rulers, if they act with the tools to finish them and at the time to do them? The tools are the three powers and the four means. He names the tools to show that even with them the time is needed. All work is then easily done.
en.4: Where is the thing called impossible if thou start on thy enterprise with a knowledge of the right season and employ the proper means?
en.5:
Can any work be hard in very fact,
If men use fitting means in timely act?
en.6: Is there any thing difficult for him to do, who acts, with (the right) instruments, at the right time?

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் ஞாலம் முழுதும் தானே ஆளக் கருதினான் ஆயினும், அஃது அவன் கையகத்ததாம்
அதற்குச் செய்யும் வினையைக் காலமறிந்து இடத்தோடு பொருந்தச் செய்வானாயின்

en.1: Even if you aim at the whole world, it will come into your hands, if you act with an eye to the time and the place.
en.2: Even someone who means to rule the whole world alone will have it in his hands, if he does what it takes knowing the time and suiting the place. What can’t be grasped comes within his grasp.
en.4: Thou canst conquer even the whole world if thou choose the proper time and the proper objectives.
en.5:
The pendant world’s dominion may be won,
In fitting time and place by action done.
en.6: Though (a man) should meditate (the conquest of) the world, he may accomplish it, if he acts in the right time, and at the right place.

padaccheda.m: தப்பாது ஞாலமெல்லாம் கொள்ளக்கருதும் அரசர்
தம் வலிமிகுமாயினும், அது கருதாது, அதற்கேற்ற காலத்தையே கருதி அது வருந்துணையும் பகைமேற் செல்லார்

en.1: Those who have their eye on the world stay still, unshaken, and watch for the time.
en.2: Rulers who mean to take the whole world without fail don’t count on their greater strength. They look only for the fitting time, and until it comes they won’t march on the enemy. If they march anyway, both kinds of their greatness shrink and they suffer. Staying still is the one of the six courses of a ruler that is opposed to marching.
en.4: Those that are intent on conquests will be quietly watching their opportunity: they will know neither confusion nor hurry.
en.5:
Who think the pendant world itself to subjugate,
With mind unruffled for the fitting time must wait.
en.6: They who thoughtfully consider and wait for the (right) time (for action,) may successfully meditate (the conquest of) the world.

reading.note: கலங்காது can go with the waiting, unshaken, or, as he takes it, with the aim, without fail.

padaccheda.m: வலிமிகுதி உடைய அரசன் பகைமேற் செல்லாது காலம் பார்த்து இருக்கின்ற இருப்பு
பொருகின்ற தகர், தன்பகைகெடப் பாய்தற்பொருட்டுப் பின்னே கால்வாங்குந் தன்மைத்து

en.1: When a person of spirit holds back, it is like a fighting ram drawing back to charge.
en.2: When a ruler of great strength doesn’t march but sits watching for the time, it is like a fighting ram stepping back so that it can leap and destroy its enemy. As the ram draws back to charge, the ruler holds back to win.
en.4: The ram steppeth back before it delivereth the crushing blow: even such is the inaction of the man of energy.
en.5:
The men of mighty power their hidden energies repress,
As fighting ram recoils to rush on foe with heavier stress.
en.6: The self-restraint of the energetic (while waiting for a suitable-opportunity,) is like the drawing back of a fighting-ram in order to butt.

padaccheda.m: அறிவுடைய அரசர்
பகைவர் மிகை செய்தபொழுதே விரைவாக அவர் அறியப் புறத்து வெகுளார்
தாம் அவரை வெல்லுதற்கு ஏற்ற காலத்தினை அறிந்து அது வரும் துணையும் உள்ளே வெகுள்வர்

en.1: The wise don’t flare up outwardly on the spot. They watch for the time and burn within.
en.2: When enemies overstep, wise rulers don’t show anger at once where the enemy can see it. They learn the time that suits their victory and stay angry inside until it comes. If they show anger, the enemy guards himself. If they let the anger go, they can’t stop him overstepping again.
en.4: The wise show not their anger on the spot: they will nurse it within their hearts and wait for their opportunity.
en.5:
The glorious ones of wrath enkindled make no outward show,
At once; they bide their time, while hidden fires within them glow.
en.6: The wise will not immediately and hastily shew out their anger; they will watch their time, and restrain it within.

padaccheda.m: தாம் வெல்லக்கருதிய அரசர், பகைவர்க்கு இறுதிக்காலம் வருந்துணையும் அவரைக்கண்டால் பணிக
பணியவே, அக்காலம் வந்திறும்வழி அவர் தகைவின்றி இறுவர்

en.1: When you see your enemies, carry them. When you see their end, they will fall head first.
en.2: Rulers who mean to win should bow low whenever they see their enemies, until the enemies’ last days come. Seeing this, the enemies neglect to guard themselves, and when the time comes they surely fall. A load carried on the head falls head down when it is thrown off. While you wait, let no hostility show.
en.4: Bend down before thy adversaries till the day of their decline: when that day is come thou mayest easily throw them down headlong.
en.5:
If foes’ detested form they see, with patience let them bear;
When fateful hour at last they spy,—the head lies there.
en.6: If one meets his enemy, let him show him all respect, until the time for his destruction is come; when that is come, his head will be easily brought low.

padaccheda.m: பகையை வெல்லக் கருதும் அரசர் தம்மால் எய்துதற்குஅரிய காலம் வந்து கூடியக்கால்
அது கழிவதற்கு முன்பே, அது கூடாவழித் தம்மால் செய்தற்கு அரிய வினைகளைச் செய்க

en.1: When what is hard to come by comes your way, do at that very moment what is hard to do.
en.2: When the time that rulers bent on beating an enemy can’t obtain for themselves comes to them, they should at once, before it passes, do the deeds they couldn’t do without it. Strength can’t make such a time, it rarely comes on its own, and it runs off once it has come. So when the time comes, act fast.
en.4: When thou hast got an unusual chance, hesitate not but straightway attempt even the impossible.
en.5:
When hardest gain of opportunity at last is won,
With promptitude let hardest deed be done.
en.6: If a rare opportunity occurs, while it lasts, let a man do that which is rarely to be accomplished (but for such an opportunity.)

padaccheda.m: ஒருவினைமேல் செல்லாது இருக்கும் காலத்துக் கொக்கு இருக்குமாறுபோல இருக்க

padaccheda.w: மற்றுச் சீர்த்த இடத்து அதன் குத்து ஒக்க
padaccheda.m: மற்றைச் செல்லும் காலம் வாய்த்தவழி அது செய்து முடிக்குமாறுபோலத் தப்பாமல் செய்து முடிக்க

en.1: In the time for holding still, be like the heron. When your moment comes, be like its strike.
en.2: When it isn’t time to move, sit still as the heron does. When the time comes, finish the work without fail, as it finishes with its strike. Waiting for a fish it stands as if lifeless, so as not to miss it, and when the fish arrives it strikes at once, before it can escape. So it serves as the image for both waiting and acting.
en.4: When the time is against thee feign inaction like the stork: but when the tide is on, strike with the swiftness of its souse.
en.5:
As heron stands with folded wing, so wait in waiting hour;
As heron snaps its prey, when fortune smiles, put forth your power.
en.6: At the time when one should use self-control, let him restrain himself like a heron; and, let him like it, strike, when there is a favourable opportunity.

padaccheda.m: பகைவரை முற்றுதற்கு ஆவதோர் இடம் பெற்றபின் அல்லது
அவர்மாட்டு யாதொரு வினையும் தொடங்காது ஒழிக
அவரைச் சிறியர் என்று இகழாது ஒழிக

en.1: Start nothing and scorn no one until you have found the ground for a siege.
en.2: Until you have found ground from which to besiege your enemies, start no work against them and don’t scorn them as small. Such ground lets many camps, safe and supporting each other, ring the fort so that no one gets in or out by gate or postern, and it has the land and water for a royal camp with wall and moat. Once you have it, do both.
en.4: Provoke no war and begin no operation except after making a thorough reconnaissance of the theatre of operations.
en.5:
Begin no work of war, despise no foe,
Till place where you can wholly circumvent you know.
en.6: Let not (a king) despise (an enemy,) nor undertake any thing (against him,) until he has obtained (a suitable) place for besieging him.

padaccheda.m: மாறுபாட்டோடு கூடிய வலியினை உடையார்க்கும்
அரணைச் சேர்ந்தாகின்ற ஆக்கம் பல பயன்களையும் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: Even to the strong and warlike, a gain that rests on a stronghold brings many benefits.
en.2: Even for those whose strength goes with hostility, the gain made from a stronghold yields many results. Hostility is what rulers feel who can’t bear to share the world, so he means rulers marching on an enemy. The gain is the siege that brings it. Its results are that the enemy can’t harm you, and that you can stand firm and wear him down.
en.4: It is an immense advantage even to the powerful and the strong to be based on fortified places.
en.5:
Though skill in war combine with courage tried on battle-field,
The added gain of fort doth great advantage yield.
en.6: Even to those who are men of power and expedients, an attack in connection with a fortification will yield many advantages.

padaccheda.m: வலியர் அல்லாதாரும், வலியராய் வெல்வர்
அதற்கு ஏற்ற இடத்தினை அறிந்து தம்மைக் காத்துப் பகைவர்மாட்டு வினைசெய்வராயின்

en.1: Even the weak grow strong and win, if they know the place, guard themselves and act against their enemies.
en.2: Even those without strength become strong and win, if they find the ground that suits, guard themselves and act against their enemies. Guarding means using forts and armies so that the enemy can’t hurt them. If they act this way, they win even without the strength named before.
en.4: Even the weak can hold their own and triumph over a powerful foe if they choose the proper theatre and operate cautiously.
en.5:
E’en weak ones mightily prevail, if place of strong defence
They find, protect themselves, and work their foes offence.
en.6: Even the powerless will become powerful and conquer, if they select a proper field (of action), and guard themselves, while they make war on their enemies.

padaccheda.m: தாம் வினைசெய்தற்கு ஏற்ற இடத்தினை அறிந்து சென்ற அரசர்
அரணைப் பொருந்திநின்று அதனைச் செய்வராயின்
அவரை வெல்வதாக எண்ணியிருந்த பகைவர் அவ்வெண்ணத்தினை இழப்பர்

en.1: Those who had it all planned lose their plan, when the other side learns the place, closes in and acts.
en.2: When rulers have chosen the ground that suits their work, gone there and acted from a stronghold, the enemies who expected to beat them lose that expected victory, because those rulers have kept themselves safe. So the enemies are beaten. These four couplets are about finding ground from which to camp outside an enemy’s fort.
en.4: The plans of thy adversaries will be baffled if thou fall back on strong positions and base thyself on them.
en.5:
The foes who thought to triumph, find their thoughts were vain,
If hosts advance, seize vantage ground, and thence the fight maintain.
en.6: If they who draw near (to fight) choose a suitable place to approach (their enemy), the latter, will have to relinquish the thought which they once entertained, of conquering them.

padaccheda.m: முதலை ஆழமுடைய நீரின்கண் ஆயின் பிறவற்றை எல்லாம் தான் வெல்லாநிற்கும்
அப்புனலின் நீங்குமாயின் அதனைப் பிறவெல்லாம் வெல்லாநிற்கும்

en.1: In deep water the crocodile beats everything. Out of the water, everything else beats it.
en.2: In deep water the crocodile beats all others, and out of it all others beat it. So everyone is strong on their own ground. It says something else by this: rulers who march to ground where the enemy can’t stand find him easy, and if they go where they can’t stand, they are easy for him. So go and beat him where he can’t stand.
en.4: All-powerful is the crocodile in deep water: but out of it, it is the plaything of its foes.
en.5:
The crocodile prevails in its own flow of water wide,
If this it leaves, ’tis slain by any thing beside.
en.6: In deep water, a crocodile ‘will conquer (all other animals); but if it leave the water, other animals will conquer it.

padaccheda.m: நிலத்தின்கண் ஓடும் கால் வலிய நெடிய தேர்கள் கடலின்கண் ஓடமாட்டா
இனி, அக்கடலின்கண் ஓடும் நாவாய்கள் தாமும், நிலத்தின்கண் ஓடமாட்டா

en.1: Tall chariots with strong wheels can’t run on the sea. Ships that run on the sea can’t run on land.
en.2: Tall chariots that run on land can’t run on the sea, for all their strong wheels and size, and ships that run on the sea can’t run on land. It says something else by this: rulers on the march should learn the enemy’s ground and act with the means that suit it.
en.4: The strong-wheeled chariot runneth not on the sea: nor saileth the oceangoing ship on dry land.
en.5:
The lofty car, with mighty wheel, sails not o’er watery main,
The boat that skims the sea, runs not on earth’s hard plain.
en.6: Wide chariots, with mighty wheels, will not run on the ocean; neither will ships that traverse the ocean, move on the earth.

padaccheda.m: பகையிடத்து வினைசெய்யும் திறங்களை எல்லாம் ஒழியாது எண்ணி அவற்றை அரசர் இடத்தொடு பொருந்தச் செய்வராயின்
அச்செயற்குத் தம் திண்மையல்லது பிறிதொரு துணை வேண்டுவதில்லை

en.1: You need no help but fearlessness, if you think everything through and act to suit the place.
en.2: If rulers think through every way of acting in the enemy’s ground, leaving nothing out, and act to suit the place, they need no helper but their own firmness. All that is needed is to stand firm and finish, because nothing is left to make the work go wrong.
en.4: Behold the prince that hath planned everything beforehand and striketh at the proper objective: he wanteth no other ally than his own valour.
en.5:
Save their own fearless might they need no other aid,
If in right place they fight, all due provision made.
en.6: You will need no other aid than fearlessness, if you thoroughly reflect (on what you are to do), and select (a suitable) place for your operations.

padaccheda.m: பெரும்படையுடைய அரசன்
ஏனைச் சிறுபடை உடையானை அழித்தல் கருதி, அவன் புகலைச் சென்று சாருமாயின்
அவனால் தன்பெருமை அழியும்

en.1: When the one with a small army reaches ground that suits it, the one with a great army loses heart.
en.2: If a ruler with a great army, meaning to destroy one with a small army, goes to the place where the small army takes refuge, he loses his greatness. If he looks at the size of his army and not at the ground, the army can’t move together there or isn’t trained for it, so its size is useless and he is destroyed.
en.4: If the prince whose army is weak only betaketh himself to a proper theatre of war, all the endeavours of his strong foe would be vain against him.
en.5:
If lord of army vast the safe retreat assail
Of him whose host is small, his mightiest efforts fail.
en.6: The power of one who has a large army will perish, if he goes into ground where only a small army can act.

reading.note: Who reaches the ground can go either way. The plain reading has the small force reach it. He has the great force go in after the small one.

padaccheda.m: அரண் அழித்தற்கு, அருமையும் பெருமையுமாகிய ஆற்றலும் உடையர் அல்லராயினும்
வினைக்குரிய மாந்தரை அவர் உறைகின்ற நிலத்தின்கண் சென்று தாக்குதல் அரிது

en.1: Even if they lack good defences and renown, it is hard to attack people on the land where they live.
en.2: Even if they lack a strong fort and great power, it is hard to go and attack people in the land where they live. Attack brave men in their home because they look small, and they won’t leave it. They resolve to die there instead, and so a great army breaks against them.
en.4: Even if they have no proper defences and other advantages it is hard to beat a people on their own soil.
en.5:
Though fort be none, and store of wealth they lack,
’Tis hard a people’s homesteads to attack!
en.6: It is a hazardous thing to attack men in their own country, although they may neither have power nor a good fortress.

padaccheda.m: பாகர்க்கு அடங்காவுமாய், வேலாட்களைக் கோத்த கோட்டவுமாய களிறுகளை
அவை, கால்ஆழும் இயல்பிற்றாய சேற்றுநிலத்துப்பட்டுழி நரி கொல்லும்

en.1: A fearless tusker with spearmen on its tusks can be killed by a jackal, in mud where its legs sink.
en.2: A bull elephant that obeys no driver and has spearmen impaled on its tusks is killed by a jackal once it is caught in mud where its legs sink. Even the brave and great, on ground that doesn’t suit them, are destroyed by the very weak. He rejects the reading “spears sunk in its face”, because those wounds would then be what let the jackal kill it.
en.4: Behold the high-mettled elephant that hath faced without wincing a whole multitude of lancers: even a jackal will triumph over him when he is entangled in marshy ground.
en.5:
The jackall slays, in miry paths of foot-betraying fen,
The elephant of fearless eye and tusks transfixing armèd men.
en.6: A fox can kill a fearless, warrior-faced, elephant, if it go into mud in which its legs sink down.

en.1: Test someone by these four, righteousness, wealth, pleasure and fear for their life, and then trust them.
en.2: A ruler should trust a man only after four trials of his mind, each put to him under oath. Priests say the ruler is unrighteous and must go. The general says he is a miser and must go. An old ascetic woman says a palace lady wants him. A minister says the ruler plans their deaths. If he never wavers, he never will. He rejects the variant உயிரெச்சம்.
en.4: Love of the right, gold, pleasure, and fear of life, these four are the tests of a man: give thy confidence therefore to men that satisfy all these tests.
en.5:
How treats he virtue, wealth and pleasure? How, when life’s at stake,
Comports himself? This four-fold test of man will full assurance make.
en.6: Let (a minister) be chosen, after he has been tried by means of these four things, viz,—his virtue, (love of) money, (love of) sexual pleasure, and fear of (losing) life.

padaccheda.m: உயர்ந்த குடியிற் பிறந்து
குற்றங்களினின்று நீங்கி

padaccheda.w: வடுப் பரியும் நாண் உடையான் கட்டே தெளிவு
padaccheda.m: நமக்கு வடு வருங்கொல் என்று அஞ்சாநிற்கும் நாண் உடையவன்கண்ணதே அரசனது தெளிவு

en.1: Trust the one who is born of good family, free of faults, and has the shame that dreads a scar.
en.2: A ruler’s trust belongs with the man born of a high family, free of faults, who has the shame that fears a stain. The faults are the six named for rulers, with sloth, forgetfulness and error. Shame means a mind that won’t turn to low acts. These are learned mostly by hearing from worthy people. Trust only one who has all four.
en.4: Behold the man who is born of a good family, who is free from faults and who dreadeth disgrace: he is the man for thee.
en.5:
Of noble race, of faultless worth, of generous pride
That shrinks from shame or stain; in him may king confide.
en.6: (The king’s) choice should (fall) on him, who is of good family, who is free from faults, and who has the modesty which fears the wounds (of sin).

padaccheda.m: கற்றற்கு அரிய நூல்களைக் கற்று மேற்சொல்லிய குற்றங்கள் அற்றார் மாட்டும்
நுண்ணிதாக ஆராயும் இடத்து வெண்மை இல்லாமை அரிது

en.1: Even among those who have learned hard things and have no flaw, look closely and you will rarely find anyone with no ignorance at all.
en.2: Even in those who have studied hard books and are free of the faults named, it is rare, if you examine closely, to find no ignorance. It shows in them only now and then, through the mind’s unsteadiness. The hint is that only those shown by direct observation to be free even of that should be trusted.
en.4: Even men of rare learning and of pure hearts will not be found, when thou dost test them, to be absolutely exempt from all ignorance.
en.5:
Though deeply learned, unflecked by fault, ’tis rare to see,
When closely scanned, a man from all unwisdom free.
en.6: When even men, who have studied the most difficult works, and who are free from faults, are (carefully) examined, it is a rare thing to find them without ignorance.

padaccheda.m: குணம் குற்றங்களுள் ஒன்றே உடையார் உலகத்து இன்மையின் ஒருவன் குணங்களை ஆராய்ந்து
ஏனைக் குற்றங்களையும் ஆராய்ந்து
பின் அவ்விரு பகுதியுள்ளும் மிக்கவற்றை ஆராய்ந்து
அவனை அம்மிக்கவற்றானே அறிக

en.1: Look at their good points, look at their faults, see which are more, and judge them by that.
en.2: No one in the world has only virtues or only faults. So examine someone’s virtues, then their faults, find which side is greater, and know them by it. Greater means greater in importance or in number. If the virtues are greater they are fit for the work, and if the faults are, they are not. Since those with only virtues are rare, this is how to trust anyone.
en.4: Weigh a man’s good and weigh his evil: whichever is more, take that to be his nature.
en.5:
Weigh well the good of each, his failings closely scan,
As these or those prevail, so estimate the man.
en.6: Let (a king) consider (a man’s) good qualities, as well as his faults, and then judge (of his character) by that which prevails.

padaccheda.m: பிறப்பு, குணம், அறிவு என்பனவற்றான் மக்கள் எய்தும் பெருமைக்கும் மற்றைச் சிறுமைக்கும் உரைகல்லாவது
தாம்தாம் செய்யும் கருமமே, பிறிதில்லை

en.1: For a person’s greatness or smallness, their own deeds are the touchstone.
en.2: The touchstone for the greatness people reach by birth, character and understanding, and for their smallness, is the deeds they do, and nothing else. There are other ways of knowing, but deeds are the final one.
en.4: Dost thou want to find out whether a man is noble or little-minded? Know that conduct is the touchstone of character.
en.5:
Of greatness and of meanness too,
The deeds of each are touchstone true.
en.6: A man’s deeds are the touchstone of his greatness and littleness.

padaccheda.m: சுற்றம் இல்லாரைத் தெளிதலை ஒழிக
அவர் உலகத்தோடு தொடர்பிலர்
ஆகலாற் பழிக்கு அஞ்சார்

en.1: Do not trust those who have no one. They have no ties and feel no shame at blame.
en.2: Don’t trust those with no kin. They have no bond with the world, so they don’t fear blame. People avoid what the world blames and do what it praises through the ways of life among kin, and those with no kin lack this. So they can’t be trusted.
en.4: Beware of trusting men that have no kindred: for their hearts will be without attachment and they will be callous to shame.
en.5:
Beware of trusting men who have no kith or kin;
No bonds restrain such men, no shame deters from sin.
en.6: Let (a king) avoid choosing men who have no relations; such men have no attachments, and therefore have no fear of crime.

padaccheda.m: அன்புடைமை பற்றுக்கோடாகத் தமக்கு அறிய வேண்டுவன அறியாதாரைத் தெளிதல்
அரசனுக்கு எல்லா அறியாமையையும் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: To trust those who don’t know what they should, leaning on your fondness for them, brings every kind of folly.
en.2: To trust those who don’t know what they need to know, with loving-kindness as your prop, gives a ruler every kind of ignorance. If he hands work to the unwise out of the loving-kindness between them, it fails through their ignorance. Then the ignorance isn’t only theirs. He too is shown not to know whom to appoint or what would follow.
en.4: If thou choose a fool for thy confidential adviser because that thou lovest him, he will lead thee to endless follies.
en.5:
By fond affection led who trusts in men of unwise soul,
Yields all his being up to folly’s blind control.
en.6: To choose ignorant men, through partiality, is the height of folly.

padaccheda.m: தன்னொடு இயைபுடையன் அல்லாதானைப் பிறப்பு முதலியவற்றானும், செயலானும் ஆராய்ந்து தெளிந்த அரசனுக்கு
அத்தெளிவு தன் வழிமுறையினும் நீங்காத துன்பத்தைக் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: Trust a stranger without testing them, and the suffering won’t end, even for those who come after you.
en.2: A ruler who trusts a man with no tie to him, without testing him by birth and deeds, gets suffering that lasts even into his line. The tie is a lineage joined to his own family, and this is needed too. Trusting means handing him the work. When it fails, those born of his family fall into enemy hands and are brought low.
en.4: Behold the man that trusteth another without trying him: he createth endless evils even unto his posterity.
en.5:
Who trusts an untried stranger, brings disgrace,
Remediless, on all his race.
en.6: Sorrow that will not leave even his posterity will come upon him who chooses a stranger whose character he has not known.

padaccheda.m: யாவரையும் ஆராயாது தெளியாது ஒழிக
ஆராய்ந்தபின் தெளியும் பொருட்களை ஐயுறாது ஒழிக

en.1: Trust no one without testing them. After testing, trust them with what they can be trusted with.
en.2: Don’t trust anyone without examining them, in any task. After examining, have no doubt about them in the tasks fit to give them. “Trust” here means setting doubt aside. What can be trusted means the work that suits each one’s ability.
en.4: Trust not a man without trying him: and after trying your men, give each of them the work for which he is fit.
en.5:
Trust no man whom you have not fully tried,
When tested, in his prudence proved confide.
en.6: Let (a king) choose no one without previous consideration; after he has made his choice, let him unhesitatingly select for each such duties as are appropriate.

padaccheda.m: அரசன் ஒருவனை ஆராயாது தெளிதலும்
ஆராய்ந்து தெளிந்தவன்மாட்டு ஐயப்படுதலும் இவ்விரண்டும்
அவனுக்கு நீங்காத துன்பத்தைக் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: To trust without testing, and to doubt someone you have come to trust, both bring suffering that doesn’t end.
en.2: For a ruler to trust someone untested, and to doubt someone he has tested and trusted, both bring him lasting suffering. If he doubts a man after giving him work, with no fault seen, the man notices, decides the post won’t last and lets the work slide. Enemies can also easily turn him away. So doubt is wrong as well.
en.4: To trust a man whom thou hast not tried and to suspect a man whom thou hast found worthy lead alike to endless ills.
en.5:
Trust where you have not tried, doubt of a friend to feel,
Once trusted, wounds inflict that nought can heal.
en.6: To make choice of one who has not been examined, and to entertain doubts respecting one who has been chosen, will produce-irremediable sorrow.

padaccheda.m: அரசன் முதற்கண் ஒருவினையைத் தன்கண் வைத்தால், அதன்கண் ஆவனவும் ஆகாதனவும் ஆய செயல்களை ஆராய்ந்தறிந்து
அவற்றுள் ஆவனவற்றையே விரும்பிய இயல்பினை உடையான்
பின் அவனாற் சிறந்த வினைகளிலே ஆளப்படும்

en.1: The one who looks at both the good and the bad, and whose nature is to choose the good, is the one to employ.
en.2: A ruler first gives a man a middling task, between his inner and outer affairs, to learn if he is fit. If the man examines what is and isn’t proper in it and shows a nature that wants only what is proper, he should then be employed in the higher work of the inner affairs. The past tense “chose” shows that a trial has gone before.
en.4: Behold the man that seeth the good and seeth the evil also and chooseth only that which is good: employ thou him in thy service.
en.5:
Who good and evil scanning, ever makes the good his joy;
Such man of virtuous mood should king employ.
en.6: He should be employed (by a king), whose nature leads him to choose the good, after having weighed both the evil and the good in any undertaking.

padaccheda.m: பொருள் வரு வாயில்களை விரியச் செய்து
அப்பொருளாற் செல்வங்களை வளர்த்து
அவ்வாயில்கட்கும் பொருட்கும் செல்வங்கட்கும் உற்ற இடையூறுகளை நாள்தோறும் ஆராய்ந்து நீக்கவல்லவன்
அரசனுக்கு வினைசெய்க

en.1: Let the work go to the one who can widen the sources of income, build up prosperity and look into whatever trouble comes.
en.2: Let the man serve the ruler who can widen the sources of wealth, use that wealth to increase prosperity, and each day look into and remove the troubles that threaten them all. The sources are those named before, with farming, cattle-keeping and trade. The troubles come from the ruler, those who work for him, kin, enemies and thieves.
en.4: Behold the man that is able to develop the resources of thy kingdom and to cure the ills that may befall it: set him to manage thy affairs.
en.5:
Who swells the revenues, spreads plenty o’er the land,
Seeks out what hinders progress, his the workman’s hand.
en.6: Let him do (the king’s) work who can enlarge the sources (of revenue,) increase wealth and considerately prevent the accidents (which would destroy it).
