padaccheda.m: அரசன்மாட்டு அன்பும்
அவனுக்காவன அறியும் அறிவும்
அவை செய்தற்கண் கலங்காமையும்
அவற்றாற் பொருள் கையுற்றவழி அதன்மேல் அவா இன்மையுமாகிய
இந்நான்கு குணங்களையும் நிலைபெற உடையான் மேலதே வினையை விட்டிருக்கும் தெளிவு

en.1: Place your trust in the one who truly has these four: loving-kindness, understanding, firmness and freedom from craving.
en.2: A ruler can rest his trust on the man who firmly has these four: loving-kindness towards the ruler, knowledge of what will help him, steadiness in doing it, and no craving for the wealth that comes to hand through it. With these, he can leave the work to the man without having to check any of it.
en.4: Let him alone be selected for service who is endowed with kindness and intelligence and decision, and who is free from greed.
en.5:
A loyal love with wisdom, clearness, mind from avarice free;
Who hath these four good gifts should ever trusted be.
en.6: Let the choice (of a king) fall upon him who largely possesses these four things, love, knowledge, a clear mind, and freedom from covetousness.

padaccheda.m: எல்லா வகையானும் ஆராய்ந்து தெளிந்து வினைவைத்த பின்னும்
அவ்வினையின் இயல்பானே வேறுபடும் மாந்தர் உலகத்துப் பலர்

en.1: Even after you have trusted them in every way, many people change with the nature of the work.
en.2: Even after being tested every way and given a post, many people in the world change through the nature of the work. Few see the pleasures of kingship as a fault and stay as they were, instead of craving them and turning. So give those who seem to have every virtue a middling task first, find them out and remove them.
en.4: Many are the men that satisfy every test and yet alter in the actual performance of duty.
en.5:
Even when tests of every kind are multiplied,
Full many a man proves otherwise, by action tried!
en.6: Even when (a king) has tried them in every possible way, there are many men who change, from the nature of the works (in which they may be employed).

padaccheda.m: செய்யும் உபாயங்களை அறிந்து செயலானும் இடையூறுகளானும் வரும் துன்பங்களைப் பொறுத்து முடிவுசெய்ய வல்லானை அல்லது
வினைதான் இவன்நம்மாட்டு அன்புடையன் என்று பிறன்ஒருவனை ஏவும் இயல்புடைத்துஅன்று

en.1: Work is not something to hand to a favourite. It goes only to one who knows how and can endure to the end.
en.2: By its nature a task can’t be given to a man because he has loving-kindness towards you. It goes only to one who knows the means and can bear the pains of the doing and of its obstacles until it is finished. Work is done by knowledge and power, not by loving-kindness.
en.4: Work should be entrusted to men in consideration of their expert knowledge and capacity for patient exertion, and not of their love towards thy person.
en.5:
No specious fav’rite should the king’s commission bear,
But he that knows, and work performs with patient care.
en.6: (A king’s) work can only be accomplished by a man of wisdom and patient endurance; it is not of a nature to be given to one from mere personal attachment.

padaccheda.m: முதற்கண்ணே செய்வானது இலக்கண்த்தை ஆராய்ந்து
பின்செய்யப்படும் வினையினது இயல்பை ஆராய்ந்து
பின் அவனையும் அதனையும், காலத்தொடு படுத்துப் பொருந்த அறிந்து அவனை அதன்கண் ஆடலைச் செய்க

en.1: Look closely at the doer, look closely at the work, match them to the time, and then act.
en.2: First examine the marks of the one who will do it, then the nature of the work, then see how they fit together with the time, and put him to it. That means reasoning that at this time, one with these marks will finish a work of this kind.
en.4: Choose the expert and give him the work for which he is fit: see that the time is ripe for performance and then get him to begin it.
en.5:
Let king first ask, ‘Who shall the deed perform?’ and ‘What the deed?’
Of hour befitting both assured, let every work proceed.
en.6: Let (a king) act, after having considered the agent (whom he is to employ), the deed (he desires to do), and the time which is suitable to it.

padaccheda.w: இதனை இதனால் இவன் முடிக்கும் என்று ஆய்ந்து
padaccheda.m: இவ்வினையை இக்கருவியால் இவன் முடிக்கவல்லன் எனக் கூறுபடுத்து ஆராய்ந்து
மூன்றும் தம்முள் இயைந்தவழி அவ்வினையை அவன்கண்ணே விடுக

en.1: Work out that this person can finish this task by this means, then leave it in their hands.
en.2: Examine point by point that this man can finish this work with these means, and when the three fit together, leave the work to him. The means are helpers, wealth and the like. Leaving it means making him the one responsible for it.
en.4: Determine first the capacity of the servant and the work for which he is fit: and then leave him in responsible charge of the same.
en.5:
‘This man, this work shall thus work out,’ let thoughtful king command;
Then leave the matter wholly in his servant’s hand.
en.6: After having considered, “this man can accomplish this, by these means,” let (the king) leave with him the discharge of that duty.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனை அரசன், தன் வினை செய்தற்கு உரியனாக ஆராய்ந்து துணிந்தால்
பின் அவனை அதற்கு உரியனாக உயரச் செய்க

en.1: Once you have found someone right for a task, make that task theirs.
en.2: Once a ruler has examined a man and decided he is fit to do the work, he should raise him to it, giving him the power to finish it himself. Failing to do this also brings ruin.
en.4: After thou hast decided that a man is fit for an office, make him worthy to fill it.
en.5:
As each man’s special aptitude is known,
Bid each man make that special work his own.
en.6: Having considered what work a man is fit for, let (the king) employ him in that work.

padaccheda.m: எப்பொழுதும் தன்வினையின்கண்ணே முயறலை உடையான் அவ்வுரிமையால் தனக்குக் கேளாய் ஒழுகுகின்ற தன்மையை
அது பொறாதார் சொற்கேட்டு அரசன் மாறுபடக் கருதுமாயின், திருமகள் அவனை விட்டு நீங்கும்

en.1: If you misread the closeness of someone devoted to the work, good fortune will leave you.
en.2: A man who always strives at the work behaves like kin, by right of that work. If the ruler listens to those who resent this and thinks otherwise of him, the goddess of fortune leaves the ruler. If he takes the man’s ease for disrespect and turns on him, no one will work with heart any more, and his wealth is lost.
en.4: Behold the man who resenteth the friendly advances of the servant who is skilful at his work: Fortune will depart from him.
en.5:
Fortune deserts the king who ill can bear
Informal friendly ways of men his toils who share.
en.6: Prosperity will leave (the king) who doubts the friendship of the man who steadily labours in the discharge of his duties.

padaccheda.m: வினை செய்வான் கோடாது ஒழிய உலகம் கோடாது
ஆதலான் அரசன் அவன் செயலை நாள்தோறும் ஆராய்க

en.1: Let the ruler look into it every day. If the one who does the work doesn’t go crooked, the world won’t.
en.2: If the man who does the work doesn’t go crooked, the world doesn’t go crooked, so the ruler should examine his work every day. By examining this one thing he has examined the whole world that depends on it. Let him do this quietly, without harming the man’s standing.
en.4: Let the prince oversee everything every day: for there will be nothing wrong with the country so long as there is nothing wrong with the officers of the State.
en.5:
Let king search out his servants’ deeds each day;
When these do right, the world goes rightly on its way.
en.6: Let a king daily examine the conduct of his servants; if they do not act crookedly, the world will not act crookedly.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் செல்வம் தொலைந்து வறியனாய வழியும் விடாது தம்மோடு அவனிடைப் பழைமையை எடுத்துக் கொண்டாடும் இயல்புகள்
சுற்றத்தார்மாட்டே உளவாவன

en.1: Only kin go on cherishing old ties even when you have lost everything.
en.2: The habit of staying with a man when his wealth is gone and he is poor, and of fondly recalling the old bond, is found only among kin. The old bond is what he did for them in better days. Everyone else cuts their ties the moment he loses his means.
en.4: Constancy of attachment even in adversity belongeth only unto kindred.
en.5:
When wealth is fled, old kindness still to show,
Is kindly grace that only kinsmen know.
en.6: Even when (a man’s) property is all gone, relatives will act towards him with their accustomed (kindness).

padaccheda.m: அன்பு அறாத சுற்றம் ஒருவற்கு எய்துமாயின்
அஃது அவற்குக் கிளைத்தல் அறாத செல்வங்கள் பலவற்றையும் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: If you have kin whose fondness never ends, they will bring you many gains that go on sprouting.
en.2: If a man finds kin whose loving-kindness doesn’t end, they give him many kinds of wealth that never stop branching. “If he finds” shows how rare this is. Unending sets them apart from enemies within. The many are the six limbs of a kingdom, which keep branching because many people raise them together.
en.4: If a man is blessed with kindred whose love for him bateth not, his fortunes will never cease to grow.
en.5:
The gift of kin’s unfailing love bestows
Much gain of good, like flower that fadeless blows.
en.6: If (a man’s) relatives remain attached to him with unchanging love, it will be a source of everincreasing wealth.

padaccheda.m: அச்சுற்றத்தோடு நெஞ்சு கலத்தல் இல்லாதவன் வாழ்க்கை
குளப்பரப்புக் கரையின்றி நீர் நிறைந்தாற் போலும்

en.1: A life with no sharing of hearts is like a broad tank filling with water and no bank around it.
en.2: The life of a man whose heart doesn’t mingle with his kin is like a wide tank filled with water and no banks. Kin comes from the subject of the chapter. Life means the wealth that supports it. Mingling comes from talking over each other’s state. The wealth of a man with no kin has no one to hold it, and it flows away.
en.4: The man who rejoiceth not in the intimacy of his kindred is like a tank without bunds: the waters of prosperity will flow away from him.
en.5:
His joy of life who mingles not with kinsmen gathered round,
Is lake where streams pour in, with no encircling bound.
en.6: The wealth of one who does not mingle freely with his relatives, will be like the filling of water in a spacious tank, that has no banks.

padaccheda.m: செல்வம் பெற்ற அதனால் ஒருவன் பெற்ற பயனாவது
தன் சுற்றத்தால் தான் சூழப்படும்வகை அதனைத் தழீஇ ஒழுகுதல்

en.1: The reward of having wealth is to live so that your kin gather round you.
en.2: What a man gains from gaining wealth is to embrace his kin and live surrounded by them. It is called the reward of wealth because such conduct lets him rule without enemies.
en.4: To gather and attach one’s kindred to oneself: that is the use and purpose of prosperity.
en.5:
The profit gained by wealth’s increase,
Is living compassed round by relatives in peace.
en.6: To live surrounded by relatives, is the advantage to be derived from the acquisition of wealth.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் சுற்றத்திற்கு வேண்டுவன கொடுத்தலையும், இன்சொற் சொல்லுதலையும் வல்லனாயின்
தம்மின் தொடர்ந்த பலவகைச் சுற்றத்தானே சூழப்படும்

en.1: If you can give and speak sweetly, you will be surrounded by kin, rank upon rank.
en.2: If a man is able to give his kin what they need and to speak sweet words, he is surrounded by many kinds of kin who follow one from another. “Able” shows that doing both in the right measure is hard. Following means the kin of kin, and their kin in turn, bound to him through each other.
en.4: If a man have a sweet tongue and a liberal hand his kinsmen will gather round him in serried ranks.
en.5:
Who knows the use of pleasant words, and liberal gifts can give,
Connections, heaps of them, surrounding him shall live.
en.6: He will be surrounded by numerous relatives who manifests generosity and affability.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன்மிக்க கொடையை உடையனுமாய், வெகுளியை விரும்பானும் ஆயின்
அவன்போலக் கிளையுடையார் இவ்வுலகத்தில் இல்லை

en.1: No one on this wide earth has more people at their side than a great giver who doesn’t cherish anger.
en.2: If a man gives greatly and doesn’t favour anger, no one in this world has kin like his. Great giving means giving so that not one of them goes poor. Not favouring anger means not going beyond measure in the belief that a ruler needs it.
en.4: Behold the man that giveth freely and entertaineth not anger: the world hath none who hath a more attached kindred than he.
en.5:
Than one who gifts bestows and wrath restrains,
Through the wide world none larger following gains.
en.6: No one, in all the world, will have so many relatives (about him), as he who makes large gifts, and does not give way to anger.

padaccheda.m: காக்கைகள் தமக்கு இரையாயின கண்டவழி, மறையாது இனத்தை அழைத்து அதனோடும்கூட உண்ணாநிற்கும்
சுற்றத்தான் எய்தும் ஆக்கங்களும் அப்பெற்றித்தாய இயல்பினை உடையார்க்கே உளவாவன

en.1: The crow doesn’t hide its food. It calls the others and eats. Gains come only to those with a nature like that.
en.2: When crows find food they don’t hide it but call their kind and eat with them. The gains that come through kin belong only to those of that nature, who see that their kin enjoy all that they enjoy. The gains are having no enemies, great wealth and the like. Wealth comes to them along with righteousness and pleasure.
en.4: The crow concealeth not its food selfishly from its fellows but shareth it lovingly with them: prosperity will abide only with men of a like nature.
en.5:
The crows conceal not, call their friends to come, then eat;
Increase of good such worthy ones shall meet.
en.6: The crows do not conceal (their prey), but will call out for others (to share with them) while they eat it; wealth will be with those who show a similar disposition (towards their relatives).

padaccheda.m: எல்லாரையும் ஒருதன்மையராக நோக்காது, அரசன் தத்தம் தகுதிக்கு ஏற்ப நோக்குமாயின்
அச்சிறப்பு நோக்கி அவனை விடாது வாழும் சுற்றத்தார் பலர்

en.1: If a ruler looks on people not all alike but each by their rank, many will live by that regard.
en.2: If a ruler doesn’t regard everyone alike but regards each according to his fitness, many kin will live by him for that honour and never leave. He rules out treating all alike because the higher ones would go, and he calls for ranked regard so that all will stay.
en.4: It is good if the prince treateth not all his kinsmen alike but hath a graduated scale for each: for there are many that have an eye to privilege.
en.5:
Where king regards not all alike, but each in his degree,
’Neath such discerning rule many dwell happily.
en.6: Many relatives will live near a King, when they observe that he does not look on all alike, but that he looks on each man according to his merit.

padaccheda.m: முன் தமராய் வைத்துத் தன்னோடு அமராது யாதானும் ஒருகாரணத்தான் தன்னைப்பிரிந்து போயவர், பின்னும் வந்து சுற்றமாதல்
அவ்வமராமைக் காரணம், தன்மாட்டு இல்லையாகத் தானே உளதாம்

en.1: Those who were your own and left you will come back as kin, once the cause of the rift is gone.
en.2: When those who were his own leave him for some cause, they come back and are kin once that cause no longer lies with him. The cause is such things as the ruler going astray or doing what they hate. Kin have loving-kindness by nature, so a break made by circumstance ends with its cause. No wooing is needed, and they return to what they were.
en.4: The estrangement of a kinsman is easily remedied: remove the cause of the coolness and he will come back to thee.
en.5:
Who once were his, and then forsook him, as before
Will come around, when cause of disagreement is no more.
en.6: Those who have been friends and have afterwards forsaken him, will return and join themselves (to him), when the cause of disagreement is not to be found in him.

padaccheda.m: காரணமின்றித் தன்னிடத்து நின்றும் பிரிந்துபோய்ப் பின் காரணத்தான் வந்த சுற்றத்தானை
அரசன் அக்காரணத்தைச் செய்துவைத்து ஆராய்ந்து தழீஇக் கொள்க

en.1: When someone who left comes back for a reason, a ruler should meet that reason, think it through and take them in.
en.2: When a kinsman who left for no cause comes back for a cause, the ruler should do what he came for, then consider him and take him in. If he doesn’t, the man leaves again and joins the enemy. He left without loving-kindness and came back with a motive, so he needs thought. Those who left to do harm and those who come back to do good are both to be taken in.
en.4: When a kinsman that hath broken with thee cometh back to thee for a reason, accept thou him, but with caution.
en.5:
Who causeless went away, then to return, for any cause, ask leave;
The king should sift their motives well, consider, and receive!
en.6: When one may have left him, and for some cause has returned to him, let the king fulfil the object (for which he has come back) and thoughtfully receive him again.

padaccheda.m: மிக்க உவகைக்களிப்பான் வரும் மறவி
அரசனுக்கு அளவிறந்த வெகுளியினும் தீது

en.1: Worse than boundless rage is the carelessness that comes from the high spirits of great delight.
en.2: For a ruler, the forgetfulness that comes from excessive delight is worse than rage beyond measure. Such delight comes from great wealth, great pleasure and great pride. Anger in measure is needed to crush enemies and punish the wicked. Excessive anger at least sometimes kills the enemy, but this kills only you, so it is worse.
en.4: Worse than excessive rage is the unguardedness that cometh of self-complacency.
en.5:
’Tis greater ill, if rapture of o’erweening gladness to the soul
Bring self-forgetfulness, than if transcendent wrath control.
en.6: More evil than excessive anger, is forgetfulness which springs from the intoxication of great joy.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் புகழினை அவன் மறவி கெடுக்கும்
அறிவினை நிச்சநிரப்புக் கெடுக்குமாறு போல

en.1: Carelessness kills glory, as daily want kills understanding.
en.2: A man’s forgetfulness destroys his glory, as daily begging to fill his belly destroys understanding. If a wise man has to beg each day, the disgrace and sin bring him scorn and his standing goes. In the same way a man of glory who is forgetful fails to guard himself and ruins his affairs, and scorn destroys his standing.
en.4: A false sense of security killeth glory even as indigence crusheth the understanding.
en.5:
Perpetual poverty is death to wisdom of the wise;
When man forgets himself his glory dies!
en.6: Forgetfulness will destroy fame, even as constant poverty destroys knowledge.

padaccheda.m: பொச்சாந்து ஒழுகுவார்க்குப் புகழுடைமை இல்லை
அவ்வின்மை இந்நீதிநூல் உடையார்க்கேயன்றி உலகத்து எவ்வகைப்பட்ட நூலுடையார்க்கும் ஒப்பமுடிந்தது

en.1: There is no glory for the careless. The learned of every kind in the world agree on that.
en.2: Those who live forgetfully have no glory. Not only writers on statecraft but the learned of every kind in the world agree on this. It shows that the rule holds not only for rulers but for anyone striving at any of the four aims, righteousness and the rest, since they fail in them and so have no glory.
en.4: Glory is not for the unwatchful: that is the conclusion of every school of thinkers in the world.
en.5:
‘To self-oblivious men no praise’; this rule
Decisive wisdom sums of every school.
en.6: Thoughtlessness will never acquire fame; and this tenet is upheld by all treatises in the world.

padaccheda.m: காடு மலை முதலிய அரண்களுக்குள்ளே நிற்பினும் மனத்தின்கண் அச்சம் உடையார்க்கு அவற்றால் பயன் இல்லை. ஆங்கு நன்கு பொச்சாப்பு உடையார்க்கு இல்லை= அதுபோலச் செல்வம்எல்லாம் உடையராயினும், மனத்தின்கண் மறவியை உடையார்க்கு அவற்றான் பயனில்லை

en.1: There is no fort for those who are afraid. Just so, there is no good for the careless.
en.2: Those with fear in their minds get no use from forts of forest or hill, even standing inside them. In the same way those with forgetfulness in their minds get no use from wealth of every kind. Good here means what brings good. As the fort of the fearful falls, the wealth of the forgetful is lost.
en.4: Of what use are fortresses to the cowardly? or abundance of resources to the incautious?
en.5:
‘To cowards is no fort’s defence’: e’en so
The self-oblivious men no blessing know.
en.6: Just as the coward has no defence (by whatever fortifications he may be surrounded), so the thoughtless has no good (whatever advantages he may possess.)

padaccheda.m: தன்னாற் காக்கப்படும் துன்பங்களை அவை வருவதற்கு முன்னே அறிந்து காவாது மறந்திருந்தான்
பின் வந்துற்ற காலத்துக் காக்கலாகாமையின் அப்பிழைப்பினை நினைந்து இரங்கிவிடும்

en.1: One who fails to guard in advance will regret that mistake when the blow lands.
en.2: One who forgets and doesn’t guard in advance against troubles he could have prevented will grieve over that mistake when they come, because it is then too late to guard. The troubles are what enemies do when they see a lapse.
en.4: He who faileth to guard against everything beforehand will deplore his negligence when he is surprised by disaster.
en.5:
To him who nought foresees, recks not of anything,
The after woe shall sure repentance bring.
en.6: The thoughtless man, who provides not against the calamities that may happen, will afterwards repent for his fault.

padaccheda.m: அரசர்க்கு மறவாமைக் குணம் யாவர்மாட்டும் எக்காலத்தும் ஒழிவின்றி வாய்க்குமாயின்
அதனை ஒக்கும் நன்மை பிறிது இல்லை

en.1: If you can keep from slipping, with everyone, at all times, without fail, nothing else compares.
en.2: If rulers manage a mind that doesn’t forget, with anyone, at any time and without a lapse, no other good equals it. With anyone, because it must hold for their own workers and kin. At any time, because it must hold when they are growing and when they are shrinking. Without a lapse, because it must hold in all their affairs.
en.4: If thou relax not in thy vigilance at all times and against all men, there is nothing like it.
en.5:
Towards all unswerving, ever watchfulness of soul retain,
Where this is found there is no greater gain.
en.6: There is nothing comparable with the possession of unfailing thoughtfulness at all times, and towards all persons.

padaccheda.m: இவை செய்தற்கு அரியன என்று சொல்லப்பட்டு ஒருவற்கு முடியாத காரியங்கள் இல்லை
மறவாத மனத்தானே எண்ணிச் செய்யப்பெறின்

en.1: Nothing is too hard to do, if you take care and use the tool of unbroken attention.
en.2: No task is so hard that it can’t be done, if you think it through with a mind that doesn’t forget. The mind is called a tool because it is the inner organ. For those with unbroken thought and unfailing planning, everything is easily done.
en.4: Nothing is impossible to the man who can bring unto his work a mind that is ever wakeful and cautious.
en.5:
Though things are arduous deemed, there’s nought may not be won,
When work with mind’s unslumbering energy and thought is done.
en.6: There is nothing too difficult to be accomplished, if a man set about it carefully, with unflinching endeavour.

padaccheda.m: நீதி நூலுடையார் இவை அரசர்க்கு உரியன என்று உயர்த்துக்கூறிய செயல்களைக் கடைப்பிடித்துச் செய்க
அங்ஙனம் செய்யாது மறந்தவர்க்கு எழுமையினும் நன்மையில்லை ஆகலான்

en.1: Hold to what is praised and do it. Those who scorn it and don’t do it have nothing, in all seven births.
en.2: Hold firm to the acts that writers on statecraft exalt as proper to rulers. Those who forget them have no good in any of seven births. The acts are the three powers, four means, five tasks and six courses. Those who stray from the duty of their caste have only the pains of hell, which is why he says seven births.
en.4: The prince shall devote himself assiduously to works that are commended by the wise: if he neglect them he will suffer in all his future births.
en.5:
Let things that merit praise thy watchful soul employ;
Who these despise attain through sevenfold births no joy.
en.6: Let (a man) observe and do these things which have been praised (by the wise); if he neglects, and fails to perform them, for him there will be no (happiness) throughout the seven births.

padaccheda.w: தம் மகிழ்ச்சியின் தாம் மைந்து உறும் போழ்து
padaccheda.m: அரசர் தம் மகிழ்ச்சிக்கண் தாம் வலியுறும்பொழுது
முற்காலத்து அதனின்ஆய சோர்வாற் கெட்டவர்களை நினைக்க

en.1: When your delight makes you feel strong, remember those who were ruined by neglect.
en.2: When rulers grow strong in their delight, let them think of those who were ruined in the past by the lapse it brings. Thinking of them, they see that they would be ruined the same way, and so they don’t grow strong in it. Neglect and ruin appear together.
en.4: When thou art tempted to be self-complacent and elated, call to thy kind those that have perished by their supineness.
en.5:
Think on the men whom scornful mind hath brought to nought,
When exultation overwhelms thy wildered thought.
en.6: Let (a king) think of those who have been ruined by neglect, when his mind is elated with joy.

en.1: Getting what you have set your mind on is easy, if you can keep your mind on it.
en.2: It is easy for a ruler to get what he has thought of getting, just as he thought it, if he can go on thinking of that alone. It hints that people can’t manage this. Keeping it in mind means striving at it without forgetting.
en.4: Verily it is easy for a man to achieve all that he desireth, provided he keepeth his purpose constantly before his mind.
en.5:
’Tis easy what thou hast in mind to gain,
If what thou hast in mind thy mind retain.
en.6: It is easy for (one) to obtain whatever he may think of, if he can again think of it.

padaccheda.m: தன்கீழ் வாழ்வார் குற்றஞ்செய்தால் அக்குற்றத்தை நாடி
யாவர்மாட்டும் கண்ணோடாது
நடுவுநிலைமையைப் பொருந்தி
அக்குற்றத்திற்குச் சொல்லிய தண்டத்தை நூலோரோடும் ஆராய்ந்து
அவ்வளவிற்றாகச் செய்வதே முறையாம்

en.1: To look into it, show no favour to anyone, hold to fairness and act after weighing it: that is justice.
en.2: When those under him do wrong, a ruler looks into the offence, shows no favour to anyone, even those dearer than life, and holds to the fairness that is a ruler’s nature. He weighs with the learned the punishment set for that offence and gives exactly that much. This is justice.
en.4: Deliberate well and lean not to either side: be impartial and consult with the men of law: that is the way to administer justice.
en.5:
Search out, to no one favour show, with heart that justice loves.
Consult, then act; this is the rule that right approves.
en.6: To examine into (the crimes which may be committed), to show no favor (to any one), to desire to act with impartiality towards all, and to inflict (such punishments) as may be wisely resolved on, constitute rectitude.

padaccheda.m: உலகத்து உயிர் எல்லாம் மழை உளதாயின் உளவாகாநிற்குமே எனினும்
குடிகள் அரசன் செங்கோல் உளதாயின் உளவாகா நிற்கும்

en.1: All the world lives looking to the sky. A ruler’s people live looking to his sceptre.
en.2: All living things in the world depend on rain, and subjects depend on the ruler’s straight sceptre. The sky stands for the food it brings, and the sceptre for the safety it brings. Without that safety, even food is no use to the people.
en.4: The world looketh up to the rain-cloud for life: even so do men look up to the sceptre of the prince for protection.
en.5:
All earth looks up to heav’n whence raindrops fall;
All subjects look to king that ruleth all.
en.6: When there is rain, the living creation thrives; and so when the king rules justly, his subjects thrive.

padaccheda.m: அந்தணர்க்கு உரித்தாய வேதத்திற்கும், அதனாற் சொல்லப்பட்ட அறத்திற்கும் காரணமாய் நிலைபெற்றது
அரசனாற் செலுத்தப்படுகின்ற செங்கோல்

en.1: The ruler’s sceptre stands at the root of the books of the sages and of righteousness.
en.2: The ruler’s straight sceptre stands as the cause of the Vedas of the sages and of the righteousness they teach. The Vedas belong to rulers and merchants too, but they are named for the sages as the foremost. The Vedas and righteousness have no beginning, yet they can’t go on without the sceptre, so it is called their source. Nothing is the source of it.
en.4: The sceptre of the prince is the mainstay of the science of the Brahmans and of righteousness also.
en.5:
Learning and virtue of the sages spring,
From all-controlling sceptre of the king.
en.6: The sceptre of the king is the firm support of the Vedas of the Brahmin, and of all virtues therein described.

padaccheda.w: குடி தழீஇக் கோல் ஓச்சும் மாநில மன்னன் அடி
padaccheda.m: தன் குடிகளையும் அணைத்துச் செங்கோலையும் செலுத்தும் பெருநில வேந்தன் அடியை
பொருந்தி விடார் உலகத்தார்

en.1: The world clings to the feet of the great ruler who holds his people close and wields the sceptre.
en.2: People won’t let go of the feet of the ruler of the great earth who embraces his subjects and wields the straight sceptre. Embracing means speaking sweetly and giving what they need when they are weak. One who does both without fail rules the whole earth, and all have a loving-kindness for him that never leaves.
en.4: Behold the noble prince who ruleth the people of his dominions with loving care: sovereignty will never depart from him.
en.5:
Whose heart embraces subjects all, lord over mighty land
Who rules, the world his feet embracing stands.
en.6: The world will constantly embrace the feet of the great king who rules over his subjects with love.

padaccheda.m: பருவமழையும் குன்றாதவிளைவும் ஒருங்குகூடி
நூல்கள் சொல்லிய இயல்பாற் செங்கோலைச் செலுத்தும் அரசனது நாட்டின்கண்ணவாம்

en.1: Rain and harvest come together in the land of a ruler who wields the sceptre as it should be wielded.
en.2: Rain in season and undiminished harvests come together in the land of a ruler who wields the straight sceptre in the way the books lay down. Sky and earth work as one and plenty flows.
en.4: Behold the prince who wieldeth the sceptre in accordance with the law: seasonal rains and rich harvests have their home in his land.
en.5:
Where king, who righteous laws regards, the sceptre wields,
There fall the showers, there rich abundance crowns the fields.
en.6: Rain and plentiful crops will ever dwell together in the country of the king who sways his sceptre with justice.

padaccheda.m: மன்னவனுக்குப் போரின்கண் வெற்றியைக் கொடுப்பது அவன் எறியும் வேல்அன்று, கோல்
அஃதும் அப்பெற்றித்தாவது, தான் கோடாதாயின்

en.1: It is not the spear that brings a ruler victory. It is the sceptre, and that only if it doesn’t bend.
en.2: What gives a ruler victory in battle is not the spear he throws but the sceptre, and that only if it doesn’t lean. The spear finds its mark only when the sceptre is straight.
en.4: It is not the lance that bringeth victory unto the prince: it is rather his sceptre, and that provided it is straight and leaneth not to either side.
en.5:
Not lance gives kings the victory,
But sceptre swayed with equity.
en.6: It is not the javelin that gives victory, but the king’s sceptre, if it do no injustice.

padaccheda.m: வையகத்தை எல்லாம் அரசன் காக்கும்
அவன்தன்னை அவனது செங்கோலே காக்கும்
அதனை முட்டவந்துழியும் முட்டாமற் செலுத்துவானாயின்

en.1: The ruler guards the whole world. Justice guards him, if he keeps it up without a break.
en.2: The ruler guards all the world, and his own straight sceptre guards him, if he keeps it going even when it meets a block. Think of the ruler who gave justice against his own son, and the one who cut off his own hand.
en.4: The prince is the protector of all his people: and him his sceptre shall guard, provided he alloweth it not ever to lean to either side.
en.5:
The king all the whole realm of earth protects;
And justice guards the king who right respects.
en.6: The king defends the whole world; and justice, when administered without defect, defends the king.

padaccheda.m: முறைவேண்டினார்க்கு எளிய செவ்வியை உடையனாய் அவர் சொல்லியவற்றை நூலோர் பலரோடும் ஆராய்ந்து, நின்ற உண்மைக்கொப்ப முறைசெய்யாத அரசன்
தாழ்ந்த பதத்திலே நின்று தானே கெடும்

en.1: A ruler who isn’t easy to reach, and doesn’t look into things and give justice, will sink low and fall by himself.
en.2: A ruler who doesn’t make himself easy to approach for those seeking justice, and doesn’t examine what they say with many learned men and judge by the truth, stands in a low state and perishes by himself. The low state is one of sin and blame. Righteousness is death to wrongdoers, so he falls even with no enemies.
en.4: Behold the prince who is not easy of access and who judgeth not causes with care: he will fall from his place and perish, even when he hath no enemy.
en.5:
Hard of access, nought searching out, with partial hand
The king who rules, shall sink and perish from the land.
en.6: The king who gives not facile audience (to those who approach him), and who does not examine and pass judgment (on their complaints), will perish in disgrace.

padaccheda.w: குடி புறம் காத்து ஓம்பிக் குற்றம் கடிதல்
padaccheda.m: குடிகளைப் பிறர் நலியாமற் காத்துத் தானும் நலியாது பேணி, அவர்மாட்டுக் குற்றநிகழின் அதனை ஒறுப்பான் ஒழித்தல்
வேந்தனுக்குப் பழியன்று, தொழிலாகலான்

en.1: To protect his people from others, care for them and punish wrongdoing is no stain on a ruler. It is his work.
en.2: To guard his subjects from others, not to harm them himself, and to punish them when they do wrong is no blame to a ruler, because it is his work. There are three punishments: pain, taking property and death. Here the first two are meant. Punishing those under him may seem unrighteous, but cleansing them of wrong is the duty of his caste.
en.4: Behold the prince that guardeth his subjects from enemies both within and without: if he punish them when they go wrong it is not a blemish: it is his duty.
en.5:
Abroad to guard, at home to punish, brings
No just reproach; ’tis work assigned to kings.
en.6: In guarding his subjects (against injury from others), and in preserving them himself, to punish crime is not a fault in a king, but a duty.

padaccheda.m: அரசன் கொடியவர்களைக் கொலையான் ஒறுத்துத் தக்கோரைக் காத்தல்
உழவன் களையைக் களைந்து பைங்கூழைக் காத்ததனோடு ஒக்கும்

en.1: A ruler who punishes the wicked with death is like someone pulling weeds from a green crop.
en.2: A ruler who punishes the wicked with death and protects the worthy is like a farmer who pulls the weeds and saves his green crop. The wicked are arsonists, poisoners, armed killers, thieves, highway robbers, plunderers, adulterers and the like. If he spares them out of pity the world suffers, like a crop among weeds. So killing, too, is the duty of a ruler’s caste.
en.4: Punishing the wicked with death is like the removing of weeds from the cornfield.
en.5:
By punishment of death the cruel to restrain,
Is as when farmer frees from weeds the tender grain.
en.6: For a king to punish criminals with death, is like pulling up the weeds in the green corn.

padaccheda.m: பகைமை பற்றிக் கொல்லுதல் தொழிலை தம்மேற்கொண்டு ஒழுகுவாரினும் கொடியன்

padaccheda.w: அலை மேற்கொண்டு அல்லவை செய்து ஒழுகும் வேந்து
padaccheda.m: பொருள் வெஃகிக் குடிகளை அலைத்தல் தொழிலைத் தன்மேற்கொண்டு முறையல்லவற்றைச் செய்தொழுகும் வேந்தன்

en.1: A ruler who takes to tormenting people and doing wrong is crueller than those who have taken up killing.
en.2: A ruler who covets wealth, takes up tormenting his subjects and does what is not justice is crueller than those who make killing their work out of hatred. What they do is the pain of a moment, and what he does is pain at all times. So tormenting is crueller than killing.
en.4: Behold the prince who oppresseth his subjects and doth iniquity: he is worse than an assassin.
en.5:
Than one who plies the murderer’s trade, more cruel is the king
Who all injustice works, his subjects harassing.
en.6: The king who gives himself up to oppression and acts unjustly (towards his subjects) is more cruel than the man who leads the life of a murderer.

padaccheda.m: ஆறலைக்கும் இடத்துத் தனியே வேல்கொண்டு நின்ற கள்வன்
ஆறுசெல்வானை நின் கைப்பொருள் தாவென்று வேண்டுதலோடு ஒக்கும்
ஒறுத்தல் தொழிலோடு நின்ற அரசன் குடிகளைப் பொருள்வேண்டுதல்

en.1: When one who stands with a sceptre asks, it is like one who stands with a spear saying, “Hand it over.”
en.2: A ruler who stands ready to punish and asks his subjects for wealth is like a thief who stands alone with a spear on a lonely road and tells a traveller to give up what he carries. “Asks” shows this isn’t the tax that is due. He means to punish them if they don’t give, so taking by asking is also crooked rule.
en.4: A request from him who holdeth the sceptre is like the stand and deliver of the highway robber.
en.5:
As ‘Give’ the robber cries with lance uplift,
So kings with sceptred hand implore a gift.
en.6: The request (for money) of him who holds the sceptre, is like the word of a highway robber who stands with a weapon in hand and says ‘‘give up your wealth.”

padaccheda.m: தன் நாட்டு நிகழும் தீமைகளை நாள்தோறும் ஆராய்ந்து அதற்கொக்க முறைமையைச் செய்யாத அரசன்
நாள் தோறும் நாடு இழக்கும்

en.1: When a ruler doesn’t look into things daily and do justice, his land goes to ruin day by day.
en.2: A ruler who doesn’t examine each day the wrongs done in his land and give justice to match loses his land day by day. Losing means getting no benefit from it. Some read it as the land perishing day by day along with the ruler.
en.4: Behold the prince who doth not oversee his administration every day and remove the irregularities therein: his sovereignty will wear away day by day.
en.5:
Who makes no daily search for wrongs, nor justly rules, that king
Doth day by day his realm to ruin bring.
en.6: The country of the king who does not daily examine into the wrongs done and distribute justice, will daily fall to ruin.

padaccheda.m: மேல்விளைவு எண்ணாது, முறைதப்பச் செய்யும் அரசன்
செயலான் முன் ஈட்டிய பொருளையும் பின் ஈட்டுதற்கு ஏதுவாகிய குடிகளையும் சேர இழக்கும்

en.1: A ruler who bends the sceptre and acts without thinking will lose his riches and his people together.
en.2: A ruler who doesn’t think of what will follow and acts against justice loses, all at once, the wealth he has stored and the subjects who would bring him more. What takes the stored wealth is told in the next couplet.
en.4: Behold the thoughtless prince whose rule swerveth from the ways of justice: he will lose his kingdom and his substance also.
en.5:
Whose rod from right deflects, who counsel doth refuse,
At once his wealth and people utterly shall lose.
en.6: The king, who, without reflecting (on its evil consequences), perverts justice, will lose at once both his wealth and his subjects.

padaccheda.m: அரசன் முறைசெய்யாமையான் குடிகள் துன்பமுற்று அதனைப் பொறுக்கமாட்டாது அழுதகண்ணீ்ர் அன்றே
அவன் செல்வத்தைக் குறைக்கும் கருவி

en.1: The tears wept by those who suffer and can’t bear it: are they not the weapon that wears away wealth?
en.2: The tears wept by subjects who suffer because the ruler gives no justice, and who can’t bear it: aren’t these the tool that cuts down his wealth? Wealth is pictured as a tree. The work of the sin is laid on the tears, because nothing is crueller than those tears. So wealth wears away quickly.
en.4: Verily it is the tears of those groaning under oppression that wear away the prosperity of the prince.
en.5:
His people’s tears of sorrow past endurance, are not they
Sharp instruments to wear the monarch’s wealth away?
en.6: Will not the tears, shed by a people who cannot endure the oppression which they suffer (from their king), become a saw to waste away his wealth?

padaccheda.m: அரசர்க்குப் புகழ்கள்தாம் நிலைபெறுதல் செங்கோன்மையான் ஆம்
அச்செங்கோன்மை இல்லையாயின், அவர்க்கு அப்புகழ்கள்தான் உளவாகா

en.1: What makes rulers last is the straight sceptre. Without it, their light won’t last.
en.2: The renown of rulers lasts through the straight sceptre, and without it they have no renown. Once they are blamed their light goes, and so they don’t last either. He puts renown in the plural because it comes from victory, giving and the like, and all of it goes without the straight sceptre.
en.4: It is just rule that bringeth renown unto princes: and an unjust government darkeneth their glory.
en.5:
To rulers’ rule stability is sceptre right;
When this is not, quenched is the rulers’ light.
en.6: Righteous government gives permanence to (the fame of) kings; without that their fame will have no endurance.

padaccheda.m: மழையில்லாமை வையத்து வாழும் உயிர்கட்கு எவ்வகைத் துன்பம் பயக்கும்
அவ்வகைத் துன்பம் பயக்கும், அரசன் தண்ணளி இல்லாமை அவன் நாட்டு வாழும் குடிகட்கு

en.1: What no rain is to the earth, a ruler with no tenderness is to living beings.
en.2: The suffering that a lack of rain brings to living things on earth, a ruler’s lack of tenderness brings to the people of his land. This says in reverse what was said of living by looking to the sky.
en.4: How fareth the earth under a rainless sky? even so fare the people under the rule of a cruel prince.
en.5:
As lack of rain to thirsty lands beneath,
Is lack of grace in kings to all that breathe.
en.6: As is the world without rain, so live a people whose king is without kindness.

padaccheda.m: முறை செய்யாத அரசனது கொடுங்கோலின்கீழ் வாழின்
யாவர்க்கும் பொருளினது இன்மையினும் உடைமை இன்னாது

en.1: Under the sceptre of a ruler who does no justice, having is more painful than having nothing.
en.2: Under the crooked sceptre of a ruler who does no justice, owning wealth is worse for anyone than owning none. In the land of one who isn’t content with his own and craves more, being bound until the hands ache and the like fall only on those who own. So owning is worse than having nothing.
en.4: The condition of the rich man is more galling than that of the poor under the rule of the tyrant prince.
en.5:
To poverty it adds a sharper sting,
To live beneath the sway of unjust king.
en.6: Property gives more sorrow than poverty, to those who live under the sceptre of a king without justice.

padaccheda.m: மன்னவன் தான்செய்யும் பொருளை முறைதப்பச் செய்யுமாயின்
அவன்நாட்டுப் பருவமழை இன்றாம்வகை மேகம் பொழிதலைச் செய்யாது

en.1: If the ruler acts against justice, the sky will fail its season and won’t rain.
en.2: If a ruler acts crookedly in what he does, the clouds don’t pour in season in his land. Rain turned aside means rain not falling when it should. The reason is given in the next couplet.
en.4: The heavens will not send showers in their season if the prince swerveth from justice and right.
en.5:
Where king from right deflecting, makes unrighteous gain,
The seasons change, the clouds pour down no rain.
en.6: If the king acts contrary to justice, rain will become unseasonable, and the heavens will withhold their showers.

padaccheda.m: காத்தற்குஉரிய அரசன் உயிர்களைக் காவான் ஆயின்
அறன் இல்லாத அவன் நாட்டுப் பசுக்களும் பால் குன்றும்
அந்தணரும் நூல்களை மறந்து விடுவர்

en.1: If the protector doesn’t protect, cows give less and those of the six duties forget their books.
en.2: If the ruler who should protect living things doesn’t, the cows of his land, which has no righteousness, give less milk, and the sages forget their books. The six duties are studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating, giving and receiving. With less milk there is no offering, and with no recitation no sacrifice, and so the sky won’t rain.
en.4: The udders of the cow will be dried up and the Brahman will forget his science if the prince ruleth not with justice.
en.5:
Where guardian guardeth not, udder of kine grows dry,
And Brahmans’ sacred lore will all forgotten lie.
en.6: If the guardian (of the country) neglects to guard it, the produce of the cows will fail, and the men of six-duties viz. the brahmins will forget the vedas.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் தன்னின் மெலியார் மேல் சென்றவழி அதனை நடுவாக நின்று ஆராய்ந்து
பின்னும் அது செய்யாமற் பொருட்டு அவனை அக்குற்றத்திற்கு ஒப்ப ஒறுப்பானே அரசனாவான்

en.1: A ruler is one who looks into a wrong fairly and punishes to fit it, so that it won’t be done again.
en.2: When a man goes against someone weaker, the true ruler looks into it impartially and, so that he won’t do it again, punishes him in measure with the offence. It follows that failing to examine fairly, and punishing too much for some other reason, are acts that frighten subjects.
en.4: The prince shall measure the guilt of the offender and punish him so that he offend not again: but the punishment shall not be excessive.
en.5:
Who punishes, investigation made in due degree,
So as to stay advance of crime, a king is he.
en.6: He is a king who having equitably examined (any injustice which has been brought to his notice), suitably punishes it, so that it may not be again committed.

padaccheda.m: அவ்வொத்தாங்கு ஒறுத்தல் தொடங்குங்கால் அளவிறப்பச் செய்வார்போல் தொடங்கி
செய்யுங்கால் அளவிறவாமல் செய்க
ஆக்கம் தங்கண் நெடுங்காலம் நிற்றலை வேண்டுவார்

en.1: Raise the blow sharply but let it land softly, if you want your gains to stay with you for long.
en.2: Those who want prosperity to stay long with them should begin a punishment as if to go beyond the measure, but keep within it when they carry it out. Raising it sharply makes wrongdoers afraid, and striking softly keeps everyone else from dread. Raising and striking are images.
en.4: Those that desire that their power shall last, let them brandish the rod smartly but lay it on soft.
en.5:
For length of days with still increasing joys on Heav’n who call,
Should raise the rod with brow severe, but let it gently fall.
en.6: Let the king, who desires that his prosperity may long remain, commence his preliminary enquiries with strictness, and then punish with mildness.

padaccheda.m: குடிகள் வெருவிய செயல்களைச் செய்துநடக்கும் வெங்கோலனாம் ஆயின்
அரசன் ஒருதலையாகக் கடிதிற் கெடும்

en.1: A wielder of the cruel sceptre, who lives by what terrifies people, is sure to fall, and soon.
en.2: If a ruler lives by acts that terrify his subjects and is cruel in his sceptre, he is certain to fall quickly. Those acts and that ruin are told in what follows.
en.4: Behold the prince who ruleth with a rod of iron and causeth anguish unto his people: he shall stand without a friend and perish forthwith.
en.5:
Where subjects dread of cruel wrongs endure,
Ruin to unjust king is swift and sure.
en.6: The cruel-sceptred king, who acts so as to put his subjects in fear, will certainly and quickly come to ruin.

padaccheda.w: இறை கடியன் என்று உரைக்கும் இன்னாச் சொல்வேந்தன்
padaccheda.m: குடிகளான் நம்மிறைவன் கடியன் என்று சொல்லப்படும் இன்னாத சொல்லையுடைய வேந்தன்
ஆயுளும்குறைந்து செல்வமும் கடிதின் இழக்கும்

en.1: A ruler of whom people say the bitter words “Our ruler is harsh” will see his days shortened and soon fall.
en.2: A ruler of whom his subjects speak the bitter words “our ruler is harsh” has his life cut short and quickly loses his wealth. The words are bitter because they come from hurt hearts and bring harm. His span becomes shorter than that of rulers not spoken of this way.
en.4: Behold the prince whose cruelty is a byword among his people: his days will be shortened and he will perish forthwith.
en.5:
‘Ah! cruel is our king,’ where subjects sadly say,
His age shall dwindle, swift his joy of life decay.
en.6: The king who is spoken of as cruel will quickly perish, his life becoming shortened.

padaccheda.m: தன்னைக் காண வேண்டுவார்க்குக் காலம் அரியனாய்க் கண்டால் இன்னாத முகத்தினை உடையானது பெரிய செல்வம்
பேயாற் காணப்பட்டாற் போல்வதொரு குற்றம் உடைத்து

en.1: The great wealth of someone hard to see, with a sour face, is like something a demon has laid eyes on.
en.2: The great wealth of a man whom those who want to see him can rarely see, and whose face is unpleasant when they do, has the fault of something a demon has seized. No one goes near him, so his wealth is of no use to him or to anyone else. Seeing here means taking possession.
en.4: Behold the dour-faced prince who is inaccessible to his people: the wealth in his hands is like treasure guarded by a demon.
en.5:
Whom subjects scarce may see, of harsh forbidding countenance;
His ample wealth shall waste, blasted by demon’s glance.
en.6: The great wealth of him who is difficult of access and possesses a sternness of countenance, is like that which has been obtained by a devil.

padaccheda.m: அரசன் கடிய சொல்லையும் உடையனாய்க் கண்ணோட்டமும் இலன் ஆயின்

padaccheda.w: நெடுஞ் செல்வம் நீடு இன்றி ஆங்கே கெடும்
padaccheda.m: அவனது பெரிய செல்வம் நீடுதலின்றி அப்பொழுதே கெடும்

en.1: If you have a harsh tongue and no kind eye, even vast wealth will perish at once, without lasting.
en.2: If a ruler has harsh speech and no kindly regard, his great wealth doesn’t last but perishes then and there. Harsh speech and excessive punishment, two of the seven vices, are counted here among the acts that frighten. “Great” shows that wealth is not so small that these should end it at once, and yet they do.
en.4: If the prince is harsh of word and unforgiving, his prosperity, be it ever so great, will come to an end quickly.
en.5:
The tyrant, harsh in speech and hard of eye,
His ample joy, swift fading, soon shall die.
en.6: The abundant wealth of the king whose words are harsh and whose looks are void of kindness, will instantly perish instead of abiding long, with him.

padaccheda.m: கடிய சொல்லும் குற்றத்தின் மிக்க தண்டமும்
அரசனது பகை வெல்லுதற்கு ஏற்ற மாறுபாடாகிய இரும்பினைத் தேய்க்கும் அரமாம்

en.1: Harsh words and punishment past all measure are the file that wears away a ruler’s conquering strength.
en.2: Harsh words and punishment beyond the offence are files that wear down the iron of a ruler’s strength to beat his enemies. Harsh words ruin his army, excessive punishment ruins his land, and so his strength shrinks. He calls that strength iron to show that even hard things wear away. The ruler who does these loses life, strength and wealth.
en.4: Words that are harsh and punishments that are excessive are the files that file away the iron of power.
en.5:
Harsh words and punishments severe beyond the right,
Are file that wears away the monarch’s conquering might.
en.6: Severe words and excessive punishments will be a file to waste away a king’s power for destroying (his enemies).

padaccheda.m: அப்பிழைப்பால் தன்காரியம் தப்பியவழித் தன்னைச் சினமாகிய குற்றத்தின்கண்ணே செலுத்தி அவரை வெகுளுமாயின்
அவன் செல்வம் நாள்தோறும் சுருங்கும்

en.1: If a ruler who doesn’t think things through with his circle flies into a rage, his good fortune shrinks.
en.2: A ruler who doesn’t share the thinking with his ministers and work it through with them, and who rages at them when the work fails, sees his wealth shrink daily. Ministers are his circle because they share his burden. If he blames them and rages, they take fright and leave, and then he has no way to set it right or to carry the burden.
en.4: Behold the prince who will not take counsel with his councillors but who falleth into a passion when his projects fail: his prosperity will wane away.
en.5:
Who leaves the work to those around, and thinks of it no more;
If he in wrathful mood reprove, his prosperous days are o’er!
en.6: The prosperity of that king will waste away, who without reflecting (on his affairs himself), commits them to his ministers, and (when a failure occurs) gives way to anger, and rages against them.

padaccheda.m: செருவருதற்கு முன்னே தனக்குப் புகல் ஆவதோர் அரண் செய்துகொள்ளாத அரசன்
அது வந்த காலத்து ஏமம் இன்மையான் வெருவிக் கடிதிற் கெடும்

en.1: A ruler who doesn’t build defences before war comes will take fright when it does, and quickly fall.
en.2: A ruler who doesn’t build a fort as his refuge before war comes takes fright when it comes, having no safety, and falls quickly. Those with him fear the enemy and leave, so he is alone and afraid, and he falls into the enemy’s power.
en.4: Behold the prince who looketh not to his defences while yet there is time: when he is surprised by a war be will be seized with trembling and perish quickly.
en.5:
Who builds no fort whence he may foe defy,
In time of war shall fear and swiftly die.
en.6: The king who has not provided himself with a place of defence, will in times of war be seized with fear and quickly ‘perish.

padaccheda.m: கடுங்கோலனாய அரசன் நீதிநூன் முதலிய கல்லாதாரைத் தனக்குப் பகுதியாகக் கூட்டாநிற்கும்
அக்கூட்டம்அல்லது நிலத்திற்கு மிகையாய பாரம் பிறிது இல்லை

en.1: A harsh sceptre binds the unlearned to itself. The earth has no burden but that.
en.2: A ruler of the harsh sceptre gathers round him as officers men unlearned in statecraft and other books. The earth has no extra burden but that gathering. He gathers only those who will do such work with him. The earth bears everything else by nature, so this alone is a burden to it.
en.4: The tyranny that yoketh to itself charlatans is the only burden under which the earth groaneth: there is none other beside.
en.5:
Tyrants with fools their counsels share:
Earth can no heavier burthen bear!
en.6: The earth bears up no greater burden than ignorant men whom a cruel sceptre attaches to itself (as the ministers of its evil deeds.)

padaccheda.w: கண்ணோட்டம் என்னும் கழி பெரும் காரிகை உண்மையான்
padaccheda.m: கண்ணோட்டம் என்று சொல்லப்படுகின்ற சிறப்புடைய அழகு அரசர் மாட்டு உண்டாகலான்
இவ்வுலகம் உண்டாகாநின்றது

en.1: This world exists because of the surpassing beauty called kindly regard.
en.2: Because the surpassing beauty called kindly regard is found in rulers, this world exists. A ruler without it does terrifying things, and the people of his land have no more safety than a herd of deer that has met a tiger.
en.4: Behold that ravishing Beauty called Considerateness: the world cannot go on smoothly without her.
en.5:
Since true benignity, that grace exceeding great, resides
In kingly souls, the world in happy state abides.
en.6: The world exists through that greatest ornament (of princes,) a gracious demeanour.

padaccheda.m: உலகநடை கண்ணோட்டத்தின்கண் நிகழ்வது
ஆகலான், அக்கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாதார் உளராதல் இந்நிலத்துக்குப் பாரமாதற்கே, பிறிது ஒன்றற்கு அன்று

en.1: The way of the world rests on kindly regard. Those without it exist only as a burden on the earth.
en.2: The ways of the world, such as helping others, protecting them and forgiving their mistakes, go on through kindly regard. So those without it exist only to load this earth, for nothing else, since they are of no use to themselves or to anyone.
en.4: In considerateness have the amenities of life their existence: those who possess it not are a burden unto the earth.
en.5:
The world goes on its wonted way, since grace benign is there;
All other men are burthen for the earth to bear.
en.6: The prosperity of the world springs from the kindliness, the existence of those who have no (kindliness) is a burden to the earth.

padaccheda.m: பண் என்ன பயத்ததாம் பாடல்தொழிலோடு பொருத்தம் இன்றாயின்
அதுபோலக் கண் என்னபயத்ததாம் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத இடத்து

en.1: What use is a melody that doesn’t fit the song? What use is an eye without kindly regard?
en.2: What use is a melody that doesn’t fit the work of singing? In the same way, what use is an eye where there is no kindly regard? A melody is useless unless joined to the techniques of voice and harp, and an eye is useless unless joined to kindly regard.
en.4: To what end is the song that cannot be sung? and what is the worth of the eye that showeth not indulgence?
en.5:
Where not accordant with the song, what use of sounding chords?
What gain of eye that no benignant light affords?
en.6: Of what avail is a song if it be inconsistent with harmony? What is the use of eyes which possess no kindliness?

padaccheda.m: கண்டார்க்கு முகத்தின்கண் உளபோல் தோன்றல் அல்லது வேறுஎன்ன பயனைச் செய்யும்
அளவிறவாத கண்ணோடுதலை உடையவல்லாத கண்கள்

en.1: Eyes without kindly regard, in due measure, only seem to be there in the face. What else do they do?
en.2: Eyes without a kindly regard that keeps within measure do nothing except seem, to those who look at them, to be in the face. They serve no other purpose. “In measure” rules out too much kindly regard.
en.4: What is the use of eyes that merely show in the face, if they show not consideration for others according to their measure?
en.5:
The seeming eye to face gives no expressive light,
When not with duly meted kindness bright.
en.6: Beyond appearing to be in the face, what good do they do, those eyes in which is no well-regulated kindness?

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் கண்ணிற்கு அணியும் கலமாவது கண்ணோட்டம்
அக்கலம் இல்லையாயின் அஃது அறிவுடையோரால் புண் என்று அறியப்படும்

en.1: Kindly regard is the eye’s jewel. Without it, an eye is taken for a sore.
en.2: Kindly regard is the jewel an eye wears, and it has no other. Without it, the wise know that eye for a sore. It may look like an eye, but it brings suffering through its diseases and its clinging to what the senses seize.
en.4: Indulgence is the ornament of the eye: the eye that hath it not will be looked upon as a mere sore.
en.5:
Benignity is eyes’ adorning grace;
Without it eyes are wounds disfiguring face.
en.6: Kind looks are the ornaments of the eyes; without these they will be considered (by the wise) to be merely two sores.

padaccheda.m: ஓடுதற்கு உரிய கண்ணோடு பொருந்திவைத்து அஃது ஓடாதவர்
இயங்காநின்றார் ஆயினும், மண்ணோடு பொருந்திநிற்கின்ற மரத்தினை ஒப்பர்

en.1: People who have eyes, yet whose eyes never turn kindly to others, are like trees fixed in the soil.
en.2: Those who have eyes made for turning towards others, and don’t turn them, are like trees standing in the soil, though they walk about. A tree has its “eyes” too, and they don’t turn. He rejects the reading of a wooden doll coated in plaster, because that rests on a hidden core, not on the eye that is seen.
en.4: Behold the men whose eyes show not consideration towards others: verily they are no better than the trees of the earth.
en.5:
Whose eyes ’neath brow infixed diffuse no ray
Of grace; like tree in earth infixed are they.
en.6: They resemble the trees of the earth, who, although they have eyes, never look kindly (on others).

padaccheda.m: கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாதவர் கண்ணுடையரும் அல்லர்
கண்ணுடையவர் கண்ணோட்டம் இலராதலும் இல்லை

en.1: Those without kindly regard have no eyes. Those who have eyes are never without it.
en.2: Those without kindly regard don’t even have eyes, and those who have eyes are never without it. In people who have eyes, kindly regard moves in the very act of seeing.
en.4: Verily they are blind, those who are not considerate towards others: and there are none that truly see but are indulgent to others’ faults.
en.5:
Eyeless are they whose eyes with no benignant lustre shine;
Who’ve eyes can never lack the light of grace benign.
en.6: Men without kind looks are men without eyes: those who (really) have eyes are also not devoid of kind looks.

padaccheda.m: முறைசெய்தலாகிய தம்தொழில் அழியாமல் கண்ணோடவல்ல வேந்தர்க்கு
உரித்தாம் தன்மைஉடைத்து இவ்வுலகம்

en.1: This world belongs to those who can show kindly regard without ruining the work they must do.
en.2: This world is the rightful possession of rulers who can show kindly regard without ruining their work of justice. Justice is ruined when a ruler spares friends who have harmed others. To withhold it where justice would suffer and show it elsewhere is rare, and the whole world comes to such rulers for a long time.
en.4: Behold the man who can be considerate towards others without derogating from any of his duties: he will inherit the earth.
en.5:
Who can benignant smile, yet leave no work undone;
By them as very own may all the earth be won.
en.6: The world is theirs (kings) who are able to show kindness, without injury to their affairs, (administration of justice.)

padaccheda.m: தம்மை ஒறுக்கும் இயல்புடையார் இடத்தும்
கண்ணோட்டம் உடையராய்க் குற்றத்தைப் பொறுக்கும் இயல்பே அரசர்க்குத் தலையாய இயல்பாவது

en.1: Even with people whose way is to hurt you, the highest quality is to show kindly regard and put up with it.
en.2: Even towards those whose nature is to hurt them, showing kindly regard and bearing the fault is the foremost quality of a ruler. These are people the ruler knows well, as “whose nature” implies.
en.4: It is nobility to forbear and show indulgence even unto those that have offended thee.
en.5:
To smile on those that vex, with kindly face,
Enduring long, is most excelling grace.
en.6: Patiently to bear with, and shew kindness to those who grieve us, is the most excellent of all dispositions.

padaccheda.m: பயின்றார் தமக்கு நஞ்சிடக் கண்டுவைத்தும் கண் மறுக்கமாட்டாமையின் அதனை உண்டு பின்னும் அவரோடு மேவுவர்
யாவரானும் விரும்பத்தக்க கண்ணோட்டத்தினை வேண்டுமவர்

en.1: Those who want the courtesy everyone admires will watch poison being poured, drink it and stay content.
en.2: Those who want the kindly regard that all desire, even seeing friends put poison in for them, can’t bring themselves to refuse. They drink it and stay close to those friends after. He takes நாகரிகம் as kindly regard. A ruler should spare people in this way only when the wrong is against himself.
en.4: Those who desire to be styled the very pink of courtesy will drink off even the poison that hath been mixed for them before their very eyes.
en.5:
They drink with smiling grace, though poison interfused they see,
Who seek the praise of all-esteemed courtesy.
en.6: Those who desire (to cultivate that degree of) urbanity which all shall love, even after swallowing the poison served to them by their friends, will be friendly with them.

padaccheda.m: ஒற்றும், புகழமைந்த நீதிநூலுமாகிய இவை இரண்டனையும்
அரசன் தன் இரண்டு கண்ணுமாகத் தெளிக

en.1: Spies and books of high repute: a ruler should be clear that these two are his eyes.
en.2: A ruler should settle on spies and the renowned books of statecraft as his two eyes. Spies go through all the expanse his own eyes can’t reach and report what happened. The books tell him what to do about it, where his own understanding can’t reach. They are his eye of flesh and his eye of wisdom.
en.4: Let the prince understand that Political Science and his Intelligence Corps are the eyes wherewith he seeth.
en.5:
These two: the code renowned, and spies,
In these let king confide as eyes.
en.6: Let a king consider as his eyes these two things, a spy and a book (of laws) universally esteemed.

padaccheda.w: எல்லார்க்கும் எல்லாம் நிகழ்பவை எஞ்ஞான்றும் வல் அறிதல்
padaccheda.m: எல்லார்கண்ணும் நிகழ்வன எல்லாவற்றையும், நாள்தோறும் ஒற்றான் விரைந்தறிதல்
அரசனுக்கு உரிய தொழில்

en.1: To know quickly, every day, all that happens to everyone is a ruler’s work.
en.2: A ruler’s proper work is to learn quickly through spies, every day, everything that happens among all people, whether enemies, neutrals or friends: good and bad words and deeds alike. He must know at once, so that he can show favour or punish as each deserves.
en.4: It is the duty of the prince to learn betimes everything that befalleth every man and every day.
en.5:
Each day, of every subject every deed,
’Tis duty of the king to learn with speed.
en.6: It is the duty of a king to know quickly (by a spy) what all happens, daily, amongst all men.

padaccheda.m: ஒற்றினானே எல்லார்கண்ணும் நிகழ்ந்தவற்றை ஒற்றுவித்து அவற்றான் எய்தும் பயனை ஆராயாத அரசன்
வென்றியடையக் கிடந்தது வேறொரு நெறியில்லை

en.1: A ruler who doesn’t spy through his spies and weigh what they find has no road to victory.
en.2: A ruler who doesn’t have spies watch what happens among all people, and doesn’t weigh what can be gained from it, has no other road to victory. Knowing neither, he lies open to his enemies, and nothing else can cure that. He allows the reading “there is no victory for him to win” as well.
en.4: Behold the prince that learneth not the happenings about him by means of scouts and spies: conquests are not for him.
en.5:
By spies who spies, not weighing things they bring,
Nothing can victory give to that unwary king.
en.6: There is no way for a king to obtain conquests, who knows not the advantage of discoveries made by a spy.

padaccheda.w: தம் வினை செய்வார் சுற்றம் வேண்டாதார் என்ற அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது
padaccheda.m: தம் காரியம் செய்வார், சுற்றத்தார், பகைவர் என்று சொல்லப்பட்ட அனைவரையும் சொல், செயல்களான் ஆராய்வானே
ஒற்றனாவான்

en.1: A spy is someone who watches everyone alike: those who do your work, your own kin, and those who wish you ill.
en.2: A spy is the one who examines, through their words and deeds, all those who do the ruler’s work, his kin and his enemies. The ruler must know what his workers do, what his kin do to him and his land, and how his enemies probe his weak moments. So none of the three may be left out.
en.4: The prince shalt set spies to watch closely the officers of the realm, his own kindred, and his enemies.
en.5:
His officers, his friends, his enemies,
All these who watch are trusty spies.
en.6: He is a spy who watches all men, to wit, those who are in the king’s employment, his relatives, and his enemies.

padaccheda.m: ஒற்றப்பட்டார் கண்டால், ஐயுறாத வடிவோடு பொருந்தி
அவர் ஐயுற்று அறியலுறின் செயிர்த்து நோக்கிய அவர் கண்ணிற்கு அஞ்சாது நின்று
நான்கு உபாயமும் செய்தாலும், மனத்துக் கொண்டவற்றை உமிழாமை வல்லவனே ஒற்றனாவான்

en.1: A spy is someone with a look that draws no suspicion, who doesn’t flinch under a stare, and who never lets anything spill.
en.2: A spy is one who takes a form the people he watches won’t suspect, such as a Brahmin’s or a merchant’s. If they do grow suspicious he doesn’t fear their angry stare, and whichever of the four means they try on him, he doesn’t spit out what is in his mind.
en.4: Behold the man who can wear an unsuspicious appearance, who will not know confusion before any man, and who can guard his secrets from ever leaking out: he is the proper man for the work of Intelligence.
en.5:
Of unsuspected mien and all-unfearing eyes,
Who let no secret out, are trusty spies.
en.6: A spy is one who is able to assume an appearance which may create no suspicion (in the minds of others), who fears no man’s face, and who never reveals (his purpose).

padaccheda.m: முற்றத் துறந்து ஆராயும் விரத ஒழுக்கினராயும், உள்புகுதற்கு அரியஇடங்கள் எல்லாம் உள்புக்கு ஆராயவேண்டுவன ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்து
ஆண்டையார் ஐயுற்றுப்பிடித்து எல்லாத் துன்பமும் செய்துகேட்டாலும் தன்னை வெளிப்படுத்தாதவனே ஒற்றனாவான்

en.1: A spy takes the form of those who have renounced, goes where others can’t and searches, and gives nothing away, whatever is done to them.
en.2: A spy keeps the vows of those who have wholly renounced, such as pilgrimage to sacred waters, gets into every place hard to enter and finds out what he must. People seldom harm one they take for holy, but even if they suspect him, seize him and torture him, he doesn’t reveal himself. Some take படிவம் as only a disguise.
en.4: Spies and scouts shall disguise themselves as ascetics and holy men, and their investigation shall be thorough: and whatever is done them, they shall not let out their secrets.
en.5:
As monk or devotee, through every hindrance making way,
A spy, whate’er men do, must watchful mind display.
en.6: He is a spy who, assuming the appearance of an ascetic, goes into (whatever place he wishes), examines into (all that is needful), and never discovers himself, whatever may be done to him.

reading.note: படிவம் can mean a form or a vow. The plain reading takes form. He takes vow.

padaccheda.m: ஒற்றப்பட்டார் மறையச்செய்த செயல்களை அவர்களுக்கு உள்ளாயினாரால் கேட்க வல்லனாய்
கேட்டறிந்த செயல்களில் பின் ஐயப்படாது துணியவல்லவனே ஒற்றனாவான்

en.1: A spy is someone who can hear what has been hidden, and has no doubt about what they have learned.
en.2: A spy can hear what those he watches did in secret, from people close to them, and then settle on what he heard without doubt. He finds who knows, gets near without raising suspicion, leads them on with fitting words and deeds until they tell it themselves, and listens as if it were nothing to him. If he reports with doubts, the ruler can’t act.
en.4: Behold the man who can draw out secrets from others and whose information is ever unconfused and clear: he is the man for the work of intelligence.
en.5:
A spy must search each hidden matter out,
And full report must render, free from doubt.
en.6: A spy is one who is able to discover what is hidden, and who retains no doubt concerning what he has known.

padaccheda.m: ஓர் ஒற்றன் ஒற்றிவந்து அறிவித்த காரியம் தன்னையும்
பிறன்ஓர் ஒற்றனாலும் ஒற்றுவித்து ஒப்புமை கண்டுகொள்க

en.1: What one spy has spied out and brought you, have another spy find out too.
en.2: Have what one spy has found and reported spied out by another spy as well, and see whether the two match. A spy may side with those he watches and report falsely, so one man’s word can’t be trusted.
en.4: Even the information that hath been obtained by a spy shall be tested by that of another.
en.5:
Spying by spies, the things they tell
To test by other spies is well.
en.6: Let not a king receive the information which a spy has discovered and made known to him, until he has examined it by another spy.

padaccheda.m: ஒற்றரை ஆளுமிடத்து ஒருவனை ஒருவன் அறியாமல் ஆள்க
அங்ஙனம் ஆண்ட ஒற்றர் மூவரை ஒருபொருள்மேல் விட்டால், அம்மூவர் சொல்லும், பயனால் ஒத்தனவாயின் அதுமெய்யென்று தெளியப்படும்

en.1: Use spies so that one spy doesn’t know another. When three agree, believe it.
en.2: Employ spies so that none knows another. Send three such spies on one matter, and if what all three say agrees in substance, trust it as true. Spies who knew each other would agree among themselves. Three can’t easily become of one mind, or stay so. If their words don’t agree, look further.
en.4: See that no spy knoweth the others engaged in the same work: when three reports agree, thou mayest give credence to them.
en.5:
One spy must not another see: contrive it so;
And things by three confirmed as truth you know.
en.6: Let a king employ spies so that one may have no knowledge of the other; and when the information of three agrees together, let him receive it.

padaccheda.m: மறைந்தவை அறிந்து கூறிய ஒற்றின்கண் செய்யும் சிறப்பினை, அரசன் பிறர்அறியச் செய்யாது ஒழிக
செய்தானாயின், தன்னகத்து அடக்கப்படும் மறையைத் தானே புறத்திட்டானாம்

en.1: Don’t honour a spy where others can see. If you do, you have brought your own secret out into the open.
en.2: A ruler shouldn’t honour a spy who has reported hidden things where others can know of it. If he does, he himself throws out the secret he should keep: that the man is a spy, and what he said. People will ask who this man is and why he was honoured, and those who ask and answer are outsiders.
en.4: Reward not openly thy officers of Intelligence: for if thou do, thou merely lettest out thy own secret.
en.5:
Reward not trusty spy in others’ sight,
Or all the mystery will come to light.
en.6: Let not a king publicly confer on a spy any marks of his favor; if he does, he will divulge his own secret.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவரை உடையர் என்று சொல்லச் சிறந்தது ஊக்கம்
அவ்வூக்கம் இல்லாதார் வேறுடையது தானும் உடையர் ஆவாரோ? ஆகார்

en.1: Drive is what truly counts as having. Do those without it really have whatever else they have?
en.2: What most deserves the word “having” is drive. Those who lack it can’t be said to have even the other things they own. They have no power to keep them, so they will lose them too.
en.4: Those that possess energy are alone to be called rich: as to those that possess it not, do they really possess what they own?
en.5:
’Tis energy gives men o’er that they own a true control;
They nothing own who own not energy of soul.
en.6: Energy makes out the man of property; as for those who are destitute of it, do they (really) possess what they possess?

padaccheda.m: ஊக்கம் உடைமையே ஒருவனுக்கு நிலைநின்ற உடைமையாவது
மற்றைப் பொருளுடைமை நிலைநில்லாது நீங்கிப்போம்

en.1: To have spirit is to truly have something. Having wealth doesn’t last. It slips away.
en.2: Having drive is the possession that stays with you. Having wealth won’t stay, but goes. Drive is a quality of the mind, so it lasts. Wealth is separate from the body and given to perishing, so it doesn’t, and it isn’t truly a possession at all.
en.4: Energy is the veritable possession of a man: for wealth endureth not forever and will depart from him one day.
en.5:
The wealth of mind man owns a real worth imparts,
Material wealth man owns endures not, utterly departs.
en.6: The possession of (energy of) mind is true property; the possession of wealth passes away and abides not.

padaccheda.m: இழந்தாராயினும் யாம் கைப்பொருளை இழந்தேம் என்று அலமரார்
நிலைபெற்ற ஊக்கத்தைக் கைப்பொருளாக உடையார்

en.1: Those who hold lasting drive in their hand don’t fret, saying “Our prosperity is lost.”
en.2: Even when it is gone, those who hold lasting drive as their wealth in hand don’t fret, saying “We have lost our wealth.” He gives the reason in the next couplet.
en.4: Behold the men that hold in their hands the resource called energy: they will never despair, saying, Alas, we are ruined!
en.5:
‘Lost is our wealth,’ they utter not this cry distressed,
The men of firm concentred energy of soul possessed.
en.6: They who are possessed of enduring energy will not trouble themselves saying, “we have lost our property.”

padaccheda.m: அசைவில்லாத ஊக்கத்தை உடையான் மாட்டு
பொருள்தானே வழி வினவிக்கொண்டு செல்லும்

en.1: Prosperity asks the way and goes by itself to someone whose drive never wavers.
en.2: Wealth itself goes, asking the way like a traveller, to the one whose drive doesn’t weaken in hardship. So drive, which causes wealth, is greater than any wealth already gained.
en.4: Behold the man who remitteth not ever from his activity: Good Fortune inquireth the way to his home.
en.5:
The man of energy of soul inflexible,
Good fortune seeks him out and comes a friend to dwell.
en.6: Wealth will find its own way to the man of unfailing energy.

padaccheda.m: நின்ற நீரின் அளவினவாம் நீர்ப்பூக்களின் தாளினது நீளங்கள்
அதுபோல் மக்கள்தம் ஊக்கத்து அளவினதாம் அவர் உயர்ச்சி

en.1: The stem of a water flower is as long as the water is deep. People rise as high as their spirit.
en.2: The stems of water flowers are as long as the standing water is deep. In the same way, people’s height is as great as their drive. As the stem lengthens with the water, people rise as their drive grows. Rising here means growing in wealth and armies.
en.4: The water with which a plant is watered is the measure of the luxuriance of its flower: even so, the spirit of a man is the measure of his fortunes.
en.5:
With rising flood the rising lotus flower its stem unwinds;
The dignity of men is measured by their minds.
en.6: The stalks of water-flowers are proportionate to the depth of water; so is mens’ greatness proportionate to their minds.

padaccheda.m: அரசராயினார் கருதுவது எல்லாம் தம் உயர்ச்சியையே கருதுக
அவ்வுயர்ச்சி பால்வகையாற் கூடிற்றில்லையாயினும், அக்கருத்துத் தள்ளாமை நீர்மை உடைத்து

en.1: Let all your thoughts be of rising higher. Even when it fails, it has the nature of not failing.
en.2: Rulers should think of nothing but their own rising. Even if fate keeps it from coming about, that aim has the nature of not failing. Mostly it doesn’t fail, and when it does there has been no lapse in effort, so good people don’t blame them.
en.4: Let all thy purposes be grand: for then even if they fail, their glory will tarnish never.
en.5:
Whate’er you ponder, let your aim be lofty still,
Fate cannot hinder always, thwart you as it will.
en.6: In all that a king thinks of, let him think of his greatness, and if it should be thrust from him (by fate), it will have the nature of not being thrust from him.

padaccheda.w: களிறு புதை அம்பின் பட்டுப் பாடு ஊன்றும்
padaccheda.m: களிறு புதையாகிய அம்பாற் புண்பட்ட இடத்துத் தளராது தன் பெருமையை நிலைநிறுத்தும்
அதுபோல ஊக்கமுடையார், தாம்கருதிய உயர்ச்சிக்குச் சிதைவு வந்தவிடத்துத் தளராது தம் பெருமையை நிலைநிறுத்துவர்

en.1: The strong don’t falter when things fall apart. An elephant struck by a mass of arrows stands its ground.
en.2: An elephant wounded by a sheaf of arrows doesn’t weaken, but holds to its greatness. In the same way, those with drive don’t weaken when the rising they aimed at meets ruin, but hold to their greatness. Even if it fails, they go on and finish what they set out to do.
en.4: Men of spirit flinch not before a defeat: the elephant planteth his legs only more firmly when he is hit by the deep-piercing arrow.
en.5:
The men of lofty mind quail not in ruin’s fateful hour,
The elephant retains his dignity mid arrows’ deadly shower.
en.6: The strong-minded will not faint, even when all is lost; the elephant stands firm, even when wounded by a shower of arrows.

padaccheda.m: ஊக்கம் இல்லாத அரசர்
இவ்வுலகத்தாருள் யாம் வண்மையுடையேம் என்று தம்மைத்தாம் மதித்தலைப் பெறார்

en.1: Those without spirit will never have the pride of thinking, “In this world, we are the generous ones.”
en.2: Rulers without drive never reach the pride of rating themselves generous among the people of this world. Without drive there is no effort, without effort no wealth, without wealth no giving, and without giving no pride. The joy of winning through giving is known only to the giver, so he puts it in the first person.
en.4: Behold the men that are wanting in energy: the glory of an exhaustless liberality can never be theirs.
en.5:
The soulless man can never gain
Th’ ennobling sense of power with men.
en.6: Those who have no (greatness of) mind, will not acquire that joy of saying in the world, “we have exercised liberality.”

padaccheda.m: எல்லா விலங்கினும் தான் பேருடம்பினது
யானைத் தன்னைப் புலி எதிர்ப்படின் அதற்கு அஞ்சும்

en.1: An elephant may be huge and sharp of tusk, yet it fears a tiger’s attack.
en.2: The elephant has the largest body of all beasts and sharp tusks as well, yet it fears the tiger it meets. It has more strength and better weapons, but no drive, and the tiger has drive. This is said of something else: rulers stronger and better armed than their enemies, if they have no drive, fear enemies who have it.
en.4: What availeth his size and his sharp tapering tusks? The heart of the elephant sinketh when he seeth the tiger spring.
en.5:
Huge bulk of elephant with pointed tusk all armed,
When tiger threatens shrinks away alarmed.
en.6: Although the elephant has a large body, and a sharp tusk; yet it fears the attack of the tiger.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவற்குத் திண்ணிய அறிவாவது ஊக்கம்மிகுதி
அவ்வூக்கம் மிகுதிஇல்லாதார் மக்கள் ஆகார், மரங்களாவார்
சாதிமரங்களோடு, இம்மரங்களிடை வேற்றுமை, வடிவுமக்கள்வடிவே, பிறிதில்லை

en.1: A person’s strength is wealth of spirit. Those without it are trees. Only their human shape sets them apart.
en.2: A person’s firm understanding is abundance of drive. Those without it aren’t people but trees, differing only in human shape. They lack the good sense and effort of people, so they are trees. They lack a tree’s use too, its fruit and its timber for temples, houses, chariots and ships, so they differ from trees.
en.4: Exuberance of spirit, that alone is strength: those that have it not are mere stocks: their human bodies alone make the difference.
en.5:
Firmness of soul in man is real excellence;
Others are trees, their human form a mere pretence.
en.6: Energy is mental wealth; those men who are destitute of it are only trees in the form of men.

reading.note: He takes உரம், strength, as firm understanding.

padaccheda.m: தான் பிறந்த குடியாகிய நந்தாவிளக்கு

padaccheda.w: மடி என்னும் மாசு ஊர மாய்ந்து கெடும்
padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் மடியாகிய இருள் அடர நந்திப்போம்

en.1: The unfailing lamp called family goes out and is lost when the grime called laziness creeps over it.
en.2: The unfailing lamp of the family you were born into dies when the darkness of your laziness presses on it. A family lights up those born in it for as long as the world goes on. Laziness comes from the dull quality in us, and unlike other darkness it can smother the lamp itself. “Lost” means not even the name is left.
en.4: The perennial light called Family will be extinguished if it is invaded by the foul vapour of sloth.
en.5:
Of household dignity the lustre beaming bright,
Flickers and dies when sluggish foulness dims its light.
en.6: By the darkness, of idleness, the indestructible lamp of family (rank) will be extinguished.

padaccheda.m: தாம் பிறந்த குடியை மேன்மேலும் நற்குடியாக வேண்டுவார்
மடியை மடியாகவே கருதி முயற்சியோடு ஒழுகுக

en.1: Those who want their family to be a true family should treat laziness as the laziness it is.
en.2: Those who want the family they were born in to grow ever better should regard laziness as laziness and live by effort. Nothing is worse than it, as nothing is crueller than fire, so he calls it only by its own name. If they strive they rise, and the family rises. If not, it falls. Some read மடியா as “destroying it”.
en.4: Let them call sloth by its real name and avoid it, those who desire to establish their family on a solid foundation.
en.5:
Let indolence, the death of effort, die,
If you’d uphold your household’s dignity.
en.6: Let those, who desire that their family may be illustrious, put away all idleness from their conduct.

padaccheda.w: மடி மடிக்கொண்டு ஒழுகும் பேதை பிறந்த குடி
padaccheda.m: விடத்தகுவதாய மடியைத் தன்னுள்ளே கொண்டொழுகும் அறிவில்லாதான் பிறந்த குடி
அவன்தன்னினும் முந்துற அழியும்
