en.1: The family of a fool who carries laziness within will perish before the fool does.
en.2: The family of the ignorant man who carries within him the laziness he ought to drop perishes even before he does. He is a fool because he keeps inside him what destroys him. The family goes first because he is the one who sustains it. It rises after him but falls before him.
en.4: Behold the fool who huggeth assassin sloth unto his heart: his family will fall even before his day is ended.
en.5:
Who fosters indolence within his breast, the silly elf!
The house from which he springs shall perish ere himself.
en.6: The (lustre of the) family of the ignorant man, who acts under the influence of destructive laziness will perish, even before he is dead.

padaccheda.m: மடியின்கண்ணே வீழ்தலான் திருந்திய முயற்சி இலராயினார்க்கு
குடியும் மடிந்து குற்றமும் பெருகும்

en.1: For those who fall into laziness and make no fine effort, the family dies and faults multiply.
en.2: Those who have fallen into laziness have no refined effort. Their family perishes and their faults multiply. He names those faults later.
en.4: Behold the men who are sunk in sloth and who turn not their hand to any noble undertakings: their family will go to ruin and their vices will grow apace.
en.5:
His family decays, and faults unheeded thrive,
Who, sunk in sloth, for noble objects doth not strive.
en.6: Family (greatness) will be destroyed, and faults will increase, in those men who give way to laziness, and put forth no dignified exertion.

padaccheda.m: மடியும், விரைந்துசெய்வதனை நீட்டித்துச் செய்யும் இயல்பும், மறப்பும், துயிலும்ஆகிய இந்நான்கும்
இறக்கும் இயல்பினை உடையார் விரும்பி ஏறும் மரக்கலம்

en.1: Delay, forgetfulness, laziness and sleep: these four are the boat that those bound for ruin desire.
en.2: Laziness, dragging out what should be done quickly, forgetting and sleep are the ship that people whose days are ending gladly board. They look like pleasure to those bound for suffering, then drop them in it, as a ship seems to promise gain, then drops them in the sea. Some read கலன் as a jewel worn with desire.
en.4: Procrastination, forgetfulness, sloth, and sleep, these four are the cosy pleasure boats of those that are fated to perish.
en.5:
Delay, oblivion, sloth, and sleep: these four
Are pleasure-boat to bear the doomed to ruin’s shore.
en.6: Idleness, procrastination, forgetfulness, and sleep, these four things, form the vessel which is desired by those who are destined to destruction.

padaccheda.m: நிலம் முழுதும் ஆண்டாராது செல்வம் தானே வந்து எய்தியவிடத்தும்

padaccheda.w: மடி உடையார் மாண் பயன் எய்தல் அரிது
padaccheda.m: மடியுடையார் அதனான் மாண்ட பயனை எய்துதல் இல்லை

en.1: Even when they hold all that the lords of the earth hold, the lazy won’t easily win any great good.
en.2: Even when wealth like that of those who rule the whole earth comes to them unsought, the lazy get no great joy from it. They make no effort to guard that wealth, so it goes, and their suffering stays. Some read this as “even when rulers of the whole earth become their allies”.
en.4: The slothful can never thrive in the world even though they have the favour of princes.
en.5:
Though lords of earth unearned possessions gain,
The slothful ones no yield of good obtain.
en.6: It is a rare thing for the idle, even when possessed of the riches of kings who ruled over the whole earth, to derive any great benefit from it.

reading.note: The Tamil can also mean the support of the earth’s rulers. He mentions that reading and takes பற்று as wealth.

padaccheda.m: மடியை விரும்புதலான் மாண்ட முயற்சி இல்லாதார்
தம் நாட்டார்முன் கழறுதலை மிகச்செய்து அதனாற் பயன் காணாமையின் பின் இகழ்ந்து சொல்லும் சொல்லைக் கேட்பர்

en.1: Those who love laziness and make no fine effort will hear words of rebuke and scorn.
en.2: Those who love laziness and so have no fine effort will hear their friends reproach them again and again before their own people, and then, when that does no good, speak of them with scorn. If friends scorn them, others surely will. They have no power to answer any of it, so they can only hear it.
en.4: Behold the men who are slothful and who turn not their hand to any noble undertakings: they will listen to much reproof and contumely.
en.5:
Who hug their sloth, nor noble works attempt,
Shall hear reproofs and words of just contempt.
en.6: Those who through idleness, do not engage themselves in dignified exertion, will subject themselves to rebukes and reproaches.

padaccheda.m: மடியினது தன்மை குடிமை உடையான்கண்ணே தங்குமாயின்
தன் பகைவர்க்கு அடியனாம் தன்மையை அடைவித்து விடும்

en.1: If laziness settles in someone of good family, it will make them a slave to their enemies.
en.2: Laziness means neglecting the work. If it settles in a ruler who ought to be raising his family, it brings him to be a slave of his enemies, bowing low and taking their orders.
en.4: If sloth find a home in a family, the family will soon be in bondage to its foes.
en.5:
If sloth a dwelling find mid noble family,
Bondsmen to them that hate them shall they be.
en.6: If idleness take up its abode in a king of high birth, it will make him a slave of his enemies.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் தன் மடியாளும் தன்மையை ஒழிக்கவே
அவன் குடியுள்ளும், ஆண்மையுள்ளும் வந்த குற்றங்கள் கெடும்

en.1: When a man ends the rule of laziness over him, the faults that have entered his family and his manhood are gone.
en.2: When a man gets rid of his habit of being ruled by laziness, which comes from the dull quality in him, the faults in his family and his manhood go. These are faults that arose earlier from other causes, not from laziness. They too leave once he drops it and takes up effort.
en.4: The afflictions that may have befallen a man’s family will cease to exist the moment he giveth up sloth.
en.5:
Who changes slothful habits saves
Himself from all that household rule depraves.
en.6: When a man puts away idleness, the reproach which has come upon himself and his family will disappear.

padaccheda.m: தன் அடியளவானே எல்லாவகை உலகையும் அளந்த இறைவன் கடந்த பரப்பு முழுதையும்
மடியிலாத அரசன் முறையான் அன்றி, ஒருங்கே எய்தும்

en.1: A ruler free of laziness will gain, all at once, everything the one who measured with his feet strode over.
en.2: A ruler without laziness gains, all at once and not by stages, the whole expanse crossed by the god who measured every world with his foot. He is always striving at his work, so he gains it without a break.
en.4: Behold the prince that knoweth not sloth: he will bring within his sway all that hath been measured by the steps of Trivikrama.
en.5:
The king whose life from sluggishness is rid,
Shall rule o’er all by foot of mighty god bestrid.
en.6: The king who never gives way to idleness will obtain entire possession of (the whole earth) passed over by Him who measured (the worlds) with His foot.

padaccheda.m: தஞ்சிறுமை நோக்கி நாம் இவ்வினைமுடித்தல் அருமை உடைத்துஎன்று கருதித் தளராது ஒழிக
அது முடித்தற்கு ஏற்ற பெருமையைத் தமக்கு முயற்சி உண்டாக்கும்

en.1: Don’t lose heart and say “This is too hard.” Effort will give you greatness.
en.2: Don’t look at your own smallness, think that finishing this work is too hard, and lose heart. Effort will give you the greatness to finish it. Keep trying and you become great, and then even hard things are easily done.
en.4: Shrink not from any work saying, It is impossible: for labour will give thee the strength to achieve everything.
en.5:
Say not, ‘’Tis hard,’ in weak, desponding hour,
For strenuous effort gives prevailing power.
en.6: Yield not to the feebleness which says, “this is too difficult to be done;” labour will give the greatness (of mind) which is necessary to do it.

padaccheda.m: வினையாகிய குறையைச் செய்யாதுவிட்டாரை உலகம் விட்டது
ஆதலால், செய்யப்படும் வினைக்கண் தவிர்ந்து இருத்தலை ஒழிக

en.1: In any work, take care not to let the work fail. The world leaves those who leave work undone.
en.2: The world leaves those who leave undone the work they can’t do without. So in the work at hand, don’t stop and sit idle.
en.4: Beware of leaving any work unfinished: for the world careth not for those that do not complete the work that they have once begun.
en.5:
In action be thou ’ware of act’s defeat;
The world leaves those who work leave incomplete!
en.6: Take care not to give up exertion in the midst of a work; the world will abandon those who abandon their unfinished work.

padaccheda.m: முயற்சி என்று சொல்லப்படுகின்ற உயர்ந்த குணத்தின் கண்ணே நிலைபெற்றது
எல்லார்க்கும் உபகாரம்செய்தல் என்னும் மேம்பாடு

en.1: The pride called helping others rests in the fine quality called effort.
en.2: The distinction of doing good to everyone rests in the high quality called effort. Those who make the effort have wealth in hand, so they are the ones able to help. It isn’t found in anyone else.
en.4: The proud pleasure of being able to serve all men belongeth only to the greatness that shrinketh not from any exertion.
en.5:
In strenuous effort doth reside
The power of helping others: noble pride!
en.6: The lustre of munificence will dwell only with the dignity of laboriousness or efforts.

padaccheda.m: முயற்சி இல்லாதவன் உபகாரியாம் தன்மை
படை கண்டால் அஞ்சும் பேடி அதனிடைத் தன்கையில் வாளை ஆளுதல்தன்மைபோல இல்லையாம்

en.1: Helping others, in someone without effort, will come to nothing, like a sword in a eunuch’s hand.
en.2: A man without effort can no more be a helper than a eunuch who fears the sight of weapons can wield a sword among them. The eunuch means to use the sword, but fear stops her. He means to help many, but poverty stops him. Some read வாளாண்மை as valour with the sword.
en.4: Like unto a sword in the hands of a eunuch is the liberality of the indolent man: it will not endure.
en.5:
Beneficent intent in men by whom no strenuous work is wrought,
Like battle-axe in sexless being’s hand availeth nought.
en.6: The liberality of him, who does not labour, will fail, like the manliness of a hermaphrodite, who has a sword in its hand.

padaccheda.m: தனக்கு இன்பத்தை விரும்பானாகி, வினை முடித்தலையே விரும்புவான்

padaccheda.w: தன் கேளிர் துன்பம் துடைத்து ஊன்றும் தூண்
padaccheda.m: தன் கேளிராகிய பாரத்தின் துன்பத்தினை நீக்கி, அதனைத் தாங்கும் தூணாம்

en.1: Someone who wants work, not pleasure, wipes away their kin’s suffering and is the pillar that holds them up.
en.2: One who wants no pleasure for himself but only to finish the work clears the suffering of his kin, his load, and is the pillar that bears it. He can end the poverty of kin and friends and protect them, so he needn’t speak of himself. Whoever wants the cause and not the effect gains everything. Whoever wants the effect and not the cause gains nothing.
en.4: The man who loveth not pleasure but loveth work is a pillar of strength unto his friends and will wipe away their tears of grief.
en.5:
Whose heart delighteth not in pleasure, but in action finds delight,
He wipes away his kinsmen’s grief and stands the pillar of their might.
en.6: He who desires not pleasure, but desires labour, will be a pillar to sustain his relations, wiping away their sorrows.

padaccheda.m: அரசர்மாட்டு உளதாய முயற்சி அவரது செல்வத்தினை வளர்க்கும்
அஃது இல்லாமை வறுமையை அடைவித்துவிடும்

en.1: Effort builds prosperity. Lack of effort lets want in.
en.2: The effort of rulers makes their wealth grow, and lack of it brings them poverty. Wealth here means the six parts of a kingdom, and poverty means being without them. Once that happens, their enemies destroy them.
en.4: Industry is the mother of Prosperity: but Indolence only bringeth forth Misery.
en.5:
Effort brings fortune’s sure increase,
Its absence brings to nothingness.
en.6: Labour will produce wealth; idleness will bring poverty.

padaccheda.m: கரியசேட்டை ஒருவன் மடியின்கண்ணே உறையும்

padaccheda.w: தாமரையினாள் மடி இலான் தாள் உளாள் என்ப
padaccheda.m: திருமகள் மடியிலானது முயற்சி்க்கண்ணே உறையும் என்று சொல்லுவர் அறிந்தோர்

en.1: They say dark Misfortune lives in laziness, and she of the lotus in the effort of those without it.
en.2: The dark goddess of misfortune lives in a person’s laziness, and the goddess of fortune in the effort of one who isn’t lazy, say those who know. Her darkness is the darkness of sin, carried over to sin’s fruit.
en.4: In sloth hath the Genius of Wretchedness her home: but the Lotus-born One resideth in the labour of him who yieldeth not to sloth.
en.5:
In sluggishness is seen misfortune’s lurid form, the wise declare;
Where man unslothful toils, she of the lotus flower is there!
en.6: They say that the black Múdévi (the goddess of adversity) dwells with laziness, and that Latchmi (the goddess of prosperity) dwells with the labour of the industrious.

padaccheda.m: பயனைத் தருவதாய விதியில்லாமை ஒருவற்கும் பழியாகாது
அறிய வேண்டும் அவற்றை வினைசெய்யாமையே பழியாவது

en.1: The lack of a favouring fate disgraces no one. The disgrace is to know what must be known and make no effort.
en.2: Lacking the fate that gives results disgraces no one. The disgrace is to know what must be known, such as your strength, and not do the work. To those who say effort is useless when the gods don’t favour you, he answers that the world blames no one for past deeds, only for present faults. So keep trying.
en.4: It is no shame if fortune faileth a man but it is a disgrace if he abstain deliberately from exertion.
en.5:
’Tis no reproach though unpropitious fate should ban;
But not to do man’s work is foul disgrace to man!
en.6: Adverse fate is no disgrace to any one; to be without exertion and without knowing what should be known, is disgrace.

reading.note: பொறி can also mean the senses or limbs. The plain reading follows him in taking it as fate.

padaccheda.m: முயன்றவினை, பால்வகையாற் கருதிய பயனைத் தாராதாயினும்
முயற்சி தனக்கு இடமாகிய உடம்பு வருந்திய வருத்தத்தின் கூலியளவு தரும், பாழாகாது

en.1: Even if god won’t allow it, effort pays the wages of your body’s toil.
en.2: Even if fate keeps the work you tried from giving the result you wanted, the effort pays at least the wages of your body’s pains and isn’t wasted. If god favours it, it gives more than its measure. Either way nothing is lost, so strive and don’t wait on god.
en.4: Even though the Gods be against, Industry is bound to pay the wages of labour.
en.5:
Though fate divine should make your labour vain:
Effort its labour’s sure reward will gain.
en.6: Although it be said that, through fate, it cannot be attained, yet labour, with bodily exertion, will yield its reward.

reading.note: He reads தெய்வம் here as fate.

padaccheda.m: பயனை விலக்குவதாய ஊழினையும் புறங் காண்பர்
அவ்விலக்கிற்கு இளையாது வினையைத் தாழ்வற முயல்வார்

en.1: Those who strive without faltering and without delay will see the back of fate itself.
en.2: Those who don’t weaken before its resistance, and strive at the work without lapse, will see the back even of the fate that blocks the result. Lapse means flaws in planning, in judging strength and the like, and in action. Fate can block you only once or twice, so those who try many times gain the result.
en.4: They will snap their fingers even at Destiny who succumb not to it but labour unremittingly in despite of it.
en.5:
Who strive with undismayed, unfaltering mind,
At length shall leave opposing fate behind.
en.6: They who labour on, without fear and without fainting, will see even fate (put) behind their back.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் வினையான் தனக்கு இடுக்கண் வருமிடத்து அதற்கு அழியாது உள்மகிழ்க

padaccheda.w: அதனை அடுத்து ஊர்வது அஃது ஒப்பது இல்
padaccheda.m: அவ் இடுக்கணை மேன்மேல் அடரவல்லது அம்மகிழ்ச்சி போல்வது பிறிது இல்லையாகலான்

en.1: Laugh when trouble comes. Nothing presses on it and rides it down like that.
en.2: When your work brings you trouble, don’t break, but rejoice inside. Nothing else can press down on trouble again and again like that joy. Bring to the trouble the joy that belongs to finishing the work. Then you stay unbroken, your rising spirit thrusts it aside, and you have the strength to complete the task.
en.4: When thou meetest with misfortune face it with thy best smile: for there is nothing like a smile to enable a man to hold his own against it.
en.5:
Smile, with! patient, hopeful heart, in troublous hour;
Meet and so vanquish grief; nothing hath equal power.
en.6: If troubles come, laugh; there is nothing like that, to press upon and drive away sorrow.

padaccheda.m: வெள்ளம்போலக் கரையிலவாய இடும்பைகள் எல்லாம்
அறிவுடையவன் தன் உள்ளத்தான் ஒன்றனை நினைக்க, அத்துணையானே கெடும்

en.1: Even a flood of trouble dies away once a wise person sets their mind to it.
en.2: Troubles shoreless as a flood all perish the moment a wise man thinks one thought in his mind. Suffering is nothing but a stance held in the mind, and it goes when that stance is reversed. He must know this, so he is called wise. “Thinks in his mind” shows how easy the means is.
en.4: A whole sea of troubles will abase themselves the moment a shifty mind collecteth itself to face them.
en.5:
Though sorrow, like a flood, comes rolling on,
When wise man’s mind regards it,—it is gone!
en.6: A flood of troubles will be overcome by the (courageous) thought which the minds of the wise will entertain, even in sorrow.

padaccheda.m: வினைசெய்யுங்கால் அதற்கிடையே வந்த துன்பத்திற்கு வருந்தாதவர்
அத்துன்பந்தனக்கு தாம் துன்பம் விளைப்பர்

en.1: Those who aren’t troubled by trouble will give trouble trouble.
en.2: Those not distressed by the trouble that comes in the middle of their work bring trouble on the trouble. Distress here means thinking of weakening and giving up. With a firm mind they keep striving, the work is finished and bears fruit, and then every trouble is gone. Take the next two couplets the same way.
en.4: Troubles they send away troubled who trouble not themselves at the sight of troubles.
en.5:
Who griefs confront with meek, ungrieving heart,
From them griefs, put to grief, depart.
en.6: They give sorrow to sorrow, who in sorrow do not suffer sorrow.

padaccheda.m: விலங்கிய இடங்கள் எல்லாவற்றினும் சகடம் ஈர்க்கும் பகடுபோல வினையை எடுத்துக்கொண்டு உய்க்கவல்லானை
வந்துற்ற இடுக்கண் தானே இடர்ப்படுதலை உடைத்து

en.1: Trouble itself is in trouble when it meets someone who, like an ox, pulls through every blocked place.
en.2: One who takes up the work and carries it through every obstacle, as an ox drags a cart through mire, leaves the trouble that comes to him in trouble itself. The ox scrapes its sides, plants its muzzle and crawls on its legs to drag the load through. So he strives, not minding the pain in his body.
en.4: Behold the man who is prepared to strain his every nerve like the bull-buffalo to wade through every difficulty: he may meet with obstacles but he will send them away disappointed.
en.5:
Like bullock struggle on through each obstructed way;
From such an one will troubles, troubled, roll away.
en.6: Troubles will vanish [i. e., will be troubled] before the man who (struggles against difficulties) as a buffalo (drawing a cart) through deep mire.

padaccheda.m: இடைவிடாது மேன்மேல் வந்தனவாயினும்
தன் உள்ளக் கோட்பாடு விடாதான் உற்ற இடுக்கண்தாம் இடுக்கணிலே பட்டுப்போம்

en.1: Even if they come heaped one on another, the troubles that reach an unbroken person are themselves in trouble.
en.2: Even if they come without a break, the same one many times or different ones mixed, the troubles that reach one who holds to his resolve are themselves caught in trouble and pass away.
en.4: Behold the man whose heart sinketh not even at a whole host of troubles arrayed against him: the obstacles in his path have themselves met with an obstacle.
en.5:
When griefs press on, but fail to crush the patient heart,
Then griefs defeated, put to grief, depart.
en.6: The troubles of that man will be troubled (and disappear) who, however thickly they may come upon him, does not abandon; (his purpose.)

padaccheda.m: வறுமைக்காலத்து யாம் வறியம் ஆயினேம் என்று மனத்தான் துயர் உழப்பாரோ?
செல்வக்காலத்து இது பெற்றேம் என்று இவறுதலை அறியாதார்

en.1: Will those who never clung to what they gained, saying “We have got it,” grieve and say “We have lost it”?
en.2: In poor times, will they suffer in their minds, saying “We have become poor”? These are people who in rich times never knew how to cling, saying “We have got this.” They kept that temper when they gained, and they keep it when all is gone, so they have no grief. This is how to stand against trouble from lack of wealth.
en.4: The men that exult not at good fortune, can they ever fret themselves saying, Alas! we are ruined?
en.5:
Who boasted not of wealth, nor gave it all their heart,
Will not bemoan the loss, when prosperous days depart.
en.6: Will those men ever cry out in sorrow, “we are destitute,” who, (in their prosperity,) give not way to (undue desire) to keep their wealth.

padaccheda.m: நாற்கதியினும் உள்ள உடம்புகள் இடும்பை என்னும் வாளுக்கு இலக்கு என்று தெளிந்து
தம்மேல் வந்த இடும்பையை இடும்பையாகக் கொள்ளார் அறிவுடையார்

en.1: Those who know the body is a target for suffering don’t treat the turmoil that comes on them as distress.
en.2: The wise see clearly that bodies, in all four states of birth, are targets for the sword of suffering. So they don’t take the suffering that comes on them as suffering, but accept it as natural. Some read கையாறு as a path of conduct.
en.4: The wise know that the body is a target unto misfortune: and so they worry themselves not when they meet with a calamity.
en.5:
‘Man’s frame is sorrow’s targe,’ the noble mind reflects,
Nor meets with troubled mind the sorrows it expects.
en.6: The great will not regard trouble as trouble, knowing that the body is but the butt of trouble.

padaccheda.m: தன் உடம்பிற்கு இன்பமாயவற்றை விரும்பாதே வினையால் இடும்பை எய்துதல் இயல்பு என்று தெளிந்திருப்பான்
தன் முயற்சியான் துன்பம் உறான்

en.1: Someone who doesn’t crave pleasure, and says suffering is natural, never comes to sorrow.
en.2: One who wants no pleasures for his body, and is clear that work naturally brings suffering, doesn’t come to sorrow through his effort. Wanting pleasure brings sorrow, and so does refusing to call suffering natural and trying to ward it off. He has done neither.
en.4: Behold the man who loveth not pleasure and who knoweth that difficulties are a part of the law of things: he smarteth not ever under any check.
en.5:
He seeks not joy, to sorrow man is born, he knows.
Such man will walk unharmed by touch of human woes.
en.6: That man never experiences sorrow, who does not seek for pleasure, and who considers distress to be natural (to man).

padaccheda.m: வினையால் தனக்கின்பம் வந்துழி அதனை அனுபவியாநின்றே மனத்தான் விரும்பாதான்
துன்பம் வந்துழியும், அதனை அனுபவியாநின்றே மனத்தான் வருந்தான்

en.1: Someone who doesn’t crave joy in times of joy won’t feel sorrow in times of sorrow.
en.2: One who, when his work brings joy, lives through it without wanting it in his mind also lives through sorrow, when it comes, without grieving in his mind. Sorrow here means the trouble that comes with effort. He takes both as the same, so neither has any effect on him.
en.4: The man who runneth not after pleasure in the day of success suffereth not pain in the day of failure.
en.5:
Mid joys he yields not heart to joys’ control,
Mid sorrows, sorrow cannot touch his soul.
en.6: He does not suffer sorrow in sorrow, who does not look for pleasure in pleasure.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் வினைசெய்யும் இடத்து முயற்சியான் வரும் துன்பம்தன்னையே தனக்கு இன்பமாகக் கற்பித்துக் கொள்வானாயின்
அதனான் தன் பகைவர் நன்கு மதித்தற்கு ஏதுவாய கவர்ச்சி உண்டாம்

en.1: If you take what hurts as joy, you will have the distinction your enemies prize.
en.2: If, when you do your work, you make yourself treat the suffering of effort as joy, you gain the quality that makes your enemies respect you. Suffering isn’t natural to the soul. It is a passing stance in the mind. Reverse it and you stay unbroken and glad, with the strength to finish what you began.
en.4: Behold the man who looketh upon the stress and strain of exertion as a veritable joy: he will be extolled by his very enemies.
en.5:
Who pain as pleasure takes, he shall acquire
The bliss to which his foes in vain aspire.
en.6: The elevation, which even his enemies will esteem, will be gained by him, who regards pain as pleasure.

padaccheda.m: வினைசெய்யுங்கால் அதற்கு வேண்டுங் கருவிகளும்
அதற்கேற்ற காலமும்
அது செய்யுமாறும்
அவ்வாற்றிற் செய்யப்படும் அவ்வரிய வினைதானும்
வாய்ப்ப எண்ணவல்லவனே அமைச்சனாவான்

en.1: A minister is someone who excels in the means, the time, the method and the rare work to be done.
en.2: A minister is one who can rightly plan the means a task needs, its proper time, the way to do it and the rare task itself. The means are armies and wealth. The time is when to begin. The way covers how to begin, how to clear obstacles and how to finish. A rare task gives great results for little effort.
en.4: Behold the man who judgeth aright the ways and means of achieving great enterprises and the proper season to commence them: he is the proper man for the Council.
en.5:
A minister is he who grasps, with wisdom large,
Means, time, work’s mode, and functions rare he must discharge.
en.6: The minister is one who can make an excellent choice of means, time, manner of execution, and the difficult undertaking (itself.)

padaccheda.m: வினைசெய்தற்கண் அசைவின்மையும்
குடிகளைக் காத்தலும்
நீதிநூல்களைக் கற்றுச் செய்வன தவிர்வன அறிதலும்
முயற்சியும்
மேற்சொல்லிய அவ்வங்கங்கள் ஐந்துடனே திருந்தவுடையானே அமைச்சனாவான்

en.1: Firmness, guarding the people, learning and knowing, and effort: a minister excels in all five.
en.2: A minister has firmness in his work, guards the people, studies the books of statecraft and knows what to do and avoid, and makes effort, along with the five parts of the last couplet. He rejects making five of these alone, by splitting guarding the people into good birth and keeping it by conduct, or learning and knowing in two.
en.4: Study, resolution, manly exertion, and loving attention to the welfare of the people, these four make along with the last the five qualifications of the Councillor.
en.5:
A minister must greatness own of guardian power, determined mind,
Learn’d wisdom, manly effort with the former five combined.
en.6: The minister is one who in addition to the aforesaid five things excels in the possession of firmness, protection of subjects, clearness by learning, and perseverance.

reading.note: The plain reading counts five in this couplet. He adds these four to the five parts of K631.

padaccheda.m: வினைவந்துழிப் பகைவர்க்குத் துணையாயினாரை அவரிற் பிரிக்கவேண்டிற் பிரித்தலும்
தம்பாலரை அவர் பிரியாமற் கொடை இன்சொற்களாற் பேணிக்கொள்ளுதலும்
முன்னே தம்மினும் தம்பாலாரினும் பிரிந்தாரை மீண்டும் பொருத்தவேண்டிற் பொருத்தலும்
வல்லவனே அமைச்சனாவான்

en.1: A minister is someone who can split others apart, keep friends close, and bring back those who have split away.
en.2: A minister is one able, when the work demands it, to part his enemies’ allies from them, to keep his own side from leaving through gifts and sweet words, and to bring back those who left earlier. Knowing what each moment needs, and carrying it out unnoticed by a fitting means, is hard, so he says “able”.
en.4: He is the able minister who possesseth the capacity to disunite allies, to cherish and keep up existing friendships, and to reunite those who have become enemies.
en.5:
A minister is he whose power can foes divide,
Attach more firmly friends, of severed ones can heal the breaches wide.
en.6: The minister is one who can effect discord (among foes), maintain the good-will of his friends and restore to friendship those who have seceded (from him).

padaccheda.m: ஒரு காரியச்செய்கை பலவாற்றால் தோன்றின், அவற்றுள் ஆவது ஆராய்ந்து அறிதலும்
அது செய்யுங்கால் வாய்க்குந் திறன்நாடிச் செய்தலும்
சிலரைப் பிரித்தல் பொருத்தல் செயற்கண், அவர்க்கு இதுவே செயற்பாலது என்று துணிவுபிறக்கும் வகை சொல்லுதலும்
வல்லவனே அமைச்சனாவான்

en.1: A minister is someone able to see clearly, act after weighing, and speak with certainty.
en.2: A minister is one able to find, when a task can be done in many ways, the way that will work, to do it after seeing how it can succeed, and, when parting or joining others, to speak so that they are convinced this alone is what they must do.
en.4: Judgment in the choice of projects and the means of their execution, and positiveness in the expression of opinion are necessary qualities in the Councillor.
en.5:
A minister has power to see the methods help afford,
To ponder long, then utter calm conclusive word.
en.6: The minister is one who is able to comprehend (the whole nature of an undertaking), execute it in the best manner possible, and offer assuring advice (in time of necessity).

padaccheda.m: அரசனாற் செய்யப்படும் அறங்களை அறிந்து, தனக்கு ஏற்ற கல்வியான் நிறைந்தமைந்த சொல்லை உடையனாய்
எக்காலத்தும் வினை செய்யும் திறங்களை அறிந்தான்
அவர்க்குச் சூழ்ச்சித் துணையாம்

en.1: Someone who knows righteousness, whose words are full and measured, and who knows at all times how to act, is a companion in counsel.
en.2: One who knows the righteous acts a ruler should perform, whose words are filled with the learning that suits him, and who knows at all times how work is done, is a help to rulers in planning. “At all times” means when his ruler is reduced, when he flourishes and in between.
en.4: Behold the man who knoweth the law and aboundeth in instruction, is deliberate in his speech and always understandeth what is fit for each occasion: he is the Councillor for thee.
en.5:
The man who virtue knows, has use of wise and pleasant words,
With plans for every season apt, in counsel aid affords.
en.6: He is the best helper (of the king) who understanding the (duties) of the latter, is, by his special learning, able to tender the fullest advice, and at all times conversant with the best method (of performing actions.)

padaccheda.m: இயற்கையாகிய நுண்ணறிவைச் செயற்கையாகிய நூலறிவோடு உடையராய அமைச்சர்க்கு

padaccheda.w: அதி நுட்பம் முன் நிற்பவை யா உள
padaccheda.m: மிக்க நுட்பத்தையுடைய சூழ்ச்சிகளாய் முன்னிற்பன யாவை உள?

en.1: What subtlety can stand before those who have sharp wit and book learning too?
en.2: What plots of great subtlety can stand before ministers who have fine natural wit along with book learning? God must give the wit, so it comes first. They see through their enemies’ plots and destroy them, and devise plots their enemies can’t. He rejects the variant அதினுட்பம், “what is subtler than that”, because nothing has been named for “that” to point to.
en.4: What is there that is too subtle for men who add knowledge of books unto natural intelligence?
en.5:
When native subtilty combines with sound scholastic lore,
’Tis subtilty surpassing all, which nothing stands before.
en.6: What (contrivances) are there so acute as to resist those who possess natural acuteness in addition to learning.

padaccheda.m: நூல்நெறியான் வினசெய்யும் திறஙகளை அறிந்தவிடத்தும்
அப்பொழுது நடக்கின்ற உலகவியற்கையை அறிந்து அதனோடு பொருந்தச் செய்க

en.1: Even when you know the methods, know the nature of the world and then act.
en.2: Even when you know from the books how work is done, know how the world runs at that time and act in keeping with it. Even if a thing is by the book, don’t do what doesn’t fit the ways of the world. The world will blame it.
en.4: Even though thou art wise in thy knowledge of books, gather thou the wisdom of experience and act in accordance therewith.
en.5:
Though knowing all that books can teach, ’tis truest tact
To follow common sense of men in act.
en.6: Though you are acquainted with the (theoretical) methods (of performing an act), understand the ways of the world and act accordingly.

padaccheda.m: அறிந்து சொல்லியாரது அறிவையும் அழித்து, அரசன் தானும் அறியானே ஆயினும்
அக்குற்றம் நோக்கி யொழியாது அவனுக்கு உறுதியாயின கூறுதல் அமைச்சனுக்கு முறைமை

en.1: Even if he kills what others know and knows nothing himself, it is the duty of the one at his side to tell him what is good for him.
en.2: Even if the ruler destroys the knowledge of those who speak to him and knows nothing himself, a minister mustn’t give up over that fault, but tell him what is good for him. Destroying it means rejecting it and mocking it too. If he stays silent, the world lays the guilt of the ruler’s end on him.
en.4: The prince may be a fool and may thwart him at every step: but the duty of the Councillor is always to point to him what is just and proper.
en.5:
’Tis duty of the man in place aloud to say
The very truth, though unwise king may cast his words away.
en.6: Although the king be utterly ignorant, it is the duty of the minister to give (him) sound advice.

padaccheda.m: பக்கத்திருந்து பிழைப்ப எண்ணும் அமைச்சன் ஒருவனில்
அரசனுக்கு எதிர்நிற்பார் ஓர் எழுபது கோடி பகைவர் உறுவர்

en.1: Seven hundred million enemies are better than one minister at your side who plots harm.
en.2: Better to have seven hundred million enemies facing the ruler than one minister at his side who plans his fall. The number stands for a very great many. Open enemies can be guarded against, but he is an enemy within, so no guard is possible. Some read this as “seven hundred million times better”, and some read a different text.
en.4: Behold the minister that sitteth in the Council and plotteth the ruin of his prince: he is more dangerous than seven hundred million enemies.
en.5:
A minister who by king’s side plots evil things
Worse woes than countless foemen brings.
en.6: . Far better are seventy crores of enemies (for a king) than a minister at his side who intends (his) ruin.

padaccheda.w: முறைப் படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவு இலவே செய்வர்
padaccheda.m: செய்யப்படும் வினைகளை முன் அடைவுபட எண்ணி வைத்தும், செய்யுங்கால் அவை முடிவு இலவாகவே செய்யாநிற்பர்
முடித்தற்கு ஏற்ற கூறுபாடு இல்லாதார்

en.1: Even when they plan things in good order, those without skill in doing will leave them unfinished.
en.2: Those who lack what finishing takes, though they have planned the work in good order, do it in such a way that it stays unfinished. What it takes is knowing the fitting remedy for each obstacle as it comes, and being firm themselves. Some can plan without error and still can’t complete anything.
en.4: The irresolute may even plan perfectly: but they will waver in the course of the execution and will never accomplish their designs.
en.5:
For gain of end desired just counsel nought avails
To minister, when tact in execution fails.
en.6: Those ministers who are destitute of (executive) ability will fail to carry out their projects, although they may have contrived aright.

padaccheda.m: அமைச்சர்க்கு இன்றியமையாக் குணமாவது, சான்றோரான் நாநலம் என்று சிறப்பித்துச் சொல்லப்படும் நலத்தினை உடையராதல்
அந்நலம் பிறர்க்கும் பிறநலமெல்லாவற்றுள்ளும் அடங்குவதன்றி மிக்கதாகலான்

en.1: To have the good called a good tongue is a good not found among any other goods.
en.2: The quality ministers can’t do without is what the wise call the good of the tongue. Even in others it isn’t counted among other goods, but stands above them. Ministers must bring the world under them, so they need it as a thing apart. If even those with no work of parting and joining need it, those who have that work surely do.
en.4: The blessing of the tongue is a blessing indeed: for it is a blessing apart and formeth not part of other blessings.
en.5:
A tongue that rightly speaks the right is greatest gain,
It stands alone midst goodly things that men obtain.
en.6: The possession of that goodness which is called the goodness of speech is (even to others) better than any other goodness.

padaccheda.m: தம் அரசற்கும், அங்கங்கட்கும் ஆக்க அழிவுகள் தம் சொல்லான் வரும்ஆகலான்
அப்பெற்றித்தாய சொல்லின்கண் சோர்தலை, அமைச்சர் தம்கண் நிகழாமற் போற்றிக் காக்க

en.1: Gain and ruin both come from it, so guard carefully against any slip in your speech.
en.2: Rise and ruin for their ruler and his kingdom come from what ministers say, so they must guard against any lapse in speech. Good words bring gain and bad words ruin, yet both are speech. A lapse by others harms few, but theirs falls on all living beings at once, so he says “guard carefully”.
en.4: Death and life are in the power of the tongue: guard thou therefore against imprudence of speech.
en.5:
Since gain and loss in life on speech depend,
From careless slip in speech thyself defend.
en.6: Since (both) wealth and evil result from (their) speech, ministers should most carefully guard themselves against faultiness therein.

padaccheda.m: நட்பாய் ஏற்றுக்கொண்டாரைப் பின் வேறுபடாமற் பிணிக்கும் குணங்களை அவாவி
மற்றைப் பகையாய் ஏற்றுக்கொள்ளாதாரும் பின் அப்பகைமை ஒழிந்து நட்பினை விரும்பும் வண்ணம் சொல்லப்படுவதே
அமைச்சர்க்குச் சொல்லாவது

en.1: Speech is that which holds its hearers fast, and is said so that even those who haven’t heard it long for it.
en.2: For ministers, true speech seeks the qualities that bind those who took them as friends, and is said so that even enemies drop their enmity and want friendship. Those qualities are freedom from error, brevity, clarity, sweetness and great use. He rejects reading தகையவாய் as “being worthy”, a plural that can’t go with the singular மொழிவது.
en.4: Behold the speech that bindeth friends more closely and fascinateth even enemies: that alone is worthy of its name.
en.5:
’Tis speech that spell-bound holds the listening ear,
While those who have not heard desire to hear.
en.6: The (minister’s) speech is that which seeks (to express) elements as bind his friends (to himself) and is so delivered as to make even his enemies desire (his friendship).

reading.note: கேட்டார் and கேளார் are those who heard and those who haven’t in the plain reading. He takes them as those who accepted you as friends and those who didn’t, your enemies.

padaccheda.m: அப்பெற்றித்தாய சொல்லை அமைச்சர் தம்முடையுவம் கேட்பாருடையவுமாய திறங்களை அறிந்து சொல்லுக
அங்ஙனம் சொல்லுதற்கு மேற்பட்ட அறனும், பொருளும் இல்லையாகலான்

en.1: Know the right way and speak your words. No righteousness and no wealth is greater than that.
en.2: Ministers should speak knowing their own standing and their hearers’, the differences that come from birth, learning, conduct, wealth, looks and age, and address each as is fitting. Nothing brings more righteousness and wealth. It is righteousness because it keeps step with the world and pleases, and wealth because it gets their work done.
en.4: Weigh each circumstance aright and then speak the speech that is fit: for the increase of righteousness and profit there is no other thing of more worth to thee than it.
en.5:
Speak words adapted well to various hearers’ state;
No higher virtue lives, no gain more surely great.
en.6: Understand the qualities (of your hearers) and (then make your speech; for, superior to it, there is neither virtue nor wealth.

padaccheda.w: சொல்லைப் பிறிது ஓர் சொல் வெல்லும்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து
padaccheda.m: தாம் சொல்லக் கருதிய சொல்லைப் பிறிதோர் சொல்லாய் வெல்லவல்லதொரு சொல் இல்லாமை அறிந்து
பின் அச்சொல்லைச் சொல்லுக

en.1: Say your word only when you know that no other word can beat it.
en.2: Say the word you have in mind once you know that no word can defeat it. The other word is a rival’s contrary word, and to defeat is to surpass in quality. So speak so that yours wins. Some read this as “speak so that there is no equal word and no better word”.
en.4: Speak thou the speech that cannot be silenced by any other speech.
en.5:
Speak out your speech, when once ’tis past dispute
That none can utter speech that shall your speech refute.
en.6: Deliver your speech, after assuring yourself that no counter speech can defeat your own.

padaccheda.w: வேட்பத் தாம் சொல்லிப் பிறர்சொற் பயன் கோடல்
padaccheda.m: பிறர்க்குத் தாம் சொல்லுங்கால் அவர் பின்னும் கேட்டலை விரும்புமாறு சொல்லி, அவர் தமக்குச் சொல்லுங்கால் அச்சொல்லின் பயனைக் கொண்டொழிதல்
அமைச்சியலுள் குற்றம் அற்றாரது துணிபு

en.1: To speak so that others want to hear, and to take what is useful from what others say, is the way of the flawless.
en.2: When you speak to others, speak so that they want to hear more. When they speak to you, take the use of their words and leave the rest. That is the settled way of those without fault in a minister’s calling. They don’t scorn others’ words even if they have flaws, because scorning those less able doesn’t suit the able.
en.4: To speak so as to captivate one’s own hearers and to seize the sense in the words of others, that is the part of the consummate statesman.
en.5:
Charming each hearer’s ear, of others’ words to seize the sense,
Is method wise of men of spotless excellence.
en.6: It is the opinion of those who are free from defects in diplomacy that the minister should speak so as to make his hearers desire (to hear more,) and grasp the meaning of what he hears himself.

padaccheda.m: தான் எண்ணிய காரியங்களைப் பிறர்க்கு ஏற்பச்சொல்லுதல் வல்லனாய்
அவைமிகப் பலவாயவழி ஒன்றினும் சோர்வு இலனாய்
அவைக்கு அஞ்சானாயினான் யாவன்
அவனை மாறுபாட்டின்கண் வெல்லுதல் யாவர்க்கும் அரிது

en.1: A man who speaks well, never slips and has no fear is hard for anyone to beat in a contest.
en.2: One who can say what he has in mind so that others accept it, even against their interest, who forgets no point however many there are, and who isn’t afraid: no one can beat him in a dispute. No rival can win against a man with these three qualities by splitting his allies or drawing them away.
en.4: Behold the man who is eloquent of speech and knoweth neither confusion nor fear: it is impossible for anyone to beat him in debate.
en.5:
Mighty in word, of unforgetful mind, of fearless speech,
Tis hard for hostile power such man to overreach.
en.6: It is impossible for any one to conquer him by intrigue who possesses power of speech, and is neither faulty nor timid.

padaccheda.m: சொல்லப்படுங் காரியங்களை நிரல்படக் கோத்து இனிதாகச் சொல்லுதல் வல்லாரைப் பெறின்
உலகம் அவற்றை விரைந்து ஏற்றுக்கொள்ளும்

en.1: The world quickly does as it is asked, if it finds those who can speak in good order and sweetly.
en.2: If you find those who can set out what is to be said in order, and sweetly, the world quickly accepts it. Order means knowing what comes first and what after. Sweetness means pleasing the hearers. A Sanskrit saying has it that one in a hundred thousand can speak well, so he says “if it finds”.
en.4: Behold the men whose speech is well ordered and couched in persuasive language: the world will be at their beck and call.
en.5:
Swiftly the listening world will gather round,
When men of mighty speech the weighty theme propound.
en.6: If there be those who can speak on various subjects in their proper order and in a pleasing manner, the world would readily accept them.

padaccheda.m: குற்றமற்றனவாய்ச் சிலவாய வார்த்தைகளை அவ்வாற்றாற் சொல்லுதலை அறியாதார்
பலவாய வார்த்தைகளைத் தொகுத்துச் சொல்ல விரும்புவர்

en.1: Those who don’t know how to say a few flawless words surely desire to say many.
en.2: Those who don’t know how to say a few faultless words in this way want to gather many. Some prize speaking at length without a pause as skill. He says “surely” to insist that only those who can’t speak in this way do that, and the able don’t.
en.4: Verily they have a passion for much speaking who know not to say their mind in few and well chosen words.
en.5:
Who have not skill ten faultless words to utter plain,
Their tongues will itch with thousand words men’s ears to pain.
en.6: They will desire to utter many words, who do not know how to speak a few faultless ones.

padaccheda.m: கற்றுவைத்த நூலைப் பிறரறியும் வண்ணம் விரித்துரைக்க மாட்டாதவர்
கொத்தின்கண்ணே மலர்ந்து வைத்தும் நாறாத பூவை ஒப்பர்

en.1: Those who can’t unfold what they have learned so that others grasp it are like flowers that bloom in clusters but have no scent.
en.2: Those who can’t explain the books they have learned so that others understand are like flowers that bloom in a cluster but have no scent. A flower in full bloom without scent isn’t worn, and one who has studied but can’t speak isn’t held in esteem.
en.4: Behold the men who cannot expound unto others the knowledge that they have acquired: they are like unto the flower that blossometh but giveth forth no fragrance.
en.5:
Like scentless flower in blooming garland bound
Are men who can’t their lore acquired to others’ ears expound.
en.6: Those who are unable to set forth their acquirements (before others) are like flowers blossoming in a cluster and yet without fragrance.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்குத் துணையது நன்மை செல்வம் ஒன்றனையும் கொடுக்கும்
அவ்வளவன்றி வினையது நன்மை அவன் வேண்டியன யாவற்றையு்ம் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: Good allies bring prosperity. Good deeds bring all you want.
en.2: The goodness of your allies gives you wealth alone. The goodness of your actions gives you all you want: righteousness, wealth and pleasure in this life, and the state you desire in the next. So the unseen goodness of action is greater than the visible goodness of allies.
en.4: Alliances bring success unto a man: but purity of action fulfilleth his every desire.
en.5:
The good external help confers is worldly gain;
By action good men every needed gift obtain.
en.6: The efficacy of support will yield (only) wealth; (but) the efficacy of action will yield all that is desired.

padaccheda.m: தம் அரசனுக்கு இம்மைக்கண் புகழும் மறுமைக்கண் அறமும் பயவாத வினைகளை
அமைச்சர்க்கு எக்காலத்தும் ஒழிதல் வேண்டும்

en.1: Always keep away from work that doesn’t bring good along with fame.
en.2: Ministers must at all times keep clear of work that doesn’t bring their ruler fame in this life and righteousness in the next. He says “always” because good times, bad times and times between all come. “Must” means there is no doing without this.
en.4: Always turn thy face away from those deeds that bring not glory as well as profit.
en.5:
From action evermore thyself restrain
Of glory and of good that yields no gain.
en.6: Ministers should at all times avoid acts which, in addition to fame, yield no benefit (for the future).

padaccheda.m: மேலாகக் கடவேம் என்று கருதுவார்

padaccheda.w: ஒளி மாழ்கும் வினை செய் ஓஒதல் வேண்டும்
padaccheda.m: தம் ஒளி கெடுதற்கு்க் காரணமாய வினையைச் செய்தலைத் தவிர்க

en.1: Those who say “We will rise” must stop doing what dims their light.
en.2: Those who mean to rise higher should give up the work that causes their light to fade. Light means being esteemed by everyone in their own time. Anything that dims it isn’t gain.
en.4: Those that desire to rise in the world, let them abjure all action that can tarnish their glory.
en.5:
Who tell themselves that nobler things shall yet be won,
All deeds that dim the light of glory must they shun.
en.6: Those who say “we will become (better)” should avoid the performance of acts that would destroy (their) fame.

padaccheda.m: தாம் இடுக்கண் படவரினும், அது தீர்தற்பொருட்டு முன் செய்தார்க்கு இளிவந்த வினைகளைச் செய்யார்
துளக்கம் அற்ற தெளிவினை உடையார்

en.1: Even when they are in trouble, those of unshaken vision won’t do anything shameful.
en.2: Even when trouble comes, those of unshaken clarity won’t escape it by what has shamed those who did it before. They see that you mustn’t take on a disgrace that never passes because of a trouble that soon will, and that even then what is to come will come.
en.4: Behold the men who see things in their right proportions: even when fallen on evil days they stoop not to action that is dishonourable and mean.
en.5:
Though troubles press, no shameful deed they do,
Whose eyes the ever-during vision view.
en.6: Those who have an infallible judgment though threatened with peril will not do acts which have brought disgrace (on former ministers).

padaccheda.m: யான் செய்தது எத்தன்மைத்து, என்று பின் தானே இரங்கும் வினைகளை ஒருகாலும் செய்யாது ஒழிக
அன்றி ஒருகால் மயங்கி அவற்றைச் செய்யும் தன்மையன் ஆயினான்ஆயின், பின்னிருந்து அவ் இரங்கல்களைச் செய்யாது ஒழிதல் நன்று

en.1: Don’t do what will make you cry “What have I done?” If you do, it is good not to do the like again.
en.2: Never do what will later make you grieve, “What have I done?” If in a moment of confusion you do, it is good not to go on grieving afterwards. Everyone will scorn you for it: you know no remedy, you lack firmness, you do useless things, you spread your own shame. He rejects “don’t do the like again” as not fitting the words.
en.4: Let not a man do those things which make him cry afterwards, what is it that I have done? and if he hath done any such thing, it is good for him if he doth it not once again.
en.5:
Do nought that soul repenting must deplore,
If thou hast sinned, ’tis well if thou dost sin no more.
en.6: Let a minister never do acts of which he would have to grieve saying, ‘‘What is this I have done!”; (but) should he do (them), it were good that he grieved not.

reading.note: The plain reading takes the second line as “don’t do it again”. He takes it as “don’t go on grieving”, and rejects the other.

padaccheda.m: தன்னைப் பயந்தாளது பசியை வறுமையாற் கண்டிரங்குந் தன்மையன் ஆயினான் எனினும்
அது சுட்டி அறிவுடையார் பழிக்கும் வினைகளை ஒருவன் செய்யாது ஒழிக

en.1: Even if you see the mother who bore you go hungry, don’t do what the worthy condemn.
en.2: Even if poverty brings a man to see the mother who bore him go hungry, he must not do what the wise condemn. The general rule of the law books says that when aged parents, a chaste wife and an infant are starving, you may do many evil things to keep them. That rule doesn’t reach ministers, who follow statecraft, serve rulers and are held in esteem.
en.4: Let not a man do those things that good men condemn, even to save the mother that bore him from starvation.
en.5:
Though her that bore thee hung’ring thou behold, no deed
Do thou, that men of perfect soul have crime decreed.
en.6: Though a minister may see his mother starve, let him do not act which the wise would (treat with contempt).

reading.note: The words have no exception. He limits this to ministers, and cites a rule that lets others do evil to feed their dependants.

padaccheda.m: சாலாதார் தீய வினைகளைச் செய்து, அதனாற் பழியைத் தம்மேற் கொண்டு பெற்றசெல்வத்தின்
அது மேற்கொ்ளளாத சான்றோர் அனுபவிக்கும் மிக்க நல்குரவே உயர்ந்தது

en.1: Better the deep poverty of the worthy than prosperity gained by wearing disgrace.
en.2: The bitter poverty the worthy endure, refusing disgrace, is higher than the wealth the unworthy win by doing evil and taking disgrace on themselves. To take on lasting disgrace for the sake of passing wealth doesn’t go with worth.
en.4: The indigence of the worthy is better far than wealth that is amassed by dishonourable means.
en.5:
Than store of wealth guilt-laden souls obtain,
The sorest poverty of perfect soul is richer gain.
en.6: Far more excellent is the extreme poverty of the wise than wealth obtained by a heaping up of sinful deeds.

padaccheda.m: நூலோர் கடிந்த வினைகளைத் தாமும் கடிந்துஒழியாது, பொருள்நோக்கிச் செய்த அமைச்சர்க்கு
அவை தூயவன்மையின் முடியா, ஒருவாற்றான் முடியினும் பின் துன்பத்தையே கொடுக்கும்

en.1: Those who do what is forbidden, not shunning what has been shunned, will find it brings pain even if it succeeds.
en.2: Ministers don’t shun what the learned have forbidden, but do it for wealth. Those deeds aren’t pure, so they won’t succeed. Even if they somehow succeed, they bring only suffering later. To succeed here means to yield the wealth intended.
en.4: Behold the men that shun not those things that are forbidden by good morals: they will come to grief even if they succeed in their designs.
en.5:
To those who hate reproof and do forbidden thing,
What prospers now, in after days shall anguish bring.
en.6: The actions of those, who have not desisted from doing deeds forbidden (by the great), will, even if they succeed, cause them sorrow.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் தீவினைகளைச் செய்து பிறர் இரங்கக்கொண்ட பொருள் எல்லாம், இம்மையிலே அவன்தான் இரங்கப் போகாநிற்கும்
மற்றைத் தூயவினையான் வந்த பொருள்கள் முன் இழந்தான் ஆயினும், அவனுக்குப் பின்னர் வந்து பயன்கொடுக்கும்

en.1: All that was taken with tears leaves with tears. What is good, even if lost, bears fruit afterwards.
en.2: All the wealth someone takes by evil deeds, making others weep, goes in this life and leaves him weeping. Wealth that came by pure deeds, even if lost at first, comes back later and gives its fruit. “Later” includes the next life.
en.4: All that is wrong in the midst of tears will depart also accompanied by weepings: but that which is acquired by righteous ways, even if lost in the middle, increaseth in the latter end.
en.5:
What’s gained through tears with tears shall go;
From loss good deeds entail harvests of blessings grow.
en.6: All that has been obtained with tears (to the victim) will depart with tears (to himself); but what has been obtained by fair means, though with loss at first, will afterward yield fruit.

padaccheda.m: அமைச்சன் தீய வினைகளாற் பொருள் படைத்து, அதனால் அரசனுக்கு ஏமஞ்செய்தல்
பசிய மட்கலத்துள்ளே நீரைப்பெய்து அதற்கு ஏமம் செய்ததனோடு ஒக்கும்

en.1: Trying to stay safe on wealth made by deceit is like pouring water into a pot of raw clay and keeping it there.
en.2: A minister who makes wealth by evil deeds to keep his ruler safe is like one who pours water into a pot of raw clay to keep it safe. Such deeds are deceit because they seem to bring gain and then bring ruin. Ruler and wealth perish together. He rejects the text ஏமாத்தல், “rejoicing”, because it breaks the comparison.
en.4: To try to lay by wealth by means of guile is like trying to preserve water in a pot of clay that is not baked.
en.5:
In pot of clay unburnt he water pours and would retain,
Who seeks by wrong the realm in wealth and safety to maintain.
en.6: (For a minister) to protect (his king) with wealth obtained by foul means is like preserving a vessel of wet clay by filling it with water.

padaccheda.m: வினைசெய்தற்கண் திண்மை என்று சொல்லப்படுவது, அதனை முடித்தற்குரியானொருவன் மனத்தினது திண்ணம்
அஃது ஒழிந்தன எல்லாம் அதற்குத் திண்மையென்று சொல்லப்படா

en.1: Firmness in action is a person’s firmness of mind. Everything else is something else.
en.2: What is called firmness in work is firmness in the mind of the one who is to finish it. The strength of armies, forts, friendships and the like can’t be called that. They are needed and belong with it, so he says “the rest”. Without it they are of no use, so he says “something else”.
en.4: Greatness of achievement is nought else but the greatness of the will that striveth therefor: all other things come not near the mark.
en.5:
What men call ‘power in action’ know for ‘power of mind’;
Externe to man all other aids you find.
en.6: Firmness in action is (simply) one’s firmness of mind; all other (abilities) are not of this nature.

padaccheda.m: முன் நீதி ஆராய்ந்த அமைச்சரது துணிபு

padaccheda.w: ஊறு ஒரால் உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை இவ்விரண்டின் ஆறு என்பர்
padaccheda.m: பழுதுபடும் வினைகளைச் செய்யாமையும், செய்யும் வினை தெய்வத்தான் பழுதுபட்டவழி அதற்குத் தளராமையுமாகிய இவ்விரண்டின் வழியென்பர் நூலோர்

en.1: Avoiding harm, and not giving way once it comes: those who have looked into it say these two are the path.
en.2: The learned say the settled view of ministers who studied statecraft runs along these two: not doing work that will go wrong, and not weakening when god spoils the work you do. This sums up what the ministers of the gods and the demons taught, so it includes clean action too. He rejects the variant ஊறொரார், which doesn’t fit a count of two.
en.4: To avoid all action that is bound to fail and not to turn away from one’s purpose because of obstacles: these two are said to be the guiding principles of the wise.
en.5:
‘Each hindrance shun,’ ‘unyielding onward press, if obstacle be there,’
These two define your way, so those that search out truth declare.
en.6: Not to perform a ruinous act, and not to be discouraged by the ruinous termination of an act, are the two maxims which, the wise say, form the principles of those who have investigated the subject.

padaccheda.m: செய்யப்படும் வினையை முடிவின்கண் புலப்படும் வகை முன்னெல்லாம் மறைத்துச் செய்வதே திட்பமாவது
அங்ஙனமின்றி இடையே புலப்படுமாயின், அப்புலப்பாடு செய்வானுக்கு நீங்காத இடும்பையைக் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: Real strength is to do the work so that it shows only at the end. If it shows midway, it brings trouble that won’t go.
en.2: Firmness is to do the work in secret all along, so that it comes to light only at the end. If it shows midway, the doer gets suffering he can’t shake off. Others mustn’t learn how it was planned, or guess from his gestures, looks, acts and words. Enemies who know early will block the work or the man.
en.4: The man of action letteth his purpose appear only when that purpose is achieved: for an untimely disclosure would create obstacles that cannot be surmounted.
en.5:
Man’s fitting work is known but by success achieved;
In midst the plan revealed brings ruin ne’er to be retrieved.
en.6: So to perform an act as to publish it (only) at its termination is (true) manliness; for to announce it beforehand, will cause irremediable sorrow.

padaccheda.m: யாம் இவ்வினையை இவ்வாற்றாற் செய்துமென நிரல்படச் சொல்லுதல் யாவர்க்கும் எளிய
அதனை அவ்வாற்றானே செய்தல் யாவர்க்கும் அரியவாம்

en.1: Saying it is easy for anyone. Doing it as you said is hard.
en.2: To set out in order “We will do this work in this way” is easy for anyone. To do it that way is hard for anyone. Even those without firmness can plan hard things and speak of them, so he says “easy”.
en.4: To say a thing is easy for any man: but to do it in the manner undertaken is a rare thing indeed.
en.5:
Easy to every man the speech that shows the way;
Hard thing to shape one’s life by words they say!
en.6: To say (how an act is to be performed) is (indeed) easy for any one; but far difficult it is to do according to what has been said.

padaccheda.m: எண்ணத்தால் சிறப்பெய்திப் பிற இலக்கணங்களாலும் மாட்சிமைப்பட்ட அமைச்சரது வினைத்திட்பம்
வேந்தன்கண்ணே உறுதலை எய்தலான், எல்லாரானும் நன்கு மதிக்கப்படும்

en.1: The firmness in action of those who have risen to excellence reaches the ruler and is held in mind.
en.2: The firmness of ministers who excel in thought and in their other marks is esteemed by all, because it reaches the ruler. It reaches him when the work is finished through it, and the wealth and fame become his. “Held in mind” means not forgotten, out of esteem.
en.4: Behold the man who hath acquired a name for the doing of great deeds: his services will be greatly in request with the prince and will be esteemed by all.
en.5:
The power in act of men renowned and great,
With king acceptance finds and fame through all the state.
en.6: The firmness in action of those who have become great by the excellence (of their counsel) will, by attaining its fulfilment in the person of the king, be esteemed (by all).

padaccheda.m: தாம் எய்த எண்ணிய பொருள்கள் எல்லாவற்றையும், அவ்வெண்ணியவாறே எய்துவர்
எண்ணியவர் அவற்றிற்கு வாயிலாகிய வினைக்கண் திண்மை உடையராகப் பெறின்

en.1: Those who plan will get what they planned, just as they planned it, if they are firm.
en.2: Those who have planned will get all they planned to get, just as they planned it and with ease, if they are firm in the work that leads there. They plan only well, so if they are firm the work is finished, and once it is, everything comes to hand.
en.4: That which they will, men acquire even in the manner that they will, provided they will with all their might.
en.5:
Whate’er men think, ev’n as they think, may men obtain,
If those who think can steadfastness of will retain.
en.6: If those who have planned (an undertaking) possess firmness (in executing it), they will: obtain what they have desired even as they have desired it.

padaccheda.w: உருள் பெரும் தேர்க்கு அச்சாணி அன்னார் உடைத்து
padaccheda.m: உருளாநின்ற பெரிய தேர்க்கு அச்சின்கண் ஆணி போல வினைக்கண் திண்ணியாரை உடையது உலகம்
அதனால் அவரை வடிவின் சிறுமைநோக்கி இகழ்தலை ஒழிக

en.1: Don’t scorn people for how they look. There are those who are the axle pin of the great rolling chariot.
en.2: The world has people firm in work, like the pin on the axle of a great rolling chariot, so don’t scorn them for being small. The pin that keeps the wheel on is small, yet firm enough to carry a great load. In the same way there are ministers, small in form, who carry great tasks. Know them by that firmness.
en.4: Despise not a man for his look: for there are men who are even as the axle pin of the mighty rolling car.
en.5:
Despise not men of modest bearing;
Look not at form, but what men are:
For some there live, high functions sharing,
Like linch-pin of the mighty car!
en.6: Let none be despised for (their) size; (for) the world has those who resemble the linch-pin of the big rolling car.

padaccheda.m: மனந்தெளிந்து செய்வதாகத் துணிந்த வினையின்கண்
பின் அசைதலின்றி நீட்டித்தலை ஒழிந்து செய்க

en.1: Once you have settled on a task with a clear mind, don’t waver or delay. Do it.
en.2: Once your mind is clear and you have resolved on a task, do it without wavering and without dragging it out. To a confused mind, what should be dropped can look like what should be done. So he means work examined clearly many times and then decided on. Not wavering is firmness.
en.4: When thou hast resolved upon a thing with all thy wits about thee, waver not but pursue thy purpose with vigour.
en.5:
What clearly eye discerns as right, with steadfast will,
And mind unslumbering, that should man fulfil.
en.6: An act that has been firmly resolved on must be as firmly carried out without delay.

padaccheda.m: முதற்கண் மெய்ம் முயற்சியான் தமக்குத் துன்பம் மிகவருமாயினும்

padaccheda.w: இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை துணிவு ஆற்றிச் செய்க
padaccheda.m: அது நோக்கித் தளராது, முடிவின்கண் இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினையைத் திட்பமுடையராய்ச் செய்க

en.1: Even if great pain comes, be resolute and do the work that brings joy.
en.2: Even if your bodily effort brings great suffering at first, don’t weaken at it, but firmly do the work that brings joy at the end. Only the unshaken can look past the passing pain of effort to the lasting joy that follows.
en.4: Take up the doing of works that increase happiness: and even if thou have to suffer cruel mortification in the doing of them, steel thy heart and persevere to the end.
en.5:
Though toil and trouble face thee, firm resolve hold fast,
And do the deeds that pleasure yield at last.
en.6: Though it should cause increasing sorrow (at the outset), do with firmness the act that yields bliss (in the end).

padaccheda.m: வினைத்திட்பத்தை இது நமக்குச் சிறந்தது என்று கொள்ளாத அமைச்சரை
ஒழிந்த திட்பங்கள் எல்லாம் உடையராய இடத்தும்
நன்கு மதியார் உயர்ந்தோர்

en.1: However firm they are in other ways, the world doesn’t want those who don’t want firmness in action.
en.2: Ministers who don’t value firmness in action, though they have every other firmness, are not esteemed by the great. Without firmness of mind, even strong armies, forts and friendships won’t finish the work, and all of it is lost.
en.4: Behold the men that have not the ambition to do great deeds: the world will not care for them whatever their other virtues may be.
en.5:
The world desires not men of every power possessed,
Who power in act desire not,—crown of all the rest.
en.6: The great will not esteem those who esteem not firmness of action, whatever other abilities the latter may possess.

padaccheda.m: விசாரத்திற்கு எல்லையாவது, விசாரிக்கின்றான் இனி இது தப்பாது என்னும் துணிவினைப் பெறுதல்
அங்ஙனந் துணிவு பெற்ற வினை, பின் நீட்டிப்பின்கண் தங்குமாயின், அது குற்றமுடைத்து

en.1: The end of deliberation is to reach a decision. For that decision to sit in delay is wrong.
en.2: Deliberation ends when you reach the firm view that this can’t fail, so go on deliberating until then. If work so decided then lingers, that is a fault. To delay is not to act at the time for action. The moment passes and enemies learn of it and destroy it, so it isn’t finished.
en.4: The end of all deliberation is to arrive at a decision: and when a decision is come to, it is wrong to delay the execution thereof.
en.5:
Resolve is counsel’s end. If resolutions halt
In weak delays, still unfulfilled, ’tis grievous fault.
en.6: Consultation ends in forming a resolution (to act); (but) delay in the execution of that resolve is an evil.

padaccheda.m: நீட்டித்துச் செய்யும் பகுதியவாய வினைகளுள் நீட்டிக்க
நீட்டியாது செய்யும் வினைகளுள் நீட்டியாது ஒழிக

en.1: Take your time over what should be done slowly. Don’t delay over what must be done without delay.
en.2: Delay in the kinds of work that are done slowly, and don’t delay in the kinds that aren’t. Which is which can be known from strength and time. Do them the wrong way round and they won’t succeed. He said earlier not to delay, and here he divides that rule in two.
en.4: Do with deliberation those things that ought to be done in a leisurely way: but put not off even for a moment those things that require prompt action.
en.5:
Slumber when sleepy work’s in hand: beware
Thou slumber not when action calls for sleepless care!
en.6: Sleep over such (actions) as may be slept over; (but) never over such as may not be slept over.

padaccheda.m: வினைசெய்யுங்கால், இயலும் இடத்தெல்லாம் போராற் செய்தல் நன்று
அஃது இயலாவிடத்து, ஏனை மூன்று உபாயத்துள்ளும் அது முடிவதோர் உபாயநோக்கிச் செய்க

en.1: Action is good wherever it is possible. Where it isn’t, look for the way that will work and do that.
en.2: Wherever possible, it is good to do the work by war. It is possible when you are stronger than your enemy, and force is best then, because force is what they fear. Where it isn’t possible, when you are equal or weaker, look among conciliation, division and gifts for the means that will succeed.
en.4: Go straight for the goal whenever circumstances permit: but when circumstances are against, follow along the path that offereth the least resistance.
en.5:
When way is clear, prompt let your action be;
When not, watch till some open path you see.
en.6: Whenever it is possible (to overcome your enemy) the act (of fighting) is certainly good; if not, endeavour to employ some more successful method.

reading.note: The words say only “work”. He reads வினை here as war, and the other way as the three other means of statecraft.

padaccheda.m: செய்யத் தொடங்கிய வினையும், களையத்தொடங்கிய பகையும் என்று சொல்லப்பட்ட இரண்டனது ஒழிவும்
ஆராயுங்கால் தீயினது ஒழிவுபோலப் பின் வளர்ந்து கெடுக்கும்

en.1: Think about it: what is left of a task or an enemy burns you as what is left of a fire does.
en.2: What remains of work begun, and of an enemy you began to root out, will grow and destroy you, as what remains of a fire does. So don’t scorn it and ask what this remnant can do, but finish it. They grow back alike, so he names the enemy too. This is how the strong should work.
en.4: Uncompleted work and enemies that are left unsubdued are like unextinguished sparks of fire: they will grow betimes and overwhelm the perfunctory man.
en.5:
With work or foe, when you neglect some little thing,
If you reflect, like smouldering fire, ’twill ruin bring.
en.6: When duly considered, the incomplete execution of an undertaking and hostility will grow and destroy one like the (unextinguished) remnant of a fire.

padaccheda.w: பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடனொடு ஐந்தும்
padaccheda.m: வினைசெய்யுமிடத்துப் பொருளும் கருவியும் காலமும் வினையும் இடனுமாகிய இவ்ஐந்தனையும்
மயக்கம் அற எண்ணிச் செய்க

en.1: Wealth, means, time, the work and the place: weigh all five until the darkness clears, then act.
en.2: Weigh these five without confusion and then act: the wealth to be spent and gained, your forces and the enemy’s, the time that suits you and the time that suits them, the work you do well and the work they do well, the place where you win and the place where they win. Weigh them without error, so that you win.
en.4: Five things should be carefully considered in the doing of all action, namely, the resources in band, the instrument, the nature of the action itself, the proper time and the proper place for its execution.
en.5:
Treasure and instrument and time and deed and place of act:
These five, till every doubt remove, think o’er with care exact.
en.6: Do an act after a due consideration of the (following) five, viz., money, means, time, execution and place.

padaccheda.m: வினை செய்யுங்கால் அது முடிதற்கு உளதாம் முயற்சியும்
அதற்கு வரும் இடையூறும்
அது நீங்கி முடிந்தாற் தான் எய்தும் பெரும்பயனும்
சீர்தூக்கிச் செய்க

en.1: Look at the finish, the obstacles, and the gain you will reach when it is done, and then act.
en.2: Weigh the effort it takes to finish, the obstacles that will come, and the great gain you will reach once they are cleared and the work is done, and then act. Do it if the gain is larger than the effort and the obstacles.
en.4: Determine first the exertion necessary, the obstacles in the way, and the expected profit, and then undertake thy enterprise.
en.5:
Accomplishment, the hindrances, large profits won
By effort: these compare,—then let the work be done!
en.6: An act is to be performed after considering the exertion required, the obstacles to be encountered, and the great profit to be gained (on its completion.)

padaccheda.m: அவ்வாற்றாற் செய்யப்படும் வினையைத் தொடங்கினான் செய்யும் முறைமையாவது
அதனது உளப்பாட்டினை அறிவான் கருத்தினைத் தானறிதல்

en.1: The way to do a task is this: take in the mind of someone who knows that task from the inside.
en.2: Someone who has begun such work should proceed like this: learn the thinking of one who knows its inner workings. That means someone who has done it before, and his thinking is the means he used. Knowing that, you can use it too and gain the result.
en.4: The way to succeed in any undertaking is to learn the secret thereof from the man who is an expert in it.
en.5:
Who would succeed must thus begin: first let him ask
The thoughts of them who throughly know the task.
en.6: The method of performance for one who has begun an act is to ascertain the mind of him who knows the secret thereof.

padaccheda.m: செய்கின்ற வினையாலே அன்னது பிறிதும் ஓர் வினையை முடித்துக் கொள்க
அது மதத்தான் நனைந்த கபோலத்தினையுடைய யானையாலே அன்னது பிறிதுமோர் யானையைப் பிணித்ததனோடு ஒக்கும்

en.1: To get one task done by means of another is to bind a wet-cheeked elephant with another elephant.
en.2: Use the work you are doing to finish another like it. That is like using an elephant with cheeks wet with must to bind another such elephant. The wet cheeks show how hard the binding is. Plan so that each task begun becomes the means of finishing another, and all work is easily done.
en.4: Men decoy one elephant by means of another: even so make one enterprise the means of achieving a second.
en.5:
By one thing done you reach a second work’s accomplishment;
So furious elephant to snare its fellow brute is sent.
en.6: To make one undertaking the means of accomplishing another (similar to it) is like making one rutting elephant the means of capturing “another.

padaccheda.m: வினைசெய்வானால், தன் நட்டார்க்கு இனியவற்றைச் செய்தலினும் விரைந்து செய்யப்படும்
தன் பகைவரோடு ஒட்டாரைத் தனக்கு நட்பாக்கிக் கோடல்

en.1: Be quicker to win over those not with you than to do good to your friends.
en.2: For one at work, making friends of those opposed to his enemy is to be done even faster than doing good to his own friends. Both help the work, and both should be done before the enemy sees his weakness. It may also mean keeping his own opponents from joining others.
en.4: Placate enemies even more swiftly than thou rewardest friends.
en.5:
Than kindly acts to friends more urgent thing to do,
Is making foes to cling as friends attached to you.
en.6: One should rather hasten to secure the alliance of the foes (of one’s foes) rather than perform good offices to one’s friends.

reading.note: The plain reading takes ஒட்டார் as those not with you. He takes them first as those not with your enemy, and allows your own opponents as a second reading.

padaccheda.m: ஆளுமிடம் சிறியராய அமைச்சர்
தம்மின் வலியராய் எதிர்ந்தவழித் தம் பகுதி நடுங்கலை அஞ்சி
அந்நிலைக்கு வேண்டுவதாய சந்து கூடுமாயின், அவரைத் தாழ்ந்து அதனை ஏற்றுக் கொள்வர்

en.1: Those who hold little, fearing the trembling within, will bow to the great and take the terms, if they can get them.
en.2: Ministers with little land and fort, facing someone stronger, fear their own side will tremble. If peace can be had, they bow and accept it. The strong rarely agree to it, so he says “if”. If their side flees in fear they are lost, root and all, so give a little and take peace. The proud don’t wish to bow, so he states this as the way of the world.
en.4: The weak should not care to live in the midst of constant alarms: when an opportunity offereth itself they should submit to an alliance with the strong.
en.5:
The men of lesser realm, fearing the people’s inward dread,
Accepting granted terms, to mightier ruler bow the head.
en.6: Ministers of small states, afraid of their people being frightened, will yield to and acknowledge their superior foes, if the latter offer them a chance of reconciliation.

padaccheda.m: தன் சுற்றத்தார் மாட்டு அன்புடையனாதலும்
அமைச்சுப் பூணற்கமைந்த குடியின்கட் பிறத்தலும்
அரசர் சாதி விரும்பும் பண்புடையனாதலும்
தூது வார்த்தை சொல்வானுக்கு இலக்கணம்

en.1: Loving-kindness, birth in a good family, and the qualities rulers desire: these are the qualities of an envoy.
en.2: The marks of an envoy are loving-kindness towards his own kin, birth in a family fit for a minister’s office, and the qualities the caste of rulers desires. The first means he sees that no harm comes to his kin. The second means he has heard from his forebears how envoys act. The third brings foreign rulers under his sway.
en.4: A kind heart, high birth, and manners that captivate princes, these are the qualifications of the ambassador.
en.5:
Benevolence, high birth, the courtesy kings love:—
These qualities the envoy of a king approve.
en.6: The qualifications of an ambassador are affection (for his relations), a fitting birth, and the possession of attributes pleasing to royalty.

padaccheda.m: தம்மரசன் மாட்டு அன்புடைமையும்
அவனுக்கு ஆவன அறியும் அறிவுடைமையும்
அவற்றை வேற்றரசரிடைச் சொல்லுங்கால் ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுதல் வன்மையும் என
தூதுரைக்க உரியார்க்கு இன்றியமையாத குணங்கள் மூன்று

en.1: Loving-kindness, understanding and skill in well-weighed speech: envoys can’t do without these three.
en.2: Loving-kindness for his own ruler, the understanding to know what serves him, and skill in weighing his words before foreign rulers: an envoy can’t do without these three. Weighing means choosing the words they will agree to. “Can’t do without” implies that he needs the other marks of ministers too.
en.4: A loving nature, a wise understanding, and skill in speech, these three are indispensable to the envoy.
en.5:
Love, knowledge, power of chosen words, three things,
Should he possess who speaks the words of kings.
en.6: Love (to his sovereign), knowledge (of his affairs), and a discriminating power of speech (before other sovereigns) are the three sine qua non qualifications of an ambassador.

padaccheda.m: வேலையுடைய வேற்றரசரிடைச் சென்று தன்அரசனுக்கு வென்றிதரும் வினையைச் சொல்லுவானுக்கு இலக்கணமாவது
நீதி நூலையுணர்ந்த அமைச்சரிடைத் தான் அந்நூலை வல்லனாதல்

en.1: To be a master of the books among those who know the books: that is the quality of one who speaks for victory among men of the spear.
en.2: One who goes among foreign rulers and their spears, and says what will win victory for his own ruler, must be a master of statecraft among ministers who know it. “Spear” shows they are given to killing. “Victory” covers both tasks of an envoy. Mastery means being able to expound it before those who only know it.
en.4: Behold the man who undertaketh to speak before princes words that shall profit his master: he shall be a scholar among scholars.
en.5:
Mighty in lore amongst the learned must he be,
Midst jav’lin-bearing kings who speaks the words of victory.
en.6: To be powerful in politics among those who are learned (in ethics) is the character of him who speaks to lance-bearing kings on matters of triumph (to his own sovereign.)

padaccheda.m: இயற்கையாகிய அறிவும்
கண்டார் விரும்பும் தோற்றப் பொலிவும்
பலரோடும் பலகாலும் ஆராயப்பட்ட கல்வியும் என
நன்கு மதித்தற்கேதுவாய இம்மூன்றனது கூட்டத்தையுடையான்
வேற்று வேந்தரிடைத் தூது வினைக்குச் செல்க

en.1: Let the one who has all three, understanding, presence and well-tested learning, go on this work.
en.2: Natural understanding, a look that pleases the eye, and learning tested with many people many times: let the one who has these together go as envoy to foreign rulers. They are rarely found in one man. They win him esteem, and then the work is easily finished.
en.4: Let that man go on embassies who possesseth intelligence and learning and a commanding presence.
en.5:
Sense, goodly grace, and knowledge exquisite,
Who hath these three for envoy’s task is fit.
en.6: He may go on a mission (to foreign rulers) who has combined in him all these three, viz., (natural) sense, an attractive bearing and well-tried learning.

padaccheda.m: வேற்றரசர்க்குப் பல காரியங்களைச் சொல்லும்வழிக் காரணவகையான் தொகுத்துச் சொல்லியும்
இன்னாத காரியங்களைச் சொல்லும்வழி வெய்ய சொற்களை நீக்கி இனிய சொற்களான் மனமகிழச் சொல்லியும்
தன் அரசனு்க்கு நன்மையைப் பயப்பவனே தூதனாவான்

en.1: An envoy sums up, drops what is harsh, speaks so that people smile, and brings about good.
en.2: An envoy, with many matters to put to foreign rulers, gathers them under one cause. With unwelcome matters, he drops harsh words and uses sweet ones that gladden. Those who refuse many things agree to one cause, not seeing what follows. Those who refuse the unwelcome agree when gladdened, not seeing the sting. So he brings his ruler good.
en.4: Conciseness of speech, sweetness of tongue and a careful eschewing of all disagreeable language, these are the means by which the ambassador shall work his master’s profit.
en.5:
In terms concise, avoiding wrathful speech, who utters pleasant word,
An envoy he who gains advantage for his lord.
en.6: He is an ambassador who (in the presence of foreign rulers) speaks briefly, avoids harshness, talks so as to make them smile, and thus brings good (to his own sovereign).

padaccheda.m: நீதிநூல்களைக் கற்று
தான்சென்ற கருமத்தைப் பகைவேந்தர் மனங்கொளச் சொல்லி
அவர் செயிர்த்து நோக்கின் அந்நோக்கிற்கு அஞ்சாடு
காலத்தோடு பொருந்த அது முடியத்தக்க உபாயம் அறிவானே தூதனாவான்

en.1: An envoy is learned, unafraid of a hard stare, speaks so that it goes home, and knows what suits the time.
en.2: An envoy has learned statecraft, says what he came for so that hostile rulers take it in, doesn’t fear their angry gaze, and knows the means that suit the time. Learning shows him the means, and if the time comes when the work must be finished some other way, he must know that too.
en.4: Learning, sangfroid, persuasive speech, and a just instinct for what is meet for each occasion, all these are necessary qualifications in the envoy.
en.5:
An envoy meet is he, well-learned, of fearless eye,
Who speaks right home, prepared for each emergency.
en.6: He is an ambassador who having studied (politics), talks impressively, is not afraid of angry looks, and knows (to employ) the art suited to the time.

padaccheda.m: வேற்றரசர் இடத்துத் தான்செய்யும் முறைமை அறிந்து
அவர் செவ்வி பார்த்து
சென்ற கருமஞ் சொல்லுதற்கேற்ற இடம் அறிந்து
சொல்லுமாற்றை முன்னே விசாரித்து
அவ்வாறு சொல்லுவான் தூதரின் மிக்கான்

en.1: The finest is the one who knows his duty, watches the time, knows the place, thinks it through and then speaks.
en.2: The highest envoy weighs the standing of foreign rulers, of his own ruler and of himself, and acts to fit. He watches for the moment they will listen, chooses a place where his helpers are present, and works out in advance what he will say, their reply and his answer. Sanskrit books rank envoys highest, middle and lowest, so he says “finest”.
en.4: He is the fittest ambassador who hath a just eye for time and place, who knoweth his duty, and who weigheth his words before uttering them.
en.5:
He is the best who knows what’s due, the time considered well,
The place selects, then ponders long ere he his errand tell.
en.6: He is chief (among ambassadors) who understands the proper decorum (before foreign princes), seeks the (proper) occasion, knows the (most suitable) place, and delivers his message after (due) consideration.

padaccheda.m: தன் அரசன் வார்த்தையை அவன் சொல்லியவாறே வேற்றரசர்க்குச் சென்று சொல்லுவானது இலக்கணமாவன
பொருள் காமங்களான் தூயனாதலும்
தனக்கு அவர்அமைச்சர் துணையாந் தன்மையும்
துணிதல்உடைமையு்ம்
இம்மூன்றோடு கூடிய மெய்ம்மையும் என இவை
