en.1: Purity, support and resolve, with truth alongside: these are the marks of one who carries a message.
en.2: One who carries his ruler’s words unchanged to foreign rulers needs four things. Purity from wealth and desire, so he won’t alter them. The support of their ministers, to ease the anger his ruler’s boasts arouse. Resolve, so he won’t drop a word for fear of harm. And truth, so that everyone trusts him.
en.4: The man that is sent on embassies shall be firm of mind, pure of heart, and engaging in his ways.
en.5:
Integrity, resources, soul determined, truthfulness;
Who rightly speaks his message must these marks possess.
en.6: The qualifications of him who faithfully delivers his (sovereign’s) message are purity, the support (of foreign ministers), and boldness, with truthfulness in addition to the (aforesaid) three.

padaccheda.m: தன்அரசன் சொல்லிவிட்ட வார்த்தையை வேற்றரசர்க்குச் சென்று சொல்லவுரியான்
தனக்கு வரும் ஏதத்திற்கு அஞ்சி அவனுக்குத் தாழ்வான வார்த்தையை வாய்சோர்ந்துஞ் சொல்லாத திண்மையை உடையான்

en.1: The one who delivers a message to rulers is a man of firm heart, whose mouth lets no scarring word slip.
en.2: The one fit to deliver his ruler’s message to foreign rulers is a man of firmness, who won’t, in fear of harm to himself, let slip even by accident a word that lowers his ruler. Lowering him isn’t the duty of his caste, so such a word is a scar.
en.4: Behold the firm-minded man that will never let fall from his lips words that are weak and unbecoming: he is the fit man to deliver the messages of princes at foreign courts.
en.5:
His faltering lips must utter no unworthy thing,
Who stands, with steady eye, to speak the mandates of his king.
en.6: He alone is fit to communicate (his sovereign’s) reply, who possesses the firmness not to utter even inadvertently what may reflect discredit (on the latter).

padaccheda.m: அவ்வார்த்தை தன் உயிர்க்கு இறுதி தருமாயினும், அதற்கு அஞ்சி ஒழியாது
தன்னரசன் சொல்லியவாறே, அவனுக்கு மிகுதியை வேற்றரசரிடைச் சொல்லுவானே தூதன்ஆவான்

en.1: An envoy is one who, even if it brings his death, holds nothing back and brings about what is good for his ruler.
en.2: An envoy is one who, even if the words will end his life, doesn’t fall back in fear, but says to foreign rulers just what his ruler told him, to his ruler’s advantage. If death won’t stop him, nothing less needs mentioning.
en.4: Even when threatened with death the perfect ambassador will not fail in his duty but will endeavour to secure his master’s profit.
en.5:
Death to the faithful one his embassy may bring;
The envoy gains assured advantage for his king.
en.6: He is the ambassador who fearlessly seeks his sovereign’s good though it should cost him his life (to deliver his message).

padaccheda.m: மாறுபடுதலை உடைய அரசரைச் சேர்ந்து ஒழுகும் அமைச்சர்
அவரை மிகநீங்குவதும், மிகச்செறிவதும் செய்யாது தீக்காய்வார்போல இடைநிலத்திலே நிற்க

en.1: Those who live close to quarrelsome rulers should be like people warming themselves at a fire, neither too far nor too near.
en.2: Ministers who live close to quick-tempered rulers should stand midway, like people warming themselves at a fire. Go too far and the ruler gives you nothing. Go too near and he destroys you for disrespect. A fire too far leaves you cold, and a fire too near burns you.
en.4: Whoever desireth to move with princes, let him be like unto the men that warm themselves at a fire: let him not approach too near nor stand too far away.
en.5:
Who warm them at the fire draw not too near, nor keep too much aloof;
Thus let them act who dwell beneath of warlike kings the palace-roof.
en.6: Ministers who serve under fickle-minded monarchs should, like those who warm themselves at the fire, be neither (too) far, nor (too) near.

padaccheda.m: தம்மால் சேரப்பட்ட மன்னர் விரும்புவனவற்றைத் தாம் விரும்பாது ஒழிதல்
அமைச்சர்க்கு அவரானே நிலைபெற்ற செல்வத்தைக் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: Not wanting what rulers want will bring you lasting prosperity from those rulers.
en.2: For ministers, not wanting what rulers want brings lasting wealth from those rulers. What they want here means what belongs to them alone: their pleasures, adornment and eminence. If ministers fear to rival them and don’t want these, the rulers are pleased and give all wealth themselves. To want these brings ruin.
en.4: Not to itch for those things that the prince desireth: that is the secret of acquiring his lasting favour and thereby growing in affluence.
en.5:
To those who prize not state that kings are wont to prize,
The king himself abundant wealth supplies.
en.6: For ministers not to covet the things desired by their kings will through the kings themselves yield them everlasting wealth.

padaccheda.m: அமைச்சர் தம்மைக் காக்கக் கருதின் அரிய பிழைகள் தங்கண் வாராமற் காக்க
அவற்றை வந்தனவாகக் கேட்டு, அவ்வரசர் ஐயுற்றால் அவரைப் பின் தெளிவித்தல் யாவர்க்கும் அரிதாகலான்

en.1: If you guard yourself, guard against the grave faults. Once suspicion has set in, no one can easily clear it.
en.2: Ministers who want to protect themselves should guard against grave faults, because once rulers hear of these and suspect, no one can reassure them. Grave faults are treachery, intimacy with the royal women and taking rare treasure. Even if you are cleared, it comes back whenever they see you, as a loan comes to mind on seeing the debtor.
en.4: If thou desire not to fall into disgrace steer clear of all graver failings: for once suspicion is roused, it is impossible for anyone to remove it.
en.5:
Who would walk warily, let him of greater faults beware;
To clear suspicions once aroused is an achievement rare.
en.6: Ministers who would save themselves should avoid (the commission of) serious errors; for if the king’s suspicion is once roused, no one can remove it.

padaccheda.m: அமைந்த அரசர் அருகிருந்தால்

padaccheda.w: செவிச் சொல்லும் சேர்ந்த நகையும் அவித்து ஒழுகல்
padaccheda.m: அவர்காண ஒருவன் செவிக்கட் சொல்லுதலையும், ஒருவன் முகநோக்கி நகுதலையும் தவிர்ந்து ஒழுகுக

en.1: In the presence of the truly great, put a stop to whispers in the ear and shared laughter.
en.2: When near rulers of full worth, don’t whisper in someone’s ear or laugh looking into someone’s face where they can see. If you do, they will take it that you did so because you saw some fault in them.
en.4: Speak not in whispers in the presence of the great ones: nor smile to another’s face when they are near.
en.5:
All whispered words and interchange of smiles repress,
In presence of the men who kingly power possess.
en.6: While in the presence of the sovereign, ministers should neither whisper to nor smile at others.

padaccheda.m: அரசனுக்குப் பிறரோடு மறை நிகழ்வுழி
யாதொரு பொருளையும் செவி கொடுத்து்க் கேளாது
அவனை முடுகி வினவுவதுஞ் செய்யாது
அம்மறைப்பொருளை அவன் தானே அடக்காது சொல்லியக்கால் கேட்க

en.1: Don’t listen in on anything, don’t press, and hear the secret when it is let out to you.
en.2: When the ruler is in secret talk with others, don’t lend an ear to anything, even what might seem fit to hear, and don’t pursue him with questions. Hear that secret only when he himself tells it, holding nothing back.
en.4: Do not try to overhear any conversation nor to fish out that which is withheld from thee: and then only receive the secret when it is imparted to thee.
en.5:
Seek not, ask not, the secret of the king to hear;
But if he lets the matter forth, give ear!
en.6: (When the king is engaged) in secret counsel (with others), ministers should neither over-hear anything whatever nor pry into it with inquisitive questions, but (wait to) listen when it is divulged (by the king himself).

padaccheda.m: அரசனுக்குக் காரியம் சொல்லுங்கால் அப்பொழுது நிகழ்கின்ற அவன் குறிப்பினை அறிந்து
சொல்லுதற்கேற்ற காலத்தையும் நோக்கி
வெறுப்பிலவுமாய் வேண்டுவனவுமாய காரியங்களை அவன் மனம் விரும்பும் வகை சொல்லுக

en.1: Read the signs, consider the time, and say what is needed and not disliked, in a way that pleases.
en.2: When you speak to the ruler on business, read his present mood, watch for the right time, and say what he won’t dislike and what is needed, so that his mind wants it. Speaking while he is taken up with desire, anger and the like, or at an unfit time, is useless. What he rejects won’t go through. Use sweet, brief, clear words.
en.4: Take into thy consideration the humour of the prince and the season that is, and then speak the words that will please him.
en.5:
Knowing the signs, waiting for fitting time, with courteous care,
Things not displeasing, needful things, declare.
en.6: Knowing the (king’s) disposition, and seeking the right time, (the minister) should in a pleasing manner suggest things such as are desirable and not disagreeable.

padaccheda.m: பயன் பெரியனவுமாய், அரசன் விரும்புவனவுமாய காரியங்களை அவன் கேட்டிலனாயினும் சொல்லி, எஞ்ஞான்றும் வினை இல கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்= எஞ்ஞான்றும் பயனிலவாயவற்றைத் தானே கேட்டாலும் சொல்லாது விடுக

en.1: Say what is wanted. What is of no use, never say, even if asked.
en.2: Say things of great use that the ruler wants, even if he hasn’t asked. Useless things, never say, even if he himself asks. “Never” includes times of want.
en.4: Speak those things before the prince that are pleasant to him; but things that are unprofitable, speak not ever even if he demandeth.
en.5:
Speak pleasant things, but never utter idle word;
Not though by monarch’s ears with pleasure heard.
en.6: Ministers should (always) give agreeable advice but on no occasion recommend useless actions, though requested (to do so).

padaccheda.m: இவர் எம்மின் இளையர் என்றும், எமக்கு இன்னமுறையினை உடையரென்றும் அரசரை அவமதியாது
அவர் மாட்டு நின்ற ஒளியோடு பொருந்த ஒழுகுதல் செயப்படும்

en.1: Don’t scorn someone as young or as your kin. Live in keeping with the light that stands in them.
en.2: Don’t scorn rulers, thinking “He is younger than us” or “He is our kin”. Act in keeping with the light in them. That light is their nature as gods, guarding the world even while they sleep. So act as though they are gods and you are mortals. The light has cast off their youth and kinship, and whoever scorns them for these will be cast off too.
en.4: Trifle not with the prince because he is young or because he is thy kinsman or connection: but walk with awe before the light that is within him.
en.5:
Say not, ‘He’s young, my kinsman,’ despising thus your king;
But reverence the glory kingly state doth bring.
en.6: Ministers should behave in accordance with the (Divine) light in the persons of kings and not despise them saying “He is our junior (in age) and connected with our family!”

padaccheda.m: அரசனால் யாம் நன்கு மதிக்கப்பட்டேம் என்று கருதி அவன் விரும்பாதவற்றைச் செய்யார்
நிலைபெற்ற அறிவினை உடையார்

en.1: Those of steady vision won’t think “We have been accepted” and do what isn’t acceptable.
en.2: Those of steady understanding don’t think “The ruler esteems us” and then do what he doesn’t want. Those who ruin themselves in this way think of themselves, once favoured, as new men. Those who think of themselves as they were before, and go in fear, are the ones of steady vision.
en.4: Behold the men whose vision is unconfused and clear: they never do things that displease the prince, saying, we are favoured of him.
en.5:
‘We’ve gained his grace, boots nought what graceless acts we do.’
So deem not sages who the changeless vision view.
en.6: Those whose judgment is firm will not do what is disagreeable (to the sovereign) saying (within themselves,) “We are esteemed by the king.”

padaccheda.w: பழையம் எனக்கருதிப் பண்பு அல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை
padaccheda.m: அரசனுக்கு யாம் பழையம்எனக் கருதித் தமக்கு இயல்புஅல்லாதவற்றைச் செய்யும் உரிமை
அமைச்சர்க்குக் கேட்டினைப் பயக்கும்

en.1: The intimacy that says “We go back a long way” and does what isn’t fitting brings ruin.
en.2: The licence that makes ministers think “We are old to the ruler” and do what doesn’t suit them brings them ruin. When he loses patience and strikes, he doesn’t look on that old bond with kindly regard, but takes their life. So don’t do what rulers hate, trusting that they will bear it.
en.4: The men that rely on their intimacy with the prince and do unworthy deeds will perish.
en.5:
Who think ‘We’re ancient friends,’ and do unseemly things;
To these familiarity sure ruin brings.
en.6: The (foolish) claim with which a minister does unbecoming acts because of his (long) familiarity (with the king) will ensure his ruin.

padaccheda.m: அரசனால் குறித்த கருமத்தை அவன் கூறவேண்டாவகை அவன் முகத்தானும் கண்ணானும் நோக்கி அறியும் அமைச்சன்
எஞ்ஞான்றும் வற்றாத நீரால் சூழப்பட்ட வையத்துள்ளார்க்கு ஓர் ஆபரணமாம்

en.1: Someone who can look and know what is meant, with nothing said, is an ornament to the world of unfailing waters.
en.2: The minister who can tell from a ruler’s face and eyes what he intends, so that he doesn’t have to say it, is an ornament to the people of the world, which unfailing water surrounds. His clear mind adorns everyone.
en.4: Behold the man who divineth what is in the mind before the voice uttereth it: he is an ornament unto all the world.
en.5:
Who knows the sign, and reads unuttered thought, the gem is he
Of earth round traversed by the changeless sea.
en.6: The minister who by looking (at the king) understands his mind without being told (of it), will be a perpetual ornament to the world which is surrounded by a never-drying sea.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் மனத்தின்கண்நிகழ்வதனை ஐயப்படாது ஒருதலையாக உணரவல்லானை
மகனே ஆயினும், தெய்வத்தோடு ஒப்ப நன்கு மதிக்க

en.1: Hold anyone who knows without doubt what is in another’s heart as equal to a god.
en.2: Someone who can know for certain what goes on in another’s mind may be only human, but hold him in honour as equal to a god. He doesn’t match a god in body and the like, but he has the divine power of knowing what others think.
en.4: Look upon that man as a God who divineth with certitude that which is in the heart.
en.5:
Undoubting, who the minds of men can scan,
As deity regard that gifted man.
en.6: He is to be esteemed a god who is able to ascertain without a doubt what is within (one’s mind).

padaccheda.m: தம் குறிப்பு நிகழுமாறு அறிந்து
அரசர் தம் உறுப்பினுள் அவர் வேண்டுவது ஒன்றனைக் கொடுத்தாயினும், தமக்குத் துணையாகக் கொள்க

en.1: To gain those who can read a thought from its signs, give any of your limbs.
en.2: Those who know how their own thoughts arise, and so can read the thoughts of others, are worth any of the parts of the realm they ask for. Rulers should give it and take them as helpers. The inner working is the same in everyone, so your own mind is the tool. The parts are outer things: wealth, land, elephants, horses and the like.
en.4: Behold the men that can judge a man’s intentions from his looks: take them into thy council at whatever cost.
en.5:
Who by the sign the signs interprets plain,
Give any member up his aid to gain.
en.6: The king should even give whatever (is asked) of his belongings and secure him who by the indications (of his own mind) is able to read those of another.

reading.note: The Tamil can go two ways on the sign: he takes the first sign to be your own thought, others, like the plain reading, the other person’s. உறுப்பு is a limb. He takes it as the outer parts of a realm.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் மனத்துக் கருதிய அதனை அவன் கூறவேண்டாமல் அறியவல்லாரோடு
மற்றை மாட்டாதார் உறுப்பால் ஒருதன்மையாராக ஒப்பாராயினும்
அறிவான் வேறு

en.1: Those who grasp a thought unspoken match other people limb for limb, yet they are different.
en.2: Those who can’t grasp what someone has in mind without being told may be like those who can in body, but they differ in understanding. He says “different” because, lacking the highest understanding, such people are beasts.
en.4: The men that understand without words may have the same features with the men that do not so understand: but they form a class apart.
en.5:
Who reads what’s shown by signs, though words unspoken be,
In form may seem as other men, in function nobler far is he.
en.6: Those who understand one’s thoughts without being informed (thereof) and those who do not may (indeed) resemble one another bodily; still are they different (mentally.)

padaccheda.m: குறித்தது காணவல்ல தம் காட்சியாற் பிறர் குறிப்பினை உணரமாட்டாவாயின்
ஒருவன் உறுப்புக்களுள் சிறந்த கண்கள் வேறென்ன பயனைச் செய்வன?

en.1: If eyes can’t read a thought from its signs, what use are they among the body’s parts?
en.2: If the eyes, which can see what is shown to them, can’t read the thoughts of others, what else do they do, these finest parts of the body? He gives the eyes the soul’s power of knowing because they help it most in reading signs. Such eyes are of no use.
en.4: What is the place of the eve among the organs of sense, if it divineth not by a look that which is in the heart?
en.5:
By sign who knows not signs to comprehend, what gain,
’Mid all his members, from his eyes does he obtain?
en.6: Of what use are the eyes amongst one’s members, if they cannot by their own indications divine those of another?

padaccheda.m: தன்னை அடுத்த பொருளது நிறத்தைத் தானே கொண்டு காட்டும் பளிங்குபோல
ஒருவன் நெஞ்சத்து மிக்கதனை அவன் முகம்தானே கொண்டுகாட்டும்

en.1: As crystal shows what lies beside it, the face shows what is strongest in the heart.
en.2: Crystal takes on the colour of whatever is beside it and shows it. In the same way a person’s face takes on and shows what is uppermost in the heart.
en.4: Even as the crystal changeth and assumeth the colour of that which is near, even so doth the face alter and show that which overfloweth the heart.
en.5:
As forms around in crystal mirrored clear we find,
The face will show what’s throbbing in the mind.
en.6: As the mirror reflects what is near so does the face show what is uppermost in the mind.

en.1: Is there anything wiser than the face? In gladness or in anger, it gets there first.
en.2: Nothing knows more than the face. When the soul turns to gladness or anger towards someone, the face knows and gets there first. To those who say only the soul knows, and a face made of the five elements can’t, he answers that it blooms in gladness and darkens in anger. So the face is the means of reading thought.
en.4: What is there that is subtler than the face? for whether the heart is angry or glad it is the face that expresseth it first.
en.5:
Than speaking countenance hath aught more prescient skill?
Rejoice or burn with rage, ’tis the first herald still!
en.6: Is there anything so full of knowledge as the face? (No.) it precedes the mind, whether (the latter is) pleased or vexed.

en.1: If you have someone who can look within and know what has happened to you, it is enough to stand and look at their face.
en.2: Someone in need who finds those who can read his mind from signs and end his trouble need only stand and look at their faces as they look at his. To go past that and speak would shame both of them, so there is no need. The face is the means of reading.
en.4: If thou canst find a man that is able to read the inside of thy heart without words, it is enough that thou merely lookest towards him and thy wishes will be fulfilled.
en.5:
To see the face is quite enough, in presence brought,
When men can look within and know the lurking thought.
en.6: If the king gets those who by looking into his mind can understand (and remove) what has occurred (to him), it is enough that he stand looking at their face.

en.1: The eyes themselves will tell enmity and friendship, if you have those who know the ways of the eye.
en.2: If rulers have ministers who can tell one kind of look from another, the eyes of foreign rulers will tell the enmity or friendship in those rulers’ hearts, though they say nothing. The kinds of look are the look of dislike and the look of delight.
en.4: If there are men who understand its moods and tricks, the eye alone will declare whether there is hatred in the heart or friendship.
en.5:
The eye speaks out the hate or friendly soul of man;
To those who know the eye’s swift varying moods to scan.
en.6: If a king gets ministers who can read the movements of the eye, the eyes (of foreign kings) will (themselves) reveal (to him) their hatred or friendship.

en.1: Look into it, and those who call themselves subtle have no measuring rod but the eye.
en.2: Ministers who think their understanding subtle have, on inquiry, only their eyes as the rod to measure a ruler’s mind. Gesture, form, action, speech and many other measures exist, but a person who knows of them can hide them. A look mingles with the mind and can’t be hidden, so he names it alone.
en.4: The measuring rod of those that call themselves subtle is, when thou search for it, nought else but their eye.
en.5:
The men of keen discerning soul no other test apply
(When you their secret ask) than man’s revealing eye.
en.6: The measuring rod of those (ministers) who say “we are acute” will on inquiry be found to be their (own) eyes and nothing else.

padaccheda.m: சொல்லின் குழுவினை அறிந்த தூய்மையினை உடையார்
தாம் ஒன்று சொல்லுங்கால் அப்பொழுதை அவையினை அறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுதல்

en.1: Those pure in speech, who know the range of words, should know the assembly, weigh it up, and then speak.
en.2: Those with the purity of knowing the whole body of words, plain, figurative and suggestive, should drop what doesn’t suit them. Before speaking they should measure the assembly against themselves, as higher, equal or lower, and weigh what to say there, how to say it and where it will lead.
en.4: O ye that know how to weigh your words! study well your audience and suit your speech to it.
en.5:
Men pure in heart, who know of words the varied force,
Should to their audience known adapt their well-arranged discourse.
en.6: Let the pure who know the arrangement of words speak with deliberation after ascertaining (the nature of) the court (then assembled.)

padaccheda.m: சொற்களின் நடையினை ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்த நன்மையினை உடையார்
அவைக்கண் ஒன்று சொல்லுங்கால் அதன் செவ்வியை ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்து வழுப்படாமல் மிகவும் தெளிந்து சொல்லுக

en.1: Those good at the ways of words should judge the moment, understand it well, and then speak.
en.2: Those with the goodness of having studied how words work should, when they speak in an assembly, find the right moment and speak very clearly, without error. How words work is how each kind yields its meaning. The moment is when the hearers want to listen. Errors are of word and of meaning.
en.4: O ye that have the gift of eloquence! ascertain the mood of your audience first and then speak after careful deliberation.
en.5:
Good men to whom the arts of eloquence are known,
Should seek occasion meet, and say what well they’ve made their own.
en.6: Let the good who know the uses of words speak with a clear knowledge after ascertaining the time (suited to the court.)

padaccheda.w: அவை அறியார் சொல்லல் மேற்கொள்பவர் சொல்லின் வகை அறியார்
padaccheda.m: அவையினது அளவையறியாது ஒன்று சொல்லுதலைத் தம் மேற்கொள்வார் அச்சொல்லுதலின் கூறுபாடும் அறியார்
கற்றுவல்ல கலையும் அவர்க்கு இல்லை

en.1: Those who take on speaking without knowing the assembly don’t know the kinds of speech, and have no skill at all.
en.2: Those who take on speaking without knowing the measure of the assembly don’t know the kinds of speech, because speech varies with what the hearers can grasp. They have no learned skill either, because everyone scorns them for this ignorance.
en.4: Behold the men that take upon themselves to address an assembly without studying its nature: they know not the art of speaking nor are they good for anything else.
en.5:
Unversed in councils, who essays to speak,
Knows not the way of suasive words,—and all is weak.
en.6: Those who undertake to speak without knowing the (nature of the) court are ignorant of the quality of words as well as devoid of the power (of learning).

padaccheda.m: அறிவான் ஒள்ளியார் அவைக்கண் தாமும் ஒள்ளியாராக

padaccheda.w: வெளியார் முன் வான் சுதை வண்ணம் கொளல்
padaccheda.m: ஏனை வெள்ளைகள் அவைக்கண் தாமும் வாலிய சுதையின் நிறத்தைக் கொள்க

en.1: Be bright before the bright. Before the blank, take on the colour of white lime.
en.2: Before those bright in understanding, your superiors and equals, be bright yourself, and set out your learning and eloquence at length. The petty, who can’t judge an assembly, he calls white, after timber with no heartwood. Before them take on the colour of white lime: be blanker than they are, so that they think well of you.
en.4: Discuss wisdom in the congregation of the wise: but answer fools according to the measure of their folly.
en.5:
Before the bright ones shine as doth the light!
Before the dull ones be as purest stucco white!
en.6: Ministers should be lights in the assembly of the enlightened, but assume the pure whiteness of mortar (ignorance) in that of fools.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவர்க்கு இது நன்றுஎன்று சிறப்பித்துச் சொல்லப்பட்ட குணங்கள் எல்லாவற்றுள்ளும் நன்றே
தம்மின் மிக்கார் அவைக்கண் அவரின் முற்பட்டு ஒன்றனைச் சொல்லாத அடக்கம்

en.1: Better even than all that is called good is the restraint of not speaking first among elders.
en.2: Of all the qualities praised as good, the best is the restraint of not speaking ahead of those greater than you in an assembly. You know your own lack, their greatness, the disgrace of speaking first and the good of holding back. Only speaking first is forbidden, so you may speak with them or after them.
en.4: Behold the self-control that denieth itself the lead in an assembly of ancients: it is a virtue that outshineth even other virtues.
en.5:
Midst all good things the best is modest grace,
That speaks not first before the elders’ face.
en.6: The modesty by which one does not rush forward and speak in (an assembly of) superiors is the best among all (one’s) good qualities.

en.1: Stumbling before those who have taken in wide learning is like losing your footing on the path.
en.2: When a skilled speaker’s words slip in the assembly of those who take in wide learning and know its truth, it is like someone on the good path to liberation losing his footing and falling, a person who guarded his five senses and then fell into false conduct. He loses the reward and is scorned as well.
en.4: A failure before men of understanding is like falling off from the way of righteousness.
en.5:
As in the way one tottering falls, is slip before
The men whose minds are filled with varied lore.
en.6: (For a minister) to blunder in the presence of those who have acquired a vast store of learning and know (the value thereof) is like a good man stumbling (and falling away) from the path (of virtue).

padaccheda.w: கசடு அறச் சொல் தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து
padaccheda.m: வழுப்படாமல் சொற்களை, ஆராய்தல் வல்லார் அவைக்கண் சொல்லின்
பல நூல்களையும் கற்று அவற்றின் ஆய பயனை அறிந்தாரது கல்வி யாவர்க்கும் விளங்கித் தோன்றும்

en.1: The learning of the well-read shines among those who can weigh words without fault.
en.2: If they speak in the assembly of those who can examine words without fault, the learning of those who have studied many books and grasped what they yield shines out for everyone. So speak there.
en.4: The learning of the scholar shineth forth in all its brilliance only in an assembly of accomplished critics.
en.5:
The learning of the learned sage shines bright
To those whose faultless skill can value it aright.
en.6: The learning of those who have read and understood (much) will shine in the assembly of those who can faultlessly examine (the nature of) words.

padaccheda.m: பிறர் உணர்த்தலின்றிப் பொருள்களைத் தாமே உணரவல்ல அறிவினை உடையார் அவைக்கண், கற்றார் ஒன்றனைச் சொல்லுதல்
தானே வளர்வதொரு பயிர் நின்ற பாத்திக்கண் நீரினைச் சொரிந்தாற்போலும்

en.1: To speak before those with understanding is like pouring water on a bed where something is already growing.
en.2: When a learned person speaks in the assembly of those who can understand things unaided, it is like pouring water on a bed where a crop grows by itself. Learning that would grow anyway grows greatly. So among your equals, speak by every means.
en.4: Delivering an address of good counsel to men of understanding is like watering the roots of living plants.
en.5:
To speak where understanding hearers you obtain,
Is sprinkling water on the fields of growing grain!
en.6: Lecturing to those who have the ability to understand (for themselves) is like watering a bed of plants that are growing (of themselves.)

padaccheda.m: நல்லார் இருந்த அவைக்கண் நல்ல பொருள்களை அவர் மனங்கொள்ளச் சொல்லுதற்கு உரியார்
அவை அறியாத புல்லர் இருந்த அவைக்கண் அவற்றை மறந்தும் சொல்லாது ஒழிக

en.1: If you can speak so that a good assembly takes it in, don’t speak in a petty one, even by forgetting.
en.2: Those fit to say good things so that the good take them in should not, even by forgetting, say them among the petty. If they do, the good assembly scorns them for not knowing their audience, and the petty one scorns them too, because it can’t follow the matter. They become fit for neither.
en.4: O ye that desire to delight the wise by your discourses! beware of addressing even by mistake an audience of fools.
en.5:
In councils of the good, who speak good things with penetrating power,
In councils of the mean, let them say nought, e’en in oblivious hour.
en.6: Those who are able to speak good things impressively in an assembly of the good should not even forgetfully speak them in that of the low.

padaccheda.w: தம் கணத்தார் அல்லார் முன் கோட்டி கொளல்
padaccheda.m: நல்லார் தம்இனத்த அல்லாதார் அவைக்கண் ஒன்றனையும் சொல்லற்க
சொல்லின் அது தூய்தல்லாத முற்றத்தின்கண் உக்க அமிழ்தத்தினை ஒக்கும்

en.1: Speaking before those not of your own kind is like ambrosia spilled in a filthy yard.
en.2: Say nothing at all before those who aren’t of your own kind, the good. If you do, it is ambrosia spilled in an unclean yard: the medicine against death, wasted, reaching no one who would enjoy it. Such speech is useless. He rejects the reading that likens the act of speaking to ambrosia, because an act can’t match a thing.
en.4: A discourse spoken before the unworthy is like unto ambrosia spilled on filthy ground.
en.5:
Ambrosia in the sewer spilt, is word
Spoken in presence of the alien herd.
en.6: To utter (a good word) in the assembly of those who are of an inferior rank is like dropping nectar on the ground.

en.1: Those pure in speech, who know the range of words, know the kinds of assembly and don’t slip before an able one.
en.2: Those with the purity of knowing the whole body of words know which assemblies are learned and which aren’t, and in a learned one they don’t speak wrongly out of fear. Some take the able things to be the subjects they have mastered.
en.4: Behold the men that know how to weigh their words: they will also know how to order their discourse and will not fail before a wise audience.
en.5:
Men, pure in heart, who know of words the varied force,
The mighty council’s moods discern, nor fail in their discourse.
en.6: The pure who know the classification of words having first ascertained the nature (of the court) will not (through fear) falter in their speech before that powerful body.

padaccheda.m: கற்றார் எல்லாரினும் இவர் நன்கு கற்றார் என்று உலகத்தாரான் சொல்லப்படுவார்
கற்றார் அவைக்கண் அஞ்சாதே தாம் கற்றவற்றை அவர் மனம் கொள்ளும்வகை சொல்லவல்லார்

en.1: Those who can say what they have learned so that the learned take it in are called the learned among the learned.
en.2: Those who can fearlessly say what they have learned in an assembly of the learned, so that the hearers take it in, are called by the world the best learned of all. They are the ones the world knows, so they are the ones it praises.
en.4: Behold the man who can sustain his conclusions in the congregation of the learned: he will be called a scholar among scholars.
en.5:
Who what they’ve learned, in penetrating words have learned to say,
Before the learn’d, among the learn’d most learn’d are they.
en.6: Those who can agreeably set forth their acquirements before the learned will be regarded as the most learned among the learned.

padaccheda.m: பகையிடை அஞ்சாது புக்குச் சாவவல்லார் உலகத்துப் பலர்
அவையிடை அஞ்சாது புக்குச் சொல்லவல்லார் சிலர்

en.1: Those who die among the enemy are common. Those who have no fear in an assembly are rare.
en.2: Many in the world can go among enemies without fear and die there. Few can go into an assembly without fear and speak.
en.4: They are common, those that can brave death on the battlefield: but they are rare who can face an audience without trembling.
en.5:
Many encountering death in face of foe will hold their ground;
Who speak undaunted in the council hall are rarely found.
en.6: Many indeed may (fearlessly) die in the presence of (their) foes; (but) few are those who are fearless in the assembly (of the learned).

padaccheda.m: பல நூல்களையும் கற்றார் அவைக்கண் தாம் கற்றவற்றை அவர் மனம் கொள்ளுமாற்றாற் சொல்லி
அவற்றின் மிக்க பொருள்களை அம் மிகக் கற்றாரிடத்து அறிந்து கொள்க

en.1: Say what you have learned so that the learned take it in, and from those who have learned more, take that more.
en.2: Say what you have learned so that an assembly of those learned in many books takes it in, and get from those deeper in learning what goes beyond it. No one can learn everything. Where many with different learning sit, speak in a way that suits them. They will speak too, and you can hear what you never got to learn.
en.4: Place before the learned that which thou hast mastered: and that which thou knowest not, learn from them that excel therein.
en.5:
What you have learned, in penetrating words speak out before
The learn’d; but learn what men more learn’d can teach you more.
en.6: (Ministers) should agreeably set forth their acquirements before the learned and acquire more (knowledge) from their superiors in (learning).

padaccheda.m: சொல் இலக்கணநெறியானே அளவை நூலை அமைச்சர் உட்பட்டுக் கற்க
வேற்று வேந்தர் அவையிடை அஞ்சாது அவர் சொல்லிய சொற்கு உத்தரம் சொல்லுதற் பொருட்டு

en.1: Learn by the right path and know the measure, so that you can answer in an assembly without fear.
en.2: Ministers should study logic, which is reached by way of grammar, so that they can answer without fear what foreign rulers say in their assemblies. Logic must come after grammar, so grammar is the path. Only those learned in the forms of debate and its tricks can say the word that beats another’s, so study them without error.
en.4: Master thou the science of reasoning that thou mayest speak without fear in any assembly.
en.5:
By rule, to dialectic art your mind apply,
That in the council fearless you may make an apt reply.
en.6: In order to reply fearlessly before a foreign court, (ministers) should learn logic according to the rules (of grammar.)

reading.note: He takes அளவு, measure, to be logic, and ஆறு, the path, to be grammar. The Tamil names neither.

padaccheda.m: வன்கண்மை உடையர் அல்லாதார்க்கு வாளோடு என்ன இயைபு உண்டு? நுண்ணவை அஞ்சுபவர்க்கு நூலொடு என்= அதுபோல நுண்ணியாரது அவையை அஞ்சுவார்க்கு நூலோடு என்ன இயைபு உண்டு?

en.1: What has a sword to do with those who lack hard courage? What have books to do with those who fear a subtle assembly?
en.2: What has a sword to do with those who lack hard courage? In the same way, what have books to do with those who fear an assembly of subtle minds? They have no right to books.
en.4: What have they to do with swords, those who have no mettle in them? and what have they to do with books, those who are afraid to face the assembly of the wise?
en.5:
To those who lack the hero’s eye what can the sword avail?
Or science what, to those before the council keen who quail?
en.6: What have they to do with a sword who are not valiant, or they with learning who are afraid of an intelligent assembly?

en.1: The learning of a man who fears the assembly is a bright sword in a eunuch’s hand among the enemy.
en.2: The books learned by a man who fears the assembly he should speak in are like the sharp sword held by a eunuch who fears the enemy she should strike. He defines a eunuch as mostly female in nature, with some male nature too. The battlefield is right and the sword is good, yet the holder’s fault makes it worthless. So too the assembly and the books.
en.4: Even as the sword in the hand of the eunuch on the battlefield is the learning of him who is afraid to face an audience.
en.5:
As shining sword before the foe which ‘sexless being’ bears,
Is science learned by him the council’s face who fears.
en.6: The learning of him who is diffident before an assembly is like the shining sword of an hermaphrodite in the presence of his foes.

en.1: Those who can’t speak so that a good assembly takes it in are of no use, however much they have learned.
en.2: Those who, out of fear, can’t say good things in an assembly of the good in a way that suits it are of no use to the world, though they have learned many books. They don’t speak before those who could judge, so no one knows their learning is real. Some read it as: they get no fruit from their learning.
en.4: Behold the men who cannot drive home their point before a learned assembly: even if they possess varied learning they are good for nothing.
en.5:
Though many things they’ve learned, yet useless are they all,
To men who cannot well and strongly speak in council hall.
en.6: Those who cannot agreeably speak good things before a good assembly are indeed unprofitable persons in spite of all their various acquirements.

padaccheda.m: நூல்களைக் கற்று வைத்தும், அவற்றாற் பயன் அறிந்து வைத்தும் நல்லார் இருந்த அவையினை அஞ்சி ஆண்டுச் சொல்லாதாரை
உலகத்தார் கல்லாதவரினும் கடையர் என்று சொல்லுவர்

en.1: They say those who have learned and understood, yet fear an assembly of the good, are lower than the unlearned.
en.2: Those who have learned books and grasped their use, yet fear an assembly of the good and don’t speak there, are called lower than the unlearned by the world. They neither gain the fruit of learning nor pass it to others, and are left with only the pain of having studied.
en.4: Behold the men that possess learning but fear to face an assembly of learned men: they will be esteemed lower than even the ignorant.
en.5:
Who, though they’ve learned, before the council of the good men quake,
Than men unlearn’d a lower place must take.
en.6: They who, though they have learned and understood, are yet afraid of the assembly of the good, are said to be inferior (even) to the illiterate.

padaccheda.m: அவைக்களத்தை அஞ்சித் தாம் கற்றவற்றை அதற்கு ஏற்கச் சொல்லமாட்டாதார்
உயிர் வாழ்கின்றார் ஆயினும், உலகத்தாரால் எண்ணப்படாமையின் இறந்தாரோடு ஒப்பர்

en.1: Those who fear the assembly and can’t get across what they have learned are alive, yet they are like those who are not.
en.2: Those who fear the assembly and can’t say what they have learned in a way that suits it are alive, but the world doesn’t count them, so they are like the dead.
en.4: Behold the men that are afraid before an assembly and are unable to expound what they have learned: though they breathe, they are no better than dead men.
en.5:
Who what they Ve learned, in penetrating words know not to say,
The council fearing, though they live, as dead are they.
en.6: Those who through fear of the assembly are unable to set forth their learning in an interesting manner, though alive, are yet like the dead.

padaccheda.m: குன்றாத விளையுளைச் செய்வோரும்
அறவோரும்
கேடில்லாத செல்வம் உடையோரும்
ஒருங்கு வாழ்வதே நாடாவது

en.1: A country is where unfailing harvests, worthy people and the rich who never decline all come together.
en.2: A country is where three live together. Farmers whose harvests never fall short mean no one is poor. The righteous, ascetics, sages and the like, mean it doesn’t perish. The rich, merchants who bring rare goods by ship and by land, supply wealth to the ruler and the people.
en.4: That is the great country which never faileth in its yield of harvests, and which is the abode of sages and of rich men that are worthy.
en.5:
Where spreads fertility unfailing, where resides a band
Of virtuous men, and those of ample wealth, call that a ‘land.’
en.6: A kingdom is that in which (those who carry on) a complete cultivation, virtuous persons, and merchants with inexhaustible wealth, dwell together.

padaccheda.m: அளவிறந்த பொருளுடைமையாற் பிற தேயத்தாரானும் விரும்பத்தக்கதாய்
கேடின்மையோடு கூடி மிகவிளைவதே நாடாவது

en.1: A country is a land desired for its great wealth, which yields abundantly because ruin rarely touches it.
en.2: A country is desired even by other lands for its boundless wealth and yields abundantly, free from ruin. Ruin comes from too much rain, no rain, rats, locusts, parrots and a hostile ruler close by. The ruler’s righteousness keeps away the first five, and his valour the last.
en.4: That is the great country which attracteth men to itself by the greatness of its wealth and which yieldeth abundantly for that it is free from pests.
en.5:
That is a ‘land’ which men desire for wealth’s abundant share,
Yielding rich increase, where calamities are rare.
en.6: A kingdom is that which is desired for its immense wealth, and which grows greatly in prosperity, being free from destructive causes.

padaccheda.m: பிற நாடுகள் பொறுத்த பாரம் எல்லாம் ஒருங்கே தன்கண் வருங்கால் அவற்றைத் தாங்கி
அதன்மேல் தன் அரசனுக்கு, இறைப்பொருள் முழுதையும் உடம்பட்டுக் கொடுப்பதே நாடாவது

en.1: A country bears every burden that falls on it at once, and still gives its ruler his whole tax.
en.2: When all the burdens other lands have carried come on a country at once, it takes them in, and on top of that freely pays its ruler all his dues. The burdens are people and herds of cattle and buffalo fleeing invasion, a crooked sceptre or want of food in their own lands. It lets them live as well as they did at home.
en.4: Behold the great nation: even if burdens upon burdens press down upon it, it will support them bravely and pay its taxes in full withal.
en.5:
When burthens press, it bears; yet, with unfailing hand,
To king due tribute pays: that is the ‘land.’
en.6: A kingdom is that which can bear any burden that may be pressed on it (from adjoining kingdoms) and (yet) pay the full tribute to its sovereign.

padaccheda.m: மிக்க பசியும்
நீங்காத நோயும்
புறத்து நின்று வந்து அழிவுசெய்யும் பகையும் இன்றி
இனிது நடப்பதே நாடாவது

en.1: A country runs free of deep hunger, endless sickness and destroying enemies.
en.2: A country goes on happily without great hunger, unending sickness or enemies from outside. Hunger stays away because it has farmers and abundant yields. Sickness stays away because its winds, cold, heat and food do no harm. Enemies stay away because of the ruler’s strength, the standing army, forests and fortresses.
en.4: That is the great country which is free from famines and plagues, and which is safe from the invasions of enemies.
en.5:
That is a ‘land’ whose peaceful annals know,
Nor famine fierce, nor wasting plague, nor ravage of the foe.
en.6: A kingdom is that which continues to be free from excessive starvation, irremediable epidemics, and destructive foes.

padaccheda.m: சங்கேத வயத்தான் மாறுபட்டுக் கூடும் பல கூட்டமும்
உடனுறையாநின்றே பாழாகச் செய்யும் உட்பகையும்

padaccheda.w: வேந்து அலைக்கும் கொல் குறும்பும் இல்லது நாடு
padaccheda.m: அளவு வந்தால் வேந்தனை அலைக்கும் கொல்வினைக் குறும்பரும் இல்லாததே நாடாவது

en.1: A country has no rival factions, no ruinous enemies within and no murderous rebels who harry the ruler.
en.2: A country has no factions gathered against each other, bound by caste or god. It has no enemies within who lay it waste: highwaymen, thieves, slanderers, and boars, tigers and bears. It has no killers who harry the ruler when the chance comes. A country is where ruler and people drive these out.
en.4: That is the great nation which is not divided into warring sects, which is free from murderous anarchists, and which hath no traitors within its bosom to ruin it.
en.5:
From factions free, and desolating civil strife, and band
Of lurking murderers that king afflict, that is the ‘land.’
en.6: A kingdom is that which is without various (irregular) associations, destructive internal enemies, and murderous savages who (sometimes) harass the sovereign.

padaccheda.m: பகைவரால் கெடுதல் அறியாததாய்
அரிதிற் கெட்டதாயினும் அப்பொழுதும் தன் வளம் குன்றாத நாட்டினை
எல்லா நாட்டினும் தலை என்று சொல்லுவர் நூலோர்

en.1: The land that knows no ruin, and whose riches hold even when it is ruined, is called the first of countries.
en.2: The learned call the first of all countries the one that knows no ruin from enemies, and whose riches don’t fall even on the rare day it is ruined. The ruler’s strength, worship of the gods and righteous acts keep ruin away. Its riches, from mines, fields and groves, don’t fall because they come by nature or have been stored up.
en.4: Behold the land that hath known no devastation by its foes, and which, even should it suffer any, would not bate one whit in its yield: it will be called a jewel among the countries of the world.
en.5:
Chief of all lands is that, where nought disturbs its peace;
Or, if invaders come, still yields its rich increase.
en.6: The learned say that the best kingdom is that which knows no evil (from its foes), and, if injured (at all), suffers no diminution in its fruitfulness.

padaccheda.m: கீழ்நீர், மேனீர் எனப்பட்ட தண்ணீரும்
வாய்ப்புடைத்தாய மலையும்
அதனின்றும் வருவதாய நீரும்
அழியாத நகரியும்
நாட்டிற்கு அவயவமாம்

en.1: The two waters, a well-placed hill, running water and a strong fortress are the limbs of a country.
en.2: Water below and above the ground, a well-placed hill, the water that comes from it and a walled city that can’t fall are the limbs of a country. The waters are wells, tanks and rivers, so there is plenty even if the sky fails. The hill stands to one side, gives its own riches, and pours out in summer what it drank in the rains.
en.4: The waters of the surface, the waters that flow underground, rainwater, well-situated mountains, and strong fortifications, these are indispensable to every country.
en.5:
Waters from rains and springs, a mountain near, and waters thence;
These make a land, with fortress’ sure defence.
en.6: The constituents of a kingdom are the two waters (from above and below), well situated hills and an indestructible fort.

padaccheda.w: பிணி இன்மை செல்வம் விளைவு இன்பம் ஏமம் இவ் ஐந்து
padaccheda.m: நோயின்மையும், செல்வம் விளைதல், இன்பம், காவல் என்று இவை உடைமையும் ஆகிய இவ்வைந்தினையும்
நாட்டிற்கு அழகு என்று சொல்லுவர் நூலோர்

en.1: They say five things are a country’s ornament: freedom from sickness, wealth, harvest, happiness and safety.
en.2: The learned say these five adorn a country: no sickness, wealth, yield, happiness and protection. Good land keeps sickness away. Happiness comes from festivals, sacrifices, worthy people, things to enjoy and good land and water. Protection is the ruler’s, the people’s and the fortress’s. This beauty makes people of other lands long for it and forget their own.
en.4: Wealth, richness of yield, happiness, immunity from diseases, and safety from invasions, these five are the ornaments of a kingdom.
en.5:
A country’s jewels are these five: unfailing health,
Fertility, and joy, a sure defence, and wealth.
en.6: Freedom from epidemics, wealth, produce, happiness, and protection (to subjects); these five, the learned say, are the ornaments of a kingdom.

padaccheda.m: தங்கண் வாழ்வார் தேடி வருந்தாமல் அவர்பால் தானே அடையும் செல்வத்தை உடையவற்றை நூலோர் நாடு என்று சொல்லுவர்

padaccheda.w: நாட வளம் தரும் நாடு நாடு அல்ல
padaccheda.m: ஆதலான் தேடி வருந்தச் செல்வம் அடைவிக்கும் நாடுகள் நாடாகா

en.1: A country is a land whose riches come without seeking. Land that gives riches only when sought is no country.
en.2: The learned call a country the land whose wealth comes to the people living there without their toiling after it. So lands that give wealth only to those who seek and toil are not countries. Seeking, in both lines, means toil.
en.4: That alone deserveth to be called country which produceth abundantly without the labour of the people: that which yieldeth only unto labour deserveth not that name.
en.5:
That is a land that yields increase unsought,
That is no land whose gifts with toil are bought.
en.6: The learned say that those are kingdoms whose wealth is not laboured for, and those not, whose wealth is only obtained through labour.

padaccheda.m: வேந்தனோடு மேவதல் இல்லாத நாடு

padaccheda.w: ஆங்கு அமைவு எய்தியக் கணணும் பயம் இன்றே
padaccheda.m: மேற்சொல்லிய குணங்கள் எல்லாவற்றினும் நிறைந்து இருந்ததாயினும் அவற்றாற் பயனுடைத்தன்று

en.1: Even with all of this, a country is of no use if it isn’t well matched with its ruler.
en.2: A country without accord with its ruler is of no use, even if it is full of all the qualities named above. Accord means the people have loving-kindness for him and he has compassion for them. Without these no one stays to live there, so all the rest is useless.
en.4: Even if a country hath all these blessings it is worth nothing if it is not blessed in its ruler.
en.5:
Though blest with all these varied gifts’ increase,
A land gains nought that is not with its king at peace.
en.6: Although in possession of all the above mentioned excellences, these are indeed of no use to a country, in the absence of harmony between the sovereign and the subjects.

padaccheda.m: மூவகை ஆற்றலும் உடையராய்ப் பிறர்மேல் செல்வார்க்கும் அரண் சிறந்தது
அவையின்றித் தம்மேல் வருவார்க்கு அஞ்சித் தன்னையே அடைவார்க்கும் அரண் சிறந்தது

en.1: A fortress is of value to those who are strong, and of value to those who fear and look after themselves.
en.2: A fortress matters to those with the three kinds of strength who march on others, because they must leave family and wealth safe behind them. It matters to those without strength who shelter in it from attackers. When power is gone, they would find no safety, like the shipwrecked in mid-ocean. He names the strong first, because even they perish without one.
en.4: Fortresses are helpful to the weak who are thinking only of their defence: but they are also no less helpful to the strong and powerful.
en.5:
A fort is wealth to those who act against their foes;
Is wealth to them who, fearing, guard themselves from woes.
en.6: A fort is an object of importance to those who march (against their foes) as well as to those who through fear (of pursuers) would seek it for shelter.

padaccheda.w: மணிநீரும் மண்ணும் மலையும் அணிநிழல் காடும் உடையது அரண்
padaccheda.m: மணிபோலும் நிறத்தினை உடைய நீரும், வெள்ளிடை நிலமும், மலையும், குளிர்ந்த நிழலையுடைய காடும் உடையதே அரணாவது

en.1: A fortress has water bright as a gem, open ground, a hill, and a forest of fine shade.
en.2: A fortress has gem-coloured water that never dries up, bare land with no water or shade so that enemies can’t settle outside the wall, a hill, and a dense forest of cool shade. It is a place ringed by these four defences of water, land, hill and forest, natural and built.
en.4: Watercourses, deserts, mountains, and thick jungles, all these constitute various kinds of defensive barriers.
en.5:
A fort is that which owns a fount of waters crystal clear,
An open space, a hill, and shade of beauteous forest near.
en.6: A fort is that which has everlasting water, plains, mountains and cool shady forests.

padaccheda.w: உயர்வு அகலம் திண்மை அருமை இந்நான்கின் அமைவு
padaccheda.m: உயர்ச்சியும், அகலமும், திண்மையும், அருமையும் என்று சொல்லப்பட்ட இந்நான்கின் மிகுதியை உடைய மதிலை
அரண் என்று சொல்லுவர் நூலோர்

en.1: Height, breadth, strength and being hard to reach: the books say a fortress is what has all four.
en.2: The learned call a wall a fortress when it has these four in plenty. Height beyond any ladder. Breadth at the base so that outsiders can’t dig through, and at the top so that defenders can stand and work. Strength, from good bricks that can’t be pierced. And being hard to approach, because of the machines on it.
en.4: Height, thickness, strength, and impregnability, these are the four requisites that Science demandeth of fortresses.
en.5:
Height, breadth, strength, difficult access:
Science declares a fort must these possess.
en.6: The learned say that a fortress is an enclosure having these four (qualities) viz. height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility.

padaccheda.m: காக்கவேண்டும் இடம் சிறிதாய், அகன்ற இடத்தை உடைத்தாய்
தன்னை வந்து முற்றிய பகைவரது மனஎழுச்சியைக் கெடுப்பதே அரணாவது

en.1: A fortress needs little guarding, has ample room, and crushes the spirit of the enemy that reaches it.
en.2: A fortress has only a small part to guard, but great space, and it destroys the spirit of the enemy who come to besiege it. Apart from gates and paths, its sides are hill, forest or water. Enemies who come trusting in their strength, saying they will take it now, lose that spirit when they see it.
en.4: That is the best fortress which is vulnerable in very few places but at the same time is spacious, and which is capable of breaking the assaults of those that attempt to take it.
en.5:
A. fort must need but slight defence, yet ample be,
Defying all the foeman’s energy.
en.6: A fort is that which has an extensive space within, but only small places to be guarded, and such as can destroy the courage of besieging foes.

padaccheda.m: புறத்தாரான் கோடற்கு அரிதாய்
உட்கொண்ட பலவகை உணவிற்றாய்
அகத்தாரது போர்நிலைக்கு எளிதாய நீர்மையை உடையதே அரணாவது

en.1: A fortress is hard to take, holds stores of food, and is easy for those inside to hold.
en.2: A fortress is hard for outsiders to take, because hedges, moats and machines keep them from gaining a footing. It holds food of many kinds, and all else that people consume. It is easy for those inside to fight from: their weapons reach the attackers easily, the attackers’ weapons don’t reach them, and the ramparts are wide.
en.4: Impregnability, facility of defence for the garrison, and abundance of provisions inside, these are the essential requisites of the fortress.
en.5:
Impregnable, containing ample stores of food,
A. fort, for those within, must be a warlike station good.
en.6: A fort is that which cannot be captured, which abounds in suitable provisions, and affords a position of easy defence to its inmates.

padaccheda.m: அகத்தோர்க்கு வேண்டும் பொருள்கள் எல்லாவற்றையும் உள்ளே உடைத்தாய்
புறத்தோரால் அழிவெய்தும் எல்லைக்கண், அஃது எய்தாவகை உதவிக்காக்கும் நல்ல வீரரையும் உடையதே அரணாவது

en.1: A fortress has everything it needs, and good people who help when the moment comes.
en.2: A fortress has within it everything those inside need, and good warriors who step in and save it when outsiders are about to destroy it. They are good because of their loving-kindness for the ruler, their honour, their valour and their tirelessness.
en.4: That is the real fortress which is filled with stores of every kind and which is garrisoned by men that will make a brave defence.
en.5:
A. fort, with all munitions amply stored,
In time of need should good reserves afford.
en.6: A fort is that which has all (needful) things, and excellent heroes that can help it against destruction (by foes.)

padaccheda.m: புகலொடு போக்கு ஒழியும் வகை நெருங்கிச் சூழ்ந்தும்
அங்ஙனம் சூழாது நெகிழ்ந்த இடன் நோக்கி ஒருமுகமாகப் பொருதும்
அகத்தோரை அவர் தெளிந்தோரை விட்டுக் கீழறுத்துத் திறப்பித்தும்
புறத்தோரான் கொள்ளுதற்கு அரியதே அரணாவது

en.1: A fortress is hard to take, whether by encircling it, by attacking without encircling, or by working treachery within.
en.2: A fortress is hard for outsiders to take, whether they close in around it so that no one can come or go, or attack in one place where it looks weak, or send trusted men to subvert those inside and have it opened. Its full stores defeat the first of these, and its good men the other two.
en.4: That is the veritable fortress which cannot be reduced whether by a regular siege or by storm or even by mining.
en.5:
A fort should be impregnable to foes who gird it round,
Or aim there darts from far, or mine beneath the ground.
en.6: ‘A fort is that which cannot be captured by blockading, assaulting, or undermining it.

padaccheda.m: தானைப்பெருமையாற் சூழ்தல் வல்லராய் வந்து சூழ்ந்த புறத்தோரையும்
தன்னைப் பற்றிய அகத்தோர், தாம்பற்றிய இடம் விடாதே நின்று, பொருது வெல்வதே அரணாவது

en.1: A fortress is one where those holding it can hold fast and beat even those strong enough to surround it.
en.2: A fortress is one where those inside hold their ground, never leave it, and fight and beat even outsiders whose great armies can encircle them. There a small force doesn’t merely stand up to a great one, it beats it. Others read this differently.
en.4: That is the veritable fortress which enableth the garrison to defeat the besiegers even when they exert their utmost against it.
en.5:
Howe’er the circling foe may strive access to win,
A fort should give the victory to those who guard within.
en.6: That is a fort whose inmates are able to overcome, without losing their ground, even abler men who have besieged it.

padaccheda.w: முனை முகத்து மாற்றலர் சாய வினைமுகத்து வீறு எய்தி
padaccheda.m: போர் தொடங்கின அளவிலே, பகைவர் கெடும் வண்ணம் அகத்தோர் செய்யும் வினைவேறுபாடுகளான் வீறுபெற்று
மற்றும் வேண்டும் மாட்சியையுடையதே அரணாவது

en.1: An excellent fortress wins glory in action, and the enemy falls at the very front of the fight.
en.2: A fortress wins distinction through what those inside do, so that the enemy is ruined as soon as battle begins, and has every other excellence it needs. Those ruined at the start can’t regroup. The actions are shooting, throwing, stabbing and cutting, whichever counters the attack. The other excellences include secret tunnels for going in and out unseen.
en.4: That is the veritable fortress which hath been rendered impregnable by works of various kinds, and which enableth the defenders to fell down their adversaries even at the outermost enceintes.
en.5:
At outset of the strife a fort should foes dismay;
And greatness gain by deeds in every glorious day.
en.6: A fort is that which derives excellence from the stratagems made by (its inmates) to defeat their enemies in the battlefield.

padaccheda.m: அரண்
மேற்சொல்லப்பட்ட மாட்சி எல்லாம் உடைத்தாய இடத்தும்
வினைசெய்தற்கண் மாட்சி இல்லாதார்மாட்டு அவை இலதாம்

en.1: However excellent a fortress may be, with those who have no excellence in action it is no fortress.
en.2: Though a fortress has every excellence described above, it has none of them in the hands of those without excellence in action, who sit idle, act without measure or do what doesn’t suit. If they don’t guard it by doing the right work in the right measure, it falls and its excellences are no use. A fortress can’t do without its guards.
en.4: But however strong a fortress may be, it will avail nothing if the defenders show not vigour in action.
en.5:
Howe’er majestic castled walls may rise,
To craven souls no fortress strength supplies.
en.6: Although a fort may possess all (the above-said) excellencies it is, as it were without these, if its inmates possess not the excellency of action.

padaccheda.m: ஒரு பொருளாக மதிக்கப்படாதாரையும் படுவராகச் செய்யவல்ல பொருளை ஒழிய
ஒருவனுக்குப் பொருளாவது இல்லை

en.1: Nothing counts but wealth, which makes people who don’t count into people who do.
en.2: Apart from wealth, which can make those held of no account into people of account, a person has nothing worth the name. Those of no account are the ignorant and the low-born. Wealth makes the wise and the high-born come and stand before them. It alone is what should be earned.
en.4: There is nothing like wealth to lend so much consequence to men of no consequence.
en.5:
Nothing exists, save wealth, that can
Change man of nought to worthy man.
en.6: Besides wealth there is nothing that can change people of no importance into those of (some) importance.

padaccheda.m: எல்லாநன்மையும் உடையராயினும் பொருள் இல்லாரை யாவரும் இகழ்வர்

எல்லாத் தீமையும் உடையராயினும் அஃது உடையாரை யாவரும் உயரச் செய்வர். உயரச்செய்தல்= தாம் தாழ்ந்து நி்ற்றல். இகழ்தற்கண்ணு்ம் தாழ்தற்கண்ணும் பகைவர், நட்டார், நொதுமலர் என்னும் மூவகையாரும் ஒத்தலின், யாவரும் என்றார். பின்னும் கூறியது, அதனை வலியுறுத்தல் பொருட்டு

en.1: Everyone scorns those who have nothing. Everyone honours the rich.
en.2: Everyone scorns those without wealth, even if they have every virtue. Everyone exalts those who have it, even if they have every vice, by lowering themselves before them. Enemies, friends and strangers alike do this, so he says “everyone”, and he says it twice for force.
en.4: The indigent are decried by all: but everyone exalteth the man of substance.
en.5:
Those who have nought all will despise;
All raise the wealthy to the skies.
en.6: All despise the poor; (but) all praise the rich.

padaccheda.m: பொருள் என்று எல்லாரானும் சிறப்பிக்கப்படும் நந்தா விளக்கு
தன்னைச் செய்தவர்க்கு அவர் நினைத்த தேயத்துச் சென்று பகையென்னும் இருளைக் கெடுக்கும்

en.1: The unfailing lamp called wealth goes to whatever land you think of and cuts through the dark.
en.2: The undying lamp all people honour as wealth goes, for those who made it, to whatever land they have in mind, and destroys the darkness of enmity. It is “unfailing” because all need it at all times. Going where you think of marks how it differs from other lamps.
en.4: The unflickering light called wealth lighteth up all dark places unto him that possesseth it.
en.5:
Wealth, the lamp unfailing, speeds to every land,
Dispersing darkness at its lord’s command.
en.6: The imperishable light of wealth goes into regions desired (by its owner) and destroys the darkness (of enmity therein).

padaccheda.w: திறன் அறிந்து தீது இன்றி வந்த பொருள்
padaccheda.m: செய்யும்திறத்தினை அறிந்து அரசன் கொடுங்கோன்மை இலனாக உளதாய பொருள்
அவனுக்கு அறத்தையும் கொடுக்கும், இன்பத்தையும் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: Wealth that comes by knowing how, and without wrong, gives birth to righteousness and to happiness.
en.2: Wealth a ruler gets by knowing the proper way to earn it, without cruel rule, gives him righteousness and happiness. Righteousness, because he is praised for a just sceptre and gains merit from worship of the gods and from gifts. Happiness, because it can be enjoyed for a long time. So earn it that way.
en.4: Behold the substance that is acquired by means that are not evil: righteousness floweth therefrom and happiness also.
en.5:
Their wealth, who blameless means can use aright,
Is source of virtue and of choice delight.
en.6: The wealth acquired with a knowledge of the proper means and without foul practices will yield virtue and happiness.

padaccheda.m: தாம் குடிகள்மாட்டுச் செய்யும் அருளோடும், அவர் தம்மாட்டுச் செய்யும் அன்போடும் கூடி வாராத பொருள் ஈட்டத்தை
அரசர் பொருந்தாது கழிய விடுக

en.1: Wealth that comes without compassion and loving-kindness: don’t embrace it, let it roll away.
en.2: Rulers should not touch wealth that doesn’t come with the compassion they show their people and the loving-kindness the people show them. Coming with these means coming as the sixth share. Other wealth, like water in an unbaked pot, takes its maker down with it, so he says not only “don’t embrace it” but “let it roll away”.
en.4: Affect not the substance that is divorced from mercy and kindliness, and touch it not with thy hands.
en.5:
Wealth gained by loss of love and grace,
Let man cast off from his embrace.
en.6: (Kings) should rather avoid than seek the accumulation of wealth which does not flow in with mercy and love.

padaccheda.m: உடையார் இன்மையின் தானே வந்துற்ற பொருளும்
சுங்கமாகிய பொருளும்
தன் பகைவரைத் திறையாகக் கொள்ளும் பொருளு்ம
அரசனுக்குரிய பொருள்கள்

en.1: Wealth that comes to him unbidden, customs dues, and wealth from crushing his enemies: these are a ruler’s wealth.
en.2: A ruler’s wealth is what comes to him because it has no owner, such as treasure found in the ground long after those who buried it have died, or property with no heirs. It is also customs on goods arriving by ship and by land, and tribute taken from his enemies. These are his beyond the sixth share.
en.4: Escheats and derelicts, customs duties, and prize acquired in war, all these contribute to build up the wealth of the prince.
en.5:
Wealth that falls to him as heir, wealth from the kingdom’s dues,
The spoils of slaughtered foes: these are the royal revenues.
en.6: Unclaimed wealth, wealth acquired by taxes, and wealth (got) by conquest of foes are (all) the wealth of the king.

padaccheda.m: அன்பினால் ஈனப்பட்ட அருள் என்னும் குழவி
பொருள் என்று உயர்த்துச் சொல்லப்படும் செல்வத்தையுடைய செவிலியான் வளரும்

en.1: Compassion, the child that loving-kindness bears, thrives with the rich foster-mother called wealth.
en.2: The child compassion, born of loving-kindness, grows up with the foster-mother called wealth. Compassion reaches the suffering without any tie, and it ripens from loving-kindness, which goes by ties. Only those able to end poverty can reach the poor, so wealth is its nurse. Unlike other nurses she supplies everything herself, so she is “rich”.
en.4: Compassion which is the child of Love requireth for tending it the kindly nurse called Wealth.
en.5:
’Tis love that kindliness as offspring bears;
And wealth as bounteous nurse the infant rears.
en.6: The child mercy which is borne by love grows under the care of the rich nurse of wealth.

padaccheda.w: தன் கைத்து உண்டாக ஒன்று செய்வான் வினை
padaccheda.m: தன் கையதாகிய பொருளுண்டாக ஒரு வினையை எடுத்துக்கொண்டான் அதனைச் செய்தல்
ஒருவன் மலைமேல் ஏறிநின்று யானைப்போரைக் கண்டால் ஒக்கும்

en.1: Taking on a task with wealth in your hands is like watching elephants fight from the top of a hill.
en.2: Taking up a task with wealth in hand is like climbing a hill to watch an elephant fight. The one on the hill, free of fear and trouble, sits at ease while elephants fight on the ground. So too the one with wealth, free of fear and trouble, sets skilled people to work and finishes the task at ease.
en.4: Behold the wealthy man who taketh an enterprise on hand: he is like one who watcheth an elephant-fight from the top of a hill.
en.5:
As one to view the strife of elephants who takes his stand,
On hill he’s climbed, is he who works with money in his hand.
en.6: An undertaking of one who has wealth in one’s hands is like viewing an elephant-fight from a hill-top.

padaccheda.m: தமக்கு ஒன்று உண்டாகக் கருதுவார் பொருளை உண்டாக்குக
தன் பகைவர் தருக்கினை அறுக்கும் படைக்கலம் அதுவாம்
அதற்கு அதுபோலக் கூரிய படைக்கலம் பிறிதில்லை

en.1: Make wealth. There is no steel sharper for cutting your enemies’ pride.
en.2: Those who want to get anything should make wealth. It is the weapon that cuts the pride of enemies, and no weapon is sharper. With wealth come a great army and allies, so enemies drop their pride and submit. Other steel can’t cut what has no form, so none is sharper.
en.4: Amass wealth: for there is no sharper steel to cleave thy foeman’s pride.
en.5:
Make money! Foeman’s insolence o’er grown
To lop away no keener steel is known.
en.6: Accumulate wealth; it will destroy the arrogance of (your) foes; there is no weapon sharper than it.

padaccheda.m: நெறியான் வரும்பொருளை இறப்ப மிகப் படைத்தார்க்கு
மற்றை அறனும் இன்பமும் ஒருங்கே எளிய பொருள்களாம்

en.1: For those who have made bright wealth in plenty, the other two come easily, and together.
en.2: For those who have made wealth in great abundance by right means, the other two, righteousness and happiness, are easy to get, and come at the same time. Wealth is “bright” because it never goes without giving its fruit. The other two are its results, so they arise by themselves at once.
en.4: Behold the man that hath laid up for himself wealth in great profusion: both the other objects of life are within his reach.
en.5:
Who plenteous store of glorious wealth have gained,
By them the other two are easily obtained.
en.6: To those who have honestly acquired an abundance of riches, the other two, (virtue and pleasure), are things easy (of acquisition).

padaccheda.w: உறுப்பு அமைந்து ஊறு அஞ்சா வெல் படை
padaccheda.m: யானை முதலிய நான்கு உறுப்பானும் நிறைந்து போரின்கண் ஊறுபடுதற்கு அஞ்சாது நின்று பகையை வெல்வதாய படை
அரசன் செல்வங்கள் எல்லாவற்றுள்ளும் தலையாய செல்வம்

en.1: A complete army that fears no wound and wins is the first of all a ruler’s riches.
en.2: An army complete in its four parts, elephants and the rest, which doesn’t fear being hurt in battle and beats the enemy, is the chief of all a ruler’s riches. If it feared wounds it couldn’t win. It guards the other parts of the state and the ruler himself, so it comes first.
en.4: A well-organised and puissant army that feareth not danger is the first among the possessions of the prince.
en.5:
A conquering host, complete in all its limbs, that fears no wound,
Mid treasures of the king is chiefest found.
en.6: The army which is complete in (its) parts and conquers without fear of wounds is the chief wealth of the king.

padaccheda.m: தான் சிறிதாய வழியும் அரசற்குப் போரின்கண் உலைவு வந்தால் தன் மேல் உறுவதற்கு அஞ்சாது நின்று தாங்கும்வன்கண்மை
அவன் முன்னோரைத் தொடங்கிவரும் படைக்கல்லது உளதாகாது

en.1: The hard courage that fears no wound when the fight goes badly, even when the force is worn down, is rare except in an old army.
en.2: When the ruler is hard pressed in battle, the hard courage to stand and take the blows without fear, even when reduced to a few, is found only in the army that has come down from his ancestors. Of the six kinds of army, hereditary, hired, country, forest, allied and enemy, the hereditary is the best, so the ruler should reward it well.
en.4: It is only veterans that can hold out in desperate situations with grim determination, regardless of decimating attacks.
en.5:
In adverse hour, to face undaunted might of conquering foe,
Is bravery that only veteran host can show.
en.6: Ancient army can alone have the valour which makes it stand by its king at the time of defeat, fearless of wounds and unmindful of its reduced strength.

padaccheda.m: எலியாகிய பகை கடல்போல ஒலித்தால் நாகத்திற்கு என்ன ஏதம் வரும்
அந்நாகம் உயிர்த்த துணையானே அது தானே கெடும்

en.1: What if a host of rats roars like the sea? A cobra breathes, and they are gone.
en.2: What harm if an enemy of rats roars like the sea? When the cobra merely breathes, they perish. Many who aren’t warriors may gather and shout, but a warrior doesn’t fear them, and when he stirs they perish. One warrior is better to have than many who aren’t.
en.4: What though they roar even like the ocean? an army of rats will be annihilated at a single whiff of the cobra’s breath.
en.5:
Though, like the sea, the angry mice send forth their battle cry;
What then? The dragon breathes upon them, and they die!
en.6: What if (a host of) hostile rats roar like the sea? They will perish at the mere breath of the cobra.

padaccheda.m: போரின்கண் கெடுதல் இன்றி
பகைவரான் கீழறுக்கப்படாததாய்
தொன்றுதொட்டு வந்த தறுகண்மையை உடையதே அரசனுக்குப் படையாவது

en.1: An army is what doesn’t fall, can’t be turned by treachery, and has hard courage handed down.
en.2: A ruler’s army is what doesn’t perish in battle, isn’t subverted by the enemy, and has courage come down from of old. Not perishing shows valour and honour. Not being subverted shows loving-kindness for the ruler.
en.4: That alone deserveth the name of army which knoweth no defeat, which is incapable of being corrupted, and which hath a long tradition of valour behind it.
en.5:
That is a host, by no defeats, by no desertions shamed,
For old hereditary courage famed.
en.6: That indeed is an army which has stood firm of old without suffering destruction or deserting (to the enemy).

padaccheda.m: கூற்றுவன் தானே வெகுண்டு மேல்வந்தாலும்
நெஞ்சொத்து எதிர்நின்று தாங்கும் ஆற்றலை உடையதே படையாவது

en.1: An army is what has the strength to stand together and face even Death, coming on in rage.
en.2: An army is what has the strength to stand with one heart and hold out, even if Death himself, for whom there is no cure, comes on in rage. So many hearts are one because of loving-kindness for the ruler. Strength here is strength of mind.
en.4: That alone deserveth the name of army which can face valiantly even the God of Death if he should advance against it in all his fury.
en.5:
That is a ‘host’ that joins its ranks, and mightily withstands,
Though death with sudden wrath should fall upon its bands.
en.6: That indeed is an army which is capable of offering a united resistance, even if Yama advances against it with fury.

padaccheda.w: மறம் மானம் மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு தேற்றம் என நான்கே
padaccheda.m: தறுகண்மையும், மானமும், முன் வீரராயினார் சென்ற நன்னெறிக்கண் சேறலும் அரசனால் தேறப்படுதலும் என இந்நான்கு குணமுமே
படைக்கு அரணாவது

en.1: Valour, honour, walking the noble path and clarity of mind: these four alone protect an army.
en.2: These four alone protect an army: fierce courage, honour, going the good way past heroes went, and being trusted by the ruler. By them, in turn, it kills enemies quickly, keeps the ruler from harm, doesn’t strike at the backs of the fleeing, and can’t be subverted. Enemies don’t come near such people, so they need no other defence.
en.4: Valour, honour, a clear head, and a thorough acquaintance with the history of the great wars of the past, these four are the armours of protection for an army.
en.5:
Valour with honour, sure advance in glory’s path, with confidence:
To warlike host these four are sure defence.
en.6: Valour, honour, following in the excellent footsteps (of its predecessors) and trust-worthiness: these four alone constitute the safeguard of an army.

reading.note: தேற்றம் can mean clarity or trust. He takes it as the ruler’s trust in the army.

padaccheda.m: மாற்றாரால் வகுக்கப்பட்டுத் தன்மேல் வந்த படையின் போரை விலக்கும் வகுப்பறிந்து வகுத்துக் கொண்டு
அவர் தூசியைத தன்மேல் வாராமல் தடுத்துத் தான் அதன்மேற் செல்வதே படையாவது

en.1: An army knows how to bear the battle that comes at it, holds back the vanguard and goes forward.
en.2: Knowing the formation that counters the enemy formation coming against it, an army draws itself up, stops their vanguard reaching it and advances on them. Formation has seven parts, four kinds and thirty varieties, all set out in the northern books.
en.4: That which deserveth the name of army always goeth for the enemy: for it is confident of overcoming him when he offereth battle.
en.5:
A valiant army bears the onslaught, onward goes,
Well taught with marshalled ranks to meet their coming foes.
en.6: That is an army which knowing the art of warding off an impending struggle, can bear against the dust-van (of a hostile force).

padaccheda.m: தானை
பகைமேல் தான் சென்று அடும் தறுகண்மையும் அது தன்மேல் வந்தால் பொறுக்கும் ஆற்றலும் இல்லையாயினும்
தன் தோற்றப் பொலிவானே பெருமை எய்தும்

en.1: Even without the power to strike or the strength to hold, an army gains greatness from how it looks.
en.2: Even if an army lacks the fierce courage to go and kill the enemy and the strength to bear attack, it gains greatness by its splendid appearance. “Even if” shows these can’t really be done without. The splendour is adorned chariots, elephants and horses with banners, flags, parasols, instruments and horns. The greatness is that enemies fear it at first sight.
en.4: Superiority of armament is a compensation when the army is lacking in dash or steadiness.
en.5:
Though not in war offensive or defensive skilled;
An army gains applause when well equipped and drilled.
en.6: Though destitute of courage to fight and strength (to endure), an army may yet gain renown by the splendour of its appearance.

padaccheda.m: தான் தேய்ந்து சிறிதாகலும், மனத்தினின்று நீங்காத வெறுப்பும், நல்குரவும் தனக்கு இல்லையாயின்
படை பகையை வெல்லும்

en.1: An army wins if it has no shrinking, no grudge that won’t go, and no poverty.
en.2: An army beats the enemy if it doesn’t shrink in number, has no lasting resentment and isn’t poor. Desertion, and poverty among those who stay, come from a ruler who doesn’t give wealth. Lasting resentment comes from his seizing their women or shaming them. Where these exist they have no loving-kindness for him and won’t fight hard.
en.4: The army will always win provided that it is not inferior in numbers, hath no implacable jealousies, and is not left to starve without pay.
en.5:
Where weakness, clinging fear and poverty
Are not, the host will gain the victory.
en.6: An army can triumph (over its foes) if it is free from diminution, irremediable aversion and poverty.

padaccheda.m: போரின்கண் நிலையுடைய வீரரை மிக உடைத்தேயாயினும்
தனக்குத் தலைவராகிய வீரர் இல்லாதவழித் தானை நில்லாது

en.1: An army may have plenty of steadfast men, but without leaders it is no army.
en.2: An army may have many warriors who stand firm in battle, but without warrior leaders it won’t stand. If its commanders don’t hold but run, it won’t fight, since no one is left to see it, and it will run too.
en.4: Even if there is no lack of troops of the line, there is no army when there are no chiefs to lead.
en.5:
Though men abound, all ready for the war,
No army is where no fit leaders are.
en.6: Though an army may contain a large number of permanent soldiers, ’it cannot last if it has no generals.

padaccheda.w: தெவ்விர் என் ஐ முன் நின்று கல் நின்றவர் பலர்
padaccheda.m: பகைவீர்! இன்றினூங்கு என் தலைவன் எதிர் போரேற்று நின்று அவன் வேல்வாய் வீழ்ந்து பின் கல்லின்கண்ணே நின்ற வீரர் பலர்
நீவிர் அதன்கண் இன்றி நும் உடற்கண் நிற்றல் வேண்டின், என் தலைவன் எதிர் போர் ஏற்று நிற்றலை ஒழிமின்

en.1: Enemies, don’t stand before my lord. Many have stood before him, and now they stand in stone.
en.2: Enemies, many warriors have faced my lord in battle, fallen to his spear and now stand in memorial stones. If you want to stand in your bodies and not in a stone, don’t face him. This is a warrior speaking, who places his own valour in his ruler.
en.4: Face not my master in battle, O ye foes! for many are the men that challenged him and are now lying in stone-marked graves.
en.5:
Ye foes! stand not before my lord! for many a one
Who did my lord withstand, now stands in stone!
en.6: O my foes, stand not before my leader; (for) many are those who did so but afterwards stood (in the shape of) statues.

padaccheda.m: கானகத்தின்கண் ஓடும் முயலைப் பிழையாமல் எய்த அம்பை ஏந்தலினும்
வெள்ளிடை நின்ற யானையை எறிந்து பிழைத்த வேலை ஏந்துதல் நன்று

en.1: Better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than an arrow that hit a hare in the woods.
en.2: Better than holding the arrow that surely hit a hare running in the forest is holding a spear thrown at an elephant in the open that missed. These are the words of a warrior who fought the rival ruler’s army, felt shame when it fled, and now goes against the ruler himself.
en.4: The javelin that is aimed at a tusker but misseth bringeth more glory than the arrow that is aimed at a hare and even hitteth.
en.5:
Who aims at elephant, though dart should fail, has greater praise
Than he who woodland hare with winged arrow slays.
en.6: It is more pleasant to hold the dart that has missed an elephant than that which has hit a deer in the forest.

padaccheda.m: பகைவர்மேல் கண்ணோடாது செய்யும் மறத்தை நூலோர் மிக்க ஆண்டன்மை என்று சொல்லுவர்
அவர்க்கு ஒரு தாழ்வு வந்ததாயின் கண்ணோடி அது தீர்த்துக் கோடற்பொருட்டு ஊராண்மை செய்தலை நூலோர் அதற்குக் கூர்மை என்று சொல்லுவர்

en.1: They call fierce courage great manhood. When someone falls on hard times, generosity is the sharp edge of it.
en.2: The learned call pitiless fierceness towards enemies great manhood. If an enemy falls on hard times, they call the kindness that helps him out of them its sharp edge. So the ruler of Ayodhya, finding the ruler of Lanka alone with his whole army dead, didn’t press on but said, “Go now, and come tomorrow with your army.”
en.4: The furious courage that striketh hard, that is what they call valour: but it is chivalrous generosity to the fallen that giveth it its edge.
en.5:
Fierceness in hour of strife heroic greatness shows;
Its edge is kindness to our suffering foes.
en.6: The learned say that fierceness (in contest with a foe) is indeed great valour; but to become a benefactor in case of accident (to a foe) is the extreme (limit) of that valour.

padaccheda.m: தன் கைப்படையாய வேலைத் தன்மேல் வந்த களிற்றோடு போக்கி, வருகின்ற களிற்றுக்கு வேல் நாடித் திரிவான்
தன் மார்பின்கண் நின்ற வேலைக் கண்டு பறித்து மகிழும்

en.1: He lets the spear in his hand go with an elephant and comes on. He sees one in his own body, pulls it out and laughs.
en.2: A warrior lets his spear go with the elephant that charged him, killing it, and looks about for a spear for the next.
