He sees the one standing in his own chest, pulls it out and rejoices, having found what he sought. So he throws only at elephants, was too enraged to feel the spear go in, and still wants to fight.
en.4: The warrior hurled his spear at the elephant and was hurrying back to look for another: but he noticed the spear buried in his own body and smiled with joy as he plucked it out.
en.5:
At elephant he hurls the dart in hand; for weapon pressed,
He laughs and plucks the javelin from his wounded breast.
en.6: The hero who after casting the lance in his hand on an elephant, comes (in search of another) will pluck the one (that sticks) in his body and laugh (exultingly).

padaccheda.m: பகைவரை வெகுண்டு நோக்கிய கண்
அவர் வேலைக்கொண்டு எறிய அஃது ஆற்றாது அந்நோக்கை அழித்து இமைக்குமாயின்
அது வீரர்க்குப் புறங்கொடுத்தலாம்

en.1: If a glaring eye blinks when a spear is thrown at it, isn’t that running away, for those with hard courage?
en.2: If the eye that glares at the enemy can’t bear it when they throw a spear, breaks that look and blinks, then for warriors it is the same as turning their backs. To take back an angry look would be a retreat in battle, so they don’t do even that.
en.4: Is it not a shame to the hero if his eye doth so much as wink when the lance is hurled at him?
en.5:
To hero fearless must it not defeat appear,
If he but wink his eye when foeman hurls his spear.
en.6: Is it not a defeat to the valiant to wink and destroy their ferocious look when a lance is cast at them (by their foe)?

padaccheda.m: தனக்குச் சென்ற நாள்களை எடுத்து எண்ணி

padaccheda.w: விழுப்புண் படாத நாள் எல்லாம் வழுக்கினுள் வைக்கும்
padaccheda.m: அவற்றுள், விழுப்புண் படாத நாள்களை எல்லாம் பயன்படாது கழிந்த நாளுள்ளே வைக்கும் வீரன்

en.1: He counts over his days and sets down every day with no noble wound as a day that slipped away.
en.2: A warrior counts up his past days and puts every day without a noble wound among the days gone to waste. A noble wound is one on the face or chest. A day he had battle but no such wound, he adds to the days he had no battle at all.
en.4: The hero counteth those days as wasted on which he receiveth not deep gashes on his body.
en.5:
The heroes, counting up their days, set down as vain
Each day when they no glorious wound sustain.
en.6: The hero will reckon among wasted days all those on which he had not received severe wounds.

padaccheda.m: துறக்கத்துத் தம்மொடு செல்லாது, வையத்தைச் சூழ்ந்து நிற்கும் புகழைவேண்டி உயிர் வாழ்தலை வேண்டாத வீரர்
கழல் கட்டுதல் அலங்கார நீர்மையை உடைத்து

en.1: Those who want fame that circles the world and don’t want life: on them the warrior’s anklet has the grace of an ornament.
en.2: Fame doesn’t go with warriors to heaven but stays circling the earth. For those who want it and don’t want to go on living, tying on the warrior’s anklet is an adornment. They easily gain both heaven and fame, so this alone is their jewel.
en.4: Behold the men that care not for their lives but yearn for the fame that encompasseth the earth about: the anklet that they wear round their foot is a very feast to the eye.
en.5:
Who seek for world-wide fame, regardless of their life,
The glorious clasp adorns, sign of heroic strife.
en.6: The fastening of ankle-ring by those who desire a world-wide renown and not (the safety of) their lives is like adorning (themselves).

padaccheda.m: போர் பெறின் தம் உயிர்ப்பொருட்டு அஞ்சாது அதன்மேல் செல்லும் வீரர்
தம் இறைவன் அது வேண்டாம் என்று முனியினும், அவ் வீரமிகுதி குன்றார்

en.1: Warriors who don’t fear for their lives when the fight comes keep their excellence, even if the ruler is angry with them.
en.2: Warriors who, offered a battle, go to it with no fear for their lives don’t lose that great valour even if their ruler says no and is angry. They have long had no battle, so when they get one they won’t stop, even if he forbids it.
en.4: Behold the men of valour that fear not for their lives on the battlefield: they forget not their discipline even when their chief is severe upon them.
en.5:
Fearless they rush where’er ‘the tide of battle rolls;’
The king’s reproof damps not the ardour of their eager souls.
en.6: The heroes who are not afraid of losing their life in a contest will not cool their ardour, even if the king prohibits (their fighting.)

padaccheda.m: தாம் கூறின வஞ்சினம் தப்பாமற் பொருட்டுச் சென்று சாவவல்ல வீரரை
அது தப்பியவாறு சொல்லி எள்ளுதற்கு உரியார் யாவர்

en.1: Those who die rather than go back on their vow: who can punish them for having failed?
en.2: Who has the right to mock, for failing, those warriors who go and die so that their vow won’t be broken? The vow is saying, “If I don’t do this, may such a thing befall me.” Even if they die before they finish it, they aren’t beaten, so they count as having done it. This is the glory of such a death.
en.4: Who hath the right to blame the men who lose their lives in the attempt to accomplish that which they have undertaken?
en.5:
Who says they err, and visits them with scorn,
Who die and faithful guard the vow they’ve sworn?
en.6: Who would reproach with failure those who seal their oath with their death.

padaccheda.m: தமக்குச் செய்த நன்றிகளை நினைந்து ஆண்ட அரசர் கண்கள் நீர்மல்கும் வகை போரிடைச் சாவப் பெறின்
அச் சாக்காடு இரந்தாயினும் கொள்ளும் தகுதியை உடைத்து

en.1: If you can die so that the eyes of those who cared for you fill with tears, that death is worth begging for.
en.2: To die in battle so that the rulers who cared for you, remembering what you did, fill their eyes with tears: such a death is worth getting even by begging. Those who die of illness at home with their kin weeping get only the fruit of old deeds. This death, by a present act, wins heaven.
en.4: If one can die so as to draw tears from the eyes of one’s chief, one may even go a-begging in order to obtain for oneself such a death.
en.5:
If monarch’s eyes o’erflow with tears for hero slain,
Who would not beg such boon of glorious death to gain?
en.6: If (heroes) can so die as to fill with tears the eyes of their rulers, such a death deserves to be obtained even by begging.

padaccheda.m: நட்புப்போலச்செய்துகோடற்கு அரிய பொருள்கள் யாவை உள

padaccheda.w: அதுபோல் வினைக்கு அரிய காப்பு யா உள
padaccheda.m: செய்துகொண்டால் அதுபோலப் பகைவர் செய்யும் வினைக்குப் புகற்கரிய காவலாவன யாவை உள?

en.1: What is as hard to make as friendship? What guard is as hard to get past?
en.2: Nothing is as hard to form as friendship. Finding the right people, the means of winning them, and keeping it unchanged are all hard. Once made, no guard is as hard for enemy action to get past, because enemies fear it and start nothing. Friendship by birth is kin. What he means here is friendship made through past help.
en.4: What is there in the world that is so difficult to acquire as friendship? and what other armour equalleth it as a defence against the machinations of foes?
en.5:
What so hard for men to gain as friendship true?
What so sure defence ’gainst all that foe can do?
en.6: What things are there so difficult to acquire as friendship? What guards are there so difficult to break through by the efforts (of one’s foes)?

padaccheda.m: அறிவுடையார் நட்புக்கள் பிறைநிறையும் தன்மைபோல நாள்தோறும் நிறையும் தன்மையவாம்
மற்றைப் பேதைமை உடையார் நட்புக்கள், நிறைந்தமதி பின் குறையும் தன்மைபோல நாள்தோறும் குறையும் தன்மையவாம்

en.1: The friendship of the worthy fills out like the new moon. The friendship of fools wanes like the moon after the full.
en.2: The friendships of the wise fill out day by day like the crescent moon. Those of fools shrink day by day like the moon after the full. Both turn on knowing each other. The wise start small and grow as they come to know each other. Fools start big and shrink for the same reason.
en.4: Like unto the waxing of the moon is the friendship of the worthy: but the alliance of fools is like the waning thereof.
en.5:
Friendship with men fulfilled of good
Waxes like the crescent moon;
Friendship with men of foolish mood,
Like the full orb, waneth soon.
en.6: The friendship of the wise waxes like the new moon; (but) that of fools waxes like the full moon.

padaccheda.m: நற்குணமுடைய மக்கள், தம்முள் செய்த நட்புப் பயிலுந்தோறும் அவர்க்கு இன்பம்செய்தல்
நூற்பொருள் கற்குந்தோறும் கற்றார்க்கு இன்பம் செய்தலை ஒக்கும்

en.1: A bond with people of good character is like a book: each time you return to it, it delights you more.
en.2: The friendship good people form with one another delights them each time they meet, as the meaning of a book delights the learned each time they study it. In both, the delight grows from one time to the next.
en.4: The friendship of the worthy is like the studying of great books: the more thou approachest them, the more charms thou wilt discover in them.
en.5:
Learned scroll the more you ponder,
Sweeter grows the mental food;
So the heart by use grows fonder,
Bound in friendship with the good.
en.6: Like learning, the friendship of the noble, the more it is cultivated, the more delightful does it become.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனோடு ஒருவன் நட்புச்செய்தல் தம்முள் நகுதற்கு இயைந்தன சொல்லி நகையாடல் பொருட்டன்று
அவர்க்கு வேண்டாதன செய்கை உளதாயவழி முற்பட்டுக் கழறுதற் பொருட்டு

en.1: You make friends not to laugh together but to step in and rebuke when someone goes too far.
en.2: Friendship isn’t for saying funny things and laughing together. It is for getting in first and rebuking a friend who does what he shouldn’t. An act that brings blame and sin yields only pain, so it is “too far”. It must be stopped before it is done, so you “step in”. Sweet words won’t turn him back, so you “rebuke”.
en.4: The object of friendship is not merrymaking: but the restraining and reproving of oneself when one goeth astray.
en.5:
Not for laughter only friendship all the pleasant day,
But for strokes of sharp reproving, when from right you stray.
en.6: Friendship is to be practised not for the purpose of laughing but for that of being beforehand in giving one another sharp rebukes in case of transgression.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனோடு ஒருவன் நட்பாதற்குப் புணர்ச்சியும், பழகுதலும் ஆகிய காரணங்கள் வேண்டுவது இல்லை
இருவர்க்கும் ஒத்த உணர்ச்சிதானே நட்பாம் உரிமையைக் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: There is no need to meet or spend time together. Feeling alone gives the bond of friendship.
en.2: To be friends you needn’t live in one land, or meet and talk often. Feeling the same gives the right of friendship by itself, as with kōpperuñjōḻaṉ and pisirānḍaiyār, who had neither, and yet had a friendship in which they gave up life together. Of the three causes of friendship, the last is the greatest.
en.4: Constant meeting and companionship are superfluous: it is the union of hearts that maketh strong the bond of friendship.
en.5:
Not association constant, not affection’s token bind;
’Tis the unison of feeling friends unites of kindred mind.
en.6: Living together and holding frequent intercourse are not necessary (for friendship); (mutual) understanding can alone create a claim for it.

padaccheda.m: கண்டவழி அகம் ஒழிய, முகம் மாத்திரமே மலரும் வகை நட்கும் அது, நட்பு ஆகாது
அன்பால் அகமும் மலர நட்கும் அதே நட்பாவது

en.1: Friendship that makes the face smile is not friendship. Friendship makes the heart smile deep within.
en.2: A friendship in which only the face blooms on meeting, and not the heart, isn’t friendship. Only the one in which the heart too blooms with loving-kindness is friendship. So both must bloom together.
en.4: Friendship is not the comradeship that smileth to the face: it is rather the love that delighteth the heart.
en.5:
Not the face’s smile of welcome shows the friend sincere,
But the heart’s rejoicing gladness when the friend is near.
en.6: The love that dwells (merely) in the smiles of the face is not friendship; (but) that which dwells deep in the smiles of the heart is true friendship.

padaccheda.m: கேட்டினைத்தரும் தீநெறிகளைச் செல்லுங்கால் விலக்கி, ஏனை நன்னெறிகளைச் செல்லாக்காற் செலுத்தி
தெய்வத்தான் கேடு வந்துழி, அது விலக்கப்படாமையின் அத்துன்பத்தை உடன் அனுபவிப்பதே ஒருவனுக்கு நட்பாவது

en.1: Friendship turns you from what would ruin you, sets you on the path, and shares the pain when ruin comes.
en.2: Friendship stops you when you take the bad ways that bring ruin, and drives you onto the good ways when you don’t take them. When ruin comes from the gods and can’t be stopped, it shares that suffering with you. Some read this differently, with a different word, and take the ruin to be the body’s death.
en.4: That man alone is thy friend who turneth thee aside from wrong, directeth thee toward the right, and beareth thee company in misfortune.
en.5:
Friendship from ruin saves, in way of virtue keeps;
In troublous time, it weeps with him who weeps.
en.6: (True) friendship turns aside from evil (ways), makes (him) walk in the (good) way, and, in case of loss it shares his sorrow (with him).

padaccheda.m: அவையிடை ஆடை குலைந்தவனுக்கு அப்பொழுதே கைசென்று உதவி அவ் இளிவரல் களையுமாறு போல
நட்டவனுக்கு இடுக்கண் வந்துழி, அப்பொழுதே சென்று உதவி, அதனைக் களைவதே நட்பாவது

en.1: Like the hand of someone whose clothes slip, friendship takes away trouble on the spot.
en.2: When a man’s clothes come loose in an assembly, his hand goes at once and saves him from shame. In the same way friendship goes at once to a friend in trouble and removes it. The hand moves faster than the mind when something must be covered, and that speed is the point.
en.4: Behold the hand of the man whose garment hath been blown aside, how it hurrieth to re-cover his limbs: that is the symbol of the true friend that hasteneth to succour a man in his misfortune.
en.5:
As hand of him whose vesture slips away,
Friendship at once the coming grief will stay.
en.6: (True) friendship hastens to the rescue of the afflicted (as readily) as the hand of one whose garment is loosened (before an assembly).

padaccheda.m: நட்பினுக்கு அரசிருக்கை யாது எனின்
அஃது எஞ்ஞான்றும், திரிபின்றி இயலும் எல்லை எல்லாம் அறம் பொருள்களின் தளராமைத்? தாங்கும் தன்மை

en.1: Where does friendship sit enthroned? In standing firm, without wavering, and holding you up in every way it can.
en.2: The throne of friendship is the steady support that, without ever changing, holds a friend up in righteousness and wealth as far as it can. These secure the next world and this one. When he falters in them, nothing goes further than lifting him and setting him back, so this is the limit of friendship.
en.4: Where doth friendship hold its court? It is where two hearts beat in perfect unison and combine to lift each other up in every possible way.
en.5:
And where is friendship’s royal seat? In stable mind,
Where friend in every time of need support may find.
en.6: Friendship may be said to be on its throne when it possesses the power of supporting one at all times and under all circumstances, (in the practice of virtue and wealth).

padaccheda.w: இவர் எமக்கு இனையர் யாம் இன்னம் என்று புனையினும்
padaccheda.m: இவர் நமக்கு இத்துணை அன்பினர், யாம் இவர்க்கு இத்தன்மையம் என்று ஒருவரை ஒருவர் புனைந்து சொல்லினும்
நட்புப் புல்லிதாய்த் தோன்றும்

en.1: “They are this much to us, and we are this much to them.” Say it, however finely, and the friendship looks poor.
en.2: Two friends may praise each other, saying “He has this much loving-kindness for me, and I am like this to him”, but then the friendship looks shabby. They had no “I” and “he” between them, and even fine words of that sort make a difference where there was none.
en.4: There is beggary in the friendship that can be reckoned, though it boasteth saying, Thus much do I love him and thus much he loveth me.
en.5:
Mean is the friendship that men blazon forth,
‘He’s thus to me,’ and ‘such to him my worth.’
en.6: Though friends may praise one another saying “He is so intimate with us, and we so much (with him);” (still) such friendship will appear mean.

padaccheda.m: நட்பினை விரும்பி அதன்கண்ணே நிற்பார்க்கு ஒருவனோடு நட்புச்செய்தபின் அவனை விடுதல் உண்டாகாது
ஆகலான், ஆராயாது நட்புச்செய்தல்போலக் கேடு தருவது பிறிதில்லை

en.1: Nothing ruins you like making friends without looking into them. For those who hold to friendship, once made there is no leaving it.
en.2: For those who love friendship and stand by it, there is no leaving a friend once made. So nothing brings ruin like befriending someone without examining his character and conduct. Friends have no “I” and “he” between them, so his blame and sin become yours, and you are ruined in both worlds.
en.4: There is no greater ill than making a friend without first testing him: for, once a friendship is formed, there is no giving it up for the man of heart.
en.5:
To make an untried man your friend is ruin sure;
For friendship formed unbroken must endure.
en.6: As those who are of a friendly nature will not forsake (a friend) after once loving (him), there is no evil so great as contracting a friendship without due inquiry.

padaccheda.m: குணமும் செய்கையும் நல்லன் என்பது, பலகாலும் பலவாற்றானும் ஆராய்ந்து ஒருவனோடு நட்புக்கொள்ளாதவன்
முடிவில் தான் சாதற்கு ஏதுவாய துன்பத்தினைத் தன் மாற்றார் விளைக்கவேண்டாமல் தானே விளைக்கும்

en.1: Someone who makes a friend without looking and looking again ends in a sorrow that kills him.
en.2: If you don’t test many times and in many ways that a person’s character and conduct are good before you befriend him, you bring on yourself, with no help from your enemies, the grief that ends in your death. Befriend a bad man and all his enmities fall on you, and they kill you.
en.4: Behold the man that maketh men his friends without previously testing them: he courteth disasters which will only end in his death.
en.5:
Alliance with the man you have not proved and proved again,
In length of days will give you mortal pain.
en.6: The friendship contracted by him who has not made repeated inquiry will in the end grieve (him) to death.

padaccheda.w: குணனும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் குன்றா இனனும் அறிந்து
padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் குணத்தினையும், குடிப்பிறப்பினையும், குற்றத்தினையும், குறைவற்ற சுற்றத்தினையும் ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்து
அவனோடு நட்புச் செய்க

en.1: Know a person’s character, family, faults and the unfailing kin around them, then make them your friend.
en.2: Examine someone’s character, birth, faults and unfailing kin, then befriend him. No one in the world is faultless, so if his faults can be borne, the friendship isn’t to be dropped. People bound to their kin stay bound to their friends too. If you have to leave him later the failing is yours, so know him first.
en.4: Take into thy consideration the family of the man whom thou desirest to make thy friend, his virtues and his vices, and the whole range of his associates and connections: and then befriend him if he is worthy.
en.5:
Temper, descent, defects, associations free
From blame: know these, then let the man be friend to thee.
en.6: Make friendship (with one) after ascertaining (his) character, birth, defects, and the whole of one’s relations.

padaccheda.m: உயர்ந்த குடியின்கண் பிறந்து, தன் மாட்டு உலகர் சொல்லும் பழிக்கு அஞ்சுவானை
சில கொடுத்தாயினும் நட்புக் கோடல் சிறந்தது

en.1: Someone well-born, who shrinks from blame upon himself: win his friendship, even if you have to pay for it.
en.2: Win the friendship of someone born in a high family who fears the blame the world may put on him, even by giving something for it. His birth keeps him from doing wrong, and his fear of blame makes him bear your wrongs. Someone with both is rare, so buy his friendship.
en.4: Behold the man who is born of a good family and who dreadeth disgrace: one ought to acquire his friendship even by paying a price for it if necessary.
en.5:
Who, born of noble race, from guilt would shrink with shame,
Pay any price, so you as friend that man may claim.
en.6: The friendship of one who belongs to a (good) family and is afraid of (being charged with) guilt, is worth even purchasing.

padaccheda.m: தாம் உலகவழக்கல்லது செய்யக் கருதின், சோகம் பிறக்கும்வகை சொல்லி விலக்கியும்
செய்தக்கால் பின்னும் செய்யாவகை நெருக்கியும்
அவ்வழக்குச் செய்யாவழிச் செய்விக்கவும் வல்லாரை
ஆராய்ந்து நட்புக் கொள்க

en.1: Choose with care friends who, when you go wrong, can speak until you weep, rebuke you, and make you see the right way.
en.2: Examine and befriend those who can stop you, with words that bring grief, when you mean to go against the way of the world. They press you not to do it again if you have, and they can make you do it when you fail to. The way of the world is what people have always done.
en.4: Look for the men who know the way of the wise and can reprove and chastise thee whenever thou go astray: and make them thy friends.
en.5:
Make them your chosen friends whose words repentance move,
With power prescription’s path to show, while evil they reprove.
en.6: You should examine and secure the friendship of those who can speak so as to make you weep over a crime (before its commission), or rebuke you severely (after you have done it) and are able to teach (you the ways of) the world.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்குக் கேடென்பது தன் நட்டாராகிய புலன்களை எஞ்சாமல் அளப்பதோர் கோல்
ஆகலின் அதன்கண்ணும் அவனாற் பெறப்படுவதோர் நல்லறிவு உண்டு

en.1: Even in ruin there is one benefit: it is a rod that measures your people to their full length.
en.2: A person’s ruin is a rod that measures every one of his friends, so even it brings him a good understanding. In good times their limits don’t show. When ruin comes they act differently, and it marks them out. Having measured them, you keep only the fit, and that knowledge is the benefit.
en.4: There is a virtue even in misfortune: for it is the rod wherewith to measure thy friends.
en.5:
Ruin itself one blessing lends:
Tis staff that measures out one’s friends.
en.6: Even in ruin there is some good; (for) it is a rod by which one may measure fully (the affection of one’s) relations.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்குப் பேறென்று சொல்லப்படுவது
அறிவிலாரோடு நட்புக் கொண்டானாயின், அதனை ஒழிந்து அவரின் நீங்குதல்

en.1: What counts as gain for a person is to give up the friendship of fools and get clear of them.
en.2: If you have befriended fools, your true gain is to drop the friendship and move away from them. Even with the friendship over, staying near them brings harm, so he says “get clear”. Once clear you not only escape harm but gain the right to happiness in both worlds, so he calls it gain.
en.4: To discard the friendship of fools, that is veritable profit for a man.
en.5:
’Tis gain to any man, the sages say,
Friendship of fools to put away.
en.6: It is indeed a gain for one to renounce the friendship of fools.

padaccheda.m: தம் ஊக்கம் சுருங்குதற்குக் காரணமாய வினைகளைச் செய்ய நினையாது ஒழிக
அதுபோலத் தமக்கு ஒருதுன்பம் வந்துழிக் கைவிடுவார் நட்பினைக் கொள்ளாது ஒழிக

en.1: Don’t think of things that make your spirit small. Don’t take the friendship of those who cut away your strength in trouble.
en.2: Don’t think of doing what shrinks your spirit: tasks begun against those stronger than you, and tasks with no use. In the same way, don’t take the friendship of those who abandon you when trouble comes. They seemed a strength before and then fall away, so he says they cut your strength. Take them, and you are surely ruined.
en.4: Think not the thoughts that depress the heart: nor make the friendship of men who will abandon thee the moment thou art down.
en.5:
Think not the thoughts that dwarf the soul; nor take
For friends the men who friends in time of grief forsake.
en.6: Do not think of things that discourage your mind, nor contract friendship with those who would forsake you in adversity.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் கெடுங்காலத்து அவனை விட்டு நீங்குவார் முன் அவனோடு செய்த நட்பு
தன்னைக் கூற்று அடுங்காலத்து ஒருவன் நினைப்பினும், அந்நினைத்த உள்ளத்தைச் சுடும்

en.1: The friendship of those who desert you in your ruin burns the heart, even if you think of it when death is upon you.
en.2: The friendship of those who leave someone in his ruin burns the mind of anyone who recalls it, even at the hour Death comes to kill them. The mere thought is crueller than Death, even to someone unconnected. Such is friendship made with desertion in mind. Others read it as: when the ruin he made kills him, the memory burns worse than the ruin.
en.4: The friendship of men that betray in the day of disaster would burn the heart that thinketh on it even at the moment of death.
en.5:
Of friends deserting us on ruin’s brink,
’Tis torture e’en in life’s last hour to think.
en.6: The very thought of the friendship of those who have deserted one at the approach of adversity will burn one’s mind at the time of death.

padaccheda.m: உலகோடு ஒத்துக் குற்றமற்றார் நட்பினையே பயில்க

padaccheda.w: ஒப்பு இலார் நட்பு ஒன்று ஈத்தும் ஒருவுக
padaccheda.m: உலகத்தோடு ஒத்தில்லார் நட்பினை அறியாது கொண்டாராயின், அவர் வேண்டியது ஒன்றனைக் கொடுத்தாயினும் விடுக

en.1: Cling to the friendship of the spotless. Give something if you must, and leave the friendship of those who don’t fit.
en.2: Cultivate the friendship of those who are in accord with the world and faultless. If you have unknowingly befriended those out of accord with it, give them what they ask and get free. The first brings joy in both worlds, and the second only sorrow, so buy your way out.
en.4: Cultivate with ardour the friendship of the pure; as to men that are unworthy of thee, discard thou their association even if it be by giving them a present.
en.5:
Cling to the friendship of the spotless ones; whate’er you pay,
Renounce alliance with the men of evil way.
en.6: Continue to enjoy the friendship of the pure; (but) renounce even with a gift, the friendship of those who do not agree (with the world.)

padaccheda.m: பழைமையென்று சொல்லப்படுவது யாதென்று வினவின்ந கிழைமையை யாதும் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு= அது பழைமையோர் உரிமையான் செய்வனவற்றைச் சிறிதும் சிதையாது அவற்றிற்கு உடம்படும் நட்பு

en.1: What is old friendship? It is friendship that in no way cuts back the rights of closeness.
en.2: Old friendship is friendship that in no way stops what an old friend does by right, and agrees to it. Such acts are doing your work without asking, even doing it harm, taking what he needs, and showing no deference or fear. So old friendship isn’t a matter of time gone by, but of friendship of this kind.
en.4: That friendship is called intimacy which submitteth without resenting to all the freedoms taken by the beloved one.
en.5:
Familiarity is friendship’s silent pact,
That puts restraint on no familiar act.
en.6: Intimate friendship is that which cannot in the least be injured by (things done through the) right (of long standing intimacy).

padaccheda.m: நட்பிற்கு அவயவம் ஆவன நட்டார் உரிமையான் செய்வன
அதனால் அவ்வுரிமைக்கு இனியராதல் அமைந்தார்க்கு முறைமை

en.1: The rights of closeness are a limb of friendship. To be its salt is the duty of the worthy.
en.2: What friends do by right are limbs of friendship, not something apart from it. So it is the proper way of the worthy to be pleasant about those rights. He names the worthy because they know these are limbs of friendship, and so stay sweet.
en.4: To be free and easy with each other, that is the heart of true friendship: and it is the part of worthy men never to resent such familiarities.
en.5:
Familiar freedom friendship’s very frame supplies;
To be its savour sweet is duty of the wise.
en.6: The constituents of friendship are (things done through) the right of intimacy; to be pleased with such a right is the duty of the wise.

reading.note: உப்பு is literally salt, and he reads it as being pleasant.

padaccheda.m: தாம் உடம்படாதனவேனும் நட்டார் உரிமையாற் செய்தனவற்றிற்குத் தாம் செய்தாற்போல உடம்படாராயின்
அவரோடு பழையதாய் வந்த நட்பு என்ன பயனைச் செய்யும்?

en.1: What use is long friendship if you can’t accept what a friend does by right, as if you had done it yourself?
en.2: What use is a friendship grown old if you don’t agree, as if you had done it yourself, to what friends do by right, even what you wouldn’t otherwise accept? Agreeing in this way means agreeing by the same right you have with them.
en.4: Of what avail is friendship that is longstanding if it acquiesceth not in the liberties taken in its name?
en.5:
When to familiar acts men kind response refuse,
What fruit from ancient friendship’s use?
en.6: Of what avail is long-standing friendship, if friends do not admit as their own actions done through the right of intimacy?

padaccheda.m: தன் கருமத்தை நட்டார் உரிமையாற் கேளாது செய்தாராயின்
அச்செயலது விழையப்படுந்தன்மைபற்றி அதனை விரும்புவர் அறிவுடையார்

en.1: When friends, out of closeness, act without asking, people welcome it as something to be wished for.
en.2: When friends do your work by right, without asking, the wise want that act for how desirable it is. Nothing is better than finding your work done without knowing it. Only the wise see it so and want it, so he says it of them.
en.4: When friends rely on their intimacy and do a thing without leave, the warmhearted will think of their love and will take it in good part.
en.5:
When friends unbidden do familiar acts with loving heart,
Friends take the kindly deed in friendly part.
en.6: If friends, through the right of friendship, do (anything) without being asked, the wise will be pleased with them on account of its desirability.

padaccheda.m: தாம் வெறுக்கத்தக்கனவற்றை நட்டார் செய்தாராயின்

padaccheda.w: பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெரும் கிழமை என்று உணர்க
padaccheda.m: அதற்குக்காரணம் ஒன்றிற் பேதைமை யென்றாதல், ஒன்றின் மி்க்கஉரிமை என்றாதல் கொள்க

en.1: If friends do something that hurts, put it down to foolishness or to great closeness.
en.2: If friends do what you could resent, put it down to foolishness or to great closeness. It isn’t their nature. Everyone has the folly that comes from the fate of loss, so they have only harmed themselves. Or what fate would have sent by your hand has come by theirs, because you are so much one. Never take it as lack of loving-kindness.
en.4: When friends do a thing that paineth thee, account thou it as much to their feeling of perfect oneness with thee as to their ignorance.
en.5:
Not folly merely, but familiar carelessness,
Esteem it, when your friends cause you distress.
en.6: If friends should perform what is painful, understand that it is owing not only to ignorance, but also to the strong claims of intimacy.

padaccheda.m: நட்பு வரம்பு இகவாது அதன்கண்ணே நின்றவர்
தம்மொடு பழைமையில் திரியாது நின்றாரது நட்பினை அவரால் தொலைவு வந்த இடத்தும் விடார்

en.1: Those who keep to the bounds of friendship don’t leave those who have stood by them from of old, even in ruin.
en.2: Those who keep within the limit of friendship don’t give up the bond with those who have stayed unchanged in old closeness, even when ruin has come through them. The ruin is loss of wealth or loss in war.
en.4: The perfect friend giveth not up the friend of his heart even though he hath been the cause of his ruin.
en.5:
Who stand within the bounds quit not, though loss impends,
Association with the old familiar friends.
en.6: Those who stand within the limits (of true friendship) will not even in adversity give up the intimacy of long standing friends.

padaccheda.m: நட்டார் தமக்கு அழிவு வந்தவற்றைச் செய்தாராயினும் அவர்மாட்டு அன்பு ஒழியார்
அன்புடனே பழையதாய் வந்த நட்பினை உடையார்

en.1: Even if friends do what ruins them, those whose bond has come down through loving-kindness don’t lose their loving-kindness.
en.2: Even if friends do what brings ruin on them, those whose friendship has grown old with loving-kindness don’t give up their loving-kindness for them. The ruin is the same as before. Even when someone does you harm, the friendship isn’t to be given up.
en.4: Behold the man who hath loved dearly and long: he bateth not in his affection for his friend even though he cause him damage frequently.
en.5:
True friends, well versed in loving ways,
Cease not to love, when friend their love betrays.
en.6: Those who have (long) stood in the path of affection will not give it up even if their friends cause (them) their ruin.

padaccheda.m: நட்டார்செய்த பிழையைத் தாமாகவே அன்றிப் பிறர்சொன்னாலும் கொள்ளாத உரிமை அறியவல்லார்க்கு
அவர் பிழைசெய்வாராயின், அது பயன்பட்ட நாளாம்

en.1: For those so close that they won’t hear of a friend’s fault, the day the friend does wrong is a good day.
en.2: For those who know the right of closeness, and won’t accept a friend’s fault even when others report it, the day that friend does wrong is a day well used. The faults are taking good things without a word and showing no deference or fear. Only such an act shows that closeness, so days without one don’t count as days.
en.4: Behold the men who refuse to listen to any imputations against the friend of their bosom: the day that he doth them an injury is a feast-day unto them.
en.5:
In strength of friendship rare of friend’s disgrace who will not hear,
The day his friend offends will day of grace to him appear.
en.6: To those who understand that by which they should not listen to (tales about) the faults of their friends, that is a (profitable) day on which the latter may commit a fault.

padaccheda.m: உரிமையறாது பழையதாய் வந்த நட்பினை உடையாரது நட்பினை
அவர் பிழைநோக்கி விடுதல்செய்யாதாரை உலகம் நட்புக்குறித்து விரும்பும்

en.1: The world desires those who don’t give up the friendship of those whose bond has come down unbroken.
en.2: The world wants as friends those who, seeing faults, don’t drop the friendship of those whose closeness has stayed whole from of old. Everyone thinks they will be like that with them too, and comes to them as friends. Some read a different word, and take it as those unfailing in friendship.
en.4: Behold the man who loveth another with a deathless affection: the whole world will hold him dear.
en.5:
Friendship of old and faithful friends,
Who ne’er forsake, the world commends.
en.6: They will be loved by the world, who have not forsaken the friendship of those with whom they have kept up an unbroken long, standing intimacy.

padaccheda.m: பழைய நட்டார் பிழை செய்தாராயினும் அவர்மாட்டுத் தம் பண்பின் நீங்காதார்
பகைவரானும் விரும்பப்படுவர்

en.1: Those who don’t part from their good nature towards old friends are desired even by those who don’t desire them.
en.2: Those who keep their own nature towards old friends, even when those friends do wrong, are wanted even by enemies. Their nature is to keep the loving-kindness they had before the wrong was done. Seeing that they don’t change, even enemies become friends.
en.4: Behold the men that alter not in their affection for their old friends: even enemies will look upon them with tenderness.
en.5:
Ill-wishers even wish them well, who guard,
For ancient friends, their wonted kind regard.
en.6: Even enemies will love those who have never changed in their affection to their long standing friends.

padaccheda.m: காதன்மிகுதியான் பருகுவார் போன்றார் ஆயினும் தீக்குணமுடையார் நட்பு
வளர்தலின் தேய்தல் நன்று

en.1: Even if they seem ready to drink you up, the friendship of people without character is better shrinking than growing.
en.2: People of bad character may seem so fond that they would drink you up, but their friendship is better shrinking than growing. The harm that comes when it grows doesn’t come when it shrinks.
en.4: Behold the men who look as if they would eat thee up for very love, but who love thee not in their hearts: their friendship is sweeter in the waning than in the waxing.
en.5:
Though evil men should all-absorbing friendship show,
THeir love had better die away than grow.
en.6: The decrease of friendship with those who look as if they would eat you up (through excess of love) while they are really destitute of goodness is far better than its increase.

padaccheda.w: உறின் நட்டு அறின் ஒரூஉம் ஒப்பு இலார் கேண்மை
padaccheda.m: தமக்குப் பயன்உள்வழி நட்புச்செய்து, அஃது இல்வழி ஒழியும் ஒப்பிலாரது நட்பினை
பெற்றால் ஆக்கம் யாது? இழந்தால் கேடுயாது?

en.1: Those who don’t fit, who make friends when it pays and leave when it doesn’t: what does it matter if you gain or lose them?
en.2: What is gained by having, or lost by losing, the friendship of those who befriend you when there is use in it and leave when there isn’t? People who look only to their own gain fit with no one, so he calls them unmatched. Stay indifferent to them.
en.4: Behold the unworthy wretches who would fawn on thee when it is to their profit and forsake thee when thou canst serve them no more: what mattereth it whether thou gain their friendship or lose it?
en.5:
What though you gain or lose friendship of men of alien heart,
Who when you thrive are friends, and when you fail depart?
en.6: Of what avail is it to get or lose the friendship of those who love when there is gain and leave when there is none.

padaccheda.m: நட்பளவு பாராது அதனால்வரும் பயனளவு பார்க்கும் நட்டாரும்
கொடுப்பாரைக் கொள்ளாது விலையைக் கொள்ளும் பொதுமகளிரும்
பிறர் கேடுநோக்காது அவர் சோர்வு நோக்கும் கள்வரும்
தம்முள் ஒப்பர்

en.1: Friends who weigh what they stand to gain, those who take what they are paid, and thieves are all alike.
en.2: Friends who look not at the measure of friendship but at the measure of their gain, public women who take not the giver but the price, and thieves who look not at your loss but at your lapse of attention are all alike. They care only for wealth, and they deceive.
en.4: Behold the men that calculate how much they can gain by a friend: they are of the same class with harlots and thieves.
en.5:
These are alike: the friends who ponder friendship’s gain,
Those who accept whate’er you give, and all the plundering train.
en.6: Friends who calculate the profits (of their friendship), prostitutes who are bent on obtaining their gains, and thieves are (all) of the same character.

padaccheda.w: அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லா மா அன்னார் தமரின்
padaccheda.m: அமர் வாராத போதெல்லாம் தாங்குவது போன்று, வந்துழிக் களத்திடை வீழ்த்துப்போம் கல்வியிலலாத புரவிபோல்வாரது தமர்மையில்
தனிமை சிறப்புடைத்து

en.1: Better to be alone than to call your own those who are like an untaught horse that fails you in battle.
en.2: Better to be alone than to have as your own those like an untrained horse, which seems to carry you until battle comes, then throws you on the field and runs. Untrained means not knowing its paces, movements and battle work. Such friends seem to help until trouble comes, then leave. Being alone is bad too, but it is the better.
en.4: There are men who are like the unbroken horse which throweth down its rider on the battlefield and gallopeth away: it is far better to be lonely than to have such men for friends.
en.5:
A steed untrained will leave you in the tug of war;
Than friends like that to dwell alone is better far.
en.6: Solitude is more to be desired than the society of those who resemble the untrained horses which throw down (their riders) in the fields of battle.

padaccheda.m: செய்து வைத்தாலும் அரண்ஆகாத கீழ்மக்களது தீநட்பு
ஒருவர்க்கு உண்டாதலின் இல்லையாதல் நன்று

en.1: The shabby friendship of small people, who give no protection even when you have made it, is better not had than had.
en.2: The bad friendship of base people, which is no defence even when you have formed it, is better not to have than to have. Being no defence means leaving you when ruin comes.
en.4: Behold the vile men that forsake a trusting friend at the time of his need: it is better not to possess their friendship than to possess it.
en.5:
’Tis better not to gain than gain the friendship profitless
Of men of little minds, whose succour fails when dangers press.
en.6: It is far better to avoid than to contract the evil friendship of the base who cannot protect (their friends) even when appointed to do so.

padaccheda.m: அறிவுஇலானது மிகச்செறி்ந்த நட்பின்
அறிவுடையானது பகைமை கோடி மடங்கு நன்று

en.1: The enmity of the wise is worth ten million times the deepest friendship of a fool.
en.2: The enmity of a wise person is ten million times better than the close friendship of a fool. A wise person’s enmity does no harm, and a fool’s friendship brings every harm.
en.4: The enmity of the wise is ten million times better than the intimacy of fools.
en.5:
Better ten million times incur the wise man’s hate,
Than form with foolish men a friendship intimate.
en.6: The hatred of the wise is ten-million times more profitable than the excessive intimacy of the fool.

padaccheda.m: தாம் அறிதல் வகையர் ஆகாது, நகுதல் வகையர் ஆதற்கு ஏதுவாகிய நட்பான் வருவனவற்றின்
பகைவரான் வருவன பத்துக்கோடி மடங்கு நல்ல

en.1: What enemies bring is a hundred million times better than a friendship that is only laughter.
en.2: What comes from enemies is a hundred million times better than what comes from a friendship that makes you someone to laugh at and not someone who knows. Such friends are like rogues, rakes and jesters, who amuse you in many ways and take what they want. He rejects all other readings as against the grammar.
en.4: The hate of enemies is a hundred million times more valuable than the friendship of boon companions and flatterers.
en.5:
From foes ten million fold a greater good you gain,
Than friendship yields that’s formed with laughers vain.
en.6: What comes from enemies is a hundred million times more profitable than what comes from the friendship of those who cause only laughter.

padaccheda.m: தம்மான் முடியும் கருமத்தை முடியாதாக்கிச் செய்யாதாரோடு கொண்ட நட்பினை
அது கண்டால், அவர் அறியச் சொல்லாதே சோரவிடுக

en.1: With those who spoil work that could be done, say nothing, and let the friendship slowly slip away.
en.2: With those who pretend that work they could do can’t be done, and don’t do it, say nothing once you see it, and let the friendship wind down bit by bit without seeming to drop it. If you speak, or seem to be dropping them, they will mend matters for the moment and try to go on as friends.
en.4: Behold the men that will place obstructions on thy path while thou art at thy work: tell them not a word, but drop their friendship little by little.
en.5:
Those men who make a grievous toil of what they do
On your behalf, their friendship silently eschew.
en.6: Gradually abandon without revealing (beforehand) the friendship of those who pretend inability to carry out what they (really) could do.

padaccheda.m: வினையும் சொல்லும் ஒவ்வாது் வேறுவேறாய் இருப்பார் நட்பு
நனவின்கண்ணே அன்றிக் கனவின் கண்ணும் இன்னாது

en.1: The friendship of those whose acts are one thing and words another is bitter even in a dream.
en.2: The friendship of those whose acts and words don’t match is bitter, not only awake but even in a dream. They are enemies in deed and friends in word. It is so real in waking life that it pains even in a dream.
en.4: Behold the men whose acts belie their spoken words: it is bitter to recall their fellowship even in dreams.
en.5:
E’en in a dream the intercourse is bitterness
With men whose deeds are other than their words profess.
en.6: The friendship of those whose actions do not agree with their words will distress (one) even in (one’s) dreams.

padaccheda.m: தனியே மனைக்கண் இருந்துழி நட்பாடிப் பலரோடு மன்றின்கண் இருந்துழிப் பழிகூறுவார் நட்பு
சிறிதாயினும் தம்மை நணுகுதலைப் பரிகரிக்க

en.1: Don’t let the friendship of those who are warm at home and blame you in the assembly come near you at all.
en.2: Take care that those who are friendly when you are alone at home, and speak blame in the assembly before others, don’t come near you in the least. Both the friendliness at home and the blame in public are bad, so guard against them always.
en.4: Behold the men that speak sweet in the closet but disparage in the assembly: do not approach them in any degree.
en.5:
In anywise maintain not intercourse with those,
Who in the house are friends, in hall are slandering foes.
en.6: Avoid even the least approach to a contraction of friendship with those who would love you in private but ridicule you in public.

padaccheda.m: கூடாதிருந்தே தமக்கு வாய்க்குமிடம் பெறுந்துணையும் கூடியொழுகுவார் நட்பு
அதுபெற்றால், அற எறிதற்குத் துணையாய பட்டடையாம்

en.1: The friendship of those who keep company without agreeing at heart is an anvil. When they find their chance, you are struck on it.
en.2: The friendship of those who stay close without being at one with you, until they get their chance, then becomes an anvil. It seems to bear you up until the moment for the blow comes, and then lets you be cut right through. Some read a different word, and take the place to be the end.
en.4: The friendship that an enemy pretendeth is only an anvil whereon to hammer thee when he seeth his opportunity.
en.5:
Anvil where thou shalt smitten be, when men occasion find,
Is friendship’s form without consenting mind.
en.6: The friendship of those who behave like friends without inward affection is a weapon that may be thrown when a favourable opportunity presents itself.

padaccheda.m: தமக்கு உற்றார் போன்று உறாதாரோடு உளதாய நட்பு
இடம்பெற்றால் பெண்பாலார் மனம்போல வேறுபடும்

en.1: The friendship of those who seem your own but are not will change, like the minds of women.
en.2: Friendship with those who seem your own but aren’t changes, when they get their chance, as women’s minds change. For a friendship to change means going back to the old enmity.
en.4: Behold the men who look like friends but are enemies at heart: their friendship will alter even as the heart of a woman.
en.5:
Friendship of those who seem our kin, but are not really kind,
Will change from hour to hour like woman’s mind.
en.6: The friendship of those who seem to be friends while they are not, will change like the love of women.

padaccheda.m: நல்லன பலநூல்களைக் கற்றவிடத்தும்
அதனான் மனம்திருந்தி நட்பாதல் பகைவர்க்கு இல்லை

en.1: Even after learning many good things, it is hard for enemies to become good at heart.
en.2: Even after learning many good books, which destroy faults of the mind, enemies don’t amend their minds and become friends. Becoming good means giving up hatred. Don’t take those with hatred within as friends because they are learned.
en.4: Even if his studies are great and godly, it is impossible for an enemy to cast off the hate in his heart.
en.5:
To heartfelt goodness men ignoble hardly may attain,
Although abundant stores of goodly lore they gain.
en.6: Though (one’s) enemies may have mastered many good books, it will be impossible for them to become truly loving at heart.

padaccheda.w: முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்து இன்னா வஞ்சரை
padaccheda.m: கண்டபொழுது முகத்தால் இனியவாகச் சிரித்து எப்பொழுதும் மனத்தால் இன்னாராய வஞ்சரை
அஞ்சல் வேண்டும்

en.1: Fear the deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within.
en.2: Fear the deceivers who smile sweetly at your face when they see you and are always bitter in the heart. They put on a smile that is the opposite of the hatred within. That hatred doesn’t show even on the face, the means of reading a person, so they are to be feared.
en.4: Fear thou the hypocritical ruffians that smile to the face but nurse their spite within their bosom.
en.5:
’Tis fitting you should dread dissemblers’ guile,
Whose hearts are bitter while their faces smile.
en.6: One should fear the deceitful who smile sweetly with their face but never love with their heart.

padaccheda.m: மனத்தால் தம்மொடு மேவாதாரை
யாதொரு கருமத்தினும் சொல்லால் தெளிதல் முறைமைத்தன்று நீதிநூல்

en.1: Those who don’t join you in their minds are not to be trusted in anything, on their words alone.
en.2: The books of right conduct hold that those who don’t agree with you at heart aren’t to be trusted in any matter on the strength of their words. Don’t take deceitful words, spoken to hide enmity, as straight words and trust them with your affairs.
en.4: Behold the men whose hearts are not with thee: though their words tempt thee, place not the slightest faith in them.
en.5:
When minds are not in unison, ’tis never just,
In any words men speak to put your trust.
en.6: In nothing whatever is it proper to rely on the words of those who do not love with their heart.

padaccheda.m: நட்டார்போன்று நன்மை பயக்கும் சொற்களைச் சொன்னாராயினும்
பகைவர் சொற்கள் அது பயவாமை அச்சொல்லிய பொழுதே அறியப்படும்

en.1: They may say good things, as friends do, but the words of those who aren’t with you are soon seen for what they are.
en.2: Enemies may speak words that seem to bring good, as friends do, but as they speak it is known that those words will bring none. “May” implies that they don’t usually speak so. They are enemies, so harm is certain, and it is known at once.
en.4: An enemy will be revealed in a moment though he speak the tender language of friendship.
en.5:
Though many goodly words they speak in friendly tone,
The words of foes will speedily be known.
en.6: Though (one’s) foes may utter good things as though they were friends, one will at once understand (their evil) import.

padaccheda.m: வில்லினது வணக்கம், ஏற்றவர்க்குத் தீமைசெய்தலைக் குறித்தமையால்
பகைவர் மாட்டுப் பிறக்கும் சொல்லினது வணக்கத்தையும், தமக்கு நன்மைசெய்தலைக் குறித்தது என்று கருதற்க

en.1: Don’t trust the bowing words of enemies. The bowing of a bow means harm.
en.2: The bending of a bow means harm to whoever stands against it, so don’t think the bending of an enemy’s speech means you good. An archer’s purpose lies in the bending of his bow, and an enemy’s in the bending of his words. Take it as bending that means harm, and guard yourself in fear.
en.4: Trust not an enemy though he bendeth low in his speech: for the bending of the bow forebodeth nothing but harm.
en.5:
To pliant speech from hostile lips give thou no ear;
’Tis pliant bow that shows the deadly peril near!
en.6: Since the bending of the bow bespeaks evil, one should not accept (as good) the humiliating speeches of one’s foes.

padaccheda.m: ஒன்னார் குறி்ப்பை உணரவல்லார்க்கு அவர் தொழுத கையகத்தும் படைக்கலம் மறைந்திருக்கும்
அவர் அழுத கண்ணீரும் அவ்வாறே அதுமறைந்திருத்தற்கு இடனாம்

en.1: A weapon hides in the joined hands of enemies, and in their tears too.
en.2: To those who can read an enemy’s intent, a weapon lies hidden in his joined hands, and in his tears too. Enemies reassure you with hands and eyes, then draw the weapon to kill. Look for it and it shows even as they reassure you. They may show meekness in worship or weeping, but watch their intent and guard yourself.
en.4: Even in his joined hands thy enemy will have a weapon concealed: nor put thou more faith in his tears.
en.5:
In hands that worship weapon often hidden lies;
Such are the tears that fall from foeman’s eyes.
en.6: A weapon may be hid in the very hands with which (one’s) foes adore (him); (and) the tears they shed are of the same nature.

padaccheda.m: பகைமை தோன்றாமல் புறத்தின்கண் நட்பினை மிகச்செய்து, அகத்தின்கண் தம்மை இகழும் பகைவரை
தாமும் அந்நட்பின்கண்ணே நின்று புறத்தின்கண் அவர்மகிழும் வண்ணம்செய்து, அகத்தின்கண் அது சாம்வண்ணம் பொருந்தற்பான்மையுடைத்து அரசநீதி

en.1: Those who make much of you and despise you: make them laugh, and within that friendship hold them so that it dies.
en.2: Enemies make much of friendship outwardly and scorn you within. The law of rulers is to stay in that friendship too, please them outwardly, and hold to them so that it dies within. Being one thing inside and another outside is wrong, but the books of statecraft hold that against enemies it is right.
en.4: Behold the men that make much of thee in public but laugh thee to scorn in secret: humour thou them openly but crush them even in the embrace of friendship.
en.5:
’Tis just, when men make much of you, and then despise,
To make them smile, and slay in friendship’s guise.
en.6: It is the duty of kings to affect great love but make it die (inwardly,) as regard those foes who shew them great friendship but despise them (in their heart).

padaccheda.m: தம்பகைவர் தமக்கு நட்டாராய் ஒழுகுங்காலம் வந்தால்

padaccheda.w: முகம் நட்டு அகம் நட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்
padaccheda.m: தாமும் அவரோடு முகத்தால் நட்புச்செய்து, அகத்தால் அதனைவிட்டுப் பின் அதுவும் தவிர்க

en.1: When the time comes for an enemy to be a friend, be friends with the face, and put friendship out of the heart.
en.2: When the time comes that your enemies behave as friends, be friends with them on your face, give it up in your heart, and then drop even that. The time is when you can’t yet openly cast them off as enemies. So keep them off as far as you can.
en.4: When thou canst not yet break openly with thy foe, feign friendship to his face but keep him off from thy heart.
en.5:
When time shall come that foes as friends appear,
Then thou, to hide a hostile heart, a smiling face may’st wear.
en.6: When one’s foes begin to affect friendship, one should love them with one’s looks, and, cherishing no love in the heart, give up (even the former).

padaccheda.m: பேதைமை என்று சொல்லப்படுவது ஒருவனுக்கு ஏனைக் குற்றங்களெல்லாவற்றினும் மிக்கதொன்று

padaccheda.w: யாது எனின் ஏதம் கொண்டு ஊதியம் போகவிடல்
padaccheda.m: அதுதான் யாதென்று வினவின், தனக்குக் கேடுபயப்பனவற்றைக் கைக்கொண்டு ஆக்கம் பயப்பனவற்றைக் கைவிடுதல்

en.1: What is folly? It is taking hold of what harms you and letting go of what profits you.
en.2: Folly is the worst of all the faults a person can have. It is taking up what brings ruin and letting go of what brings gain. Ruin here means poverty, blame and sin. Gain means wealth, fame and righteousness. So the fool wrecks this life and the next by his own hand.
en.4: Dost thou want to know what folly is? It is the throwing away of that which is profitable and the holding fast to that which is hurtful.
en.5:
What one thing merits folly’s special name?
Letting gain go, loss for one’s own to claim!
en.6: Folly is one (of the chief defects); it is that which (makes one) incur loss and forego gain.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்குப் பேதைமை எல்லாவற்றுள்ளும் மிக்க பேதைமையாவது
தனக்கு ஆகாத ஒழுக்கத்தின்கண் காதன்மை செய்தல்

en.1: The worst folly of all is setting your heart on conduct that isn’t for you.
en.2: The worst of all follies is to be fond of conduct that does you no good. He means gladly doing what the learned have forbidden as harmful in this life and the next.
en.4: The chiefest among all kinds of folly is the folly of inclining the heart towards conduct that is unbecoming to oneself.
en.5:
’Mid follies chiefest folly is to fix your love
On deeds which to your station unbefitting prove.
en.6: The greatest folly is that which leads one to take delight in doing what is forbidden.

padaccheda.m: நாணவேண்டும் அவற்றுக்கு நாணாமையும்
நாடவேண்டுமவற்றை நாடாமையும்
யாவர்மாட்டும் முறிந்தசொல், செயல்உடைமையும்
பேணவேண்டுமவற்றுள் யாதொன்றனையும் பேணாமையும்

பேதையது தொழில். நாணவேண்டுமவை: பழி, பாவங்கள். நாடவேண்டுமவை: கருமங்களிற் செய்வன, தவிர்வன. முறிதல்:கண்ணறுதல். பேணவேண்டுமவை= குடிப்பிறப்பு, கல்வி, ஒழுக்கம் முதலாயின. இவை பேதைக்கு எஞ்ஞான்றும் இயல்பாய் வருதலின் 'தொழில்' என்றார்

en.1: Having no shame, looking into nothing, showing no warmth, caring for nothing: these are a fool’s habits.
en.2: The fool feels no shame at blame and sin, does not look into which tasks to do and which to avoid, is harsh in word and deed with everyone, and guards nothing worth guarding, such as family, learning and conduct. They are called his “work” because they come to him naturally, at all times.
en.4: The fool is neglectful of duties and rude of speech, and callous to all sense of shame: and he will cherish nothing that is good.
en.5:
Ashamed of nothing, searching nothing out, of loveless heart,
Nought cherishing, ’tis thus the fool will play his part.
en.6: Shamelessness, indifference (to what must be sought after), harshness, and aversion for every thing (that ought to be desired) are the qualities of the fool.

padaccheda.m: மனமொழி மெய்கள் அடங்குவதற்கு ஏதுவாய நூல்களை ஓதியும்
அவ்வடக்கத்தான் வரும் பயனை உணர்ந்தும்
அதனை அறியலுறப் பிறர்க்கு உரைத்தும்
தான் அவையடங்கி ஒழுகாத பேதை போல
பேதையார் உலகத்தில்லை

en.1: No one is a greater fool than someone who studies, understands, teaches others, and still has no self-control.
en.2: Someone studies the books that lead to control of mind, speech and body, understands what that control brings, and explains it to others who want to know, yet does not live by it. There is no greater fool in the world. The very things that cure folly have failed, and there is no other medicine.
en.4: There is a man that is learned and subtle and a teacher of others, and yet continueth to be the slave of his passions himself: there is no greater fool than he.
en.5:
The sacred law he reads and learns, to other men expounds,—
Himself obeys not: where can greater fool be found?
en.6: There are no greater fools than he who, though he has read and understood (a great deal) and even taught it to others, does not walk according to his own teaching.

padaccheda.m: பேதையாயினான்
வரும் பிறவிகள் எல்லாம் தான் புக்கு அழுந்தும் நிரயத்தினை
இவ்வொரு பிறப்புள்ளே செய்துகொள்ள வல்லனாம்

en.1: In a single birth, a fool can do enough to sink into the mire of hell for all seven births.
en.2: Within this one birth a fool can bring about the hell he will sink into through all the births to come. All births fall under seven, so “seven” means all. Even in his earthly births his cruel deeds keep him in that hell’s pain. Few others could do so quickly the deeds that earn suffering without end.
en.4: The fool hath the gift of sowing in one birth the seeds of misery for all his future incarnations.
en.5:
The fool will merit hell in one brief life on earth,
In which he entering sinks through sevenfold round of birth.
en.6: A fool can procure in a single birth a hell into which he may enter and suffer through all the seven births.

padaccheda.m: செய்யும் முறைமை அறியாத பேதை ஒரு கருமத்தை மேற்கொள்வனாயின்
அதுவும் புரைபடும், தானும் தளை பூணும்

en.1: When a fool who doesn’t know how takes on a task, the task falls apart and the fool ends up in fetters.
en.2: When a fool who doesn’t know the right way to do a thing takes on a task, it rots from within past repair, and he himself is put in fetters. He ruins it and ruins himself. This is how a fool tries to make wealth.
en.4: Behold the fool that taketh in his hand an enterprise of moment: he will not merely spoil it, he will qualify also for fetters.
en.5:
When fool some task attempts with uninstructed pains,
It fails; nor that alone, himself he binds with chains.
en.6: If the fool who knows not how to act undertakes a work, he will (certainly) fail. (But) is it all? He will even adorn himself with fetters.

padaccheda.m: பேதையாயினான் பெரிய செல்வத்தைத் தெய்வத்தான் எய்தியவழி
தான்னோடு ஒரியைபும் இல்லாதார் நிறைய, எல்லா இயைபும் உடைய தமராயினார் பசியாநிற்பர்

en.1: When a fool comes into great wealth, strangers eat their fill and the fool’s own people go hungry.
en.2: When a fool comes by great wealth through god and not his own effort, people with no tie to him are filled, while his own people, tied to him in every way, go hungry. “Great wealth” could have bought every good thing. Outsiders get all they want, and his own do not get even food.
en.4: If the fool should come by a great fortune it is strangers that will feast and his kindred will only starve.
en.5:
When fools are blessed with fortune’s bounteous store,
Their foes feed full, their friends are prey to hunger sore.
en.6: If a fool happens to get an immense fortune, his neighbours will enjoy it while his relations starve.

padaccheda.m: பேதையாயினான், தன் கைக்கண்ணே ஒன்றனை உடைமையாகப் பெற்றானாயின்
அவன் மயங்குதல், முன்னே பித்தினையுடையான் ஒருவன் அம்மயக்கத்தின் மேலே மதுவுண்டு மயங்கினாற் போலும்

en.1: When a fool gets something of their own in hand, it is like a madman getting drunk.
en.2: When a fool gets something into his hands as his own, he is like a man already mad who drinks liquor on top of his madness. “Gets” shows it came through god and not by his own effort. With folly and the giddiness of wealth together, his acts stagger like those of someone both mad and drunk.
en.4: If the fool obtaineth anything of value he will behave like a madman who is also grown tipsy.
en.5:
When folly’s hand grasps wealth’s increase, ’twill be
As when a madman raves in drunken glee.
en.6: A fool happening to possess something is like the intoxication of one who is (already) giddy.

padaccheda.m: பின் பிரிவுவந்துழி, அஃது இருவர்க்கும் தருவதொரு துன்பமில்லை
ஆதலாற் பேதையாயினார் தம்முட் கொண்ட நட்பு மிகவினிது

en.1: The friendship of fools is very sweet. When it ends, it brings no pain at all.
en.2: When fools’ friendship with each other reaches parting, it gives neither of them any pain, and so it is very sweet. It wears away day by day, so the end doesn’t hurt. This is blame that sounds like praise.
en.4: Greatly delectable is the friendship of fools: one feeleth no pangs when one parteth from them.
en.5:
Friendship of fools is very pleasant thing;
Parting with them will leave behind no sting.
en.6: The friendship between fools is exceedingly delightful (to each other); for at parting there will be nothing to cause them pain.

padaccheda.m: சான்றோர் அவையின்கண் பேதையாயினான் புகுதல்
தூயவல்ல மிதித்த காலை இன்பந்தரும் அமளிக்கண்ணே வைத்தாற் போலும்

en.1: A fool walking into a gathering of the worthy is like putting an unwashed foot on a bed.
en.2: A fool entering an assembly of the worthy is like setting a foot that has trodden filth on a bed made for pleasure. “Unwashed” is a polite way of saying it. As the foot degrades the bed, the fool degrades the assembly.
en.4: Even as is the placing of an unwashed foot on the couch, even so is the entrance of the fool in an assembly of men of worth.
en.5:
Like him who seeks his couch with unwashed feet,
Is fool whose foot intrudes where wise men meet.
en.6: The appearance of a fool in an assembly of the learned is like placing (one’s) unwashed feet on a bed.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு இல்லாமை பலவற்றுள்ளும் மிக்க இல்லாமையாவது, அறிவில்லாமை
மற்றைப் பொருள் இல்லாமையோவெனின், அதனை அப்பெற்றித்தாய இல்லாமையாகக் கொள்ளார் உலகத்தார்

en.1: The worst poverty is a lack of understanding. The world does not count any other lack as poverty.
en.2: Of all the things a person can lack, the worst is understanding, meaning sound understanding. The world doesn’t count a lack of other things, such as wealth, as the same. People of petty understanding gain nothing for this life or the next even when rich, and people of sound understanding lose none of it even when poor.
en.4: The veritable poverty is the poverty of sense: the world regardeth not other poverty as poverty.
en.5:
Want of knowledge, ’mid all wants the sorest want we deem;
Want of other things the world will not as want esteem.
en.6: The want of wisdom is the greatest of all wants; but that of wealth the world will not regard as such.

padaccheda.m: புல்லறிவுடையான் ஒருவனுக்கு மனம் உவந்து ஒன்று கொடுத்தல் கூடிற்றாயின்
அதற்குக் காரணம் பெறுகின்றவன் நல்வினையே, வேறொன்றும் இல்லை

en.1: When someone without understanding gives with a glad heart, it comes from nothing but the penance of the one who receives.
en.2: If someone of petty understanding ever does give gladly, the cause is the good deeds of the receiver and nothing else. He answers those who say such people do good too. The receiver is like someone who finds a dropped thing. The giver isn’t thinking of this life or the next.
en.4: When a fool bestoweth a gift of his own free will, it is simply the good fortune of the receiver and nothing else.
en.5:
The gift of foolish man, with willing heart bestowed, is nought
But blessing by receiver’s penance bought.
en.6: (The cause of) a fool cheerfully giving (some thing) is nothing else but the receiver’s merit (in a former birth.)

padaccheda.m: புல்லறிவுடையார் தாமே தம்மை வருத்தும் வருத்தம்
அது செய்தற்கு உரியராய தம்பகைவர்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது

en.1: The pain that people without understanding cause themselves is hard even for their enemies to cause.
en.2: The pain that people of petty understanding give themselves is hard even for their enemies, who have every reason to give it. An enemy can only wait for the moment and do the one thing he knows. He can’t bring poverty, blame, sin and all the rest at all times.
en.4: The troubles that a fool bringeth down on his head, it is hard even for his enemies to cause him.
en.5:
With keener anguish foolish men their own hearts wring,
Than aught that even malice of their foes can bring.
en.6: The suffering that fools inflict upon themselves is hardly possible even to foes.

padaccheda.m: புலலறிவுடைமையென்று சொல்லப்படுவது யாதென்று வினவின்
அது தம்மைத்தாமே யாம் நல்லறிவுடையம் என்று நன்குமதிக்கும் மயக்கம்

en.1: What is called immaturity? It is the conceit that says, “I am wise.”
en.2: What is called petty understanding? It is the delusion of thinking well of yourself and saying, “I have sound understanding.” The word means understanding that hasn’t ripened. It is called delusion because such people know the world scorns them and think this all the same.
en.4: Dost thou want to know what is shallowness of wit? It is the conceit that sayeth to itself, I am wise.
en.5:
What is stupidity? The arrogance that cries,
‘Behold, we claim the glory of the wise.’
en.6: What is called want of wisdom is the vanity which says, “We are wise.”

padaccheda.m: புல்லறிவாளர் தாம் கல்லாத நூல்களையும் கற்றாராகத் தாம் மேலிட்டுக்கொண்டு ஒழுகுதல்
கசடறக் கற்றதொரு நூலுண்டாயின், அதன்கண்ணும் பிறர்க்கு ஐயத்தை விளைக்கும்

en.1: Claiming to know what you have not learned makes people doubt even what you have truly mastered.
en.2: When people of petty understanding carry on as if they had studied books they have not, then even a book they have learned thoroughly leaves others in doubt. People wonder whether they really know it, or whether it is as they say.
en.4: Behold the fool that pretendeth unto knowledge that be possesseth not: he raiseth doubts even as to those things that he really knoweth.
en.5:
If men what they have never learned assume to know,
Upon their real learning’s power a doubt ’twill throw.
en.6: Fools pretending to know what has not been read (by them) will rouse suspicion even as to what they have thoroughly mastered.

padaccheda.m: புல்லறிவாளர் தம்கண் நிகழும் குற்றங்களை அறிந்து கடியாராயின்
ஆடையால் அற்றம் மறைத்தாராகத் தம்மைக் கருதுதலும் புல்லறிவாம்

en.1: If you leave your own faults uncovered, covering your nakedness is just petty understanding.
en.2: People of petty understanding who don’t see and stop their own faults, yet think themselves covered because clothes hide their nakedness, show petty understanding here too. To cover a fault means to get rid of it. They hide only the lowest thing that needs hiding, leave the higher ones bare, and on that alone count themselves decent people.
en.4: Where is the good of the fool covering his nakedness, if the deformities of his mind are still left uncovered?
en.5:
Fools are they who their nakedness conceal,
And yet their faults unveiled reveal.
en.6: Even to cover one’s nakedness would be folly, if (one’s) faults were not covered (by forsaking them.)

padaccheda.m: பெறுதற்குரிய உபதேசப்பொருளைப் பெற்றாலும் உட்கொள்ளாது போக்கும் புல்லறிவாளன்
அவ்வுறுதி அறியாமையான் தானே தனக்கு மிக்க வருத்தத்தைச் செய்துகொள்ளும்

en.1: Someone without understanding who lets a precious secret slip does himself great harm.
en.2: Someone of petty understanding receives precious teaching and lets it go without taking it in. Not knowing what is good for him, he brings on himself pain too hard to bear. He rejects the reading that this means blurting out a hidden plan, because that is carelessness, a kind of folly, not petty understanding.
en.4: Behold the shallow man that cannot keep a secret to himself: he will bring down great calamities on his own head.
en.5:
From out his soul who lets the mystic teachings die,
Entails upon himself abiding misery.
en.6: The fool who neglects precious counsel does, of his own accord, a great injury to himself.

reading.note: அருமறை can be a precious secret or precious teaching. He takes it as teaching that is heard and not kept, and rejects the reading that it is a secret blurted out.

padaccheda.m: புல்லறிவாளன் தனக்கு உறுதியாயவற்றை அறிவுடையார் சொல்லாநிற்கவும் செய்யான்
அதுவன்றித் தானாகவும் இவை செய்வன என்று அறியான்
அவ்வுயிர் யாக்கையின் நீங்கும் அளவும் நிலத்திற்குப் பொறுத்தற்குஅரியதொரு நோயாம்

en.1: He won’t act when told and can’t work it out himself. Until that life leaves him, he is a disease.
en.2: A man of petty understanding won’t do what is good for him even when the wise tell him, and can’t see for himself what should be done. Until that life leaves the body he is a disease hard for the earth to bear. The soul knows by nature, but the body has turned it to delusion. The earth bears the great mountains, and a sinful body is its heavy load.
en.4: Behold the man who neither listeneth to advice nor knoweth for himself what is right: all the days of his life he is a plague to his fellows.
en.5:
Advised, he heeds not; of himself knows nothing wise;
This man’s whole life is all one plague until he dies.
en.6: The fool will not perform (his duties) even when advised nor ascertain them himself; such a soul is a burden (to the earth) till it departs (from the body.)

padaccheda.m: தன்னை எல்லாம் அறிந்தானாக மதித்தலான் பிறரால் ஒன்றுஅறியும் தன்மை இலாதானை, அறிவிக்கப்புகுவான் அவனால் பழிக்கப்பட்டுத் தான் அறியானாய் முடியும்
இனி அவ்வறியுந்தன்மை இல்லாதான், கொண்டது விடாமையான், தான் அறிந்தவாற்றால் அதனை அறிந்தானாய் முடியும்

en.1: Whoever tries to show a man who can’t see ends up seeing nothing himself. That man goes on seeing it the way he saw it.
en.2: A man who thinks he knows everything can’t learn anything from others. Whoever sets out to teach him gets blamed by him and ends up as the one who doesn’t know. And the man, never letting go of what he holds, ends up knowing it just the way he knew it. There is no way to give sound understanding to people of petty understanding.
en.4: He that trieth to open the eyes of a fool is a fool himself: for the fool seeth but one way and that way is never wrong in his eyes.
en.5:
That man is blind to eyes that will not see who knowledge shows;
The blind man still in his blind fashion knows.
en.6: One who would teach a fool will (simply) betray his folly; and the fool would (still) think himself ‘‘wise in his own conceit.”

padaccheda.m: உயர்ந்தோர் பலரும் உண்டு என்பதோர் பொருளைத் தன் புல்லறிவான் இல்லையென்று சொல்லுவான்
மகன் என்று கருதப்படான், வையத்துக் காணப்படுவதோர் பேய் என்று கருதப்படும்

en.1: Someone who says “there is none” where the world says “there is” will be counted a demon on this earth.
en.2: Someone who in his petty understanding denies what many of the great say exists isn’t counted a human being. He is counted a demon seen on earth. What they affirm includes god, rebirth and the fruit of good and bad deeds. He says what he pleases, as a demon does, and looks unlike one, so he is the kind that hides its body and appears in a human one.
en.4: Behold the man who denieth what all the world doth assert: he will be looked upon as a devil in human shape.
en.5:
Who what the world affirms as false proclaim,
O’er all the earth receive a demon’s name.
en.6: He who denies the existence of what the world believes in will be regarded as a demon on earth.

padaccheda.w: எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் பகல் என்னும் பண்பு இன்மை பாரிக்கும் நோய்
padaccheda.m: எல்லா உயிர்கட்கும், பிறஉயிர்களோடு கூடாமை என்னும் தீக்குணத்தை வளர்க்கும் குற்றம்
இகல்என்று சொல்லுவர் நூலோர்

en.1: They call strife the disease that feeds, in every living being, the fault of drawing apart.
en.2: The learned call strife the fault that feeds, in all beings, the evil trait of not coming together with others. “Every living being” shows that it puts humans on a level with animals. It is called division because it comes between people and produces a divided nature.
en.4: The spirit of defiance is the peccant humour which developpeth in all men the distemper called hate.
en.5:
Hostility disunion’s plague will bring,
That evil quality, to every living thing.
en.6: The disease which fosters the evil of disunion among all creatures is termed hatred by the wise.

padaccheda.m: தம்மோடு கூடாமையைக் கருதி ஒருவன் வெறுப்பன செய்தானாயினும்
அவனோடு மாறுபடுதலைக் குறித்துத் தாம் அவனுக்கு இன்னாதவற்றைச் செய்யாமை உயர்ந்தது

en.1: Even if someone means to break with you and does what you can’t bear, it is best not to answer with harm out of strife.
en.2: Even if someone wants to break with you and does things you dislike, the highest course is not to do him harm in order to fight him. If you do, enmity grows and you sink. If you hold back, his hostile acts die away by themselves and you rise.
en.4: Even when thy neighbour injureth thee with the deliberate purpose of picking a quarrel, even then it is best not to harbour vengeance or return the injury.
en.5:
Though men disunion plan, and do thee much despite,
’Tis best no enmity to plan, nor evil deeds requite.
en.6: Though disagreeable things may be done from (a feeling of) disunion, it is far better that nothing painful be done from (that of) hatred.

padaccheda.m: மாறுபாடு என்று சொல்லப்படுகின்ற துன்பத்தைச் செய்யு நோயை ஒருவன் தன்மனத்தினின்று நீக்குமாயின்
அவனுக்கு அந்நீக்குதல், எஞ்ஞான்றும் உளனாதற்கு ஏதுவாய புகழைக் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: Get rid of the painful disease called strife, and you gain an undying, spotless brightness.
en.2: If you remove from your mind the painful disease called strife, that removal gives you the fame that makes you live forever. Everyone becomes your friend, so you gain all wealth, and giving and the like bring you fame.
en.4: The habit of defying others is verily a grievous malady: if a man freeth himself from it, he will acquire everlasting fame.
en.5:
If enmity, that grievous plague, you shun,
Endless undying praises shall be won.
en.6: To rid one-self of the distressing disease of hatred will bestow (on one) a never-decreasing imperishable fame.

padaccheda.m: மாறுபாடு என்று சொல்லப்படுகின்ற துன்பங்கள் எல்லாவற்றினும் மிக்க துன்பம் ஒருவனுக்கு இல்லையாயின்
அவ்வின்மை அவனுக்கு இன்பங்கள் எல்லாவற்றினும் மிக்க இன்பத்தினைக் கொடுக்கும்

en.1: When strife, the worst pain of all pains, is gone, it brings the greatest joy of all joys.
en.2: If you are free of strife, the greatest of all pains, that freedom gives you the greatest of all joys. The worst pain is fighting many, losing your strength and lying at everyone’s mercy, and strife brings this directly. The greatest joy is that everyone becomes a friend and you gain every benefit.
en.4: The highest joys will be within thy reach if thou reject from thy heart that greatest of evils, the defiant spirit.
en.5:
Joy of joys abundant grows,
When malice dies, that woe of woes.
en.6: If hatred which is the greatest misery is destroyed, it will yield the greatest delight.

padaccheda.m: தம்முள்ளது மாறுபாடு தோன்றியவழி அதனை ஏற்றுக்கொள்ளாது சாய்ந்து ஒழுகவல்லாரை
வெல்லக் கருதும் தன்மயுடையார் யாவர்?

en.1: Who would try to get the better of those who can turn aside from strife?
en.2: When discord arises, some can refuse to take it up and turn aside. Who would think of defeating them? Giving up strife is hard in every way for rulers, so he says “can”. Such people are friends to all, so no one thinks of beating them.
en.4: Who can desire the overthrow of the man who hath the talent to avoid hostilities?
en.5:
If men from enmity can keep their spirits free,
Who over them shall gain the victory?
en.6: Who indeed would think of conquering those who naturally shrink back from hatred?

padaccheda.m: பிறரொடு மாறுபடுதற்கண் மிகுதல் எனக்கு இனிதென்று அதனைச் செய்வானது உயிர்வாழ்க்கை
பிழைத்தலும் முற்றக்கெடுதலும் சிறிது பொழுதுள் உளவாம்

en.1: Someone who calls it sweet to press on in strife will soon see his life falter and fall to ruin.
en.2: A man who says it is sweet to go further and further in strife, meaning to win, and keeps at it, has failure and total ruin close by. Failure means the misery of poverty. Total ruin means death. Loss of wealth and loss of life come at once.
en.4: Behold the man who taketh delight in breathing defiance against his neighbours: it will not be long before he doth stumble and fall.
en.5:
The life of those who cherished enmity hold dear,
To grievous fault and utter death is near.
en.6: Failure and ruin are not far from him who says it is sweet to excel in hatred.

padaccheda.m: இகலோடு மேவுதலையுடைய இன்னாத அறிவினை உடையார்
வெற்றி பொருந்தலையுடைய நீதிநூற் பொருளை அறியமாட்டார்

en.1: People of bitter understanding who cling to strife can’t see the truth that brings victory.
en.2: People of harmful understanding, who keep to strife, can’t grasp what the books of statecraft teach, which brings victory. Such understanding hurts themselves and others. Those books are called true because those who follow the path to victory can see what they yield. Strife confuses the understanding, so they can’t see it.
en.4: Behold the prince of spiteful nature who is ever addicted to strife: he will be blind to the policy that advanceth nations.
en.5:
The very truth that greatness gives their eyes can never see,
Who only know to work men woe, fulfilled of enmity.
en.6: Those whose judgment brings misery through its connection with hatred cannot understand the triumphant nature of truth.

padaccheda.m: தன்னுள்ளத்து மாறுபாடு தோன்றியவழி, அதனை எதிர்தலை ஒழிதல் ஒருவனுக்கு ஆக்கமாம்
அது செய்யாது அதன்கண் மிகுதலை மேற்கொள்வானாயின், கேடும் தன்கண் வருதலை மேற்கொள்ளும்

en.1: Turning aside from strife brings gain. Press on with it, and ruin presses on towards you.
en.2: When strife arises in your heart, refusing to take it up is gain. If you don’t refuse, and set about increasing it, ruin sets about coming to you. Gain comes the moment you turn aside, so he calls turning aside itself gain.
en.4: The avoiding of strife leadeth unto prosperity: but if thou allow it to grow apace, ruin will not lag far behind.
en.5:
’Tis gain to turn the soul from enmity;
Ruin reigns where this hath mastery.
en.6: Shrinking back from hatred will yield wealth; indulging in its increase will hasten ruin.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் தன்கண் ஆக்கம் வரும்வழிக் காரணமுண்டாயினும் இகலை நினையான்
தனக்குக் கேடு செய்துகோடற்கண் காரணம் இன்றியும் அதன்கண் மிகுதலை நினைக்கும்

en.1: When gain is coming to him, a man doesn’t look for strife. To bring about his own ruin, he looks to increase it.
en.2: When gain is coming to a man, he doesn’t think of strife even with cause. When he is bringing ruin on himself, he thinks of increasing it even without cause. “Bring about” shows that the ruin comes through his strife, not through others. Whether strife is absent or present tells you in advance whether gain or ruin is coming.
en.4: When fortune is about to smile on a man he will ignore all provocation: but when Destiny hath decreed him ruin, he will set no bounds to his defiance of his neighbours.
en.5:
Men think not hostile thought in fortune’s favouring hour,
They cherish enmity when in misfortune’s power.
en.6: At the approach of wealth one will not think of hatred; (but) to secure one’s ruin, one will look to its increase.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு மாறுபாடு ஒன்றானே இன்னாதன எல்லாம் உளவாம்
நட்பு ஒன்றானே நல்லநீதி என்னும் பெருஞ்செல்வம் உளதாம்

en.1: Strife brings all that is bitter. Smiles bring the pride of true goodness.
en.2: Strife alone brings every bitter thing, such as poverty, blame and sin. Friendship alone brings the great wealth called good policy. By “smiles” he means the friendship that causes them, and by “pride” the wealth that causes it.
en.4: From defiance springeth all that is bitter: but good will yieldeth the glorious fruit of peace and harmony.
en.5:
From enmity do all afflictive evils flow;
But friendliness doth wealth of kindly good bestow.
en.6: All calamities are caused by hatred; but by the delight (of friendship) is caused the great wealth of good virtues.

padaccheda.m: தம்மின் வலியார்க்குப் பகையாய் எதிர்தலை ஒழிக
ஏனை மெலியார்க்குப் பகையாதலை ஒழியாது விரும்புக

en.1: Keep from opposing the strong. Without holding back, seek enmity with the weak.
en.2: Don’t stand against those stronger than you. Without holding back, seek enmity with those weaker. Strength includes allies, and weakness means lacking them. Allies are of two kinds: outer, such as army and wealth, and inner, such as sound understanding and living by statecraft. Beating those with neither costs you no strength, so enmity with them is allowed.
en.4: Strive not with the powerful: but against those that are weaker than thyself carry on wars without relaxing even for one moment.
en.5:
With stronger than thyself, turn from the strife away;
With weaker shun not, rather court the fray.
en.6: Avoid offering resistance to the strong; (but) never fail to cherish enmity towards the weak.
