padaccheda.m: அக்குறைதலை நன்று என்று அறிந்து அவ்வாறே உண்பவன்மாட்டு இன்பம்நீங்காது நிலை நிற்குமாறுபோல்
மிகப்பெரிய இரையை விழுங்குவான் மாட்டு நோய்நீங்காது நிலைநிற்கும்

en.1: Joy stays with someone who knows to eat a little less. In the same way, disease stays with someone who gorges.
en.2: As joy never leaves the man who knows that less is better and eats a little short of what he could, disease never leaves the man who swallows huge feeds. Joy means the three humours stay in place, so mind, speech and body are his own, and he gains the four aims, beginning with righteousness. The other is like an animal that feeds without measure and suffers by it.
en.4: Even as Health seeketh the man who eateth only when his stomach is empty, even so doth Disease seek the man who eateth to excess.
en.5:
On modest temperance as pleasures pure,
So pain attends the greedy epicure.
en.6: As pleasure dwells with him who eats moderately, so disease (dwells) with the glutton who eats voraciously.

padaccheda.w: தெரியான் தீ அளவு அன்றிப் பெரிது உண்ணின்
padaccheda.m: தன்பகுதியும், அதற்கு ஏற்ற உணவும் காலமும் ஆராயாது வேண்டியதோர் உணவை வேண்டியதோர் காலத்து வயிற்றுத் தீயளவன்றி ஒருவன் மிகஉண்ணுமாயின்
அவன் மாட்டு நோய்கள் எல்லையற வளரும்

en.1: Someone who eats without thought, more than the fire can take, will have diseases without measure.
en.2: A man who doesn’t consider his constitution, the right food or the right time, and eats whatever he likes, whenever he likes, far beyond the fire in his belly, will find his diseases grow without limit.
en.4: Behold the man who glutteth himself foolishly beyond the measure of his internal heat: his diseases will exceed all measure.
en.5:
Who largely feeds, nor measure of the fire within maintains,
That thoughtless man shall feel unmeasured pains.
en.6: He will be afflicted with numberless diseases, who eats immoderately, ignorant (of the rules of health.)

padaccheda.m: மருத்துவன்ஆயினான் ஆதுரன் மாட்டு நிகழ்கின்ற நோயை அதன் குறிகளான் இன்னதென்று துணிந்து
பின் அது வருதற் காரணத்தை ஆராய்ந்து தெளிந்து
பின் அது தீர்க்கும் உபாயத்தினை அறிந்து
அதனைச் செய்யும்வழிப் பிழையாமற் செய்க

en.1: Find the disease, find its cause, find the way to ease it, and act so that it works.
en.2: A physician should settle from the signs what disease the patient has, then work out its cause, then find the way to cure it, and carry that out without error. The cause is the food and activity named above. The way covers giving medicine, letting blood, cutting, burning and the like. Without error means not straying from the practice of the old physicians.
en.4: Consider the disease and its origin and the means of curing it: and then set about the cure with every precaution.
en.5:
Disease, its cause, what may abate the ill:
Let leech examine these, then use his skill.
en.6: Let the physician enquire into the (nature of the) disease, its cause and its method of cure and treat it faithfully according to (medical rule).

padaccheda.m: ஆயுள் வேதத்தினைக் கற்ற மருத்துவன்

padaccheda.w: உற்றான் அளவும் பிணி அளவும் காலமும் கருதிச் செயல்
padaccheda.m: அவ்வுபாயத்தினைச் செய்யுங்கால், ஆதுரன் அளவினையும், அவன்கண் நிகழ்கின்ற நோயின் அளவினையும், தன் செயற்கு ஏற்ற காலத்தினையும் அந்நூல் நெறியால் நோக்கி, அவற்றோடு பொருந்தச் செய்க

en.1: The one who has learned should weigh the patient, the disease and the time, and then act.
en.2: A physician learned in medicine should, as his texts direct, weigh the patient, the disease and the time for his work, and act to fit them. The patient means constitution, age and strength to bear pain. The disease means whether it is curable, incurable or manageable, its stage and its force. Weigh these by the books and by keen judgement.
en.4: Let the physician take the measure of the patient and the disease and the season that is: and then let him undertake the cure.
en.5:
The habitudes of patient and disease, the crises of the ill:
These must the learned leech think over well, then use his skill.
en.6: The learned (physician) should ascertain the condition of his patient, the nature of his disease, and the season (of the year) and (then) proceed (with his treatment).

padaccheda.m: பிணிக்கு மருந்தாவது
அதனையு்ற்றவன்
அதனைத் தீர்க்கும் மருத்துவன்
அவனுக்குக் கருவியாகிய மருந்து
அதனைப் பிழையாமல் இயற்றுவான் என்று சொல்லப்பட்ட நான்கு பகுதியையுடைய நான்கு திறத்தது

en.1: The patient, the healer, the remedy and the attendant: medicine has these four parts.
en.2: Medicine has four parts, each with four qualities. The sufferer needs wealth, obedience, clear report and endurance. The physician needs no fear, learning, experience and purity. The remedy needs broad use, potency, ease of getting and fit. The one who prepares it needs loving-kindness, purity, exactness and understanding. A cure needs them all, so all are called medicine.
en.4: The patient, the physician, the medicine, and the apothecary, on these four doth all cure depend: and four again are the attributes of each of them.
en.5:
For patient, leech, and remedies, and him who waits by patient’s side,
The art of medicine must fourfold code of laws provide.
en.6: Medical science consists of four parts, viz. patient, physician, medicine and compounder; and each of these (again) contains four sub-divisions.

padaccheda.m: செம்மையும் நாணும் சேர
குடிப்பிறந்தார் மாட்டல்லது பிறர்மாட்டு இயற்கையாக உளவாகா

en.1: Only in those born of a good family do uprightness and shame come together by nature.
en.2: Uprightness and shame together are natural only in those born of a good family, not in others. Uprightness means thought, word and deed don’t clash. Shame means shrinking from blame and sin. Those of good family have these without being taught. In others, even when taught, they don’t last long.
en.4: Rectitude and a sense of shame come by nature only to men who are born of a good family.
en.5:
Save in the scions of a noble house, you never find
Instinctive sense of right and virtuous shame combined.
en.6: Consistency (of thought, word and deed) and fear (of sin) are conjointly natural only to the high born.

padaccheda.m: உயர்ந்த குடியின்கண் பிறந்தார்
தமக்குரிய ஒழுக்கம் மெய்ம்மை நாண் எனப்பட்ட இமமூன்றன் கண்ணும் கல்வியான் அன்றித் தாமாகவே வழுவார்

en.1: Those of good family never slip from these three: good conduct, truth and shame.
en.2: Those born in a high family never slip in the three that are theirs, conduct, truth and shame, and they keep them by themselves, not through study. These belong to body, speech and mind, which is why they come in that order. They don’t even know how to slip, so he says “never slip”.
en.4: Men of family fall not from three things, namely, correct conduct, truth, and a sense of shame.
en.5:
In these three things the men of noble birth fail not:
In virtuous deed, and truthful word, and chastened thought.
en.6: The high born will never deviate from these three: good manners, truthfulness and modesty.

padaccheda.m: எக்காலத்தும் திரிபில்லாத குடியின்கண் பிறந்தார்க்கு

padaccheda.w: நகை ஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை நான்கும் வகை என்ப
padaccheda.m: வறியார் சென்றவழி முகமலர்ச்சியும், உள்ளன கொடுத்தலும், இன்சொற் சொல்லுதலும், இகழாமையுமாகிய இந்நான்கும் உரிய கூறு என்று சொல்லுவர் நூலோர்

en.1: A smile, giving, sweet words and scorning no one: they say these four belong to a true family.
en.2: The learned say four things belong to those of an unchanging family: a bright face when the poor come, giving what you have, sweet words and no scorn. Falsehood changes, so changelessness is called “true”. Everyone despises those who have nothing, so not scorning them is made one of the four.
en.4: Four are the attributes of the true gentleman: a smiling face, a liberal hand, sweetness of speech, and condescension.
en.5:
The smile, the gift, the pleasant word, unfailing courtesy:
These are the signs, they say, of true nobility.
en.6: A cheerful countenance, liberality, pleasant words, and an unreviling disposition, these four are said to be the proper qualities of the truly high born.

padaccheda.m: பலவாக அடுக்கிய கோடி அளவிற்றாய பொருளைப் பெற்றாராயினும்
உயர்ந்த குடியின்கண் பிறந்தார் தம் ஒழுக்கம் குன்றும் தொழில்களைச் செய்யார்

en.1: Even for piled-up millions, those of good family won’t do anything that lowers them.
en.2: Even if they could get wealth counted in millions upon millions, those born of a high family won’t do work that lowers their conduct.
en.4: Men of family would not tarnish their name even for the sake of tens of millions.
en.5:
Millions on millions piled would never win
The men of noble race to soul-degrading sin.
en.6: Though blessed with immense wealth, the noble will never do anything unbecoming.

padaccheda.m: தொன்றுதொட்டு வருகின்ற குடியின்கண் பிறந்தார்
தாம் கொடுக்கும் பொருள் பண்டையிற் சுருங்கிய இடத்தும்
தம் பண்புடைமையின் நீங்கார்

en.1: Even when what they have to give has shrunk, those of an old family don’t part from their good nature.
en.2: Those of a family that has come down from of old don’t leave their good nature, even when what they can give has shrunk. Such a family is like the Chera, Chola and Pandya lines, great since creation. For them, poverty simply means having less to give.
en.4: Behold the men of ancient family: they give not up their liberality even when their means of munificence are diminished.
en.5:
Though stores for charity should fail within, the ancient race
Will never lose its old ancestral grace.
en.6: Though their means fall off, those born in ancient families, will not lose their character (for liberality).

padaccheda.w: மாசு அற்ற குலம் பற்றி வாழ்தும் என்பார்
padaccheda.m: வசையற்று வருகின்ற நம் குடிமரபினோடு ஒத்து வாழக்கடவேம் என்று கருதி அவ்வாறு வாழ்வார்
வறுமையுற்றவழியும், வஞ்சனையைப் பொருந்தி, அமைவிலவாய தொழில்களைச் செய்யார்

en.1: Those who say, “We will live by our spotless family,” won’t turn to deceit and do unworthy things.
en.2: Those who resolve to live up to their family line, free of blame, won’t take to deceit and do what doesn’t suit that line, even when poor.
en.4: Behold the men who are anxious to keep pure the honourable traditions of their family: they will never take to deceit nor descend to ignoble deeds.
en.5:
Whose minds are set to live as fits their sire’s unspotted fame,
Stooping to low deceit, commit no deeds that gender shame.
en.6: Those who seek to preserve the irreproachable honour of their families will not viciously do what is detrimental thereto.

padaccheda.m: உயர்ந்த குடியின்கண் பிறந்தார்மாட்டு உளதாம் குற்றம்
தான் சிறிதேயாயினும் விசும்பின்கண் மதியிடத்து மறுப்போல ஓங்கித் தோன்றும்

en.1: A fault in those of good family stands out like the spot on the moon in the sky.
en.2: A fault in someone born of a high family, however small, stands out like the spot on the moon in the sky. The family is high, and the fault clashes with good qualities that are like the moon, so it spreads and shows across the world.
en.4: The fault of a man of noble family will show conspicuously even as the spot in the body of the moon.
en.5:
The faults of men of noble race are seen by every eye,
As spots on her bright orb that walks sublime the evening sky.
en.6: The defects of the noble will be observed as clearly as the dark spots in the moon.

padaccheda.m: குல நலமுடையனாய் வருகின்றவன்கண்ணே ஈரமின்மை உளதாம் ஆயின்
அவனை அக்குலப்பிறப்பின்கண்ணே ஐயப்படும் உலகம்

en.1: If a lack of warmth shows in someone of good character, people will doubt his family.
en.2: If someone of fine family shows no kindness, the world doubts that he was born in that family. Lack of kindness means not giving, harsh words and the like. “If” shows it doesn’t usually appear. Because these things appear in a man of good standing, even what is true of him comes into doubt.
en.4: If rudeness of speech showeth itself in a man coming of a good family, people would even suspect the legitimacy of his descent.
en.5:
If lack of love appear in those who bear some goodly name,
’Twill make men doubt the ancestry they claim.
en.6: If one of a good family betrays want of affection, his descent from it will be called in question.

padaccheda.m: நிலத்தின் இயல்பை அதன்கண் முளைத்த முளை காட்டும்
அதுபோலக் குலத்தின் இயல்பை அதன்கண் பிறந்தார் வாயி்ற் சொல் காட்டும்

en.1: A sprout shows what the soil is like. The words from a person’s mouth show what their family is like.
en.2: The sprout that rises from a field shows its nature. So the words in the mouths of those born in a family show its nature. A sprout alone shows whether the soil is good or bad, so leaves aren’t mentioned, and words alone show the family, so deeds aren’t needed. While seeming to name a way of knowing the family, he is saying that sweet speech is needed.
en.4: The nature of a soil is known by the seedling that groweth therein: even so is the family of a man known by the words that come out of his mouth.
en.5:
Of soil the plants that spring thereout will show the worth;
The words they speak declare the men of noble birth.
en.6: As the sprout indicates the nature of the soil, (so) the speech of the noble indicates (that of one’s birth.)

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் தனக்கு நலன் உடைமையை வேண்டுவனாயின், நாணுடையன் ஆதலை வேண்டுக
குலன் உடைமையை வேண்டுவன் ஆயின், பணியப்படுவார் யாவர்மாட்டும் பணிதலை வேண்டுக

en.1: If you want goodness, have shame. If you want a good family name, bow to everyone.
en.2: If you want goodness, meaning fame and merit, you must have shame. If you want family standing, bow to all who should be bowed to: sages, the worthy, great ascetics, your elders, father and mother. Bowing means rising from your seat, going to meet them and the like.
en.4: If thou desire virtue, thou must cultivate the sense of shame: and if thou want to honour thy family, thou must be respectful unto all.
en.5:
Who seek for good the grace of virtuous shame must know;
Who seek for noble name to all must reverence show.
en.6: He who desires a good name must desire modesty; and he who desires (the continuance of) a family greatness must be submissive to all.

padaccheda.m: செய்யாதவழித் தாம் அமையாத சிறப்பினை உடையவே எனினும்
தம் குடிப்பிறப்புத் தாழவரும் செயல்களை ஒழிக

en.1: Even things you can’t do without, give them up if they would lower you.
en.2: Even if leaving them undone would cost you your life, give up acts that lower your birth. He rejects the rule of the northern books that you may do something shameful to survive when death is near. Weigh the body, which doesn’t last, against honour, which does, and don’t do them.
en.4: Forbear from those things that would lower thee, even though they should be indispensable for the very preservation of thy life.
en.5:
Though linked to splendours man no otherwise may gain,
Reject each act that may thine honour’s clearness stain.
en.6: Actions that would degrade (one’s) family should not be done, though they may be so important that not doing them would end in death.

padaccheda.m: புகழ்செய்யும் இடத்தும் தம் குடிமைக்கு ஒவ்வாத இளிவரவுகளைச் செய்யார்
புகழுடனே மானத்தை நிறுத்துதலை விரும்புவார்

en.1: Those who want glory along with great strength of character won’t do anything unworthy, even for glory.
en.2: Those who want fame and want to keep their honour won’t do anything shameful and unfit for their birth, even where it would bring fame. Honour is called great strength because it stands firm everywhere. They won’t do it even for lasting fame.
en.4: Behold the men that desire to leave an honoured name behind them: they will not do that which is not right even for the sake of glory.
en.5:
Who seek with glory to combine honour’s untarnished fame,
Do no inglorious deeds, though men accord them glory’s name.
en.6: Those who desire (to maintain their) honour, will surely do nothing dishonourable, even for the sake of fame.

padaccheda.m: குடிப்பிறந்தார்க்கு நிறைந்த செல்வம் உளதாயவழி யாவர்மாட்டும் பணிவு வேண்டும்
குறைந்த நல்குரவு உளதாயவழிப் பணியாமை வேண்டும்

en.1: In plenty, bow low. When your means shrink, stand tall.
en.2: When the well-born have great wealth, they should be humble before everyone. When they fall into want, they should not bow, and should stay at their old height. Wealth raises you, so you must lower yourself. Hardship lowers you, so you must rise.
en.4: Cultivate modesty in the day of prosperity: but in the day of thy decline hold fast to thy dignity.
en.5:
Bow down thy soul, with increase blest, in happy hour;
Lift up thy heart, when stript of all by fortune’s power.
en.6: In great prosperity humility is becoming; dignity, in great adversity.

padaccheda.m: குடிப்பிறந்த மாந்தர்
தம் உயர்ந்த நிலையை விட்டு அதனினின்றும் தாழ்ந்தவழி
தலையைவிட்டு அதனினின்றும் வீழ்ந்த மயிரினை ஒப்பர்

en.1: People who fall from their standing are like hair fallen from the head.
en.2: When the well-born leave their high standing and sink from it, they are like hair dropped from the head. Hair is cared for while it stays on the head and despised once it falls, and so are they.
en.4: Behold the men that have soiled a name that was honourable: they are even as the locks of hair that have been shaven off the head and thrown away.
en.5:
Like hairs from off the head that fall to earth,
When fall’n from high estate are men of noble birth.
en.6: They who have fallen from their (high) position are like the hair which has fallen from the head.

en.1: People as high as a hill will still fall if they do something low, even a thing the size of a crab’s-eye seed.
en.2: Even those raised as high as a hill by their birth will sink if they do anything that lowers them, even an act the size of a crab’s-eye seed. The acts that lower you are the shameful ones.
en.4: Even men who are grand as a mountain will look small if they do an ignoble thing, though it should be only of the measure of a kunri seed.
en.5:
If meanness, slight as ‘abrus’ grain, by men be wrought,
Though like a hill their high estate, they sink to nought.
en.6: Even those who (are exalted) like a hill will be thought low, if they commit deeds that are debasing.

padaccheda.m: மானத்தைவிட்டுத் தன்னை அவமதிப்பார் பின்னே ஒருவன்சென்று நிற்கின்ற நிலை
இவ்வுலகத்துப் புகழ் பயவாது
ஏனைப் புத்தேள் உலகத்துச் செலுத்தாது
இனி, அவனுக்கு அது செய்வது யாது?

en.1: It brings no fame and it won’t take you to the land of the gods. So why follow behind those who despise you?
en.2: Giving up your honour and standing behind those who slight you brings no fame in this world and doesn’t lead to the world of the gods. What then does it do for you? It has neither reward and destroys your honour for nothing.
en.4: It bringeth not glory, neither doth it open the way unto heaven: why then doth a man try to live by fawning on men that despise him?
en.5:
It yields no praise, nor to the land of gods throws wide the gate:
Why follow men who scorn, and at their bidding wait?
en.6: Of what good is it (for the high-born) to go and stand in vain before those who revile him. It only brings him loss of honour and exclusion from heaven.

padaccheda.m: தன்னை இகழ்வார் பின்னே சென்று பொருள் பெற்று அதனால் ஒருவன் உயிர் வாழ்தலின்
அது செய்யாது இறந்தான் என்று சொல்லப்படுதல் அவனுக்கு நன்று

en.1: Better to be called ruined there and then than to live by trailing after those who spurn you.
en.2: It would be better for a man to be said to have died, not having done it, than to stay alive on what he gets by following those who slight him. This answers those who say that even without fame or heaven, you at least get wealth and stay alive.
en.4: It is better for a man to meet his doom at once without any ado than to maintain himself by hanging on to those that scorn him.
en.5:
Better ’twere said, ‘He’s perished!’ than to gain
The means to live, following in foeman’s train.
en.6: It is better for a man to be said of him that he died in his usual state than that he eked out his life by following those who disgraced him.

reading.note: கெட்டான் can mean ruined or dead. He takes it as dead.

padaccheda.m: உயர்குடிப் பிறப்புத் தன் வலியாகிய மானம் அழிய வந்துழி
இறத்தல் ஒழிந்து பயனில்லாத உடம்பினைக் காக்கும் வாழ்க்கை பின்னும் இறவாமைக்கு மருந்தாகுமோ?

en.1: When your great dignity is being destroyed, is a life of tending your flesh any medicine?
en.2: When honour, the strength of high birth, is being destroyed, will a life that guards a useless body instead of dying be a medicine against death? He says “flesh” because the bare body left without honour is despised, and “medicine?” because you will die anyway.
en.4: Is the skin immortal, that men desire to save it even at the cost of honour?
en.5:
When high estate has lost its pride of honour meet,
Is life, that nurses this poor flesh, as nectar sweet?
en.6: For the high born to keep their body in life when their honour is gone will certainly not prove a remedy against death.

padaccheda.m: தன் மயிர்த்திரளின் ஒருமயிர் நீங்கினும் உயிர் வாழாத கவரிமானை ஒப்பார்
உயிர் நீங்கத் தான் மானம் எய்தும் எல்லைவரின், அதனைத் தாங்காது இறப்பர்

en.1: Like the yak that won’t live if it loses its hair, there are those who give up their life when honour demands it.
en.2: They are like the yak that won’t stay alive if even one hair of its coat is lost. When it comes to the point where honour can only be had by losing life, they can’t bear it and die. Life and honour can’t both stay, so they give up life, which goes anyway, for honour, which lasts. The simile shows this is their nature.
en.4: The kavarima giveth up its life when it loseth its wool: there are men who are as sensitive and they put an end to their lives when they cannot save their honour.
en.5:
Like the wild ox that, of its tuft bereft, will pine away,
Are those who, of their honour shorn, will quit the light of day.
en.6: Those who give up (their) life when (their) honor is at stake are like the yak which kills itself at the loss of (even one of) its hairs.

padaccheda.m: தமக்கோர் இழிவு வந்துழிப் பொறுத்து உயிர் வாழாது அதனை நீத்த மானம் உடையாரது புகழ் வடிவினை
எஞ்ஞான்றும் தொழுது துதியாநிற்பர் உலகத்தார்

en.1: The world bows down and praises the radiance of those whose honour won’t let them live on in disgrace.
en.2: When disgrace came to those with honour, they did not bear it and live, but gave up life. The world bows down and praises their fame for ever. Heaven need not be mentioned, because those whose fame poets sing reach it anyway.
en.4: Behold the men of honour who refuse to outlive their good name: the world will join its hands and worship at the altar of their glory.
en.5:
Who, when dishonour comes, refuse to live, their honoured memory
Will live in worship and applause of all the world for aye!
en.6: The world will (always) praise and adore the fame of the honourable who would rather die than suffer indignity.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு ஒளியாவது, பிறரால் செயற்கு அரிய செய்வேம் என்று கருதும் ஊக்கமிகுதி

padaccheda.w: ஒருவற்கு இளி அஃது இறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்
padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு மாசாவது, அச்செயலை ஒழிந்து உயிர்வாழக் கடவேம் என்று கருதுதல்

en.1: A person’s light is a wealth of spirit. A person’s disgrace is to say, “I can live without that.”
en.2: A person’s light is the great drive that resolves to do what others can’t. A person’s stain is resolving to leave that undone and simply stay alive. The hard things here are boundless helpfulness and giving. Light means standing out while you live.
en.4: An aspiration for noble achievement, that is what is called greatness: and littleness is the thought that sayeth, I shall live without it.
en.5:
The light of life is mental energy; disgrace is his
Who says, ‘I’ll lead a happy life devoid of this.’
en.6: One’s light is the abundance of one’s courage; one’s darkness is the desire to live destitute of such (a state of mind.)

padaccheda.m: எல்லா மக்கள் உயிர்க்கும் பொதுவாகிய பிறப்பியல்பு ஒக்குமே எனினும்
பெருமை, சிறுமை எனப்பட்ட சிறப்பியல்கள் ஒவ்வா, அவை செய்யும் தொழில்களது வேறுபாட்டான்

en.1: Birth is the same for every living being. Distinction is not, because what they do is different.
en.2: All people share the same nature of birth, but the qualities of greatness and smallness are not equal, because their deeds differ. Every varna alike is joined by karma to a body of the five elements and lives out its fruits, so birth is the same. The deeds that test greatness differ with each varna and each body.
en.4: The manner of birth is the same for all men: but their reputations vary because they differ in the lives that they lead.
en.5:
All men that live are one in circumstance of birth;
Diversities of works give each his special worth.
en.6: All human beings agree as regards their birth but differ as regards their characteristics, because of the different qualities of their actions.

padaccheda.w: மேல் அல்லார் மேல் இருந்தும் மேல் அல்லர்
padaccheda.m: செயற்கு அரிய செய்கலாது சிறியராயினார், உயர்ந்து அமளி முதலியவற்றின் மிசையிருந்தவராயினும், பெரியராகார்

padaccheda.w: கீழ் அல்லவர் கீழ் இருந்தும் கீழ் அல்லார்
padaccheda.m: அவை செய்து பெரியராயினார், தாழ்ந்த வறுநிலத்து இருந்தாராயினும், சிறியர் ஆகார்

en.1: Those who aren’t high aren’t high, even sitting high. Those who aren’t low aren’t low, even sitting low.
en.2: Those who stay small because they can’t do what is hard are not great, even on a raised couch. Those made great by doing it are not small, even on bare low ground. Sitting high and low mean wealth and poverty. So greatness doesn’t come from wealth alone, as the last couplet showed it doesn’t come from birth alone.
en.4: Even if they are noble, those that are not noble are not noble; and even if they are lowborn, those that are not low are not low.
en.5:
The men of lofty line, whose souls are mean, are never great;
The men of lowly birth, when high of soul, are not of low estate.
en.6: Though (raised) above, the base cannot become great; though (brought) low, the great cannot become base.

padaccheda.m: கவராதமனத்தினை உடைய மகளிர் நிறையின் வழுவாமல் தம்மைத் தாம் காத்துக்கொண்டு ஒழுகுமாறுபோல
பெருமைக்குணனும், ஒருவன் நிறையின் வழுவாமல் தன்னைத்தான் காத்துக்கொண்டு ஒழுகுவானாயின் அவன்கண் உண்டாம்

en.1: As with women of undivided heart, greatness too comes only if you guard yourself.
en.2: Women of undivided heart guard themselves and don’t slip from their firmness, and so chastity arises. Greatness too arises in a man who guards himself and doesn’t slip from his firmness. To do this is to restrain mind, speech and body and go on doing helpful deeds.
en.4: Even as chastity in a woman, greatness can be maintained only by being true to one’s own self.
en.5:
Like single-hearted women, greatness too,
Exists while to itself itself is true.
en.6: Even greatness, like a woman’s chastity, belongs only to him who guards himself.

padaccheda.m: அவ்வாற்றான் பெருமையுடையர் ஆயினார்
தாம் வறியராயவழியும், பிறரான் செய்தற்கு அரியவாய தம் செயல்களை விடாது அவை செய்யும் நெறியான் கடைபோகச் செய்தலை வல்லராவர்

en.1: The great will carry out hard deeds, and by the right means.
en.2: Those who have become great in this way can, even when they have grown poor, keep to deeds that others find hard and see them through to the end by the right means. “The great” and “will carry out” show they have done such things before, which is how he gets “even when poor”.
en.4: Those that are great have the puissance to employ adequate means and achieve things that are impossible for others.
en.5:
The man endowed with greatness true,
Rare deeds in perfect wise will do.
en.6: (Though reduced,) the great will be able to perform, in the proper way, deeds difficult (for others to do.)

padaccheda.m: அப்பெற்றியராய பெரியாரை வழிபட்டு அவர் இயல்பினை யாம் கோடும் என்னும் கருத்து
மற்றைச் சிறியராயினார் மனத்தின்கண் உளதாகாது

en.1: It never enters the minds of the small to say, “We will honour the great and hold on to them.”
en.2: The thought of serving the great and taking on their nature doesn’t arise in the minds of the small. Those who admire themselves merely for having birth, wealth or learning can’t serve the ones who take these calmly as their nature, and so can’t gain that quality.
en.4: It is not in the grain of small men to revere the great and earn their good will and favour.
en.5:
‘As votaries of the truly great we will ourselves enroll,’
Is thought that enters not the mind of men of little soul.
en.6: It is never in the nature of the base to seek the society of the great and partake of their nature.

padaccheda.m: தனக்கு ஒக்கும் பெரியாரிடத்து அமைந்திருத்தலைச் செய்வதாய சிறப்புத்தானும்
தனக்கு ஒவ்வாத சிறியாரிடத்துப் படுமாயின்
அதனை ஒழித்துத் தருக்கின்கண்ணே மிக்கசெயலை உடைத்தாம்

en.1: Even distinction, when it falls to the unworthy, turns to nothing but excess.
en.2: Distinction means superiority in birth, wealth or learning. In the great who suit it, it brings calm. If it lands on the small who don’t suit it, it gives that up and produces only greater arrogance.
en.4: If fortune falleth to the lot of the little-minded their insolence will know no bounds.
en.5:
Whene’er distinction lights on some unworthy head,
Then deeds of haughty insolence are bred.
en.6: Even nobility of birth, wealth and learning, if in (the possession of) the base, will (only) produce everincreasing pride.

padaccheda.m: பெருமையுடையார், அச்சிறப்பு உண்டாய ஞான்றும் தருக்கின்றி அமைந்தொழுகுவர்
மற்றைச் சிறுமையுடையார் அஃது இல்லாத ஞான்றும் தம்மை வியந்து புனையாநிற்பர்

en.1: Greatness always bends low. Smallness admires itself and dresses itself up.
en.2: The great stay calm and free of arrogance even when they have distinction. The small, even without it, admire themselves and dress themselves up, claiming some superiority over others. Some read this as wonder at the way of the world, where the high stoop and the low climb.
en.4: Greatness is ever unpretending and modest: but littleness vaunteth its merits before all the world.
en.5:
Greatness humbly bends, but littleness always
Spreads out its plumes, and loads itself with praise.
en.6: The great will always humble himself; but the mean will exalt himself in self-admiration.

padaccheda.m: பெருமைக் குணமாவது, காரணம் உண்டாயவழியும் அஃது இயல்பாதல் நோக்கித் தருக்கின்றி இருத்தல்
சிறுமைக்குணமாவது, அஃது இல்வழியும் அதனை ஏற்றிக்கொண்டு தருக்கின் முடிவின்கண்ணே நின்றுவிடுதல்

en.1: Greatness is having no pride. Smallness is riding on pride, all the way to its limit.
en.2: The quality of greatness is to have no arrogance even when there is cause for it, seeing distinction as natural. The quality of smallness is to mount arrogance even without cause and stay at its furthest limit.
en.4: Greatness showeth condescension unto all: but littleness is the very acme of insolence.
en.5:
Greatness is absence of conceit; meanness, we deem,
Riding on car of vanity supreme.
en.6: Freedom from conceit is (the nature of true) greatness, (while) obstinacy therein is (that of) meanness.

padaccheda.m: பெருமையுடையார் பிறர் மானத்தையே கூறி அவமானத்தை மறையாநிற்பர்
மற்றைச் சிறுமையுடையார், பிறர் குணத்தை மறைத்துக் குற்றத்தையே கூறி விடுவர்

en.1: Greatness hides another’s shame. Smallness speaks of nothing but faults.
en.2: The great speak only of another’s honour and hide their dishonour. The small hide another’s good qualities and speak only of their faults.
en.4: Greatness is always for screening the infirmities of others: but littleness will talk nothing but scandal.
en.5:
Greatness will hide a neighbour’s shame;
Meanness his faults to all the world proclaim.
en.6: The great hide the faults of others; the base only divulge them.

padaccheda.m: நமக்குத் தகுவது இது என்று அறிந்து சான்றாண்மையை மேற்கொண்டு ஒழுகுவார்குக்
நல்லனவாய குணங்கள் எல்லாம் இயல்பாய் இருக்கும் என்று சொல்லுவர் நூலோர்

en.1: They say every good thing is a duty for those who know what is due and take up worth.
en.2: The books say that for those who know what befits them and live by worth, all good qualities are simply natural. If some were missing, or were put on by effort, the word for this quality wouldn’t apply.
en.4: Behold the men that know their duties and want to cultivate worth in themselves: everything that is good will be a duty in their eyes.
en.5:
All goodly things are duties to the men, they say,
Who set themselves to walk in virtue’s perfect way.
en.6: It is said that those who are conscious of their duty and behave with a perfect goodness will regard as natural all that is good.

reading.note: கடன் usually means duty, and the plain reading keeps that. He takes it here as what is natural: good qualities aren’t a duty for such people but their nature.

padaccheda.m: சான்றோர் நலமாவது குணங்களான் ஆய நலமே
அஃது ஒழிந்த உறுப்புக்களானாய நலம் ஒரு நலத்தினும் உள்ளதன்று

en.1: The goodness of the worthy is goodness of character. No other goodness counts as goodness at all.
en.2: The good of the worthy is the good that comes from their qualities. The other kind, the good of the body’s limbs, isn’t among good things at all, because it has no place in the list the books give, beginning with birth and learning.
en.4: The comeliness of the worthy is the comeliness of their character: the comeliness of the body addeth nothing to their comeliness.
en.5:
The good of inward excellence they claim,
The perfect men; all other good is only good in name.
en.6: The only delight of the perfect is that of their goodness; all other (sensual) delights are not to be included among any (true) delights.

padaccheda.m: சுற்றத்தார் மேலேயன்றிப் பிறர் மேலும் உளதாய அன்பும்
பழி, பாவங்களின் நாணலும்
யாவர்மாட்டும் ஒப்புரவு செய்தலும்
பழையார்மேல் கண்ணோடலும்
எவ்விடத்தும் மெய்ம்மை கூறலும் என
சால்பு என்னும் பாரத்தைத் தாங்கிய தூண்கள் ஐந்து

en.1: Loving-kindness, a sense of shame, helpfulness, considerateness and truthfulness are the five pillars that hold up worth.
en.2: Loving-kindness for others as well as your own people, shame at blame and sin, helpfulness to everyone, kind regard for old friends, and truth in every place: these five pillars bear the load of worth. They are called pillars because without them worth can’t stand.
en.4: Love to all, sensibility to shame, complaisance, indulgence to the faults of others, and truthfulness, these five are the pillars that support the edifice of a noble character.
en.5:
Love, modesty, beneficence, benignant grace,
With truth, are pillars five of perfect virtue’s resting-place.
en.6: Affection, fear (of sin), benevolence, favour and truthfulness: these are the five pillars on which perfect goodness rests.

padaccheda.m: பிற அறங்களும் வேண்டுமாயினும், தவம் ஓருயிரையும் கொல்லாத அறத்தின்கண்ணதாம்
அதுபோலப் பிற குணங்களும் வேண்டுமாயினும். சால்பு பிறர் குற்றத்தைச் சொல்லாத குணத்தின்கண்ணதாம்

en.1: The good of penance lies in not killing. The good of worth lies in not speaking of others’ wrongs.
en.2: Penance needs other virtues too, but it rests above all on the virtue of killing no living thing. In the same way worth needs other qualities too, but it rests above all on the quality of not speaking of others’ faults.
en.4: The virtue of the saint is non-killing: and the virtue of the worthy man is the abstaining from scandalous speech.
en.5:
The type of ‘penitence’ is virtuous good that nothing slays;
To speak no ill of other men is perfect virtue’s praise.
en.6: Penance consists in the goodness that kills not, and perfection in the goodness that tells not others’ faults.

padaccheda.m: ஒரு கருமத்தைச் செய்து முடிப்பாரது ஆற்றலாவது அதற்குத் துணையாவாரைத் தாழ்ந்து கூட்டிக்கொள்ளுதல்
இனிச் சால்புடையார் தம் பகைவரைப் பகைமை ஒழிக்கும் கருவியும் அது

en.1: The strength of the capable is bowing. That is the weapon the worthy use to turn enemies around.
en.2: The strength of those who finish a task is to humble themselves and win over the people who can help with it. That is also the tool by which the worthy end the enmity of their foes. He praises the humility that suits worth, and names the other use along with it.
en.4: It is humility that is the strength of the strong: and that is also the armour of the man of worth against his foes.
en.5:
Submission is the might of men of mighty acts; the sage
With that same weapon stills his foeman’s rage.
en.6: Stooping (to inferiors) is the strength of those who can accomplish (an undertaking); and that is the weapon with which the great avert their foes.

padaccheda.m: சால்பாகிய பொன்னின் அளவு அறிதற்கு உரைகல்லாகிய செயல் யாது எனின்
அது தம்மின் உயர்ந்தார்மாட்டுக் கொள்ளும் தோல்வியை இழிந்தார்மாட்டும் கோடல்

en.1: What is the touchstone of worth? Accepting defeat, even from those who are not your equals.
en.2: What is the touchstone that tests the gold of worth? Taking from your inferiors too the defeat you would take from your betters. You could win, but you accept it. Worth is measured when you don’t make yourself their equal by trying to beat them, and so stand above them through defeat.
en.4: What is the touchstone of worth? It is the acknowledgement of superiority when it is found even in men who are otherwise one’s inferiors.
en.5:
What is perfection’s test? The equal mind,
To bear repulse from even meaner men resigned.
en.6: The touch-stone of perfection is to receive a defeat even at the hands of one’s inferiors.

padaccheda.m: தமக்கு இன்னாதவற்றைச் செய்தார்க்கும் சால்புடையார் இனியவற்றைச் செய்யாராயின்
அச்சால்பு வேறு என்ன பயனை உடைத்து?

en.1: What use is worth, if you don’t do kindness even to those who have done you harm?
en.2: If the worthy don’t do pleasant things even for those who have done them unpleasant things, what other use does their worth have? If they also do harm in return, their worth is of no use at all.
en.4: Where is the superiority of the worthy man if he doth not do good even unto those that work him injury?
en.5:
What fruit doth your perfection yield you, say!
Unless to men who work you ill you good repay?
en.6: Of what avail is perfect goodness if it cannot do pleasing things even to those who have pained (it)?

padaccheda.m: சால்பு என்று சொல்லப்படும் வலி உண்டாகப்பெறின்
ஒருவனுக்கு நல்குரவு இளிவாகாது

en.1: Having nothing is no disgrace, if you have the strength called worth.
en.2: Poverty is no disgrace to someone who has the strength called worth. It is called strength because it keeps you from weakening. “Poverty” stands for what poverty brings. The worthy stand above others even when they are poor.
en.4: Poverty is no disgrace to a man if he possesseth the wealth that is called character.
en.5:
To soul with perfect virtue’s strength endued,
Brings no disgrace the lack of every earthly good.
en.6: Poverty is no disgrace to one who abounds in good qualities.

padaccheda.m: சால்புடைமையாகிய கடற்குக் கரை என்று சொல்லப்படுவார்
ஏனைக் கடலும் கரையுள் நில்லாமல் காலத்தான் திரிந்தாலும் தாம் திரியார்

en.1: Even if the age itself shifts, those called the ocean of worth will not shift.
en.2: They are called the shore of the sea of worth. Even if, as the age turns, the ordinary sea leaves its shore, they will not change. Worth is made a sea to show how great it is, and those who have it are its shore because they hold it in.
en.4: Behold the men that would not swerve from the path of rectitude even if all else should change in a general convulsion: they will be called the very palladium of worth.
en.5:
Call them of perfect virtue’s sea the shore,
Who, though the fates should fail, fail not for evermore.
en.6: Those who are said to be the shore of the sea of perfection will never change, though ages may change.

reading.note: ஆழி can mean the sea or its shore. The plain reading takes the sea. He takes the shore: worth is the sea, and these people are what holds it.

padaccheda.m: பல குணங்களானும் நிறைந்தவர் தம் தன்மை குன்றுவராயின்

padaccheda.w: இரு நிலம் தான் பொறை தாங்காது மன்னோ
padaccheda.m: மற்றை இருநிலந்தானும் தன் பொறையைத் தாங்காதாய் முடியும்

en.1: If the worthy fall from their worth, even the great earth can’t bear its load.
en.2: If those full of many qualities fall from their nature, the great earth too will fail to bear its load. But it is their nature not to fall and the earth’s to bear, so neither will ever happen. Some say the earth bears its load with the worthy as its helpers, so without them it couldn’t.
en.4: Verily even the earth itself will not be able to support the burden of human life if the worthy were to fall from their worth.
en.5:
The mighty earth its burthen to sustain must cease,
If perfect virtue of the perfect men decrease.
en.6: If there is a defect in the character of the perfect, (even) the great world cannot bear (its) burden.

padaccheda.m: யாவர்மாட்டும் எளிய செவ்வியர் ஆதலால்

padaccheda.w: பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு எய்தல் எளிது என்ப
padaccheda.m: அரிதாய பண்புடைமை என்னும் நன்னெறியினை எய்துதல் எளிது என்று சொல்லுவர் நூலோர்

en.1: They say that being easy to approach, for anyone at all, makes the way of courtesy easy to reach.
en.2: The books say that being easy for everyone to approach makes it easy to reach the rare good path called courtesy. For someone full of good qualities who is also approachable, courtesy comes of itself. It wins over the whole world, so the ancients made it a good path, and the books give this as the means.
en.4: Courteousness, they say, cometh easily to those who receive all men with open arms.
en.5:
Who easy access give to every man, they say,
Of kindly courtesy will learn with ease the way.
en.6: If one is easy of access to all, it will be easy for one to obtain the virtue called goodness.

padaccheda.m: பிறர்மேல் அன்புடையன் ஆதலும், உலகத்தோடு அமைந்த குடியின்கண் பிறத்தலும் ஆகிய இவ்விரண்டும்
ஒருவனுக்குப் பண்புடைமை என்று உலகத்தார் சொல்லும் நன்னெறி

en.1: Having loving-kindness and being born into a good family: these two are the way of courtesy.
en.2: Having loving-kindness for others and being born in a family at one with the world: these two are the good path people call courtesy. Being born here means the conduct of those so born. Neither is enough alone, only both together.
en.4: Courteousness cometh of the combination of the two virtues of kindness and good-breeding.
en.5:
Benevolence and high-born dignity,
These two are beaten paths of courtesy.
en.6: Affectionateness and birth in a good family, these two constitute what is called a proper behaviour to all.

padaccheda.m: செறியத்தகாத உடம்பால் ஒத்தல் ஒருவனுக்கு நன்மக்களோடு ஒப்பாகாமையின் அது பொருந்துவது அன்று
இனிப் பொருந்துவதாய ஒப்பாவது, செறியத்தக்க பண்பால் ஒத்தல்

en.1: Having the same limbs does not make people alike. True likeness is likeness in the courtesy that draws people close.
en.2: Matching good people in body, which isn’t fit to hold close, isn’t true likeness. The likeness that fits is matching them in courtesy, which is. The body is separate from the soul and doesn’t last. Courtesy isn’t separate and does last. So have the courtesy they have.
en.4: Men are likened to each other not by the cut of their personal appearance, but by the similarity of their manners.
en.5:
Men are not one because their members seem alike to outward view;
Similitude of kindred quality makes likeness true.
en.6: Resemblance of bodies is no resemblance of souls; true resemblance is the resemblance of qualities that attract.

padaccheda.w: நயனொடு நன்றி புரிந்த பயன் உடையார் பண்பு
padaccheda.m: நீதியையும் அறத்தையும் விரும்புதலான், பிறர்க்கும் தமக்கும் பயன்படுதல் உடையாரது பண்பினை
உலகத்தார் கொண்டாடாநிற்பர்

en.1: The world praises the courtesy of those who are useful because they care for justice and for doing good.
en.2: The world celebrates the courtesy of those who, loving justice and righteousness, are of use to others and themselves. Their justice, their goodness and their usefulness all come from courtesy, so that is what the world praises.
en.4: Behold the men who love justice and righteousness, and who are of a helpful disposition: the world setteth a high value on their manners.
en.5:
Of men of fruitful life, who kindly benefits dispense,
The world unites to praise the ‘noble excellence..’
en.6: The world applauds the character of those whose usefulness results from their equity and charity.

padaccheda.m: தன்னை இகழ்தல் ஒருவற்கு விளையாட்டின்கண்ணும் இன்னாது

padaccheda.w: பாடு அறிவார் மாட்டுப் பகையுள்ளும் பண்பு உள
padaccheda.m: ஆகலான், பிறர் பாடு அறிந்து ஒழுகுவார்மாட்டுப் பகைமை உள்வழியும், அஃது உளதாகாது இனியவாய பண்புகளே உளவாவன

en.1: Scorn hurts, even in fun. Those who know what others feel stay courteous, even in enmity.
en.2: Being scorned hurts a person even in play. So those who live knowing others’ natures keep only pleasant ways, even where there is enmity. Knowing that hurt, they won’t cause it. He rejects readings that leave the two halves unconnected, or that take “hurts” to mean “doesn’t arise”.
en.4: Disparaging words pain a man even when uttered only in jest: the well-bred therefore are never discourteous even to their foes.
en.5:
Contempt is evil though in sport. They who man’s nature know,
E’en in their wrath, a courteous mind will show.
en.6: Reproach is painful to one even in sport; those (therefore) who know the nature of others exhibit (pleasing) qualities even when they are hated.

padaccheda.m: பண்பு உடையார்கண்ணே படுதலால், உலகியல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் உண்டாய் வாராநின்றது
ஆண்டுப் படுதல் இல்லையாயின், அது மண்ணின்கண் புக்கு மாய்ந்து போவதாம்

en.1: The world goes on because of the courteous. Without them it would sink into the earth and die.
en.2: The ways of the world go on for ever because they rest on the courteous. If they didn’t rest there, they would sink into the earth and perish. The discourteous give them no support, so only this has spared them from that end.
en.4: The world goeth on smoothly because of the men of good-breeding: verily, but for them all this harmony would be dead and buried in the dust.
en.5:
The world abides; for ‘worthy’ men its weight sustain.
Were it not so, ’twould fall to dust again.
en.6: The (way of the) world subsists by contact with the good; if not, it would bury itself in the earth and perish.

padaccheda.m: நன்மக்கட்கே உரிய பண்பு இல்லாதவர்
அரத்தின் கூர்மை போலும் கூர்மையை உடையரே ஆயினும்
ஓரறிவிற்றாய மரத்தினை ஒப்பர்

en.1: Those without human courtesy are like trees, even if they are as sharp as a file.
en.2: Those without the courtesy proper to good people are like a tree, which has only one sense, even if they are as sharp as a file. A file wears down what it touches and isn’t worn itself. A tree lacks higher knowledge, and since they lack the courtesy that knowledge should yield, they lack it too.
en.4: Though they are sharp as files, the men that are lacking in good manners are no better than mere wooden stocks.
en.5:
Though sharp their wit as file, as blocks they must remain,
Whose souls are void of ‘courtesy humane.’
en.6: He who is destitute of (true) human qualities (only) resembles a tree, though he may possess the sharpness of a file.

padaccheda.m: தம்மொடு நட்பினைச் செய்யாது பகைமையைச் செய்து ஒழுகுவார் மாட்டும்
தாம் பண்புடையராய் ஒழுகாமை அறிவுடையார்க்கு இழுக்காம்

en.1: Even towards those who won’t be friends and treat you unkindly, it is low to fail in courtesy.
en.2: Even towards those who refuse friendship and act as enemies, it is a blot on the wise not to keep to courtesy. Do that and you become like them, which is why he says “low”.
en.4: Discourtesy is unbecoming in a man, even were it only against men who are unfriendly and unjust.
en.5:
Though men with all unfriendly acts and wrongs assail,
’Tis uttermost disgrace in ‘courtesy’ to fail.
en.6: it is wrong (for the wise) not to exhibit (good) qualities even towards those who bearing no friendship (for them) do only what is hateful.

padaccheda.m: பண்பின்மையான் ஒருவரோடும் கலந்து உள் மகிழ்தல் மாட்டாதார்க்கு
மிகவும் பெரிய ஞாலம், இருளில்லாத பகற்பொழுதினும் இருளின்கண் கிடந்தாம்

en.1: To those who can’t laugh, the vast wide world lies in darkness, even by day.
en.2: For those who, lacking courtesy, can’t mix with anyone and feel glad inside, the whole great world lies in darkness even in daytime. Because they never mix with people, they can’t know the ways of the world. Some read the ending differently, as “the darkness hasn’t left”.
en.4: Behold the men who cannot smile: in all the wide, wide world they will see nothing but darkness even during the day.
en.5:
To him who knows not how to smile in kindly mirth,
Darkness in daytime broods o’er all the vast and mighty earth.
en.6: To those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried in darkness even in (broad) daylight.

padaccheda.m: பண்புஇல்லாதவன் முன்னை நல்வினையான் எய்திய பெருஞ்செல்வம், அக்குற்றத்தால் ஒருவற்கும் பயன்படாது கெடுதல்
நல்ல ஆன் பால், ஏற்ற கலத்தின் குற்றத்தால் இன் சுவைத்தது ஆகாது கெட்டாற்போலும்

en.1: The great wealth gained by someone without courtesy is like good milk gone sour from a bad pot.
en.2: Great wealth that someone without courtesy has gained through past good deeds goes to waste, of no use to anyone because of that fault, as good cow’s milk spoils through a fault in its vessel. “Gained” shows he can’t create wealth himself. This points ahead to the next chapter.
en.4: Behold the wealth in the hands of the churlish man: it is even as the milk that is spoiled for being kept in an unclean vessel.
en.5:
Like sweet milk soured because in filthy vessel poured,
Is ample wealth in churlish man’s unopened coffers stored.
en.6: The great wealth obtained by one who has no goodness will perish like pure milk spoilt by the impurity of the vessel.

padaccheda.w: வாய் சான்ற பெரும்பொருள் வைத்தான் அஃது உண்ணான்
padaccheda.m: தன் மனை அகலம் எல்லாம் நிறைதற்கு ஏதுவாய பெரும்பொருளை ஈட்டிவைத்து உலோபத்தால் அதனை உண்ணாதவன்
உளனாயினும் செத்தானாம், அதன்கண் அவனால் செயக் கிடந்ததோர் உரிமை இன்மையான்

en.1: He stores up great heaps of wealth and doesn’t eat from it. He is a dead man, and there is nothing he can do with it.
en.2: A man who piles up wealth enough to fill his house and, from greed, doesn’t enjoy it is dead though he lives, because he has no claim on it. “Eating” means enjoying it with all five senses. It can also mean that if he dies without enjoying it he has no claim, so enjoy wealth when you get it.
en.4: Behold the man who hath laid by in his home treasures in abundance but enjoyeth them not: he is as good as dead, for he maketh no use of them.
en.5:
Who fills his house with ample store, enjoying none,
Is dead. Nought with the useless heap is done.
en.6: He who does not enjoy the immense riches he has heaped up in his house, is (to be reckoned as) dead, (for) there is nothing achieved (by him.)

padaccheda.m: பொருள் ஒன்றும் உண்டாக அதனால் எல்லாம் உண்டாம் என்று அறிந்து அதனை ஈட்டி
பின் பிறர்க்கு ஈயாது பற்றுள்ளம் செய்யும் மயக்கத்தாலே
ஒருவனுக்கு நிறைதல் இல்லாத பேய்ப்பிறப்பு உண்டாம்

en.1: “Wealth brings everything,” you think, and you clutch it and give nothing. That delusion brings a wretched birth.
en.2: You know that wealth alone brings everything, and you earn it. Then you grip it and give nothing, and from that confusion comes a ghost’s birth that is never filled. You watched others go hungry with wealth to hand, so you will be born to suffer hunger with food all around you.
en.4: Behold the miser that thinketh that wealth is all in all and hoardeth it without giving to any: he will be a demon in his next birth.
en.5:
Who giving nought, opines from wealth all blessing springs,
Degraded birth that doting miser’s folly brings.
en.6: He who knows that wealth yields every pleasure and yet is so blind as to lead a miserly life will be born a demon.

padaccheda.w: ஈட்டம் இவறி இசை வேண்டா ஆடவர் தோற்றம்
padaccheda.m: யாம் பிறரின் மிக ஈட்டுதும் என்று, பொருளினது ஈட்டல் மாத்திரத்தையே விரும்பி, அதன் பயனாய புகழை விரும்பாத மக்களது பிறப்பு
நிலத்திற்குப் பாரமாம் அத்துணையே

en.1: Men who crave piling up wealth and don’t want fame are only a load on the earth.
en.2: People who want only to earn more than others, and don’t want the fame that is its fruit, are born to be a burden on the land. Fame is righteousness that serves in both worlds. They don’t seek it by giving, and in their ignorance choose the pain of earning and guarding.
en.4: Behold the men that are always after hoarding but care not for fame: their existence is a burden unto the earth.
en.5:
Who lust to heap up wealth, but glory hold not dear,
It burthens earth when on the stage of being they appear.
en.6: A burden to the earth are men bent on the acquisition of riches and not (true) fame.

padaccheda.m: ஒரு பொருளும் ஈந்தறியாமையின் ஒருவராலும் நச்சப்படுதல் இல்லாதவன்
தான் இறந்தவழி ஈண்டு ஒழிந்து நிற்பதாக யாதனைக் கருதுமோ?

en.1: What does he think he will leave behind, this man whom no one wants?
en.2: A man no one wants, because he has never given anything: what does he imagine will remain here after he dies? The fame that remains stays only with those who give, so he has nothing to do with it.
en.4: The man who careth not to earn the attachment of his neighbours, what doth he hope to leave behind him when he is dead?
en.5:
Whom no one loves, when he shall pass away,
What doth he look to leave behind, I pray?
en.6: What will the miser who is not liked (by any one), regard as his own (in the world to come).

padaccheda.m: பிறர்க்கு ஈவதும் தாம் நுகர்வதுமாய இரண்டு செய்கையும் உடையர் அல்லாதார்க்கு
பலவாகிய அடுக்கிய கோடி பொருள் உண்டாயினும் ஒன்றுமில்லை

en.1: People who neither give nor enjoy have nothing, even with ten million heaped on ten million.
en.2: Those who neither give to others nor enjoy it themselves have nothing, even with many millions stacked up. Giving is named first because righteousness stands above pleasure. They lose both fruits, so they are like people who have nothing.
en.4: Behold the men that neither give unto others nor enjoy their wealth themselves: even if they possess tens of millions they really possess nothing.
en.5:
Amid accumulated millions they are poor,
Who nothing give and nought enjoy of all they store.
en.6: Those who neither give (to others) nor enjoy (their property) are (truly) destitute, though possessing immense riches.

padaccheda.w: தான் துவ்வான் தக்கார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்
padaccheda.m: தான் நுகரானாய் அதன்மேலும் தகுதியுடையார்க்கு அவர் வேண்டியது ஒன்றனை ஈதல் இயற்கை இலன் ஆயினான்
இண்டும் செய்தற்கு இடனுடைத்தாய செல்வத்திற்கு ஒரு நோய்

en.1: A man who won’t enjoy it himself and has no habit of giving to the deserving is a sickness to great wealth.
en.2: A man who doesn’t enjoy his wealth, and by nature gives the worthy nothing they ask for, is a sickness to great wealth, which could have done both. The worthy are those fit to receive gifts. Some say instead that his great wealth brings him only the pain of earning and guarding it.
en.4: There is a man that enjoyeth not his wealth nor giveth freely to men of worth: he is a disease unto a great fortune.
en.5:
Their ample wealth is misery to men of churlish heart,
Who nought themselves enjoy, and nought to worthy men impart.
en.6: He who enjoys not (his riches) nor relieves the wants of the worthy is a disease to his wealth.

padaccheda.m: ஒருபொருளும் இலர் ஆயினார்க்கு அவர் வேண்டியது ஒன்றனைக் கொடாதானது செல்வம் கொன்னே கழிதல்
பெண்டிரின் மிக்க நலத்தினைப் பெற்றாள் ஒருத்தி, கொடுப்பார் இன்மையின் கொழுநன் இன்றித் தமியளாய் மூத்த தன்மைத்து

en.1: The wealth of a man who gives nothing to those who have nothing is like a woman of great beauty growing old alone.
en.2: The wealth of a man who gives the destitute nothing they need passes away for nothing. A woman of rare beauty and goodness, whom no one gave in marriage, grows old alone without a husband. As her own life is wasted, and not only her family’s hopes and a husband’s, so the wealth’s use is lost as well as the owner’s and the receiver’s.
en.4: Behold the man that giveth not anything to the needy: the wealth in his hands is like a fair damsel that wasteth away her youth in loneliness.
en.5:
Like woman fair in lonelihood who aged grows,
Is wealth of him on needy men who nought bestows.
en.6: The wealth of him who never bestows anything on the destitute is like a woman of beauty growing old without a husband.

padaccheda.m: வறியார்க்கு அணியனாய் இருந்தும் ஒன்றும் கொடாமையின் அவரான் நச்சப்படாதவன் செல்வம் எய்துதல்
ஊரிடை நிற்பதோர் நச்சுமரம் பழுத்தாற்போலும்

en.1: The wealth of a man no one wants is like a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of the village.
en.2: A man lives close to the poor but gives them nothing, so they want nothing from him. His gaining wealth is like a poison tree ripening in the middle of the village. Being near and having plenty are no use.
en.4: The fortune of the man that is not loved of men is like the fruiting of the poison tree in the midst of the village.
en.5:
When he whom no man loves exults in great prosperity,
Tis as when fruits in midmost of the town some poisonous tree.
en.6: The wealth of him who is disliked (by all) is like the fruit-bearing of the etty tree in the midst of a town.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் கொடாமைப்பொருட்டுச் சுற்றத்தார் நட்டார்கண் அன்பு செய்தலை ஒழித்து
வேண்டுவன நுகராது தன்னைச் செறுத்து
வறியார்க்கு ஈதல் முதலிய அறத்தை நினைப்பதும் செய்யாது
ஈட்டிய ஒள்ளிய பொருளைக் கொண்டுபோய்ப் பயன்பெறுவார் பிறர்

en.1: You give up loving-kindness, punish yourself and ignore righteousness to gather bright wealth, and others take it.
en.2: To avoid giving, he drops loving-kindness for kin and friends, denies himself what he needs, and gives no thought to righteousness such as giving to the poor. Others carry off the bright wealth he gathered and get the use of it. Without righteousness or pleasure, gathering is only pain, and it doesn’t even serve his own line.
en.4: The wealth that is made without any regard to love or righteousness, and by starving oneself, is hoarded only for the behoof of strangers.
en.5:
Who love abandon, self afflict, and virtue’s way forsake
To heap up glittering wealth, their hoards shall others take.
en.6: Strangers will inherit the riches that have been acquired without regard for friendship, comfort and charity.

padaccheda.m: புகழுடைத்தாய செல்வத்தினை உடையவரது, நிற்கும் காலம் சிறிதாய வறுமை
உலகத்தை எல்லாம் நிலைநிறுத்தும் மேகம் வறுமை மிக்காற்போல்வதோர் இயல்பினை உடைத்து

en.1: A short spell of hardship for the wealthy of good name is like a rain cloud running dry.
en.2: The poverty of those with wealth and fame lasts only a little while, like the cloud that sustains the world growing poor. Those who helped everyone soon recover and help again, so wealth that does no good never helps at all. He rejects the reading that this is about the rich tiring of beggars, which doesn’t fit the chapter.
en.4: The distress of the man of wealth who hath emptied his resources by benefactions is only like the exhaustion of the rain-cloud: it will not continue for long.
en.5:
’Tis as when rain-cloud in the heaven grows dry,
When generous wealthy man endures brief poverty.
en.6: The short-lived poverty of those who are noble and rich is like the clouds becoming poor (for a while.)

padaccheda.m: நன்மக்கள் நாணாவது இழிந்த கருமம் காரணமாக நாணுதல்
அஃதன்றி மன மொழி மெய்கள் தொடுக்கத்தான் வருவனவோ எனின், அவை அவரளவல்ல, அழகிய நுதலினை உடைய குலமகளிர் நாண்கள்

en.1: Real shame is shrinking from an act. The rest is the shyness of good women with lovely foreheads.
en.2: The shame of good people is shame at a low deed. The kinds that come from holding in mind, speech and body are beyond them, and belong to women of good family with lovely foreheads. He rejects the reading that covering the body is like the shame of common women, since shame is held to ruin them and they aren’t named here.
en.4: The blush of the worthy is for action that become them not: it is therefore quite different to the blush of the fair.
en.5:
To shrink abashed from evil deed is ‘generous shame;’
Other is that of bright-browed ones of virtuous fame.
en.6: True modesty is the fear of (evil) deeds; all other modesty is (simply) the bashfulness of virtuous maids.

padaccheda.w: ஊண் உடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கு எல்லாம் வேறு அல்ல
padaccheda.m: ஊணும் உடையும் அவை ஒழிந்தனவும் மக்கள் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் பொது
நன்மக்கட்குச் சிறப்பாவது நாணுடைமையே, அவையல்ல

en.1: Food, clothing and the rest are no different for anyone alive. What marks out a person is a sense of shame.
en.2: Food, clothing and the rest are common to all human lives. The rest means sleep, fear and desire. What sets good people apart is a sense of shame, not these. Some read “fear” in place of “the rest”.
en.4: Food, clothing, and progeny are common unto all men: it is in the sensibility to shame that they differ from one another.
en.5:
Food, clothes, and other things alike all beings own;
By sense of shame the excellence of men is known.
en.6: Food, clothing and the like are common to all men; but modesty is peculiar to the good.

padaccheda.m: எல்லா உயிர்களும், உடம்பினைத் தமக்கு நிலைக்களனாகக் கொண்டு அதனை விடா
அதுபோலச் சால்பு, நாண் என்னும் நன்மைக்குணத்தைத் தனக்கு நிலைக்களனாகக் கொண்டு அதனை விடாது

en.1: All life is bound to flesh. Worth is bound to the good called shame.
en.2: Every living thing takes the body as its base and doesn’t leave it. In the same way worth takes the good quality called shame as its base and doesn’t leave it. As life gets no fruit except with a body, worth gets none except with shame.
en.4: The body is the seat of all life: but a virtuous blush is the dwelling place of worth.
en.5:
All spirits homes of flesh as habitation claim,
And perfect virtue ever dwells with shame.
en.6: As the body is the abode of the spirit, so the excellence of modesty is the abode of perfection.

padaccheda.m: சான்றோர்க்கு நாணுடைமை ஆபரணமாம்
அவ் ஆபரணம் இல்லையாயின் அவர் பெருமிதத்தையுடைய நடை, கண்டார்க்குப் பிணியாம்

en.1: Isn’t shame the ornament of the worthy? Without it, isn’t a proud walk a disease?
en.2: A sense of shame is the ornament of the worthy. Without that ornament, their proud walk is a disease to those who see it. Shame is an ornament because it beautifies, and the walk is a disease because it is hard to bear.
en.4: Is not the jewel of the worthy their sense of shame? And when a man hath it not, is not his swagger an affliction unto the eye to behold?
en.5:
And is not shame an ornament to men of dignity?
Without it step of stately pride is piteous thing to see.
en.6: Is not modesty the ornament of the noble? Without it, their haughtiness would be a pain (to others).

padaccheda.m: பிறர்க்கு வரும் பழியையும் தமக்கு வரும் பழியையும் ஒப்பமதித்து நாணுவாரை
உலகத்தார் நாணுக்கு உறைவிடம் என்று சொல்லுவார்

en.1: The world calls those who are ashamed of others’ blame as well as their own the home of shame.
en.2: Those who feel shame at blame falling on others just as at blame falling on themselves, treating it as their own, are called by the world the dwelling place of shame. Such people are great, so all those of high standing praise them.
en.4: Behold the men that blush as much for others’ disgrace as for their own: they will be called the very dwelling place of delicacy.
en.5:
As home of virtuous shame by all the world the men are known,
Who feel ashamed for others’ guilt as for their own.
en.6: The world regards as the abode of modesty him who fears his own and others’ guilt.

padaccheda.m: தமக்கு ஏமமாக நாணினைக் கொள்வதன்றி
அகன்ற ஞாலத்தைக் கொள்ள விரும்பார்

en.1: The best of people won’t want the wide world unless they have shame as their fence.
en.2: The best people take shame as their protection and don’t want the wide world instead. It is a fence because it keeps out blame and sin. If shame and the world conflict, they take shame and not the world, the road by which those enter. Some say they want the world only with that fence.
en.4: The worthy refuse to acquire even kingdoms save by means for which they shall not have to blush.
en.5:
Unless the hedge of shame inviolate remain,
For men of lofty soul the earth’s vast realms no charms retain.
en.6: The great make modesty their barrier (of defence) and not the wide world.

padaccheda.m: நாணினது சிறப்பறிந்து அதனை விடாது ஒழுகுவார்
அந்நாணும் உயிரும் தம்முள் மாறாயவழி, நாண் சிதையாமற்பொருட்டு உயிரை நீப்பர்
உயிர் சிதையாமற் பொருட்டு நாணினை நீக்கார்

en.1: Those who live by shame will give up life for shame. They won’t give up shame for life.
en.2: Those who know the worth of shame and keep to it, when shame and life conflict, will give up life so that shame isn’t harmed. They won’t give up shame so that life isn’t harmed. Shame stands above life.
en.4: Behold the men that have a delicate sense of shame: they will renounce their lives to save themselves from a disgrace, but will not swallow their shame even in order to save their lives.
en.5:
The men of modest soul for shame would life an offering make,
But ne’er abandon virtuous shame for life’s dear sake.
en.6: The modest would rather lose their life for the sake of modesty than lose modesty for the sake of life.

padaccheda.m: கேட்டாரும் கண்டாரும் நாணத்தக்க பழியை, ஒருவ்ன் தான் நாணாது செய்யுமாயின்
அந்நாணாமை, அவனை அறம் விட்டு நீங்கத்தக்க குற்றத்தினை உடைத்து

en.1: If a man feels no shame at what would shame others, righteousness has reason to feel shame.
en.2: If a man shamelessly does a blameworthy thing that would shame those who hear or see it, that shamelessness is a fault for which righteousness leaves him. Righteousness doesn’t stay near someone with no tie to shame.
en.4: If a man blush not for those things that call forth a blush in others, Righteousness will have cause to blush for him.
en.5:
Thou know’st no shame, while all around ashamed must be:
Virtue will shrink away ashamed of thee!
en.6: Virtue is likely to forsake him who shamelessly does what others are ashamed of.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு ஒழுக்கம் பிழைக்குமாயின் அப்பிழைப்பு, அவன் குடிப்பிறப்பு ஒன்றனையும் கெடுக்கும்
ஒருவன்மாட்டு நாணின்மை நின்றவழி, அந்நிலை அவன் நலம் யாவற்றையும் கெடுக்கும்

en.1: Failing in your principles burns your family’s name. Shamelessness, once it stays, burns all your good.
en.2: If a man’s conduct fails, that failure ruins one thing only, the standing of his birth. If shamelessness stays in him and never leaves, it ruins all his good, whatever comes from birth, learning, character, deeds and company. Losing shame is far worse than losing conduct.
en.4: By neglecting ceremonial observances a man loseth only his family: but every good is lost when he is lost to shame.
en.5:
’Twill race consume if right observance fail;
’Twill every good consume if shamelessness prevail.
en.6: Want of manners injures one’s family; but want of modesty injures one’s character.

padaccheda.m: தம் மனத்தின்கண் நாண் இல்லாத மக்கள் உயிருடையார் போன்று இயங்குகின்ற இயக்கம்
மரத்தாற் செய்யப்பட்ட பாவை இயந்திரக் கயிற்றினான் ஆய தன்னியக்கத்தால் உயிருடைத்தாக மயக்கினாற் போலும்

en.1: Those with no shame inside them move like a wooden puppet, whose string fools you into thinking it is alive.
en.2: People with no shame in their hearts move about as if alive, as a wooden puppet, moved by the strings of its frame, deceives you into thinking it has life. Their movement is a puppet’s and not the movement of life.
en.4: The men that are dead to shame live not: they merely feign life even as wooden marionettes that are moved by strings.
en.5:
’Tis as with strings a wooden puppet apes life’s functions, when
Those void of shame within hold intercourse with men.
en.6: The actions of those who are without modesty at heart are like those of a puppet moved by a string.

padaccheda.m: தன் குடிசெய்தற்பொருட்டுத் தொடங்கிய கருமம் முடியாமையின் எண்ணிய கருமம் செய்தற்கு யான் கையொழியேன் என்னும் ஆள்வினைப் பெருமைபோல
ஒருவனுக்கு மேம்பாடுடைய பெருமை பிறிதில்லை

en.1: Nothing is more dignified than the greatness that says, “I won’t rest my hands from the work.”
en.2: No greatness stands higher than the greatness of effort that says, “I won’t stop the work I began for my family until it is done.” Through many kinds of work the family gains wealth and fame and rises. He rejects “my own work” and “others’ work”: your own work is this work, and doing others’ bidding is no leadership.
en.4: Nothing advanceth a man’s family so much as his determination never to weary in labouring with his hands.
en.5:
Who says ‘I’ll do my work, nor slack my hand,’
His greatness, clothed with dignity supreme, shall stand.
en.6: There is no higher greatness than that of one saying, I will not cease in my effort (to raise my family).

padaccheda.m: முயற்சியும், நிறைந்த அறிவும் என்ற சொல்லப்பட்ட இரண்டினையும் உடைய இடையறாத கருமச்செயலால்
ஒருவன் குடி உயரும்

en.1: A family grows through long work that has two things in it: effort and full understanding.
en.2: A man’s family rises through unbroken work that has two things: effort and full knowledge. Knowledge is full when natural sense joins what is learned. Effort keeps laziness out. Full knowledge judges without error which acts will raise you and how to complete them.
en.4: Manly exertion and a sound understanding: it is the fullness of these two that exalteth the family.
en.5:
The manly act and knowledge full, when these combine
In deed prolonged, then lengthens out the race’s line,
en.6: One’s family is raised by untiring perseverance in both effort and wise contrivances.

padaccheda.m: என் குடியினை உயரச்செய்யக் கடவேன் என்றுகொண்டு அதற்கு ஏற்ற கருமங்களின் முயலும் ஒருவனுக்கு
தெய்வம் ஆடையைத் தற்றுக்கொண்டு தான் முந்துற்று நிற்கும்

en.1: For anyone who says, “I will raise my family,” god tucks up its cloth and goes on ahead.
en.2: For someone who resolves to raise his family and works at what that takes, god ties its garment tight and goes on ahead. Effort is named here by what it brings about. What a person walking in front would do is laid on fate.
en.4: When a man setteth out saying, I shall advance my house, the very Gods gird up their loins and march before him.
en.5:
‘I’ll make my race renowned,’ if man shall say,
With vest succinct the goddess leads the way.
en.6: The Deity will clothe itself and appear before him who resolves on raising his family.

padaccheda.m: தம் குடிக்கு ஆம் வினையை விரைந்து முயல்வார்க்கு
அவ்வினை முடிக்குந்திறம் அவர் சூழவேண்டாமல் தானே முடிவு எய்தும்

en.1: For those who strive without delay for their family, success comes of itself, without planning.
en.2: For those who hurry to the work that serves their family, the way to finish it comes of itself, and they don’t need to plan it. This is the fruit of god going on ahead of them.
en.4: Behold the men that remit not in their exertions to raise high their family: the work of their hands will prosper of itself even if they make no elaborate plans therefor.
en.5:
Who labours for his race with unremitting pain,
Without a thought, spontaneously, his end will gain.
en.6: Those who are prompt in their efforts (to better their family) need no deliberation, such efforts will of themselves succeed.

padaccheda.m: குற்றமாயின செய்யாது தன் குடியை உயரச்செய்து ஒழுகுவானை
அவனுக்குச் சுற்றமாக வேண்டித் தாமே சென்று சூழ்வர் உலகத்தார்

en.1: The world gathers round a man who raises his family and does no wrong, as if it were his kin.
en.2: The world goes to a man who does no wrong and lives raising his family, and surrounds him, wanting to be his kin. Wrong means acts against righteousness and justice. People draw near him for their own gain too.
en.4: Behold the man that setteth his family on high without doing iniquity: the whole world will be as a kindred unto him.
en.5:
With blameless life who seeks to build his race’s fame,
The world shall circle him, and kindred claim.
en.6: People will eagerly seek the friendship of the prosperous soul who has raised his family without foul means.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு நல்ல ஆண்மை என்று உயர்த்துச் சொல்லப்படுவது
தான் பிறந்த குடியினை ஆளும் தன்மையைத் தனக்கு உளதாக்கிக் கோடல்

en.1: The good kind of manliness is to make yourself master of the family you were born into.
en.2: What is praised as good manliness in a man is making himself able to rule the family he was born into. “Good” sets this apart from manliness in war. To rule a family is to raise those in it and bring them under your lead.
en.4: That is the supreme manhood which bringeth to a high estate the family wherein one is born.
en.5:
Of virtuous manliness the world accords the praise
To him who gives his powers, the house from which he sprang to raise.
en.6: A man’s true manliness consists in making himself the head and benefactor of his family.

padaccheda.m: களத்தின்கண் சென்றார் பலராயினும் போர்தாங்குதல் வன்கண்ணர்மேலது ஆனாற்போல
குடியின்கண் பிறந்தார் பலராயினும், அதன் பாரம்பொறுத்தல் அது வல்லார் மேலதாம்

en.1: As the battlefield rests on the fearless, among your own people too the load falls on those who can carry it.
en.2: Many go to the field, but bearing the battle falls to the fearless. Many are born into a family, but bearing its load falls to those able to do it. They are the ones held in high regard.
en.4: Even as the brunt of an action falleth on the courageous on the battlefield, even so the burden of keeping up the family lieth only on the shoulders of those that can bear the burden.
en.5:
The fearless hero bears the brunt amid the warrior throng;
Amid his kindred so the burthen rests upon the strong.
en.6: Like heroes in the battle-field, the burden (of protection &c.) is borne by those who are the most efficient in a family.

padaccheda.m: தம் குடியினை உயரச்செய்வார், அச்செயலையே நோக்காது காலத்தை நோக்கி மடியினைச் செய்துகொண்டு, மானத்தையும் கருதுவாராயின் குடி கெடும்
ஆகலான், அவர்க்குக் காலநியதி இல்லை

en.1: Those raising a family have no season. Be idle and think of your pride, and it is ruined.
en.2: If those raising a family watch the weather, not the work, and also think of their honour, the family falls. So they have no set season. Idleness is saying, “Sun, rain, mist: I’ll do it later.” Honour is saying, “Must I alone suffer while all here are happy?” Rulers at war need the right time. This work doesn’t.
en.4: There is no season for them that desire the advancement of their family: if they take things easy or stand upon their dignity, their house will be brought low.
en.5:
Wait for no season, when you would your house uprear;
’Twill perish, if you wait supine, or hold your honour dear.
en.6: As a family suffers by (one’s) indolence and false dignity, there is to be no season (good or bad) to those who strive to raise their family.

padaccheda.m: மூவகைத் துன்பமும் உறற்பாலதாய தன் குடியை அவை உறாமல் காக்க முயல்வானது உடம்பு
அம்முயற்சித் துன்பத்திற்கே கொள்கலமாம் அத்துணையோ, அஃது ஒழிந்து இன்பத்திற்காதல் இல்லையோ?

en.1: Is the body of the man who shields his family from harm only a vessel for suffering?
en.2: He works to keep his family from the three kinds of suffering it is open to. Is his body only a vessel for the pain of that effort, and not for joy? The wise man thinks, “If my whole family rises in joy, I gain both worlds, so this bodily pain is good for me,” and never says this, so it is said for him.
en.4: Verily, is the body of the man that would protect his family against every ill a receptacle for toils and hardships alone?
en.5:
Is not his body vase that various sorrows fill,
Who would his household screen from every ill?
en.6: Is it only to suffering that his body is exposed who undertakes to preserve his family from evil?

padaccheda.m: துன்பமாகிய நவியம் புகுந்து தன் முதலை வெட்டிச் சாய்க்க ஒரு பற்றின்றி வீழாநிற்கும்
அக்காலத்தும் பற்றாவன கொடுத்துத் தாங்கவல்ல நல்ல ஆண்மகன் பிறவாத குடியாகிய மரம்

en.1: A family with no good person to stand by and prop it up will fall when trouble cuts it at the root.
en.2: A family is a tree. If no good man is born in it, able to give it support and hold it up, it falls with nothing to hold it when the axe of trouble cuts in and fells it at the base. The base is its heirs. It is a tree because it grows and gives fruit with someone to tend it, and dies without.
en.4: Behold the family that hath no good man to prop it up: calamities will gnaw into its roots and it will fall to the ground.
en.5:
When trouble the foundation saps the house must fall,
If no strong hand be nigh to prop the tottering wall.
en.6: If there are none to prop up and maintain a family (in distress), it will fall at the stroke of the axe of misfortune.

padaccheda.m: உழுதலான் வரும் மெய்வருத்த நோக்கிப் பிறதொழில்களைச் செய்துதிரிந்தும், முடிவில் ஏருடையார் வழியதாயிற்று உலகம்
ஆதலான் எல்லா வருத்தமுற்றும், தலையாய தொழில் உழவே

en.1: The world may turn every way, but it still follows the plough. So for all its toil, ploughing comes first.
en.2: People avoid the bodily strain of ploughing and go round doing other work, but in the end the world follows those with the plough. Even with money from other work, they must go to the ploughman for food. So for all its pain ploughing is the foremost work, and other work, painless as it may be, is the lowest.
en.4: Roam where they will, men must at last stand behind the plough for their food: in spite of every hardship, therefore, husbandry is the chiefest industry.
en.5:
Howe’er they roam, the world must follow still the plougher’s team;
Though toilsome, culture of the ground as noblest toil esteem.
en.6: Agriculture, though laborious, is the most excellent (form of labour); for, people, though they go about (in search of various employments), have at last to resort to the farmer.

padaccheda.m: அவ்வுழுதலைச் செய்யமாட்டாது பிற தொழில்கள் மேல் செல்வார் யாவரையும் தாங்குதலால்
அது வல்லார் உலகத்தாராகிய தேர்க்கு அச்சாணி ஆவர்

en.1: Those who plough are the linchpin of the world, because they carry all who can’t and go off to other work.
en.2: Those able to plough are the linchpin of the chariot that is the rest of the world, because they bear all who can’t do it and go to other work. This includes those who have others plough for them. Some read it that those who can’t plough bear every insult from their patrons and can only bow to them.
en.4: Husbandmen are the linchpin of society: for they support all those that take to other work, not having the strength to plough.
en.5:
The ploughers are the linch-pin of the world; they bear
Them up who other works perform, too weak its toils to share.
en.6: Agriculturists are (as it were) the linch-pin of the world, for they support all other workers who cannot till the soil.

padaccheda.m: யாவரும் உண்ணும் வகை உழுதலைச்செய்து அதனான் தாமும் உண்டு வாழ்கின்றாரே தமக்குரியராய் வாழ்கின்றவர்
மற்றையார் எல்லாம் பிறரைத் தொழுது அதனான் தாமும் உண்டு அவரைப் பின்பற்றிச் செல்கி்ன்றவர்

en.1: Only those who plough and eat really live. All the rest bow to eat, and walk behind others.
en.2: Those who plough so that everyone can eat, and eat from it themselves, are the only ones who live as their own masters. All the others bow to someone and eat by that. People born human like anyone, who worship others, keep alive on the little they are given and walk behind them, don’t belong to themselves.
en.4: They alone live who live by tilling the ground: all others eat only the bread of dependence.
en.5:
Who ploughing eat their food, they truly live;
The rest to others bend subservient, eating what they give.
en.6: They alone live who live by agriculture; all others lead a cringing, dependent life.

padaccheda.m: உழுதல் தொழிலான், நெல்லினை உடையராய தண்ணளி உடையோர்

padaccheda.w: பல குடை நீழலும் தம் குடைக்கீழ்க் காண்பர்
padaccheda.m: பலவேந்தர் குடை நிழலதாய மண் முழுதினையும், தம் அரசன் குடைக்கீழே காண்பர்

en.1: Those who have the shade of ripe grain will see the shade of many royal parasols come under their own.
en.2: Those with grain from ploughing, whose kindness is like shade, will see the whole earth, now under the parasols of many rulers, come under the parasol of their own ruler. Their grain feeds all who ask and swells his power, so that all the land becomes his. “Their own parasol” is his, because they are one with him.
en.4: Behold the men whose fields sleep under the shadow of the rich ears of their harvests: they will see the umbrellas of other princes bow down before the umbrella of their own sovereign.
en.5:
O’er many a land they’ll see their monarch reign,
Whose fields are shaded by the waving grain.
en.6: Patriotic farmers desire to bring all other states under the control of their own king.

padaccheda.m: தம் கையால் உழுதுண்டலை இயல்பாக உடையார் பிறரைத் தாம் இரவார்
தம்மை இரப்பார்க்கு அவர் வேண்டியது ஒன்றனைக் கரவாது கொடுப்பர்

en.1: Those who by nature eat by the work of their own hands won’t beg. They give to those who beg, and hide nothing.
en.2: Those whose nature is to plough with their own hands and eat don’t beg from others. They give those who beg from them whatever they ask, and hide nothing. Living this way means they have wealth that never runs out.
en.4: Behold the men that eat the bread of husbandry: they will not only not beg themselves, but they will also give alms to those that beg, without ever saying nay.
en.5:
