en.2: He is always in my heart, without a break. Am I in his in the same way, or not? Is he staying away, though I am there, because his work isn’t done? Or is it done, and he stays away because I am not there?
en.4: Have I at all a place in his heart? As for him, there is never a doubt but he abideth in mine.
en.5:
Have I a place within his heart?
From mine, alas! he never doth depart.
en.6: He continues to abide in my soul, do I likewise abide in his?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: தம்முடைய நெஞ்சின்கண்ணே யாம் செல்லாமல் எம்மைக் காவல்கொண்ட காதலர்
தாம் எம்முடைய நெஞ்சின்கண் ஒழியாது வருதலை நாணார் கொல்லோ

en.1: He has barred me from his heart. Isn’t he ashamed to keep coming into mine?
en.2: My lover has set a guard in his heart so that I can’t enter. Isn’t he ashamed to keep coming into mine without end? To never let someone come to you, yet go to them again and again, isn’t what a person with shame does.
en.4: He excludeth me jealously from his heart: is he not ashamed then to show himself ceaselessly in mine?
en.5:
Me from his heart he jealously excludes:
Hath he no shame who ceaseless on my heart intrudes?
en.6: He who has imprisoned me in his soul, is he ashamed to enter incessantly into mine.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says that remembering the joy of their union is killing her, and she should forget it. She answers.

padaccheda.m: யான் அவரோடு புணர்ந்தஞான்றை இன்பத்தை நினைதலான் இத்துன்ப வெள்ளத்தும் உயிர்வாழ்கின்றேன்
அது இன்றாயின், வேறு எத்தால் உயிர்வாழ்வேன்

en.1: How else would I live? I live by remembering the days I was with him.
en.2: I stay alive in this flood of pain by thinking of the joy of the days I joined him. Without that, what would I live by? Other things could sustain life, such as a messenger from him or one of my own, but I have none of them. This is my only support.
en.4: It is but the recollection of our union that keepeth me alive yet: what else of life is there in me?
en.5:
How live I yet? I live to ponder o’er
The days of bliss with him that are no more.
en.6: I live by remembering my (former) intercourse with him; if it were not so, how could I live?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: அவ்வின்பத்தை மறத்தல் அறியேனாய் இன்று உள்ளாநிற்கவும், பிரிவு என் உள்ளத்தைச் சுடாநின்றது
அங்ஙனம் பிரிவு ஆற்றாத யான் மறந்தால் இறந்துபடாது உளேன் ஆவது எத்தால்

en.1: What would become of me if I forgot? I don’t know how to forget, and even remembering burns my heart.
en.2: I don’t know how to forget that joy, and even as I remember it, parting burns my heart. I can’t bear parting as it is. If I forgot, how could I stay alive and not die?
en.4: Even with my memory full of him, my heart burneth within me: what then will be my case if I forget him?
en.5:
If I remembered not, what were I then? And yet,
The fiery smart of what my spirit knows not to forget!
en.6: I have never forgotten (the pleasure); even to think of it burns my soul; could I live, if I should ever forget it?

uvacha.tr: Her friend says he will learn of her pain, come and give her joy. She answers.

padaccheda.m: தம்மை யான் எத்துணையும் மிகநினைந்தாலும் அதற்கு வெகுளார்
காதலர் எனக்குச் செய்யும் இன்பமாவது அவ்வளவன்றோ

en.1: However much I think of him, he doesn’t get angry. Isn’t that the honour my lover does me?
en.2: However much I think of him, he isn’t angry. He agrees to stay in my heart. Isn’t that all the joy my lover gives me? She knows no joy greater, so she calls it an honour. She is quietly mocking what her friend said.
en.4: How often soever I recall my beloved to my mind he will not be wroth with me: so much is the favour that my beloved bestoweth upon me!
en.5:
My frequent thought no wrath excites. Is it not so?
This honour doth my love on me bestow.
en.6: He will not be angry however much I may think of him; is it not so much the delight my beloved affords me?

uvacha.tr: She grieves that no messenger comes. Her friend urges her to be firm, and she answers.

padaccheda.w: வேறு அல்லம் என்பார் அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து
padaccheda.m: முன்பெல்லாம் நாம் இருவரும் வேறல்லம் என்று சொல்லுவாரது அளியின்மையை மிகவும் நினைந்து
எனது இனியவுயிர் கழியாநின்றது

en.1: My sweet life is ending, as I dwell on the unkindness of the one who said, “We are not separate.”
en.2: My sweet life is going, as I think so much on the unkindness of the one who used to say, “We two are not separate.” His unkindness is leaving when he could come back, staying away and sending no messenger. It is his lack of loving-kindness, she answers her friend, not the parting, that is ending her life.
en.4: When my heart thinketh on his cruelty who once said, We are not two but only one life and soul, verily my life ebbeth away.
en.5:
Dear life departs, when his ungracious deeds I ponder o’er,
Who said erewhile, ‘We’re one for evermore.’
en.6: My precious life is wasting away by thinking too much on the cruelty of him who said we were not different.

uvacha.tr: She has rejected her friend’s comfort. With desire at its height and her grief past bearing, she says this.

padaccheda.m: மதியே
என் நெஞ்சின் இடைவிடாதிருந்தே விட்டுப்போயினாரை, யான் என் கண்ணளவாயினும் எதிர்ப்படும்வகை நீ படாது ஒழிவாயாக

en.1: Long may you live, moon. Don’t set, so that my eyes may see the one who left without leaving me.
en.2: Moon, don’t set, so that I may meet with my eyes the one who stays always in my heart and yet has gone. Both of them look at the moon, so their eyes meet on it. She says “long may you live” because she is pleading. With another reading, the moon won’t set, so she can’t sleep and see him in a dream.
en.4: O Moon! set not in the horizon, I pray thee, till my eyes look again upon him who, abiding still within my heart, hath yet parted from me.
en.5:
Set not, so may’st thou prosper, moon! that eyes may see
My love who went away, but ever bides with me.
en.6: May you live, O Moon. Do not set, that I mine eyes may see him who has departed without quitting my soul.

uvacha.tr: She has seen a message from him come to her in a dream, and she says this.

padaccheda.m: யான் வருந்துகின்றது அறிந்து, அது தீரக் காதலர் விடுத்த தூதினைக்கொண்டு என்மாட்டு வந்த கனவினுக்கு
யான் விருந்தாக யாதனைச் செய்வேன்

en.1: What feast can I give the dream that came with a message from my lover?
en.2: Knowing I suffer, my lover sent a message to end it, and the dream came to me carrying it. What can I do for it as my guest? A feast means the courtesies due to a guest, and she asks because she can see nothing that could be offered to a dream.
en.4: What honours shall I do to the Dream which hath brought me a message from the beloved?
en.5:
It came and brought to me, that nightly vision rare,
A message from my love,—what feast shall I prepare?
en.6: Wherewith shall I feast the dream which has brought me my dear one’s messenger?

uvacha.tr: She has been thinking of sending him a message, and she says this.

padaccheda.m: துஞ்சாதுவருந்துகின்ற என் கயல்போலும் உண்கண்கள் யான் இரந்தால் துஞ்சுமாயின்
கனவிடைக் காதலரைக் காண்பேன், கண்டால் அவர்க்கு யான் ஆற்றியுளேனாய தன்மையை யானே விரியச் சொல்வேன்

en.1: If my eyes, carp-shaped and dark with kohl, would sleep when I beg them, I could tell the one who held me that I have survived.
en.2: My carp-like eyes won’t sleep. If they would sleep when I begged them, I would see my lover in a dream and tell him myself how I have endured the sickness of desire, in full, with all that a messenger would leave out or shorten. But the eyes won’t sleep, so it can’t be said. She calls them carp-like in grief for the beauty she has lost.
en.4: If only I could persuade my eyes to sleep, I would fly to my beloved in my dream, and tell him the story of how I manage yet to hold on to life.
en.5:
If my dark, carp-like eye will close in sleep, as I implore,
The tale of my long-suffering life I’ll tell my loved one o’er.
en.6: If my fish-like painted eyes should, at my begging, close in sleep, I could fully relate my sufferings to my lord.

uvacha.tr: Her friend fears she can’t bear the separation. She answers that she can.

padaccheda.m: நனவின்கண் வந்து தலையளி செய்யாதாரை
யான் கனவின்கட் கண்ட காட்சியானே என் உயிருண்டாகாநின்றது

en.1: He shows me no kindness when I am awake, but I see him in dreams, and that is what keeps me alive.
en.2: He won’t come and show me kindness while I am awake, but seeing him in a dream keeps the life in me. With that sight I can bear this, so you needn’t worry.
en.4: If I am able to support life yet it is only because I see him in dreams who showeth not his face in waking hours.
en.5:
Him, who in waking hour no kindness shows,
In dreams I see: and so my lifetime goes!
en.6: My life lasts because in my dream I behold him who does not favour me in my waking hours.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நனவின்கண் வந்து தலையளி செய்யாதாரை அவர்சென்றுழி நாடிக்கொண்டுவந்து கனவு தருதலான்
அக்கனவின்கண்ணே எனக்கு இன்பம் உண்டாகாநின்றது

en.1: In dreams I have the joy of desire, because a dream seeks out the man who shows no kindness when I am awake and brings him to me.
en.2: A dream finds the place he went to and brings back the man who won’t come to me in waking life, and so I have joy in it. By nature he shows no kindness, yet the dream finds him, fetches him and makes him kind. With that dream I can bear this.
en.4: Dream giveth me all the joys of love: for it bringeth back to me my beloved who refuseth to pity me in my waking state.
en.5:
Some pleasure I enjoy when him who loves not me
In waking hours, the vision searches out and makes me see.
en.6: There is pleasure in my dream, because in it I seek and obtain him who does not visit me in my wakefulness.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: முன் நனவின்கண் அவரைக்கண்டு நுகர்ந்த இன்பந்தானும் இனிதாயிற்று அப்பொழுதே
இன்று கனவின்கட் கண்டு நுகர்ந்த இன்பமும் அக்கண்டபொழுதே இனிதாயிற்று, அதனான் எனக்கு இரண்டும் ஒத்தன

en.1: Even seeing him awake was sweet only at that moment. The dream too is sweet only while I am seeing it.
en.2: The joy I had when I saw him awake was sweet at that time. The joy I have today from seeing him in a dream is sweet at that time too. So the two are equal to me. That was all I ever had before, and with this I can bear it now.
en.4: The joys of the dream last as long as the beloved appeareth in it: and what more can be said of the waking state?
en.5:
As what I then beheld in waking hour was sweet,
So pleasant dreams in hour of sleep my spirit greet.
en.6: I saw him in my waking hours, and then it was pleasant; I see him just now in my dream, and it is (equally) pleasant.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நனவு என்று சொல்லப்படுகின்ற ஒரு பாவி இல்லையாயின்
கனவின்கண் வந்துகூடிய காதலர் என்னைப் பிரியார்

en.1: If there were no such thing as waking, my lover would never leave me in my dreams.
en.2: If there were none of this wretch called waking, the lover who comes and joins me in a dream wouldn’t leave me. Waking breaks in, ends the dream and parts him from me, and the word “thing” shows how cruel it is. She is telling how she gets through by having him in dreams.
en.4: Oh that there were no waking state! For then my dream would never be cut short and my beloved would never depart from me.
en.5:
And if there were no waking hour, my love
In dreams would never from my side remove.
en.6: Were there no such thing as wakefulness, my beloved (who visited me) in my dream would not depart from me.

uvacha.tr: She wakes and he is gone. Remembering their union in the dream, she can’t bear it, and says this.

padaccheda.m: ஒருஞான்றும் நனவின்கண் வந்து தலையளி செய்யாத கொடியவர்
நாள்தோறும் கனவின்கண் வந்து நம்மை வருத்துவது எவ்வியைபுபற்றி

en.1: He is cruel, giving me no kindness when I am awake. Why does he torment me in my dreams?
en.2: This cruel man never once comes to show me kindness when I am awake. By what right does he come every day in dreams and torment me? He is cruel because he left and doesn’t think of coming back. In a dream he is on my shoulders, and when I wake he hides, and that hurts too. People say what isn’t there awake isn’t there in dreams, but we haven’t found it so.
en.4: The cruel one who pitieth me not while I am awake, why doth he haunt me in my dreams?
en.5:
The cruel one, in waking hour, who all ungracious seems,
Why should he thus torment my soul in nightly dreams?
en.6: The cruel one who would not favour me in my wakefulness, what right has he to torture me in my dreams?

uvacha.tr: Her friend has spoken ill of him to help her bear it. She defends him.

padaccheda.m: என்நெஞ்சு விடாது உறைகின்ற காதலர் யான் துஞ்சும்பொழுது வந்து என் தோள்மேலராய்
பின் விழிக்கும்பொழுது, விரைந்து பழைய நெஞ்சின்கண்ணராவர்

en.1: When I sleep, he is on my shoulders. When I wake, he rushes into my heart.
en.2: My lover never leaves my heart. When I sleep he comes and lies on my shoulders, and when I wake he hurries back into my heart, where he was before. She says he hurries because it is so harsh that he breaks off their union and vanishes. He has never once left me, so you have no cause to blame him.
en.4: He embraceth me while I am asleep and rusheth into my heart as soon as I open my eyes.
en.5:
And when I sleep he holds my form embraced;
And when I wake to fill my heart makes haste!
en.6: When I am asleep he rests on my shoulders, (but) when I awake he hastens into my soul.

uvacha.tr: She goes on defending him to her friend.

padaccheda.m: தமக்கொரு காதலர் இன்மையின் அவரைக் கனவிற்கண்டறியாத மகளிர்
தாமறிய நனவின்கண் வந்து நல்காத நங்காதலரை அன்பிலர் என நோவா நிற்பர்

en.1: Those who never see a lover in their dreams blame him for showing no kindness in waking life.
en.2: Women who have no lover of their own, and so have never seen one in a dream, blame my lover as lacking loving-kindness because he doesn’t come to me in waking life. She can’t bear the blame, and speaks as if of strangers. If they had lovers and saw them in dreams, they would know how he comforts me there, and wouldn’t blame him.
en.4: They reproach my beloved for that he doth not meet me to their knowledge: but then they see him not in dreams.
en.5:
In dreams who ne’er their lover’s form perceive,
For those in waking hours who show no love will grieve.
en.6: They who have no dear ones to behold in their dreams blame him who visits me not in my waking hours.

uvacha.tr: She goes on defending him to her friend.

padaccheda.m: இவ்வூரின்மகளிர் நனவின்கண் நம்மை நீத்தார் என்று நம்காதலரைக் கொடுமைகூறாநிற்பர்
அவர் கனவின்கண் நீங்காதுவருதல் கண்டறியாரோ

en.1: They say he left me in waking life. Do the people of this village not see him in their dreams?
en.2: The women of this village call my lover cruel, saying he has left me in waking life. Do they not know he comes to me in dreams and doesn’t leave? She says “of this village” to mark her friend as an outsider. If there were no difference between them, her friend would see what she sees and be content. Instead she calls him cruel.
en.4: These village folk say that he hath parted from me: is it that they see him not in dreams?
en.5:
They say, that he in waking hours has left me lone;
In dreams they surely see him not,—these people of the town!
en.6: The women of this place say he has forsaken me in my wakefulness. I think they have not seen him visit me in my dreams.

uvacha.tr: She quarrels with the evening, and says this.

padaccheda.m: பொழுதே! நீ மாலையோ அல்லை= நீ முன்னாள்களின் வந்த மாலையோவெனின், அல்லை

இருந்தவாற்றான் அந்நாட்காதலரை மணந்த மகளிர் உயிரை உண்ணும் இறுதிக்காலமாய் இருந்தாய். முன்னாள்= கூடியிருந்தநாள். அந்நாள் மணந்தார் எனவே, பின் பிரிந்தாரதல் பெறுதும். வாழி என்பது குறிப்புச்சொல். "வாலிழை மகளிர் உயிர்ப்பொதி அவிழ்க்குங் காலை" (கலித்தொகை, நெய்தற்கலி-2)என்றாற்போல ஈண்டுப் பொதுமையாற் கூறப்பட்டது. வேலை என்பது ஆகுபெயர். வேலை என்பதற்கு வேலாய் இருந்தாய் என்பாரும் உளர்

en.1: Long may you live, hour. You are no evening, but the time that eats the lives of those who have wed.
en.2: Hour, you are not the evening of the days when we were together. You have become the final hour that eats the lives of women joined to their lovers then and parted now. “Long may you live” is irony. Some read the word for “time” as “spear”, so that she says: you are a spear.
en.4: Evening! Bless thee, but who calleth thee Evening? Thou art really the hour that devoureth the lives of the wedded ones!
en.5:
Thou art not evening, but a spear that doth devour
The souls of brides: farewell, thou evening hour!
en.6: Live, O you evening; are you (the former) evening? No, you are the season that slays (married) women.

uvacha.tr: She lays her own inner sorrow on the evening, and says this.

padaccheda.m: மயங்கிய மாலாய்
நீயும் எம்போலப் புன்கண் உடையாய் இருந்தாய்

padaccheda.w: நின் துணை எம் கேள் போல் வன்கண்ணதோ
padaccheda.m: நின் துணையும் எந்துணை போல வன்கண்மையுடையதோ, கூறுவாயாக

en.1: You are wretched, dim evening, long may you live. Is your mate as hard-hearted as mine?
en.2: Dim evening, where day and night run together, you too have lost your brightness, as I have. Tell me, is your mate as hard-hearted as mine? From that lost brightness she imagines it has a mate. “Long may you live” carries a hidden sense: you have hurt me, and you have found no joy yourself.
en.4: Thou lookest melancholy and pale, O Eventide! Pray, tell me, dear, is thy lover also cruel even as mine?
en.5:
Thine eye is sad; Hail, doubtful hour of eventide!
Of cruel eye, as is my spouse, is too thy bride?
en.6: A long life to you, O dark evening! You are sightless. Is your help-mate (also) as hard-hearted as mine.

uvacha.tr: Her friend tells her she must bear it, and she answers.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் கூடிய நாளெல்லாம் என்முன் நடுக்கம் எய்திப் பசந்து வந்த மாலை
இந்நாள் எனக்கு இறந்துபாடு வந்துதோன்றி அதற்குளதாம் துன்பம் ஒருகாலைக்கொருகால் மிக வாரா நின்றது

en.1: Evening comes with cold budding and its light growing pale, and with it despair buds in me and pain grows.
en.2: On all the days I was with my lover, evening came before me trembling and pale. Today it brings death into view, and a loathing of life, and the pain of that grows from moment to moment. On the surface the words only say that evening comes cool and dim, but they suggest this. How am I to bear it?
en.4: The dewy evening hour that once used to come trembling and sighing before me, now advanceth boldly, bringing nought but grief and despair unto my heart.
en.5:
With buds of chilly dew wan evening’s shade enclose;
My anguish buds apace, and all my sorrow grows.
en.6: The evening that (once) came in with trembling and dimness (now) brings me an aversion for life and increasing sorrow.

reading.note: பனி can be cold or trembling, and he hears both: the surface sense is a cool, dim evening, and beneath it evening once trembled before her.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் உள்ளபொழுதெல்லாம் என்னுயிர் தளிர்ப்ப வந்தமாலை
அவரி்ல்லாத இப்பொழுது
அஃது ஒழிந்துநிற்றலேயன்றிக் கொல்லுங் களரியிற் கொலைஞர் வருமாறு போல அவ்வுயிரைக் கோடற்கு வாராநின்றது

en.1: When my lover is away, evening comes like strangers to a killing ground.
en.2: While my lover was here, evening came and my life put out new shoots. Now he is gone, it doesn’t only stop doing that. It comes to take my life, as executioners with no compassion come to the killing ground. It used to be my friend and bring me joy, and today it is my enemy and brings me pain. How am I to bear it?
en.4: When the beloved is away, evening approacheth even as the executioner advancing to the execution-ground.
en.5:
When absent is my love, the evening hour descends,
As when an alien host to field of battle wends.
en.6: In the absence of my lover, evening comes in like slayers on the field of slaughter.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: (காலையும், மாலையும் அவர் கூடியஞான்று போலாது இஞ்ஞான்று வேறுபட்டு வாராநின்றன அவற்றுள்) யான் காலைக்குச் செய்த உபகாரம் யாது
மாலைக்குச் செய்த அபகாரம் யாது

en.1: What good did I do the morning, and what harm did I do the evening?
en.2: Morning and evening both come differently now. What favour did I do the morning? When we were together it made me fear his leaving, and now it comes as a shore to the flood of night. What harm did I do the evening? It used to bring joy and now brings endless pain. Unlike morning, it hurts me through its own cruelty.
en.4: What is the kindness that I had done to the morning hour? and how have I injured eventide?
en.5:
O morn, how have I won thy grace? thou bring’ st relief!
O eve, why art thou foe? thou dost renew my grief.
en.6: What good have I done to morning (and) what evil to evening?

uvacha.tr: Her friend asks why she agreed to his leaving, if she is like this now. She answers.

padaccheda.m: முன்னெல்லாம் எனக்கு நட்பாய் இன்பம் செய்துபோந்த மாலை இன்று பகையாய்த் துன்பம்செய்தலை
காதலர் பிரிதற்குமுன்னே அறியப்பெற்றிலேன்

en.1: Before the one who wed me left, I never knew that evening brings pain.
en.2: Evening used to be my friend and bring me joy, and today it is my enemy and brings me pain. I didn’t know this before my lover left. If I had known it would change like this, I wouldn’t have agreed to his going.
en.4: Alack the day! I never knew the sting of the evening so long as my beloved was by my side.
en.5:
The pangs that evening brings I never knew,
Till he, my wedded spouse, from me withdrew.
en.6: Previous to my husband’s departure, I knew not the painful nature of evening.

uvacha.tr: Her friend asks why she suffers so at evening, and she answers.

padaccheda.m: இக்காமநோயாகிய பூ
காலைப்பொழுதின்கண் அரும்பி
பகற்பொழுதெல்லாம் பேர்அரும்பாய் முதிர்ந்து
மாலைப்பொழுதின்கண் மலராநிற்கும்

en.1: This sickness buds in the morning, fills out all day and flowers in the evening.
en.2: This sickness of desire is a flower. It buds in the morning, ripens all day into a full bud, and opens at evening. On waking she takes comfort in the union of her dream. As the day goes she forgets it and thinks of the parting. At evening she sees beasts and people drawn back to their mates, remembers her own joy, and can’t bear it.
en.4: This sickness buddeth in the morning, goeth on opening its petals the livelong day, and standeth full-blown at eventide.
en.5:
My grief at morn a bud, all day an opening flower,
Full-blown expands in evening hour.
en.6: This malady buds forth in the morning, expands all day long and blossoms in the evening.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: முன்னெல்லாம் இனியதாய்ப் போந்த ஆயன்குழல்
இதுபொழுது அழல்போலச் சுடுவதாய மாலைக்குத் தூதுமாய்
அது வந்து என்னைக் கொல்வுழிக் கொல்லும் படையும் ஆயிற்று

en.1: The cowherd’s flute is a messenger for the evening that burns like fire, and a weapon that kills.
en.2: The cowherd’s flute, once sweet, has become the messenger of evening, which now burns like fire, and the weapon that kills me when evening comes. It is a messenger because it announces evening in advance, and a weapon because it is the means of killing. If evening can burn by itself, what won’t it do with all this help?
en.4: They call it the pipe of the shepherd, but verily it is a murderous weapon to me: for it ushereth in the evening that burneth me so.
en.5:
The shepherd’s pipe is like a murderous weapon, to my ear,
For it proclaims the hour of ev’ning’s fiery anguish near.
en.6: The shepherd’s flute now sounds as a fiery forerunner of night, and is become a weapon that slays (me).

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: (இதற்கு முன்னெல்லாம் யானே மயங்கி நோயுழந்தேன்) இனிக் கண்டாரும் மதி மருளும்வகை மாலை வரும்பொழுது
இப்பதி எல்லாம் மயங்கி நோயுழக்கும்

en.1: When evening spreads and reason reels, the town reels too, and suffers.
en.2: Until now I alone was bewildered and in pain. Now evening comes so that all who see it lose their reason, and this whole town will be bewildered and suffer. She thinks of evening as Death coming for her, and she means that she will die. Some read it as: when evening comes dim, my town’s reason is shaken and it suffers.
en.4: If evening that hath already driven me mad should advance any further, the whole town will be shrouded in sorrow before long, for I shall simply die.
en.5:
If evening’s shades, that darken all my soul, extend;
From this afflicted town will sound of grief ascend.
en.6: When night comes on confusing (every one’s) mind, the (whole) town will lose its sense and be plunged in sorrow.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் பிரிவைப் பொறுத்து இறந்துபடாதிருந்த என் உயிர்
இன்று பொருள் இயல்பே தமக்கு இயல்பாக உடையவரை நினைந்து, இம்மயங்கும் மாலைக்கண்ணே இறந்துபடாநின்றது

en.1: My life has not died yet, but in this dim evening it is dying, as I think of the man whose way is wealth.
en.2: My life, which bore his leaving and didn’t die, is dying in this dim evening as I think of him. The agreed season has passed and he stays away until his wealth is won. He has lost his own nature, of never changing his word, and taken on the nature of wealth. It has come to this, and nothing you say can help now.
en.4: The life which is yet clinging on to me will soon depart: for eventide recalleth to me the image of him who is mad after wealth.
en.5:
This darkening eve, my darkling soul must perish utterly;
Remembering him who seeks for wealth, but seeks not me.
en.6: My (hitherto) unextinguished life is now lost in this bewildering night at the thought of him who has the nature of wealth.

uvacha.tr: She has changed, because the pain is more than she can bear. Her friend says this to her.

padaccheda.m: இவ்வாற்றாமை நம்கண்ணே நிற்பத் தாம் சேணிடைச் சென்ற காதலரை நீ நினைந்து அழுதலால்
நின்கண்கள் ஒளியிழந்து முன் தமக்கு நாணிய நறுமலர்கட்கு இன்று தாம் நாணிவிட்டன

en.1: He went far away and left us this misery. As you think of him, your eyes now shrink in shame before sweet flowers.
en.2: He went far away and left this misery with us. You think of him and weep, so your eyes have lost their light, and the fragrant flowers that were once ashamed before them now shame them. Anyone who sees this will call him cruel, so you must bear it.
en.4: My eyes think on him who left me saying that it was but to increase my happiness that he went, and are ashamed to show their face before flowers.
en.5:
Thine eyes grown dim are now ashamed the fragrant flow’rs to see,
Thinking on him, who wand’ring far, leaves us in misery.
en.6: While we endure the unbearable sorrow, your eyes weep for him who is gone afar, and shun (the sight of) fragrant flowers.

uvacha.tr: Her friend goes on.

padaccheda.m: பசப்பெய்தன்மேல் நீர் வார்கின்ற நின்கண்கள்
நம்மான் நயக்கப்பட்டவரது நல்காமையைப் பிறர்க்குச் சொல்லுவபோலாநின்றன. இனி, நீ ஆற்றல் வேண்டும்

en.1: Your eyes, pale and streaming with tears, seem to be telling of the unkindness of the one you long for.
en.2: Your eyes have turned pale and now run with tears. They seem to tell others that the man we long for shows us no kindness, because from them people can infer it. So you must bear this. Some have a text in which the eyes tell him.
en.4: My lacklustre eyes that are raining down tears look as if they would betray to others the unkindness of my beloved.
en.5:
The eye, with sorrow wan, all wet with dew of tears,
As witness of the lover’s lack of love appears.
en.6: The discoloured eyes that shed tears profusely seem to betray the unkindness of our beloved.

uvacha.tr: Her friend goes on.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் மணந்த ஞான்று இன்பம் மிகுதியாற் பூரித்த நின்தோள்கள்
இன்று அவர் பிரிந்தமையை விளங்க உணர்த்துவபோல மெலியாநின்றன, இது தகாது

en.1: Your arms, which swelled on the day he wed you, seem to be proclaiming that he has gone.
en.2: Your arms, which swelled with joy on the day he wed you, are thinning today as if to make his leaving plain. This is not right. If they swelled then and thin now, anyone who has seen both will soon understand, and will say he has no decency.
en.4: The arms that swelled with joy on the nuptial day now look as if they would proclaim his parting to all the world.
en.5:
These withered arms, desertion’s pangs abundantly display,
That swelled with joy on that glad nuptial day.
en.6: The shoulders that swelled on the day of our union (now) seem to announce our separation clearly (to the public).

uvacha.tr: Her friend goes on.

padaccheda.m: அன்றும் துணைவர் நீங்குதலான் அவராற்பெற்ற செயற்கை அழகேயன்றிப் பழைய இயற்கை அழகும் இழந்த இ்ததோள்கள்
இன்று அதற்கும்மேலே தம் பெருமையிழந்து வளை கழலாநின்றன. இவை இங்ஙனம் செயற்பாலன அல்ல

en.1: With your companion gone, your arms have lost their old beauty. Now they shrink and the gold bangles slip away.
en.2: When your companion left, these arms lost the beauty he gave them and their old natural beauty too. Now they have lost their fullness as well, and the gold bangles slip off. They shouldn’t do this. Then they showed that he has no loving-kindness, and now that he lied, not coming in the agreed season. Can those who say so be blamed?
en.4: The arms that lost their wonted comeliness at the parting of the beloved, are now grown so thin that their very bracelets slip off from them of themselves.
en.5:
When lover went, then faded all their wonted charms,
And armlets’ golden round slips off from these poor wasted arms.
en.6: In the absence of your consort, your shoulders having lost their former beauty and fulness, your bracelets of pure gold have become loose.

uvacha.tr: Her friend goes on.

padaccheda.m: கவவுக்கை நெகிழினும் ஆற்றாதாட்கு, இக்கால நீட்டத்து என்னாம் என்று நினையாத கொடியாரது கொடுமையைத் தாமே சொல்லாநின்றன
வளைகளும் கழன்று, பழைய இயற்கை அழகும் இழந்த இத்தோள்கள், இனி அதனை யாம் மறைக்குமாறு என்னை

en.1: Your arms, their bangles gone and their old beauty withered, tell of the cruelty of a cruel man.
en.2: You couldn’t bear it even when his embrace loosened, and the cruel man never thought what so long a time would do to you. These arms, their bangles gone and their old beauty lost, tell of his cruelty themselves, so how can we hide it? If the arms that held him say it, what need is there for outsiders to speak?
en.4: The arms which have lost their wonted comeliness together with the bracelets that they were wearing, proclaim loudly to the world the cruelty of that cruel one.
en.5:
These wasted arms, the bracelet with their wonted beauty gone,
The cruelty declare of that most cruel one.
en.6: The (loosened) bracelets, and the shoulders from which the old beauty has faded, relate the cruelty of the pitiless one.

uvacha.tr: Her friend has blamed him to help her bear it. She answers.

padaccheda.m: யான் ஆற்றவும், என் வயத்தவன்றித் தொடிகள் கழலுமாறு தோள்கள் மெலிய
அவற்றைக்கண்டு நீ அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக் கூறுதலைப் பொறாது யான் என்னுள்ளே நோவாநின்றேன்

en.1: My arms grow thin and my bangles slip, and I ache to hear him called cruel.
en.2: I do bear it, but beyond my control my arms thin and my bangles slip. You see that and call him cruel, and I can’t stand it, and I ache inside. What I can’t bear isn’t his staying away. It is what you say.
en.4: I chide my arms for growing lean and allowing the bracelets to fall off, as people now reproach him with cruelty.
en.5:
I grieve, ’tis pain to me to hear him cruel chid,
Because the armlet from my wasted arm has slid.
en.6: I am greatly pained to hear you call him a cruel man, just because your shoulders are reduced and your bracelets loosened.

uvacha.tr: She can’t bear to hear him blamed, and she says this to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே
இவள் கொடியார் என்கிறவர்க்கு, நீ சென்று என் மெலிகின்ற தோளினால் விளைகின்ற ஆரவாரத்தைச் சொல்லி
ஒரு மேம்பாடு எய்த வல்லையோ, வல்லையாயின் அதனை ஒப்பது இல்லை

en.1: Will you win glory, my heart, by telling that cruel man about the uproar over my wasting arms?
en.2: My heart, go to the man she calls cruel, tell him of the uproar over my wasting arms, and can you win some honour? If so, nothing could equal it. “Cruel” implies he isn’t, and the arms waste of themselves. Once he hears you he will come and all this will end, a good deed done in time, and you will have its whole reward.
en.4: Wouldst thou obtain glory, O my Heart? Then run to the cruel one and tell him of the bruit that hath arisen here from the wasting away of my arm.
en.5:
My heart! say ought of glory wilt thou gain,
If to that cruel one thou of thy wasted arms complain?
en.6: Can you O my soul! gain glory by relating to the (so-called) cruel one the clamour of my fading shoulders?

uvacha.tr: His work is done and he is about to return. He remembers the past and says this to himself.

padaccheda.m: தன்னை இறுக முயங்கிய கைகளை, இவட்கு நோகும் என்று கருதி ஒருஞான்று யான் நெகிழ்த்தேனாக
அத்துணையும் பொறாது, பைந்தொடிகளை அணிந்த பேதையது நுதல் பசந்தது, அப்பெற்றித்தாய நுதல் இப்பிரிவிற்கு யாது செய்யுமோ

en.1: When I loosened my arms in our embrace, the forehead of that simple girl in gold bangles turned pale.
en.2: One day I loosened the arms that held her tight, thinking it would hurt her. She couldn’t bear even that, and the forehead of that simple girl in gold bangles turned pale. What will such a forehead do in this separation? I must go back quickly.
en.4: As we were embracing each other one day, I but relaxed my arms a little, and the forehead of that artless one grew pale at once!
en.5:
One day the fervent pressure of embracing arms I checked,
Grew wan the forehead of the maid with golden armlet decked.
en.6: When I once loosened the arms that were in embrace, the forehead of the gold-braceleted woman turned sallow.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: அங்ஙனம் கைகளை ஊக்குதலான் அம்முயக்கிடையே சிறுகாற்று நுழைந்ததாக
அத்துணை இடையீடும் பொறாது, பேதையுடைய பெரிய மழைக்கண்கள் பசப்புற்றன

en.1: When a cool breeze cut through our embrace, the simple girl’s great rain-cool eyes turned pale.
en.2: As I loosened my arms, a small breeze slipped in between us. Her large cool eyes couldn’t bear even that gap and turned pale. How have such eyes borne all that lies between us now, the mountains, forests and lands? “Cut through” shows that the two bodies had become one.
en.4: But a single breath of wind cut its way between us during our embrace, and the blood fled at once from her large eyes that are full even as the rain-cloud.
en.5:
As we embraced a breath of wind found entrance there;
The maid’s large liquid eyes were dimmed with care.
en.6: When but a breath of breeze penetrated our embrace, her large cool eyes became sallow.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: தண்வளி போழவந்த கண்ணின் பசப்புத் துன்பம் உற்றது
தனக்கு அயலாய ஒண்ணுநல் விளைத்த பசப்பைக்கண்டு

en.1: Even the pallor in her eyes suffered when it saw what her bright forehead had done.
en.2: The pallor in her eyes suffered when it saw the pallor made by her bright forehead. The forehead paled as soon as my arms loosened. The eyes paled only when a breeze came between us, and they were ashamed of their hardness beside its tenderness. So her features race each other to lose their beauty, and I must hurry.
en.4: Did the eyes grow pale only? They wept also at seeing the pallor of the fair forehead above.
en.5:
The dimness of her eye felt sorrow now,
Beholding what was done by that bright brow.
en.6: Was it at the sight of what the bright forehead had done that the sallowness of her eyes became sad?

uvacha.tr: She asks how her suffering might be ended.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே
இவ் எவ்வநோயினைத் தீர்க்கும் மருந்தாவது ஒன்றனை
யான் அறியும் ஆ்றறல் இலன், எத்தன்மையது யாதொன்றாயினும் நீ அறிந்து எனக்குச் சொல்

en.1: Won’t you think of something, heart, and tell me any cure at all for this unending sickness?
en.2: My heart, I haven’t the power to find it. Whatever it may be, find out and tell me one medicine for this sickness that nothing relieves. “Any at all” means even something that gives up modesty, which is worth more than life.
en.4: Wouldst thou not think, O my Heart, and find out and tell me some remedy to cure me of this incurable disease?
en.5:
My heart, canst thou not thinking of some med’cine tell,
Not any one, to drive away this grief incurable?
en.6: O my soul, will you not think and tell me some medicine, be it what it may, that can cure this incurable malady?

uvacha.tr: Her longing to see him overwhelms her, and she says this.

padaccheda.m: என் நெஞ்சே வாழ்வாயாக
அவர் நம்கண் காதல் இலராகவும் நீ அவர் வரவு நோக்கி வருந்துதற்கு ஏது
நின் பேதைமையே பிறிதில்லை

en.1: He has no love for you, yet you go on suffering. That is foolishness, my heart, long may you live.
en.2: He has no love for us, yet you suffer, waiting for him to come. That is your own foolishness and nothing else. He doesn’t think of us, so we can tell he has no love, and you don’t see that. You don’t think of going to him either, and you bring this on yourself. “Long may you live” is mockery. The wise thing is for us to go to him.
en.4: Bless thee, my Heart! Thou art a fool to grieve at his absence when he hath no love for thee.
en.5:
Since he loves not, thy smart
Is folly, fare thee well, my heart!
en.6: May you live, O my soul! While he is without love, for you to suffer is (simple) folly.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே! அவர்பாற் செல்வதும் செய்யாது, ஈண்டு இறந்துபடுவதும் செய்யாது இருந்து அவர் வரவுநினைந்து நீ வருந்துகின்றது என்னை

padaccheda.w: பைதல் நோய் செய்தார்கண் பரிந்து உள்ளல் இல்
padaccheda.m: இப்பையுள் நோய் செய்தார்மாட்டு நமக்கு இரங்கி வரக்கருதுதல் உண்டாகாது

en.1: Why sit here thinking of him and aching, heart? The one who gave us this sickness of grief has no tender thought for us.
en.2: My heart, you neither go to him nor die here. Why sit thinking of his return and suffering? The man who gave us this sickness of grief won’t think of us with pity and come. He has no compassion for us, so he won’t come of himself. It is right now that we go to him.
en.4: What availeth our sitting here and pining away for thinking of him, O my Heart? He that caused us this grief remembereth us not.
en.5:
What comes of sitting here in pining thought, O heart? He knows
No pitying thought, the cause of all these wasting woes.
en.6: O my soul, why remain (here) and suffer thinking (of him)? There are no lewd thoughts (of you) in him who has caused you this disease of sorrow.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே, நீ அவர்பால் சேறலுற்றாயாயின் இக்கண்களையும் உடன் கொண்டு செல்வாயாக
அன்றி நீ சேறியாயின், இவைதாம் காட்சிவிதுப்பினால் அவரைக் காண்டல்வேண்டி நீ காட்டு என்று என்னைத் தின்பனபோன்று நலியாநிற்கும்

en.1: Take my eyes with you too when you go, heart. Wanting to see him, they are eating me.
en.2: My heart, if you go to him, take these eyes with you. If you go without them, their craving will torment me as if devouring me, demanding that I show him to them. She wants that torment ended, which means she herself intends to go.
en.4: If thou go to him, my Heart, take these eyes also along with thee! For they devour me in their longing to look on him.
en.5:
O rid me of these eyes, my heart; for they,
Longing to see him, wear my life away.
en.6: O my soul, take my eyes also with you. (If not), these would eat me up (in their desire) to see him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே! யாம் உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்= யாம் நம்மையுறத் தாமுறாத நம் காதலரை
வெறுத்தார் என்று கருதிப் புலந்து கைவிட்டிருக்கும் வலி நமக்கு உண்டோ, இல்லை

en.1: We are drawn to him and he isn’t drawn to us. Can we give him up as an enemy, heart?
en.2: He doesn’t return the loving-kindness we give him. Do we have the strength to decide he hates us, sulk and give him up? We don’t. Since we lack that strength, the right thing for us is to go to him.
en.4: Though he spurneth us in spite of our cleaving unto him, can we give him up as an enemy, my Heart?
en.5:
O heart, as a foe, can I abandon utterly
Him who, though I long for him, longs not for me?
en.6: O my soul, can he who loves not though he is beloved, be forsaken saying he hates me (now)?

uvacha.tr: Her heart thinks of his cruelty and won’t agree to go. She scolds it.

padaccheda.m: என்னெஞ்சே!: கலந்து உணர்த்தும் காதலர்க் கண்டாற்புலந்து உணராய்= யான் தம்மொடு புலந்தால், அப்புலவியைக் கலவிதன்னானே நீக்கவல்ல காதலரைக் காண்டாற் பொய்யேயாயினும் ஒருகாற் புலந்து பின்அதனை நீங்க மாட்டாய்
அதுவும் மாட்டாத நீ, இப்பொழுது அவர் கொடியர் எனப் பொய்க்காய்வு காயாநின்றாய், இனி அதனை ஒழிந்து அவர்பால் செல்லத் துணிவாயாக

en.1: When you see the lover who mends a sulk with an embrace, you can’t even sulk. Your anger now is a pretence, my heart.
en.2: If I sulk, my lover can end it by making love. When you see him, you can’t sulk even once in pretence and then give it up. You can’t do that, yet now you rage at him as cruel. That is false anger with no firmness in it. If you fail when you see him, hating him when you don’t is useless. Stop, and make up your mind to go to him.
en.4: When thou lookest on the beloved who is clever in the art of conciliating, my Heart, thou wouldst not even take huff but wouldst rush to his embrace, forgetting all: I fear that now too thy anger is only feigned.
en.5:
My heart, false is the fire that burns; thou canst not wrath maintain,
If thou thy love behold, embracing, soothing all thy pain.
en.6: O my soul, when you see the dear one who removes dislike by intercourse, you are displeased and continue to be so. Nay, your displeasure is (simply) false.

uvacha.tr: Her modesty holds her back, so she gives up going, and she says this.

padaccheda.m: நல்ல நெஞ்சே
ஒன்றின் நாண்விட மாட்டாயாயின் காம வேட்கையை விடு
ஒன்றின் அது விடமாட்டாயாயின், நாணினை விடு
அன்றியே இரண்டும் விடாமை நின்கருத்தாயின், ஒன்றற்கொன்று மறுதலையாய இவ்விரண்டனையும் உடன்தாங்கு மதுகை யான்இலன்

en.1: Good heart, give up desire or give up modesty. I can’t bear them both.
en.2: Good heart, if you won’t give up modesty, give up desire. If you won’t give up that, give up modesty. If you mean to keep both, I haven’t the strength to carry two opposites at once, even if you have. She calls the heart good because keeping both preserves a woman’s womanhood. That is good, but her life can’t stand it.
en.4: O my Heart! Either give up love or give up bashfulness: for, I am unable to support both of them at the same time.
en.5:
Or bid thy love, or bid thy shame depart;
For me, I cannot bear them both, my worthy heart!
en.6: O my good soul, give up either lust or honour, as for me I can endure neither.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: என் நெஞ்சே
அவர் இவ்வாற்றையை அறியாமையின் நொந்துவந்து தலையளி செய்யார் ஆயினார் என்று கருதி
அஃது அறிவித்தற் பொரு்ட்டு, நம்மைப் பிரிந்துபோயவர்பின் ஏங்கிச் செல்லலுற்ற நீ யாதும் அறியாய்

en.1: You pine because he won’t show tender kindness, and you go after the one who left. You are a fool, my heart.
en.2: My heart, you think he shows no kindness only because he doesn’t know how I suffer, and you would go pining after him to tell him. You know nothing. He saw my suffering and left without kindness. It is foolish to think he will come just because you told him, away from the sight of it.
en.4: Thou sighest that he would not return for pity sake, and wouldst go to seek him though he separated deliberately from thee: verily, thou art a simpleton, my Heart!
en.5:
Thou art befooled, my heart, thou followest him who flees from thee;
And still thou yearning criest: ‘He will nor pity show nor love to me.’
en.6: You are a fool, O my soul, to go after my departed one, while you mourn that he is not kind enough to favour you.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: என்னெஞ்சே
காதலர் நின் அகத்தாராக
முன்பு எல்லாம் கண்டுவைத்து இப்பொழுது நீ புறத்துத் தேடிச் செல்கின்றது யாரிடத்து

en.1: Your lover is within you, my heart. Whom are you thinking of, and to whom are you going?
en.2: My heart, your lover is inside you. You have seen it all before, so who is it you go searching for outside? To go looking outside for someone who lives within you, not knowing it, is laughable. Give it up.
en.4: Whom dost thou seek to join, O my Heart, when thou knowest that the beloved is seated within thy own self?
en.5:
My heart! my lover lives within my mind;
Roaming, whom dost thou think to find?
en.6: O my soul, to whom would you repair, while the dear one is within yourself.

uvacha.tr: She says this to mean that she must forget him and bear it.

padaccheda.m: நம்மைக் கூடாவண்ணம் துறந்துபோயினாரை நாம் நம் அகத்து உடையேமாக
முன் இழந்த புறக்கவினேயன்றி நின்ற அகக்கவினும் இழப்பேம்

en.1: If we keep in our heart the one who left us and won’t come near, we will lose still more of our beauty.
en.2: He left us so that we can’t be together. If we keep him within us, we will lose the inner beauty that remains as well as the outer beauty already gone. He has left and won’t come near us, and we can’t forget him, so we will lose even the composure we still have.
en.4: If we entertain any longer within our hearts the beloved that hath abandoned us, we shall only waste ourselves away yet further.
en.5:
If I should keep in mind the man who utterly renounces me,
My soul must suffer further loss of dignity.
en.6: If I retain in my heart him who has left me without befriending me, I shall lose even the (inward) beauty that remains.

uvacha.tr: Her friend tells her to bear it, so that her modesty and reserve aren’t lost. She answers.

padaccheda.m: நாணாகிய தாழினைக் கோத்த நிறையென்னும் கதவினை
காமவேட்கையாகிய கணிச்சி முறியாநின்றது, இனி அவை நிற்றலும் இல்லை, யான் ஆற்றலும் இல்லை,

en.1: The axe of desire breaks down the door of reserve, bolted with modesty.
en.2: The axe of desire is breaking the door of reserve, on which modesty is the bolt. Neither can stand now, and I can’t bear this. While modesty lasts reserve won’t fail, so it is the bolt. Reserve keeps what is inside from others, so it is the door. Both are strong and won’t go of themselves, but her longing removes them together, so it is the axe.
en.4: The door that is bolted with the bolt of modesty will yet yield to the axe of an overpowering love.
en.5:
Of womanly reserve love’s axe breaks through the door,
Barred by the bolt of shame before.
en.6: The axe of lust can break the door of chastity which is bolted with the bolt of modesty.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says desire born in the heart can be held down by the heart. She answers.

padaccheda.m: எல்லாரும் தொழில் ஒழியும் இடையாமத்தும் என் நெஞ்சத்தை ஒறுத்துத் தொழில்கொள்ளாநின்றது
ஆகலான் காமம் என்று சொல்லப்பட்ட ஒன்று கண்ணோட்டம் இன்றாய் இருந்தது

en.1: This thing called desire has no mercy. Even in the dead of night it rules my heart and puts it to work.
en.2: Even at midnight, when everyone stops work, it punishes my heart and works it, so the thing called desire has no kindly regard. The work is sending her heart to him. Desire was born in her heart, and putting your mother to work isn’t the way of the world, so she says “a thing called desire”. She means it can’t be held down.
en.4: Heartless is this thing called Love: for it oppresseth my heart even in the dead of night.
en.5:
What men call love is the one thing of merciless power;
It gives my soul no rest, e’en in the midnight hour.
en.6: Even at midnight is my mind worried by lust, and this one thing, alas! is without mercy.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says women can hide desire. She answers.

padaccheda.m: இக்காமத்தை யான் என்னுள்ளே மறைக்கக் கருதுவேன்
அதனால் என், இஃது என்கருத்தின் வாராது தும்மல்போல வெளிப்பட்டே விடாநின்றது,

en.1: I would hide my desire, but it comes out without warning, like a sneeze.
en.2: I mean to hide this desire inside me, but what use is that? It breaks out against my will, like a sneeze. It can’t be held in, any more than a sneeze can.
en.4: I try indeed to shut my love up within my heart: but like a sneeze it breaketh out of itself without a warning.
en.5:
I would my love conceal, but like a sneeze
It shows itself, and gives no warning sign.
en.6: I would conceal my lust, but alas, it yields not to my will, but breaks out like a sneeze.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: இன்றின் ஊங்கெ்ல்லாம் யான் என்னை நிறையுடையேன் என்று கருதியிருந்தேன்
அதனால் என், இன்று என்காமம் மறைத்தலைக் கடந்து மன்றின்கண் வெளிப்படாநின்றது

en.1: I used to say I had reserve. Now my desire has gone past hiding, out into the public square.
en.2: Until today I thought I had reserve. What use was that? Today my desire has gone past hiding and come out in the public square, so that many people know it. It is no longer in my power.
en.4: I was proud that I was correct and decorous in my behaviour: but alas! love rendeth every veil and showeth itself in public.
en.5:
In womanly reserve I deemed myself beyond assail;
But love will come abroad, and casts away the veil.
en.6: I say I would be firm, but alas, my malady breaks out from its concealment and appears in public.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says they should forget the man who has forgotten them. She answers.

padaccheda.m: தம்மை அகன்றுசென்றார் பின் செல்லாது தாமும் அகன்றுநிற்கும் நிறையுடைமை
காமநோயினை உறாதார் அறிவது ஒன்றன்றி உற்றார் அறிவது ஒன்றன்று

en.1: The great dignity of not going after those who hurt you is not something known to people with the sickness of desire.
en.2: The reserve that doesn’t follow those who left, but keeps away from them in turn, is known only to people of pride who don’t have the sickness of desire. She says “hurt” because he makes time that should pass in joy pass in pain. Going after him means thinking of him without a break. My heart goes even to one who doesn’t value it, and I know no other way.
en.4: The stern self-respect that refuseth to seek the beloved though he hath cruelly deserted, is a thing unknown to the lovesick fair.
en.5:
The dignity that seeks not him who acts as foe,
Is the one thing that loving heart can never know.
en.6: The dignity that would not go after an absent lover is not known to those who are stricken by love.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: என்னை அகன்று சென்றார் பின்னே யான் சேறலை வேண்டுதலான்
என்னை உற்றதுயர் எத்தன்மையது, சால நன்று

en.1: It makes me want to go after the one who hurt me. What a fine thing, this sorrow that has come to me!
en.2: What kind of sorrow has come to me, making me want to go after the one who left me? A very fine one! “Fine” is scorn. She means this sickness of desire can’t be spoken of or listened to, and is utterly cruel.
en.4: How thou lovest me, O Grief! Thou wantest me to follow after him who hath deserted me cruelly!
en.5:
My grief how full of grace, I pray you see!
It seeks to follow him that hateth me.
en.6: The sorrow I have endured by desiring to go after my absent lover, in what way is it excellent?

uvacha.tr: He came back from a courtesan, and she lost her reserve and went to him. Her friend asks why she didn’t sulk, and she answers.

padaccheda.m: நம்மால் விரும்பப்பட்டவர் வந்து, காமத்தால் நாம் விரும்பியவற்றைச் செய்யுமளவின்
நாண் என்று ஒன்றையும் அறியமாட்டேமாய் இருந்தேம்

en.1: When the one we cherish does, in desire, all we long for, we don’t even know there is such a thing as modesty.
en.2: When the man I desired came and, in desire, did what I longed for, we knew nothing at all of modesty. Modesty here is shame at touching a chest that courtesans have touched. What she longed for is the lovemaking her craving had dwelt on. Seeing her own fault in joining him unthinkingly, she says “we”, to include her friend.
en.4: If the beloved but favour us with his love, we at once forget all our reserve.
en.5:
No sense of shame my gladdened mind shall prove,
When he returns my longing heart to bless with love.
en.6: I know nothing like shame when my beloved does from love (just) what is desired (by me).

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நம் நிறையாகி அவர் அணை அழிக்கும் தானை
பல பொய்களை வல்ல கள்வனுடைய தாழ்ந்த சொற்கள் அன்றோ

en.1: Aren’t the humble words of that thief of many tricks the army that breaks down our womanhood?
en.2: The army that destroys the wall of our reserve is the humble talk of this thief, skilled in many lies, so how could it stand? Womanhood here means reserve. I had planned to sulk and not give way, but he came so that it all vanished and I was ahead of him in union. His humble words claim he has more loving-kindness than I do.
en.4: It is the subdued speech of that false one skilled in many a wily art, that breaketh through all the defences of our womanly decorum.
en.5:
The words of that deceiver, versed in every wily art,
Are instruments that break through every guard of woman’s heart!
en.6: Are not the enticing words of my trick-abounding roguish lover the weapon that breaks away my feminine firmness.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: அவர் வந்தபொழுது புலக்கக்கடவேன் என்று கருதி முன் நில்லாது பிறிது ஓர் இடத்துப் போயினேன்
போயும், என்னெஞ்சம் நிறையில்லாது அறைபோய் அவரோடு கலத்தல் தொடங்குதலை அறிந்து, இனி அது வாயாது என்று புல்லினேன்

en.1: I went off meaning to sulk. I saw my heart was ready to join him, and I embraced him.
en.2: Meaning to sulk when he came, I went off somewhere else and didn’t stand before him. But my heart, with no reserve, betrayed me and began to join him. Seeing that, I knew sulking wouldn’t work, and I embraced him. The heart is the means of sulking, and it had become the means of union.
en.4: I wanted to go away in a huff: but I went and embraced him, for I saw that my heart had already joined him.
en.5:
‘I’ll shun his greeting’; saying thus with pride away I went:
I held him in my arms, for straight I felt my heart relent.
en.6: I said I would feign dislike and so went (away); (but) I embraced him the moment I saw my mind begin to unite with him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நிணத்தைத் தீயின்கண்ணே இட்டால், அஃது உருகுமாறுபோலத் தம் காதலரைக் கண்டால் நிறையழிந்து உருகும் நெஞ்சினையுடைய மகளிர்க்கு
அவர் புணர யாம் ஊடிப் பின்பு உணராது அந்நிலையே நிற்கக்கடவேம் என்று கருதுதல் உண்டாகுமோ, ஆகாது

en.1: Can those whose hearts are like fat in a fire say, when they come together, that they will hold to their sulk?
en.2: Fat put in a fire melts, and so do the hearts of women when they see their lovers, and their reserve is gone. When he draws close, can such women think they will sulk and stay that way without relenting? They can’t. Coming together here means coming very near, or meeting. I am such a woman, so sulking wasn’t possible for me.
en.4: Can they ever think of refusing to be reconciled, whose heart melteth even as fat in the fire?
en.5:
‘We’ll stand aloof and then embrace’: is this for them to say,
Whose hearts are as the fat that in the blaze dissolves away?
en.6: Is it possible for those whose hearts melt like fat in the fire to say that they can feign a strong dislike and remain so?

uvacha.tr: She is eager to see him, and she says this.

padaccheda.w: அவர் சென்ற நாள் ஒற்றி விரல் தேய்ந்த
padaccheda.m: அவர் நம்மைப் பிரிந்துபோய நாள்கள் சுவரின்கண் இழைத்தவற்றைத் தொட்டு எண்ணுதலான் என் விரல்கள் தேய்ந்தன
அதுவேயன்றி, அவர் வரும்வழி பார்த்து என்கண்களும் ஒளியிழந்து புல்லியவாயின, இவ்வாறாயும் அவர் வரவு உண்டாயிற்றில்லை

en.1: My eyes have lost their light and grown dull, and my fingers have worn down from touching off the days since he left.
en.2: Touching the marks on the wall to count the days since he left, I have worn down my fingers. Watching the road he will come by, my eyes too have lost their light and can’t make out fine things. Even so he hasn’t come. How can I see him now? She does these things without a break, not once, and that is her eagerness.
en.4: My eyes have lost their lustre and grown dull, and my fingers have worn away for counting of the days that I have noted on the wall.
en.5:
My eyes have lost their brightness, sight is dimmed, my fingers worn,
With noting on the wall the days since I was left forlorn.
en.6: My finger has worn away by marking (on the wall) the days he has been absent while my eyes have lost their lustre and begin to fail.

uvacha.tr: Her friend tells her she can’t go on thinking of him without a break, and should forget him a little. She answers.

padaccheda.m: விளங்காநின்ற இழையினையுடையாய்
காதலரை யான் இன்று யான் மறப்பேனாயின்
மேலும், காரிகை என்னை நீப்ப என் தோள்கள் வளை கழல்வனாவாம்

en.1: You in your bright jewels, if I forget him today, my beauty will leave me and the bangles will slip from my arms.
en.2: You in your bright jewels, if I forget him today, the day I am dying, then in my next birth too beauty will leave me and the bangles will slip from my arms. “Bright jewels” hints that you care nothing for this. If I think of him at this last moment I can reach him in the next life and be happy, so I mustn’t forget him.
en.4: What if I forget today, my maid? My beauty hath already left me and my bracelet hath slipped off my arm.
en.5:
O thou with gleaming jewels decked, could I forget for this one day,
Henceforth these bracelets from my arms will slip, my beauty worn away.
en.6: O you bright-jewelled maid, if I forget (him) today, my shoulders will lose their beauty even in the other life and make my bracelets loose.

reading.note: மேல் can mean “on” or “hereafter”. He takes it as hereafter: she is dying today, and forgetting him now would cost her in her next birth.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: இன்பம் நுகர்தலை நச்சாது, வேறலை நச்சி நாம் துணையாதலை இகழ்ந்து நம் ஊக்கம் துணையாகப் போயினார்
அவற்றை இகழ்ந்து ஈண்டு வருதலை நச்சுதலான், யான் இவ் எல்லையினும் உளேன் ஆயினேன்

en.1: He left wanting victory, with his will for his companion. Wanting his return, I am still alive.
en.2: He didn’t want pleasure. He wanted victory, scorned me as his companion and went with his own will as his companion. Because I want him to scorn those things and come back here, I have lived even this long. That wanting keeps me alive. Without it I would die.
en.4: He parted from me longing for conquests: and if I live yet, it is for the longing of his return.
en.5:
On victory intent,
His mind sole company he went;
And I yet life sustain,
And long to see his face again!
en.6: I still live by longing for the arrival of him who has gone out of love for victory and with valour as his guide.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நீங்கிய காமத்தராய் நம்மைப் பிரிந்துபோயவர் மேற்கூறிய காமத்துடனே தங்கண் வருதலை நினைந்து
என்செஞ்சு வருத்தம் ஒழிந்து மேன்மேல் பணைத்து எழாநின்றது

en.1: Thinking of the return of the one who left, with all the desire we shared, my heart grows branches and climbs.
en.2: He left with desire put aside. I think of him coming back to me with that desire gathered again, and my heart drops its pain and rises, branching higher and higher. A man leaving for his work doesn’t look to the joys of desire, and when it is done he looks to nothing else. Branching is what a tree does, laid here on the heart. Without this thought I would die.
en.4: He gave my company up and parted without any regard to my feelings but yet for the mere thinking of his speedy return my heart swelleth with joy!
en.5:
‘He comes again, who left my side, and I shall taste love’s joy,’—
My heart with rapture swells, when thoughts like these my mind employ.
en.6: My heart is rid of its sorrow and swells with rapture to think of my absent lover returning with his love.

uvacha.tr: Her friend tells her he is coming, and that she mustn’t give way and grow pale. She answers.

padaccheda.m: என் கண்கள் ஆரும் வகை என்கொண்கனை யான் காண்பேனாக
அங்ஙனம் கண்டபின் என் மெ்ல்லிய தோளின்கண் பசப்புத்தானே நீங்கும்

en.1: Let me see my husband until my eyes are full. Once I have, the pallor will leave my soft shoulders.
en.2: Let me see my husband until my eyes are sated. Once I have, the pallor on my soft shoulders will go by itself. She says this as a wish. Only hearing that he is coming won’t remove it.
en.4: Only let my eyes take their fill of the sight of my beloved: pallor will then no more be seen on my wasted arm.
en.5:
O let me see my spouse again and sate these longing eyes!
That instant from my wasted frame all pallor flies.
en.6: May I look on my lover till I am satisfied and thereafter will vanish the sallowness of my slender shoulders.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: இத்துணைநாளும் வாராக் கொண்கன் ஒருநாள் என்கண் வருவானாக
வந்தால் பையுளைச் செய்கின்ற இந்நோய் எல்லாம் கெட அவ்வமிழ்தத்தை வாயில் களைந்தானும் பருகக் கடவேன்

en.1: Let my husband come, just one day. I will drink until all this sickness of grief is gone.
en.2: My husband hasn’t come in all these days. Let him come to me one day. If he comes, I will drink that ambrosia until this sickness that makes me grieve is gone. She means that within that one day she will destroy even the sickness still to come.
en.4: Let my spouse but return home: and then in one day I shall drink the nectar of his presence and bid farewell to this wasting disease.
en.5:
O let my spouse but come again to me one day!
Ill drink that nectar: wasting grief shall flee away.
en.6: May my husband return some day; and then will I enjoy (him) so as to destroy all this agonizing sorrow.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: கண்போற் சிறந்த கேளிர் வருவராயின்
அவர் வரவு நீட்டித்தமை நோக்கி யான் புலக்கக்கடவேனோ
அன்றி என் ஆற்றாமைநோக்கிப் புல்லக்கடவேனோ
அவ்விரண்டும் வேண்டுதலான் அவ்விருசெயல்களையும் விரவக்கடவேனோ, யாது செய்யக்கடவேன்

en.1: When the one as dear as my eyes comes, shall I sulk, shall I embrace him, or shall I join with him?
en.2: When the one as dear as my eyes comes, shall I sulk because he stayed away so long? Shall I embrace him because I can’t bear it? Or, wanting both, shall I blend the two? They can’t be mixed in one moment, so she asks. She means to do all three, and that is her eagerness. Some take the last as: shall I join with him as in the days before we parted?
en.4: When the beloved who is dear even as my eyes cometh home, shall I sulk for his long absence? or shall I embrace him? or shall I do both?
en.5:
Shall I draw back, or yield myself, or shall both mingled be,
When he returns, my spouse, dear as these eyes to me.
en.6: On the return of him who is as dear as my eyes, am I displeased or am I to embrace (him); or am I to do both?

reading.note: கலப்பேன் can mean to mix or to join. He takes it as mixing the sulk and the embrace.

uvacha.tr: He left to help the ruler in need, and the work drags on. He thinks of her and says this to himself.

padaccheda.m: வேந்தன் வினைசெய்தலைப் புரிந்து வெல்வானாக
யாமும் மனைவியைச் சென்று கூடி ஆண்தை மாலைப்பொழுதிற்கு விருந்து அயர்வோமாக

en.1: May the ruler throw himself into the work and win. Then I will go to my wife and give the evening a feast.
en.2: May the ruler carry out his work and win. Let me go and join my wife, and feast the evening there. Evenings on campaign have no welcome and no adorning. It is said before the work is done, and that is the eagerness. He rejects the view that she is speaking: she wouldn’t say “may the ruler win” and leave out her husband.
en.4: May the prince begin the battle at once and triumph! And may I return in the evening and feast at home with my loved one!
en.5:
O would my king would fight, o’ercome, divide the spoil;
At home, to-night, the banquet spread should crown the toil.
en.6: Let the king fight and gain (victories); (but) let me be united to my wife and feast the evening.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: சேணிடைச் சென்ற தங்காதலர் மீண்டுவரக்குறித்த நாளையுட்கொண்டு, அது வருந்துணையும் உயிர்தாங்கி வருந்தும் மகளிர்க்கு
ஒருநாள் பலநாள் போல நெடிதாகக்காட்டும்

en.1: For those who pine, counting on the day when the one far away returns, one day passes like seven.
en.2: Women who hold in mind the day set for their lover’s return from far away, and bear to stay alive until it comes, find one day feels as long as many. Seven stands for a great many. The man is laying her suffering on other women, which shows she isn’t the speaker.
en.4: To those who count the days and yearn for the return of the beloved who is away, one single day will creep along with the slowness of seven.
en.5:
One day will seem like seven, to those who watch and yearn
For that glad day when wanderers from afar return.
en.6: To those who suffer waiting for the day of return of their distant lovers one day is as long as seven days.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: காதலி நம் பிரிவினை ஆற்றாது, உள்ளம் உடைந்து இறந்துபட்டவழி
நம்மைப் பெறக்கடவள் ஆனால் என்
அதுவன்றியே பெற்றால் என்
அதுவன்றியே மெய்யுறக் கலந்தால்தான் என், இவை ஒன்றானும் பயனில்லை

en.1: Once her heart has broken and spilled, what use is it if she will have me, if she has me, if she holds me?
en.2: If my beloved can’t bear the parting and her heart breaks and she dies, what good is it if she is to have me, or if she has me, or even if we join in the body? None of these is any use. So I must get there before that, and this is his eagerness. If she were the speaker it would be grief, not eagerness.
en.4: Of what avail will be my getting back or the meeting or even the hearty embrace, if the heart of my loved one be broken before then?
en.5:
What’s my return, the meeting hour, the wished-for greeting worth,
If she heart-broken lie, with all her life poured forth?
en.6: After (my wife) has died of a broken heart, what good will there be if she is to receive me, has received me, or has even embraced me?

uvacha.tr: Reunited, he shows her fresh delight for many days, and she fears it means something. He reads this from her signs and speaks to her.

padaccheda.m: நீசொல்லாது மறைத்தாய் ஆயினும்
அதற்கு உடம்படாதே நின்னைக் கைகடந்து
நின் கண்களே எமக்குச் சொல்லல் உறுவது ஒருகாரியம் உண்டாய் இராநின்றது, இனியதனை நீயே தெளியச்சொல்வாயாக

en.1: Though you hide it, your kohl-dark eyes slip your control and refuse. There is something they want to say.
en.2: You say nothing and hide it, but your eyes won’t agree. They slip from your control, and there is something they are trying to tell me. Now say it plainly yourself. Hiding here means holding back out of modesty. She has changed because she thinks he means to leave. He sees it from her signs, and lets her know he doesn’t.
en.4: Thou mayest try to conceal, my love, but thy eye refuseth to be restrained, and telleth me that there is some strange thought in thy breast.
en.5:
Thou hid’st it, yet thine eye, disdaining all restraint,
Something, I know not what, would utter of complaint.
en.6: Though you would conceal (your feelings), your painted eyes would not, for, transgressing (their bounds), they tell (me) something.

uvacha.tr: Out of modesty she won’t say it, so he speaks to her friend.

padaccheda.w: கண் நிறைந்த காரிகைக் காம்பு ஏர் தோள் பேதைக்கு
padaccheda.m: என்கண்நிறைந்த அழகினையும், வேயை ஒத்த தோளினையும் உடைய நின்பேதைக்கு
பெண்பாலாரிடத்து நிறைந்த மடமை அவ்வளவன்றி மிகுந்தது

en.1: This simple girl, with beauty that fills my eyes and arms like bamboo, has a woman’s nature in great measure.
en.2: Your simple girl, whose beauty fills my eyes and whose arms are like bamboo, has more than the simple-mindedness that fills all women. He says this because she takes on herself a parting that doesn’t exist, and fears it.
en.4: Ah! More than a woman’s reserve hath my artless one, whose beauty filleth my eyes and whose arms are even as bamboo stems.
en.5:
The simple one whose beauty fills mine eye, whose shoulders curve
Like bambû stem, hath all a woman’s modest sweet reserve.
en.6: Unusually great is the female simplicity of your maid whose beauty fills my eyes and whose shoulders resemble the bamboo.

reading.note: பெண்நிறைந்த நீர்மை is the nature that fills a woman. He takes it as simple-mindedness, because she fears a parting that isn’t coming.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: கோக்கப்பட்ட பளிக்குமணி யகத்துக் கிடந்து புறத்துப் புலனாம் நூல்போல
இம்மடந்தையது அணியகத்துக் கிடந்து புறத்துப் புலனாகின்றதொரு குறிப்பு உண்டு

en.1: Like the thread that shows through a bead, something shows through this young woman’s adornment.
en.2: Like the thread that lies inside a strung crystal bead and shows outside, a sign lies within this young woman’s beauty and shows outside. The beauty is what comes from their union, and the sign doesn’t belong with it, yet it is there. I can’t make it out, and you must find out and tell me.
en.4: Even as the thread that is seen through the crystal bead, there is a thought that is now passing in her bosom, but which is yet plainly visible.
en.5:
As through the crystal beads is seen the thread on which they’re strung,
So in her beauty gleams some thought that cannot find a tongue.
en.6: There is something that is implied in the beauty of this woman, like the thread that is visible in a garland of gems.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: முகையது முகிழ்ப்பின் உளதாய்ப் புறத்துப் புலனாகாத நாற்றம்போல
நின் பேதை என்னொடு நகக்கருதும் நகையது முகிழ்ப்பின் உளதாய்ப் புறத்துப் புலனாகாததோர் குறிப்புண்டு

en.1: As fragrance lies inside a closed bud, something lies inside the budding smile of this simple girl.
en.2: As fragrance lies in a swelling bud and doesn’t show outside, a sign lies in the swelling smile your simple girl means to give me, and it doesn’t show outside. The swelling comes from ripeness, and the smile comes from the joy of union.
en.4: Even as the fragrance in the bud that is not yet blown, there is a secret meaning in the half-smile of this artless one.
en.5:
As fragrance in the opening bud, some secret lies
Concealed in budding smile of this dear damsel’s eyes.
en.6: There is something in the unmatured smile of this maid like the fragrance that is contained in an unblossomed bud.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நெருங்கிய வளைகளை உடையாள் என்கண் இல்லாதது ஒன்றனை உட்கொண்டு அது காரணமாக என்னை மறைத்துப்போன குறிப்பு

padaccheda.w: உறு துயர் தீர்க்கும் மருந்து ஒன்று உடைத்து
padaccheda.m: என் மிக்கதுயரைத் தீர்க்கும் மருந்தாவது ஒன்றனை உடைத்து

en.1: The stealth of the woman in close-set bangles, done and gone past me, holds a medicine for the great pain I feel.
en.2: She of the close-set bangles has taken something into her mind that isn’t in me, and has hidden from me because of it. That hidden sign holds the medicine for my pain. What she took in is a parting, and what she hides is a resolve to go with me. My pain comes from doing good and getting harm. The medicine is for you to assure her there is no parting.
en.4: The cunning with which she concealed her rising thought and left hath a charm to cure the anguish of my heart.
en.5:
The secret wiles of her with thronging armlets decked,
Are medicines by which my rising grief is checked.
en.6: The well-meant departure of her whose bangles are tight-fitting contains a remedy that can cure my great sorrow.

uvacha.tr: She has read his intent, and she tells it to her friend, who has come to reassure her.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் வந்து தம்பிரிவினான் ஆய துன்பத்தினை மிகவும் ஆற்றி நாம் மகிழும் வண்ணம் கலக்கின்ற கலவி
இருந்தவாற்றான் மேலும் அத்துன்பத்தினை அரிதாக ஆற்றியிருந்து அவர் அன்பின்மையை நினையும் தன்மை உடைத்து

en.1: He comforts me so fully and joins me so gladly, but in it I see myself bearing pain again and thinking he has no love.
en.2: He has come and eased the pain of parting, and he joins me so that I rejoice. Yet as things stand, this holds in it that I will bear that pain again, with difficulty, and think of his lack of love. It comes from his intent to leave, so in the end it turns bitter.
en.4: He is overkind and sweet to me: I fear there is something in his heart which he is hardly able to conceal: and it forebodeth to me a second departure.
en.5:
While lovingly embracing me, his heart is only grieved:
It makes me think that I again shall live of love bereaved.
en.6: The embrace that fills me with comfort and gladness is capable of enduring (my former) sorrow and meditating on his want of love.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: குளிர்ந்த துறையையுடையவன் நம்மை மெய்யாற் கூடியிருந்தே மனத்தாற் பிரிந்தமையை
அவன் குறி்பபான் அறிதற்குரிய நம்மினும் இவ்வளைகள் முன்னே அறிந்தன

en.1: My bangles knew before we did that the man of the cool shore had drawn away.
en.2: The man of the cool shore is with me in body, but in his mind he has parted from me. I should know this from his signs, but these bangles knew first. His intent is already formed, so she says he has drawn away. Her arms thinned before she clearly understood, and she puts that on the bangles and speaks as if they could feel.
en.4: My bracelet hath read the coolness in the heart of my gracious lord even sooner than my own self.
en.5:
My severance from the lord of this cool shore,
My very armlets told me long before.
en.6: My bracelets have understood before me the (mental) separation of him who rules the cool seashore.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: எங்காதலர் பிரிந்து போயினார் நெருநற்றே
அப்பிரிவிற்கு யாமும் மேனிபசந்து ஏழுநாளுடையம் ஆயினேம்

en.1: It was only yesterday my lover left, and I have been pale in body for seven days.
en.2: My lover went only yesterday, and I have been pale over it for seven days. The tenderness he showed yesterday told me his parting was decided, so she says he left yesterday. She has suspected it for seven days and turned pale that first day, so she says seven. In this way she makes his intent to leave known.
en.4: My beloved parted only yesterday: but it is seven days since my form hath lost its freshness!
en.5:
My loved one left me, was it yesterday?
Days seven my pallid body wastes away!
en.6: It was but yesterday my lover departed (from me); and it is seven days since my complexion turned sallow.

uvacha.tr: Her friend has read her signs, and she makes them known to him.

padaccheda.m: (யானது தெளிவித்தவழித் தெளியாது) அவர் பிரிய யான் ஈண்டிருப்பின் இவை நில்லாவெனத் தன் தொடியை நோக்கி
அதற்கு ஏதுவாக இவை மெலியும் எனத் தன்மென் தோள்களையும் நோக்கி
பின் இவ்விரண்டும் நிகழாமல்நீர் நடந்து காத்தல் வேண்டும் என்த் தன் அடியையும் நோக்கி
அங்ஙனம் அவள் செய்த குறிப்பு உடன்போக்காயிருந்தது

en.1: She looked at her bangles, looked at her soft arms, looked at her feet. That is what she did there.
en.2: I reassured her and she wasn’t reassured. She looked at her bangles: if he leaves and I stay, these won’t stay on. She looked at her soft arms, which will thin and cause it. She looked at her feet: you must walk and save me from both. So what she did there was a sign that she will go with you. If you mean to leave, it is there to stop you.
en.4: She looked at her bracelet and her tender arm and then she looked at her feet: these are the signs that she made to me.
en.5:
She viewed her tender arms, she viewed the armlets from them slid;
She viewed her feet: all this the lady did.
en.6: She looked at her bracelets, her tender shoulders, and her feet; this was what she did there (significantly).

uvacha.tr: He makes it known to her friend that he doesn’t mean to leave.

padaccheda.m: மகளிர், தம் காமநோயினைத் தோழியர்க்கும் வாயாற் சொல்லாது கண்ணினாற் சொல்லி அது தீர்க்கவேண்டும் என்று அவரை இரவாது உடன்போதல் குறித்துத் தம் அடியினை இரத்தல்
தமக்கு இயல்பாகிய பெண்மை மேலும் ஓர் பெண்மைஉடைத்தென்று சொல்லுவர் அறிந்தோர்

en.1: To tell the sickness of desire with the eyes and beg: they say this is womanhood on top of womanhood.
en.2: Women don’t speak their sickness of desire even to their friends. They tell it with their eyes, and instead of begging friends to end it, they beg their own feet to go with him. Those who know call this a womanhood beyond their natural womanhood. Hearing her resolve from the friend, he praises it as if of others, and shows he won’t leave.
en.4: She telleth me of the pangs of separation and prayeth for permission to accompany me if I go: how she surpasseth womanhood’s self in delicacy to tell this only with her eyes!
en.5:
To show by eye the pain of love, and for relief to pray,
Is womanhood’s most womanly device, men say.
en.6: To express their love-sickness by their eyes and resort to begging bespeaks more than ordinary female excellence.

uvacha.tr: Her friend teases her: he means to leave, so why don’t you sulk? She answers.

padaccheda.m: நினைந்த துணையானே களிப்பு எய்தலும்
கண்ட துணையானே மகிழ்வு எய்தலும்
கள்ளுண்டார்க்கு இல்லை, காமம் உடையார்க்கு உண்டு

en.1: To be drunk at a thought and elated at a glance: toddy can’t do this, but desire can.
en.2: Elation at a mere thought and joy at a mere sight don’t come to those who drink toddy. They come to those who have desire. The first leaves the senses whole, and the second doesn’t. Toddy gives both only when it is drunk. With desire like this, how could I sulk?
en.4: Rapture at the very thought and delight at the mere seeing belong not to wine: they belong only unto love.
en.5:
Gladness at the thought, rejoicing at the sight,
Not palm-tree wine, but love, yields such delight.
en.6: To please by thought and cheer by sight is peculiar, not to liquor but lust.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: மகளிர்க்குக் காமம் பனையளவினும் மிக உண்டாமாயின்
அவரால், தங்காதலரோடு தினையளவும் ஊடுதல் செய்யாமை வேண்டப்படும்

en.1: When desire comes full, as tall as a palmyra, you must not sulk even by a millet seed.
en.2: When a woman’s desire grows beyond the size of a palmyra, she must not sulk with her lover even by a millet seed. If she sulks, her suffering grows. She seems to be giving others good advice, but she is telling of her own eagerness.
en.4: When love exceedeth even the measure of a palmyra tree, the desire to sulk can never enter the heart even to the extent of a millet seed.
en.5:
When as palmyra tall, fulness of perfect love we gain,
Distrust can find no place small as the millet grain.
en.6: If women have a lust that exceeds even the measure of the palmyra fruit, they will not desire (to feign) dislike even as much as the millet.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நம்மை அவமதித்துத் தான் வேண்டியனவே செய்யுமாயினும்
கொண்கனை என்கண்கள் காணாது அமைகின்றன இல்லை

en.1: Though he shows me no regard and does just as he likes, my eyes can’t rest without seeing my husband.
en.2: Though he slights me and does only what he wants, my eyes won’t be content without seeing my husband. She lays her own eagerness on her eyes. Being like this, how could I sulk?
en.4: Though he careth not for me and doth only as he pleaseth, my eyes will not rest unless they behold him.
en.5:
Although, his will his only law, he lightly value me,
My heart knows no repose unless my lord I see.
en.6: Though my eyes disregard me and do what is pleasing to my husband, still will they not be satisfied unless they see him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: தோழீ
காதலரைக் காணாமுன் அவர்செய்த தவற்றைத் தன்னொடுநினைந்து யான் அவரோடு ஊடுதற்கண்ணே சென்றேன்
கண்டபின் என் நெஞ்சு அதனை மறந்து கூடுதற்கண்ணே சென்றது

en.1: I went there to sulk, my friend, but my heart forgot that and went to join him.
en.2: Friend, before I saw him I thought over his fault and set out to sulk with him. Once I saw him my heart forgot that and went to union. What use was my going? My heart betrayed me at that moment, so the sulk was never finished.
en.4: I wanted indeed to go away in a huff, my maid: but my heart forgot it and ran after union with the beloved.
en.5:
My friend, I went prepared to show a cool disdain;
My heart, forgetting all, could not its love restrain.
en.6: O my friend I was prepared to feign displeasure, but my mind forgetting it was ready to embrace him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: முன்னெல்லாங் கண்டிருந்தும் எழுதும் காலத்து அஞ்சனக் கோலின்இயல்பு காணமாட்டாத கண்ணேபோல்
கொண்கனது தவறு, காணாதவிடத்தெல்லாம் கண்டிருந்து, அவனைக் க்ணடவிடத்துக் காண மாட்டேன்

en.1: Like the eye that can’t see the stick painting it with kohl, I can’t see my husband’s faults when I see him.
en.2: The eye sees the kohl stick at other times, but while it is being painted it can’t see the stick’s blackness. So too I see my husband’s fault wherever he isn’t, and when I see him I can’t see it. This is my nature, so sulking won’t succeed in future either.
en.4: Even as the eye seeth not the blackness of the pencil when it is being painted, even so I see no blemish in my beloved when he is near.
en.5:
The eye sees not the rod that paints it; nor can I
See any fault, when I behold my husband nigh.
en.6: Like the eyes which see not the pencil that paints it, I cannot see my husband’s fault (just) when I meet him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: கொண்கனை யான் காணும்பொழுது அவன் தவறாயவற்றைக் காண்கின்றிலேன்
காணாதபொழுது அவையேயல்லது, பிறவற்றைக் காண்கின்றிலேன்

en.1: When I see him I see no faults. When I don’t see him I see nothing but faults.
