en.2: When I see my husband, I don’t see his faults. When I don’t see him, I see nothing else. The faults I told you about before aren’t in sight now, so I didn’t sulk.
en.4: When he is before me I can see no faults in him: but when I see him not, I can see nothing in him but faults.
en.5:
When him I see, to all his faults I’m blind;
But when I see him not, nothing but faults I find.
en.6: When I see my husband, I do not see any faults; but when I do not see him, I do not see anything but faults.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: தம்மை ஈர்த்துக்கொண்டு போதல் அறிந்துவைத்து, ஒழுகுகின்ற புனலுட் பாய்வார் செயல் போல
புலவி முடிவுபோகாமை அறிந்து வைத்துக் கொண்கனோடு புலந்து பெறுவதென்

en.1: Like people who jump into a flood knowing it will sweep them away, what use is it to sulk, knowing it will fail?
en.2: Like those who leap into a running flood knowing it will carry them off, what do I gain by sulking with my husband, knowing the sulk won’t hold to its end? If the text reads “I knew it fails”, then: like those who leap in to learn how the water carries, I once sulked to learn its end, found it fails, and shouldn’t do it again.
en.4: Who will jump into a stream knowing that it hath a treacherous undercurrent that will carry him away? and how should I take to sulking who know that I cannot hold on to it when he is near?
en.5:
As those of rescue sure, who plunge into the stream,
So did I anger feign, though it must falsehood seem?
en.6: Like those who leap into a stream which they know will carry them off, why should a wife feign dislike which she knows cannot hold out long?

uvacha.tr: Her friend sees her eagerness for union, and says this to him.

padaccheda.m: வஞ்சகா
தன்னை உண்டு களித்தார்க்கு இளிவரத்தக்க இன்னாதவற்றைச் செய்யினும், அவரால் மேன்மேல் விரும்பப்படுவதாய கள்ளுப்போலும்
எங்கட்கு நின்மார்பு

en.1: Your chest, you thief, is like toddy to those drunk on it. However shameful the harm it does, they want more.
en.2: You deceiver, your chest is to us like toddy, which does shameful harm to those who drink it and is craved all the more. That harm is the loss of modesty, reserve, good conduct and good sense. Your chest does this to us, and we want it more and more. That is why she calls him a deceiver.
en.4: Wine is never unwelcome to the drunkard though it maketh him hang down his head in shame: even so is thy bosom to me, O false one!
en.5:
Though shameful ill it works, dear is the palm-tree wine
To drunkards; traitor, so to me that breast of thine!
en.6: O you rogue! your breast is to me what liquor is to those who rejoice in it, though it only gives them an unpleasant disgrace.

uvacha.tr: She is sulking and won’t be won over by his pleading, and he says this.

padaccheda.m: காமவின்பம் மலரினும் மெல்லிதாய் இருக்கும்
அங்ஙனம் மெல்லிதாதலை அறிந்து அதன் செவ்வியைப் பெறுவார் உலகத்துச்சிலர்

en.1: Desire is softer than a flower. Few ever find it at its peak.
en.2: The joy of desire is softer than a flower, which loses its fresh scent at a touch. Few in this world know that and reach its peak. Two people must match in intent, longing, enjoyment and joy at one time, with the right place, time and means. If any of these differs a little, it wilts. Our intent doesn’t match, so I don’t have it. He says this to end her sulk.
en.4: Even tenderer than a flower is love: and few there be who know its delicacy and deal with it gently.
en.5:
Love is tender as an opening flower. In season due
To gain its perfect bliss is rapture known to few.
en.6: Sexual delight is more delicate than a flower, and few are those who understand its real nature.

uvacha.tr: She is still sulking, and he goes on.

padaccheda.m: காதலி முன்னொருஞான்று, புல்லல் விதுப்பினாற் சென்ற என்னோடு தன்கண் மாத்திரத்தான் ஊடி
புல்லுதலை என்னினும்தான் விதும்பலால், அதுதன்னையும் அப்பொழுதே மறந்து கூடிவிட்டாள்

en.1: She sulked with her eyes alone, then gave way, more eager to embrace than I was.
en.2: Once, when I went eagerly to embrace her, she sulked with her eyes alone, with no word, her eyes only reddening. Then, more eager for the embrace than I was, she forgot even that and joined me. I am the same man now, so this woman who stands sulking with no eagerness is not she. That woman wouldn’t keep up a sulk for long.
en.4: There were the sulks in her eye when she saw me: but when I approached, she flew to my arms even quicker than I myself to hers.
en.5:
Her eye, as I drew nigh one day, with anger shone;
By love o’er powered, her tenderness surpassed my own.
en.6: She once feigned dislike in her eyes, but the warmth of her embrace exceeded my own.

uvacha.tr: He is at fault, yet her heart won’t think of sulking. She says this to it.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே
அவருடைய நெஞ்சு நம்மை நினையாது அவர்க்காய்நிற்றல் கண்டு வைத்தும்
நீ எமக்காய் நில்லாது அவரை நினைத்தற்காரணம் யாது

en.1: You see how his heart stands by him. Why, heart, won’t you stand by me?
en.2: Heart, you have seen that his heart doesn’t think of us and stands by him. Why won’t you stand by me, instead of thinking of him? Standing by me here means agreeing to sulk. People who can’t work out a task for themselves will do it by watching someone else, and you won’t do even that.
en.4: Thou seest how his heart serveth his will: then, how is it that thou obeyest not me, O my Heart?
en.5:
You see his heart is his alone:
O heart, why not be all my own?
en.6: O my soul, although you have seen how his soul stands by him, how is it you do not stand by me.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: என் நெஞ்சே
மேலும் நாம்மாட்டு அன்புடையர் ஆகாதவரை உள்ளவாறு அறிந்தவிடத்தும்
நாம் சென்றால் வெகுளார் என்பதுபற்றி நீ அவர் மாட்டுச் செல்லா நின்றாய், இப்பெற்றியது மேலும் ஓர் அறியாமை உண்டோ

en.1: Even when you see he isn’t drawn to us, my heart, you go to him, sure he won’t be angry.
en.2: My heart, even when you know for certain that he has no loving-kindness for us, you go to him, sure that he won’t be angry if we come. Can there be greater ignorance? You rely on his old regard to keep him from anger. Will that get you what you want?
en.4: Thou seest, my Heart, how he neglecteth me: and yet thou consortest with him as if he were thy friend!
en.5:
’Tis plain, my heart, that he’s estranged from thee;
Why go to him as though he were not enemy?
en.6: O my soul, although you have known him who does not love me, still do you go to him, saying “he will not be displeased.”

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே
என்மாட்டு நில்லாது நீ விரும்பியவாறே அவர் மாட்டுச் செல்லுதற்குக் காரணம்
கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார் உலகத்து இல்லை என்னும் நினைவோ, நின்னியல்போ, கூறுவாயாக

en.1: Is it because the ruined have no friends, heart, that you go after him as you please?
en.2: Heart, you don’t stay with me but go to him as you wish. Is it that you think the ruined have no friends in this world, or is it your nature? Tell me. She says “as you please” because leaving her is its old habit, and “ruined” because she now has no pride. Your bond, she says, is like that of the senseless, who fall away when you fail.
en.4: Thou followest him at thy own sweet will and pleasure, my Heart: dost thou also teach me that those who are unfortunate have no friends?
en.5:
‘The ruined have no friends,’ they say; and so, my heart,
To follow him, at thy desire, from me thou dost depart.
en.6: O my soul, do you follow him at pleasure under the belief that the ruined have no friends?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே
நீ அவரைக் கண்டபொழுதே இன்பம் நுகரக் கருதுவது அல்லது, அவர் தவறுநோக்கி முன் புலவியை உண்டாக்கி அதனை அளவறிந்து பின் நுகரக் கருதாய்
ஆகலான், இனி அப்பெற்றிப்பட்டவற்றை நின்னோடு எ்ண்ணுவார் யார், யானது செய்யேன்

en.1: You won’t sulk first and enjoy him after. So who will plan such things with you from now on, heart?
en.2: Heart, as soon as you see him you think only of enjoying him. You don’t look at his fault, start a sulk first, take its measure and enjoy him after. So who will plan such things with you now? I won’t. She meant all along to sulk, and then grew eager for union, so she says this.
en.4: Thou refusest to indulge in a bouderie, my Heart, before showing thy delight in his company: who is going hereafter to take thee as a confidant in suchlike things?
en.5:
‘See, thou first show offended pride, and then submit,’ I bade;
Henceforth such council who will share with thee, my heart?
en.6: O my soul, you would not first seem sulky and then enjoy (him): who then would in future consult you about such things?

uvacha.tr: Her friend comes as his go-between, and she says this for her friend to hear.

padaccheda.m: காதலரைப் பெறாத ஞான்று அப்பெறாமைக்கு அஞ்சாநின்றது
பெற்றக்கால் வரக்கடவ பிரிவினை உட்கொண்டு அதற்கு அஞ்சா நின்றது
ஆகலான், என்னெஞ்சம் எஞ்ஞான்றும் நீங்காத இடும்பையை உடைத்தாயிற்று

en.1: My heart fears not having him, and when it has him it fears parting. Its suffering never ends.
en.2: When it doesn’t have my lover my heart fears that, and when it has him it dwells on the parting to come and fears that. So its suffering never leaves. She is agreeing to the plea, thinking it unwise to have him and lose union. Not yet sated, she also fears he may leave again. There are only these two, so the suffering never ends.
en.4: It feareth lest it should not get him, and when it hath got him, it feareth lest it should lose him: thus there is no end to the pangs that my Heart suffereth.
en.5:
I fear I shall not gain, I fear to lose him when I gain;
And thus my heart endures unceasing pain.
en.6: My soul fears when it is without him; it also fears when it is with him: it is subject to incessant sorrow.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, for her friend to hear.

padaccheda.m: என்னெஞ்சு ஈண்டு இருந்தது
காதலரைப் பிரிந்திருந்து அவர் கொடுமைகளை யான் தன்னொடு நினைத்தக்கால்
அவ்வளவறிந்து என்னைத் தின்பதுபோன்று துன்பம் செய்தற்கே

en.1: When I sat alone and thought, my heart stayed with me only to eat me up.
en.2: When I was apart from my lover and thought over his cruelties, my heart stayed here only to torment me as if devouring me. It wasn’t on my side. It took in his cruelties to make me suffer, not so that I could sulk with him over them today.
en.4: What is my Heart good for? It is good for nothing else but to devour me when I am musing alone.
en.5:
My heart consumes me when I ponder lone,
And all my lover’s cruelty bemoan.
en.6: My mind has been (here) in order to eat me up (as it were) whenever I think of him in my solitude.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, for her friend to hear.

padaccheda.w: அவர் மறக்கல்லா என் மாணா மடநெஞ்சிற் பட்டு
padaccheda.m: தன்னைமறந்த காதலரைத் தான் மறக்கமாட்டாத என் மாட்சிமை இல்லாதமட நெஞ்சுடனே கூடி
என் உயிரினும் சிறந்த நாண் தன்னையும், மறந்துவிட்டேன்

en.1: Caught up with this worthless, foolish heart that can’t forget him, I have forgotten even my modesty.
en.2: Joined to my unworthy, foolish heart, which can’t forget the lover who forgot it, I have forgotten even modesty, worth more than my life. The heart can’t hold steady. It remembers his fault when he is away and forgets it when he is here, where it should do the reverse. Modesty is shrinking from him, however long you have been together, as if seeing him for the first time.
en.4: Fallen into the company of this foolish Heart that knoweth not to preserve its self-respect by forgetting him, I have myself forgotten my dignity.
en.5:
Fall’n neath the sway of this ignoble foolish heart,
Which will not him forget, I have forgotten shame.
en.6: I have even forgotten my modesty, having been caught in my foolish mind which is not dignified enough to forget him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, for her friend to hear.

padaccheda.m: உயிர்மேல் காதலை உடைய என் நெஞ்சு
நம்மை எள்ளிச்சென்றார் என்று நாமும் எள்ளுவேமாயின், பின் நமக்கு இளிவாம் என்று கருதி
அவர் திறத்தினையே நினையாநின்றது

en.1: My heart, in love with life, thinks it would be shameful to scorn him, and so it keeps thinking of his ways.
en.2: My heart, in love with life, thinks: if we scorn him for scorning us, we will be shamed later. So it thinks only of him. To scorn him is to turn away his go-between. The shame comes from failing him, from being unable to bear parting, and from losing modesty and reserve. Fearing shame and unable to die, my heart means to join him.
en.4: My life of a Heart thinketh it a disgrace to our own selves if we humiliate the beloved: and so it is always partial to him.
en.5:
If I contemn him, then disgrace awaits me evermore;
My soul that seeks to live his virtues numbers o’er.
en.6: My soul which clings to life thinks only of his (own) gain in the belief that it would be disgraceful for it to despise him.

reading.note: உயிர்க்காதல் could also be a love as dear as life. He takes it as love of life: the heart can’t bring itself to die.

uvacha.tr: She is sulking and won’t be won over by his pleading, and he says this.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவர்க்குத் துன்பம் வந்துழி, அது நீக்குதற்கு
தாம் உரித்தாகப்பெற்ற தம்முடைய நெஞ்சம் துணையாகாவழி
வேறுதுணையாவார் ஒருவரும் இல்லை

en.1: In trouble, who will stand by you if your own heart won’t?
en.2: When trouble comes, if your own heart doesn’t help you, no one else will. The trouble here is that her sulk won’t yield to his pleading. His heart fails him by longing for union, instead of deciding she has no loving-kindness and giving her up. With no help at all, he can only bear it and let it go.
en.4: Who will support a man in his grief, if the Heart of his beloved itself refuseth him help?
en.5:
And who will aid me in my hour of grief,
If my own heart comes not to my relief?
en.6: Who would help me out of one’s distress, when one’s own soul refuses help to one?

uvacha.tr: She is still sulking, and he goes on.

padaccheda.m: தாம் உரித்தாகவுடைய நெஞ்சம், ஒருவர்க்குத் தமர் அல்லாவழி
அயலார் தமர் அல்லராதல் சொல்லவேண்டுமோ

en.1: If your own heart isn’t on your side, it is a small thing that strangers aren’t.
en.2: If the heart you own isn’t on your side, need it be said that outsiders aren’t? My own heart takes this other woman for my beloved and torments me. After that, it is a small matter that she sulks.
en.4: When my own heart is not on my side, is it a wonder that strangers care not at all for me?
en.5:
A trifle is unfriendliness by aliens shown,
When our own heart itself is not our own!
en.6: It is hardly possible for strangers to behave like relations, when one’s own soul acts like a stranger.

uvacha.tr: Her friend has come as his go-between. She teases her, to win her over to accepting him.

padaccheda.w: அவர் உறு அல்லல் நோய் சிறிது காண்கம்
padaccheda.m: அங்ஙனம் புலந்தால் காதலர் எய்தும் அல்லல் நோயினை யாம் சிறிது காணக்கடவேம்
நீ அவரை விரைந்து சென்று புல்லாதே இத்தொழிலை மேலிட்டுக்கொண்டிருப்பாயாக

en.1: Don’t embrace him. Sulk, and let us see a little of the pain and sickness he goes through.
en.2: If you sulk, we can see a little of the painful sickness of desire he will suffer. Don’t hurry to embrace him. Keep this up. She says “a little” because a sulk mustn’t be drawn out. Seeing the sulk, she takes her side and teases: he should feel a little of what we felt. In this way she brings her round.
en.4: Embrace him not, my dear, but feign to be angry: let us just see a fun how he is nettled over it.
en.5:
Be still reserved, decline his proffered love;
A little while his sore distress we’ll prove.
en.6: Let us witness awhile his keen suffering; just feign dislike and embrace him not.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says this so that she will give up sulking and accept him.

padaccheda.m: புலவி கலவி இன்பம் செயற்கு வேண்டும் அளவிற்றாதல் உப்புத் துய்ப்பனவற்றை இன்சுவைய ஆக்கற்கு வேண்டும் அளவிற்றாதல் போலும்
இனி அதனை அவ்வளவில் சிறிது மிகவிடுதல் அவ்வுப்பு அளவின் மிக்காற்போலும்

en.1: A sulk is like the right amount of salt. Drawing it out is like a little too much.
en.2: A sulk should be just enough to make union sweet, as salt is just enough to make food taste good. Stretching it even slightly past that is like too much salt. Stretching it means not knowing the measure, and going on until the impulse towards union fades. Too much salt spoils the taste, and too much sulking spoils the joy of union.
en.4: Bouderie is the salt of love: to lengthen it unduly, however, is like adding too much of salt to food.
en.5:
A cool reserve is like the salt that seasons well the mess,
Too long maintained, ’tis like the salt’s excess.
en.6: A little dislike is like salt in proportion; to prolong it a little is like salt a little too much.

uvacha.tr: He has come back from the courtesans, and she sulks with him and says this.

padaccheda.m: தம்மைப் பெறாது புலந்தமகளிரைப் புலவிநீக்கிக் கலவாது ஆடவர் சேறல்
பண்டே துன்பமுற்று அழிந்தாரை அதன்மேலும் மிக்கதுன்பத்தினைச் செய்தாற்போலும்

en.1: Not to embrace those who sulk with you is like bringing fresh pain to people already in distress.
en.2: For a man to walk away without ending the sulk of women who sulk at not having him is like bringing worse pain on those already ruined by it. She means: you go to others, so the courtesans sulk at not having you. If you don’t go and end their sulk and embrace them, they won’t be able to bear it.
en.4: It is like wounding one anew who is already wounded, it thou come away without embracing her whom thou hast left in a pet.
en.5:
’Tis heaping griefs on those whose hearts are grieved;
To leave the grieving one without a fond embrace.
en.6: For men not to embrace those who have feigned dislike is like torturing those already in agony.

reading.note: He hears this as bitter irony. The women she means are the courtesans, and she is sending him back to them.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, sulking with him.

padaccheda.m: நும்மோடு ஊடிய பரத்தையரை ஊடல் உணர்த்திக் கூடாது ஒழிதல்
பண்டே நீர்பெறாது வாடிய கொடியை அடியிலே அறுத்தாற்போலும்

en.1: Not to soothe those who sulk is like cutting a withered creeper at the root.
en.2: Not soothing and joining the courtesans who sulk with you is like cutting at the root a creeper already withered for want of water. When you are with them, we should comfort ourselves with our son. We have no right to sulk with you, so you needn’t soothe us. Soothe the courtesans, who have that right. So go there.
en.4: To come away without conciliating her who is frowning in a pet is like cutting off the roots from under the starving plant.
en.5:
To use no kind conciliating art when lover grieves,
Is cutting out the root of tender winding plant that droops.
en.6: Not to reconcile those who have feigned dislike is like cutting a faded creeper at its root.

reading.note: He hears irony again. She says she has no right to sulk, and sends him to the courtesans, who have.

uvacha.tr: He has ended her sulk and been with her, and he says this to himself.

padaccheda.m: நற்குணங்களாற் தகுதியுடையராய தலைவர்க்கும் அழகாவது
தம் பூவன்ன கண்ணார் நெஞ்சின்கண் நிகழும் புலவி மிகுதியன்றே

en.1: What graces those of fine character is the sulking in the hearts of women with eyes like flowers.
en.2: What graces even leaders of fine character is the great sulking in the hearts of women with eyes like flowers. “Even” shows that a sulk is sweet to those with no fault. The grace lies in reaching its reward of joy. He is marvelling at the sulk that brought him the joy he has just had.
en.4: The bouderie of the beloved hath an attraction even for men who are spotlessly pure.
en.5:
Even to men of good and worthy mind, the petulance
Of wives with flowery eyes lacks not a lovely grace.
en.6: An increased shyness in those whose eyes are like flowers is beautiful even to good and virtuous husbands.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

en.1: Without the deep sulk and the light one, desire is like a fruit too ripe and a fruit too green.
en.2: If there is no deep quarrel and no light quarrel, desire is like a fruit past its best and a young green fruit. Fruit so ripe it is about to fall gives little pleasure, so without the deep one desire is that. Hard green fruit isn’t ready to enjoy, so without the light one desire is that. He is praising the need for both.
en.4: If there were no frowns or pets on the part of the beloved, love would miss its fruits and its half-growns.
en.5:
Love without hatred is as ripened fruit;
Without some lesser strife, fruit immature.
en.6: Sexual pleasure, without prolonged and short-lived dislike, is like too ripe, and unripe fruit.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: இனிப்புணர்ச்சி நீட்டிக்குமோ, நீட்டியாதோ என்று கருதலான்
இன்பத்திற்கு இன்றியமையாத ஊடலின்கண்ணேயும் ஒருதுன்பம் நிகழும்

en.1: There is a pain even in sulking: the worry over whether union will be delayed.
en.2: Even in a sulk, which joy can’t do without, there is a pain, from wondering whether union will be delayed or not. So a sulk makes you hurry towards union.
en.4: There is a pain that belongeth unto bouderie: for one asketh oneself whether reconciliation is near or yet a far way off.
en.5:
A lovers’ quarrel brings its pain, when mind afraid
Asks doubtful, ‘Will reunion sweet be long delayed?
en.6: The doubt as to whether intercourse would take place soon or not, creates a sorrow (even) in feigned dislike.

uvacha.tr: She won’t give up her sulk, so he sulks back at her and says this.

padaccheda.w: நொந்தார் என்று அஃது அறியும் காதலர் இல்லாவழி
padaccheda.m: இவர் நம்பொருட்டாக நொந்தார் என்று, அந்நோவினை அறியும் அன்பு உடையாரைப் பெறாவழி
ஒருவர் நோகின்றதனால் பயன் என்

en.1: What is the use of suffering, when there is no lover to know you are suffering?
en.2: If you don’t have someone with loving-kindness who knows you are suffering for their sake, what use is suffering? To know here is to understand a sulk well. She isn’t my beloved, so she doesn’t know this pain, and so my sulking is useless. In this way he shows that he can’t bear it.
en.4: Of what avail is my grieving when there is no loving one nigh to see how much I suffer?
en.5:
What good can grieving do, when none who love
Are there to know the grief thy soul endures?
en.6: What avails sorrow when I am without a wife who can understand the cause of my sorrow.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, sulking with her.

padaccheda.m: உயிர்க்கு இன்றியமையாத நீரும் நிழலின்கண்ணே இனிதாவது, ஏனை வெயிலின்கண்ணது ஆகாது
அது போலக் கலவிக்கு இன்றியமையாத புலவியும், அன்புடையார்கண்ணே இனிதாவது, ஏனை அன்பிலார்கண் ஆகாது

en.1: Water is sweet in the shade, and sulking is sweet with those who love you.
en.2: Water, vital to life, is sweet in the shade and not in the sun. So too sulking, vital to union, is sweet with those who have loving-kindness and not with those who don’t. Those who love you are pained by your suffering and long to join you. She has neither of these for me, so even this sulk turns bitter.
en.4: Water is pleasant only in shady groves: and pettishness hath a charm only in one who loveth ardently.
en.5:
Water is pleasant in the cooling shade;
So coolness for a time with those we love.
en.6: Like water in the shade, dislike is delicious only in those who love.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, sulking with her.

padaccheda.m: தாம் ஊடற்கண்ணே மெலியாநிற்கவும்

padaccheda.w: விடுவாரோடு கூடுவேம் என்பது என் நெஞ்சம் அவா
padaccheda.m: விட்டிருக்க வல்லாரோடு கூடக்கடவேம் என்று என் நெஞ்சம் முயறற்கு ஏது, தன் அவாவே, பிறிதில்லை

en.1: My heart says we will join with the one who leaves a sulk to wither. That is only craving.
en.2: She can leave things so, even as she withers in her sulk. My heart tries to join such a woman only out of its own craving, and nothing else. To think someone has loving-kindness and compassion when she has neither, and to try to join her, is what craving does. This union won’t happen.
en.4: If my heart still yearneth for her who sootheth me not, it is due to nothing but a foolish longing.
en.5:
Of her who leaves me thus in variance languishing,
To think within my heart with love is fond desire.
en.6: It is nothing but strong desire that makes her mind unite with me who can leave her to her own dislike.

uvacha.tr: He has come back from a procession and is in bed with her, and she says this.

padaccheda.m: பரத்தமையுடையாய்
நின்னைப் பெண் இயல்பின் உடையார் யாவரும் தம் கண்ணால் பொதுவாக உண்பர்
அதனால் அவர் மிச்சிலாய நின் மார்பினைப் பொருந்தேன்

en.1: All those who are women eat you up with their eyes, as common property. I won’t go near your chest, you philanderer.
en.2: You philanderer, all those with a woman’s nature feast on you with their eyes in common. So I won’t touch your chest, which is their leavings. She says “a woman’s nature” because courtesans lack chastity, modesty and other virtues, and are women by nature alone. She fears they enjoy looking at him as she does, and this jealousy is what makes it subtle.
en.4: All that are women devour thee with their eyes, thou gallant! I shall have none of thy embrace.
en.5:
From thy regard all womankind
Enjoys an equal grace;
O thou of wandering fickle mind,
I shrink from thine embrace!
en.6: You are given to prostitution; all those who are born as womankind enjoy you with their eyes in an ordinary way. I will not embrace you.

uvacha.tr: While he is away from the bed, she tells her friend what happened there.

padaccheda.m: யாம் தம்மோடு ஊடி உரையாடாது இருந்தேமாகக் காதலர் தும்மினார்

padaccheda.w: யாம் தம்மை நீடு வாழ்க என்பாக்கு அறிந்து
padaccheda.m: அது நீங்கித் தம்மை நீடுவாழ்க என்று உரையாடுவேமாகக் கருதி

en.1: I was sulking when he sneezed. He knew I would say, “Live long.”
en.2: I was sulking and not speaking when my lover sneezed. He thought I would stop and say “Live long”. A sneeze calls for a blessing by custom, so I would have had to speak. She takes a natural sneeze as something done on purpose, and that is what makes it subtle.
en.4: I was in the sulks: he then sneezed, for he thought that I would bless him saying, Long live my beloved!
en.5:
One day we silent sulked; he sneezed:
The reason well I knew;
He thought that I, to speak well pleased,
Would say, ‘Long life to you!’
en.6: When I continued to be sulky he sneezed and thought I would (then) wish him a long life.

uvacha.tr: Her friend sees signs of sulking and asks him why, when they are together. He answers.

padaccheda.m: யான் கோடுதலைச் செய்யும் மாலையைச் சூடினேன் ஆயினும்
நும்மால் காதலிக்கப் பட்டாள் ஒருத்திக்கு இப்பூவணி காட்டல் வேண்டிச் சூடினீர் என்று வெகுளாநிற்கும், இத்தன்மையாட்கு ஒரு காரணம் வேண்டுமோ?

en.1: Even if I wear a flower from the branch she is angry. “You wear it to show some woman,” she says.
en.2: Even if I wear a garland bent in a ring, she flares up and says I wore it to show it to some woman I love. Does such a woman need a reason? It can also mean: if I wear a flower from another region, she says I wore that strange flower to show some other woman.
en.4: Even if I wear a garland she would go off in a pique saying, Thou wantest to look smart in some damsel’s eyes!
en.5:
I wreathed with flowers one day my brow,
The angry tempest lowers;
She cries, ‘Pray, for what woman now
Do you put on your flowers?’
en.6: Even if. I were adorned with a garland of branch-flowers, she would say I did so to show it to another woman.

reading.note: கோட்டுப்பூ can be a flower from a branch. He takes கோடு as bending, a garland worn in a ring, and also allows a flower from another region.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: காமம் நுகர்தற்குரிய இருவராயினார் யாவரினும் மிக்க காதல் உடையேம் என்பது கருதி யாரினும் காதலம் என்றேனாக
நின் தோழி அது கருதாது, என்னால் காதலிக்கப்பட்ட மகளிர் பலருள்ளும் நின்கண் காதலுடையேன் என்றேனாகக் கருதி, அம்மகளிர் யாரினும் என்கண் காதலுடையர் ஆனீர் என்று சொல்லிப் புலந்தாள்

en.1: “We love more than anyone,” I said, and she sulked: “Than who? Than who?”
en.2: I meant that we two love more than any pair who enjoy desire, so I said we love more than anyone. Your friend took it that I love her most among the many women I love, and she sulked, saying: than whom, than whom? I said it out of loving-kindness and she took it another way. There was no other cause.
en.4: I said to her, I love thee above all: and behold, she frowned at once asking, Above whom? and above whom?
en.5:
‘I love you more than all beside,’
’Twas thus I gently spoke;
‘What all, what all?’ she instant cried,
And all her anger woke.
en.6: When I said I loved her more than any other woman, she said “‘more than others, yes, more than others,” and remained sulky.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: காதல் மிகுதியான் இம்மையாகிய பிறப்பின்கண் யாம் பிரியேம் என்று சொன்னேனாக
அதனான் ஏனை மறுமையாகிய பிறப்பின்கண் பிரிவல் என்னும் குறிப்பினேனாகக் கருதி, அவள் தன் கண்நிறைந்த நீரினைக் கொண்டாள்

en.1: “We will not part in this life,” I said, and her eyes filled with tears.
en.2: In my great love I said we would not part in this birth. She took it to mean I would part from her in the next, and her eyes filled with tears. She takes plain words as a hint, and I am not at fault.
en.4: I told her, We shall never part in this life: alack, her eyes at once filled with tears!
en.5:
‘While here I live, I leave you not,’
I said to calm her fears.
She cried, ‘There, then, I read your thought’;
And straight dissolved in tears.
en.6: When I said I would never part from her in this life, her eyes were filled with tears.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: பிரிந்தகாலத்து நின்னை இடையின்றி நினைந்தேன் என்னும் கருத்தால், யான் உள்ளினேன் என்றேன்

padaccheda.w: மற்று என்மறந்தீர் என்று என்னைப் புல்லாள் புலத்தக்கனள்
padaccheda.m: என, அதனை ஒருகான் மறந்து பின்நினைந்தேன் என்றதாகக் கருதி, என்னையிடையே மறந்தீர் என்று சொல்லி, முன் புல்லுதற்கு அமைந்தவள் அஃது ஒழிந்து புலத்தற்கு அமைந்தாள்

en.1: “I thought of you,” I said. “So why did you forget me?” she said, and she didn’t embrace me but got ready to sulk.
en.2: I meant that I thought of her without a break while we were apart, so I said I had thought of her. She took it that I forgot and then remembered, and said I had forgotten her in between. She had been ready to embrace me, and now she was ready to sulk. She inferred the forgetting from the remembering.
en.4: I said to her, I called thee to mind when away: and she that was about to clasp me to her arms went off in a pet saying, Thou hadst forgotten me then!
en.5:
‘Each day I called to mind your charms.’
‘O, then, you had forgot,’
She cried, and then her opened arms,
Forthwith embraced me not.
en.6: When I said I had remembered her, she said I had forgotten her and relaxing her embrace, began to feign dislike.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: கூடியிருக்கின்றவள் யான் தும்மினேனாகத் தன் இயற்கைபற்றி வாழ்த்தினாள்

padaccheda.w: அழித்து யார் உள்ளித் தும்மினீர் என்று அழுதாள்
padaccheda.m: அங்ஙனவாழ்த்திய தானே மறித்து, நும்மை நினைத்து வருந்துகின்ற மகளிருள் யாவர் நினைத்தலான் தும்மினீர் என்று சொல்லிப் புலந்து அழுதாள்

en.1: I sneezed and she blessed me. Then she took it back and wept: “Who was thinking of you, that you sneezed?”
en.2: I sneezed, and she blessed me from habit. Then she reversed herself and wept in a sulk, asking which of the women pining for me had thought of me and made me sneeze. Women say that you sneeze when someone with loving-kindness thinks of you. She treated an empty saying as fact, and sulked.
en.4: I sneezed and she blessed: but then she recalled her blessing and asked with tear-filled eyes, Who thought on thee now, that thou sneezedest?
en.5:
She hailed me when I sneezed one day;
But straight with anger seized,
She cried, ‘Who was the woman, pray,
Thinking of whom you sneezed?’
en.6: When I sneezed, she blessed me, but at once changed (her mind) and wept, asking, “At the thought of whom did you sneeze?”

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: எனக்குத் தும்மல் தோன்றியவழி யாருள்ளித் தும்மினீர் என்று புலத்தலை அஞ்சி, அதனை யான் அடக்கினேன், அங்ஙனம் அடக்கவும்

padaccheda.w: நுமர் உள்ளல் எம்மை மறைத்திரோ என்று அழுதாள்
padaccheda.m: நுமர் நும்மை நினைத்தலை எம்மை மறைக்கல் உற்றீரோ என்று சொல்லிப் புலந்து அழுதாள்

en.1: I held back a sneeze and she wept: “Are you hiding from me that your own people are thinking of you?”
en.2: Fearing she would sulk and ask who was thinking of me, I held back a sneeze. Even so she wept in a sulk: are you hiding from us that your people think of you? “Us” implies she has no tie to him at all. If sneezing is a fault and not sneezing is a fault, what can be done?
en.4: I repressed my sneeze: and then aiso she wept saying, Thou wantest to conceal from me that some of thy friends are thinking on thee!
en.5:
And so next time I checked my sneeze;
She forthwith wept and cried,
(That woman difficult to please,)
‘Your thoughts from me you hide.’
en.6: When I suppressed my sneezing, she wept saying, “I suppose you (did so) to hide from me your own people’s remembrance of you’.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: இவ்வாற்றான் ஊடிய தன்னை, யான் பணிந்து உணர்த்துங்காலும் வெகுளாநிற்கும்
பிறமகளிர்க்கும் அவர் ஊடியவழி, இவ்வாறே பணிந்து உணர்த்தும் நீர்மையை உடையீர் ஆகுதிர் என்று சொல்லி

en.1: Even when I soothe her sulk she flares up: “So this is how you are with others too.”
en.2: Even when I bow and soothe her in her sulk, she flares up and says I must soothe other women this way when they sulk. She wouldn’t be reassured, so I accepted the fault laid on me and bowed. Even that became a reason to sulk. What can be done with her now?
en.4: Even if I exhaust all my arts to soothe her, she will only frown harder saying, Thou hast practised well at others’ bouderies!
en.5:
I then began to soothe and coax,
To calm her jealous mind;
‘I see,’ quoth she, ‘to other folks
How you are wondrous kind.’
en.6: Even when I try to remove her dislike, she is displeased and says, “This is the way you behave towards (other women)”.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: என் சொற்களும் செயல்களும் பற்றித் தான் வெகுடலான், அவற்றை ஒழிந்திருந்து, தன் அவயவங்களது ஒப்பின்மையை நினைந்து அவற்றையே நோக்கினும், என்னை வெகுளாநிற்கும்

padaccheda.w: அனைத்தும் நீர் நோக்கினீர் யார் உள்ளி என்று
padaccheda.m: என் அவயவம் அனைத்தும் நோக்கினீர், அவற்றது ஒப்புமையான் எம்மகளிரை நினைந்து என்று சொல்லி

en.1: Even if I just sit thinking and gazing at her, she flares up: “Who are you thinking of, looking at all of me like that?”
en.2: She is angry at what I say and do, so I stop both and gaze at her limbs, thinking how matchless they are. She flares up: you looked at all of me, thinking of which women? I can’t match one woman in every limb, so you must be thinking of many, so name them all. Even keeping quiet has become a fault.
en.4: Even if I look in rapture on her own charms, she will chide saying, To whose limbs now art thou comparing mine?
en.5:
I silent sat, but thought the more,
And gazed on her. Then she
Cried out, ‘While thus you eye me o’er,
Tell me whose form you see.’
en.6: Even when I look on her contemplating (her beauty), she is displeased and says, “With whose thought have you (thus) looked on my person.”

uvacha.tr: She has been sulking without cause. Her friend asks why, and she answers.

padaccheda.m: அவர்மாட்டுத் தவறு இல்லையாயினும்
நமக்கு அவர் தலையளி செய்கின்றவாறு, அவரோடு ஊடுதலை விளைக்கவற்றாகின்றது

en.1: He has done nothing wrong, yet sulking is what draws out his tenderness.
en.2: He has no fault, but the tenderness he shows me makes me sulk. He gives such boundless joy that I think others may receive this tenderness too, and I can’t bear it.
en.4: Even if he is free from faults, it is only bouderie that giveth me a taste of his conciliatory grace.
en.5:
Although there be no fault in him, the sweetness of his love
Hath power in me a fretful jealousy to move.
en.6: Although my husband is free from defects, the way in which he embraces me is such as to make me feign dislike.

reading.note: The Tamil can go either way. The plain reading says sulking draws out his tenderness. parimēlaḻagar says his tenderness makes her jealous, and that causes the sulk.

uvacha.tr: Her friend asks why she suffers by sulking, when she could have his tenderness anyway.

padaccheda.m: ஊடல் ஏதுவாக நம்கண் தோன்றுகின்ற சிறிய துனி தன்னால்
காதலர் செய்யும் நல்ல தலையளி வாடுமாயினும் பெருமை எய்தும்

en.1: The small hurt of sulking may dim his tenderness for a moment, but it comes back greater.
en.2: The small distress of sulking may make his tenderness wilt, but it then gains greatness. A sulk with no real fault behind it soon ends, so the pain doesn’t last, and great joy follows.
en.4: Though the tenderness of the beloved hath to wait a little, there is a charm in the pinprick that we feel in being pettish.
en.5:
My ‘anger feigned’ gives but a little pain;
And when affection droops, it makes it bloom again.
en.6: His love will increase though it may (at first seem to) fade through the short-lived distress caused by (my) dislike.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நிலத்தொடு நீர் கலந்தாற்போல ஒற்றுமையுடைய காதலர் மாட்டுப் புலத்தல் போல
நமக்கு இன்பந்தருவது ஒரு புத்தேள் உலகமும் உண்டோ, இ்ல்லை

en.1: Is there any heaven better than a lovers’ quarrel, between two people as blended as earth and water?
en.2: Is there any heaven that gives us as much joy as sulking with a lover who is one with us, as water blends with earth? Water takes on the nature of its land, and a lover takes on the nature of the woman he joins, so sulking arises, and great joy follows.
en.4: Is there a higher heaven than bouderie, provided that the beloved is one with us, even as the water with the land whereon it floweth?
en.5:
Is there a bliss in any world more utterly divine,
Than ‘coyness’ gives, when hearts as earth and water join?
en.6: Is there a celestial land that can please like the feigned dislike of those whose union resembles that of earth and water.

uvacha.tr: Someone asks her how this sulking will end.

padaccheda.m: காதலரைப் புல்லிக்கொண்டு, பின்விடாமைக்கு ஏதுவாகிய அப்புலவிக்கண்ணே உளதாம்
அதன்மேற்சென்ற என் உள்ளத்தைக் கெடுக்கும் படைக்கலம்

en.1: In the very quarrel that keeps me clinging to him is the weapon that breaks my resolve.
en.2: In the sulking that makes me hold him and not let go lies the weapon that destroys my heart’s resolve. The weapon is his bowing and his pleading words.
en.4: In my very quarrel with my beloved lieth the engine that stormeth the defences of my heart.
en.5:
Within the ‘anger feigned,’ that close love’s tie doth bind,
A weapon lurks, which quite breaks down my mind.
en.6: In prolonged dislike after an embrace there is a weapon that can break my heart.

uvacha.tr: He has made up with her and, overjoyed, says this to himself.

padaccheda.w: தவறு இலராயினும், தாம் வீழ்வார் மென்றோள் அகறலின்
padaccheda.m: ஆடவர் தங்கண் தவறு இலராயினும் உடையார்போல ஊடப்பட்டுத் தாம் விரும்பும் மகளிருடைய மெல்லியதோள்களைக் கூடப்பெறாத எல்லைக்கண்
அவர்க்கு அப்பெற்றியதோர் இன்பம் பயத்தலுடைத்து

en.1: Even when you have done nothing wrong, being kept from the soft shoulders of the one you love has a pleasure of its own.
en.2: Men with no fault, sulked at as though they had one, can’t reach the soft shoulders they love. Even then they find a pleasure too great to name.
en.4: Even when one is free from faults there is a delight when the arms of the beloved are withdrawn from one’s clasp.
en.5:
Though free from fault, from loved one’s tender arms
To be estranged awhile hath its own special charms.
en.6: Though free from defects, men feel pleased when they cannot embrace the delicate shoulders of those whom they love.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: உயிர்க்கு மேல் உண்பதனினும் முன் உண்டது அறுதல் இன்பந்தரும்
அதுபோலக் காமத்திற்கு மேற்புணர்தலினும், முன்னைத் தவறுபற்றி ஊடுதல் இன்பந்தரும்

en.1: Digesting a meal is sweeter than eating more. In desire, a quarrel is sweeter than making love.
en.2: Digesting what you have eaten is more pleasant than eating more. In desire, a quarrel over an earlier fault is more pleasant than more union. Hunger makes food better, and time apart makes union sweeter.
en.4: Sweeter is digestion than the meal: even so is the lovers’ quarrel sweeter than the embrace.
en.5:
’Tis sweeter to digest your food than ’tis to eat;
In love, than union’s self is anger feigned more sweet.
en.6: To digest what has been eaten is more delightful than to eat more; likewise love is more delightful in dislike than intercourse.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

en.1: In a lovers’ quarrel, the one who loses has won. You see it when you come back together.
en.2: Of the two lovers, the one who gives way in the quarrel is the winner. This isn’t clear at the time, but it shows later in their lovemaking. I gave way then, so now I have had great joy.
en.4: It is the one who yieldeth first who is the winner in lovers’ quarrels: thou canst see it indeed at the hour of reconciliation.
en.5:
In lovers’ quarrels, ’tis the one that first gives way,
That in re-union’s joy is seen to win the day.
en.6: Those are conquerors whose dislike has been defeated and that is proved by the love (which follows).

reading.note: The site keeps this couplet out of Reflect, because it could reach someone pressured to give in.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: இதுபொழுது இவள் நுதல் வெயர்க்கும்வகை கலவியின்கண் உளதாய இனிமையை
இன்னுமொருகால் இவள் ஊடி யாம்பெறவல்லேமோ

en.1: Will a quarrel bring back the sweetness of our lovemaking, the kind that left her forehead damp with sweat?
en.2: Can I, by her sulking once more, have again the sweetness of the lovemaking that made her forehead sweat?
en.4: Verily, will she give some piquancy to the delights of our embrace by just feigning a quarrel for some time?
en.5:
And shall we ever more the sweetness know of that embrace
With dewy brow; to which ‘feigned anger’ lent its piquant grace.
en.6: Will I enjoy once more through her dislike, the pleasure of that love that makes her forehead perspire?

reading.note: உப்பு is literally salt, and he reads it as sweetness. The plain reading follows him.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: ஒளியிழையினை உடையாள், இன்னும் எம்மோடு ஊடுவாளாக
அங்ஙனம் அவள் ஊடிநிற்றற்கும், அதனை உணர்த்துதல் பொருட்டு யாம் இரந்து நிற்றற்கும், காலம்பெறும் வகை இவ்விரவு விடியாது நீட்டித்தல் வேண்டுக

en.1: Let her go on sulking, this woman in bright jewels, and let the night run on while I plead.
en.2: Let her of the bright jewels sulk with me more, and let this night not dawn, so that there is time for her sulking and my pleading. The quarrel is enough, even better than union.
en.4: Oh, let me enjoy her frowning and her pouting a little more! Only let night prolong her reign at my prayer.
en.5:
Let her, whose jewels brightly shine, aversion feign!
That I may still plead on, O night, prolong thy reign!
en.6: May the bright-jewelled one feign dislike, and may the night be prolonged for me to implore her!

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: காமநுகர்ச்சிக்கு இன்பமாவது, அதனை நுகர்தற்கு உரியார், ஆராமைபற்றித் தம்முள் ஊடுதல்
அவ்வூடுதற்கு இன்பமாவது, அதனை அளவறிந்து நீங்கித் தம்முள் கூடி முயங்குதல் கூடுமாயின் அம்முயக்கம்

en.1: Sulking is the joy of desire, and the joy of sulking is the embrace that ends it, if you get that far.
en.2: Sulking is the joy of desire. The joy of sulking is the embrace, if you can judge the measure, let go and come together. Held too long it brings pain, and ended too soon it brings no pleasure. That balance is hard, which is why he says “if”.
en.4: Bouderie is the charm of love: and the charm of that again is the sweet embrace at its close.
en.5:
A ‘feigned aversion’ coy to pleasure gives a zest;
The pleasure’s crowned when breast is clasped to breast.
en.6: Dislike adds delight to love; and a hearty embrace (thereafter) will add delight to dislike.
